title: Tanker rams US cruise ship, capsizing it (VIDEOS)
content:
All 180 people aboard were rescued after the vessel capsized in the Mississippi River, with 32 hospitalized

An asphalt tanker rammed a docked cruise ship in New Orleans, Louisiana, on Friday, causing it to capsize and sending passengers into the Mississippi River.

Videos from the scene show the much larger Atlantic Asphalt tanker striking the American Heritage cruise ship directly in the side. The vessel, operated by American Cruise Lines, was carrying 180 passengers and crew members at the time of the collision.

The cruise ship rolled onto its side and partially sank as tugboat operators, police and other rescuers rushed to help.

Watch the moment a tanker struck a cruise ship in New Orleans. Rescues are underway. 📷: Kern Studios https://t.co/ZPspGtM0Yr https://t.co/O1qGr8kImf

— wdsu (@wdsu) November 13, 2026

New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno confirmed that everyone aboard had been rescued. She added that 32 people were hospitalized, none with critical injuries.

WATCH: Dramatic video shows passengers swimming for help as cruise ship capsizes after being struck by a tanker; 12 people hospitalized, officials say. https://t.co/2UtubUdktf

— Scope Report (@ScopeReport_) November 13, 2026

The cause of the collision remains under investigation. Initial reports suggest the tanker may have lost steering before striking the docked vessel.

title: OpenAI is betting a data center rebrand will make you hate them less
content:
Republicans weren’t the only big losers in last week’s midterms: Across the country, voters also backed restrictions on data centers and elected candidates promising tougher oversight of AI companies. Out of 41 local ballot initiatives limiting the data center buildout, 40 of them passed, according to the New York Times. 

The AI industry knows it was a tough cycle: Chris Lehane, the chief global affairs officer for OpenAI, told Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram that “I could take my shirt off and show you my [metaphorical] bruises if you want.”

Now, OpenAI is figuring out how to move forward. Lehane talked with Sean from rural Texas, where he said he was on a “listening and learning” tour of communities around the site of a massive OpenAI data center. They discussed the lessons of the midterm election, why OpenAI would prefer that we call data centers “compute campuses,” and why Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election will largely revolve around AI — just not in the same way that 2026 did.

“I just don’t think it’s going to be good enough for a candidate from either party to emerge from their primary by simply being the person who’s against things,” Lehane said. 

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.

You guys at OpenAI, in the wake of this shellacking, put out this big document saying that you’re going to be listening, you’re going to be learning, you’re going to be empowering local people and bringing jobs.

You’re also, in this document, rebranding data centers to “compute campuses,” which when I say it, I have trouble not laughing because it sounds like a bit of a joke to meet everyone’s concerns with a rebrand. Please tell us why you think this could work or why it’s a good idea.

We were very intentional in actually using that phrase. And we did it with the full knowledge that people would potentially be skeptical of it. But I do think there’s an intent behind provoking this conversation. 

Data centers have existed for 20-odd years and at some level they’re the proverbial empty box in a pasture. And they’re called data centers because that’s in fact what they were. When people talked about the cloud, this is actually where the cloud was housed, where you would load data if you were streaming a video, if you were ordering something from a delivery service. These AI facilities are really fundamentally different.

What is being generated at these facilities is something called compute. And compute is just the raw computing power that it takes to train AI systems and then run AI tools and products when you’re using them. 

Second of all, they’re different because [of] the amount of jobs that do get created directly. This is not half a dozen people in that empty box. These are real jobs, these are six-figure jobs. They are also huge opportunities for economic transformation if a community approaches it in a really strategic way and companies like ours do our part to work with those communities. We’re not just building in the communities, we’re building with the communities.

You’re out there in Texas because essentially, data centers and artificial intelligence have a PR problem. Seventy percent of the country, maybe more than that, says that they’re against data centers, or “compute campuses,” as you’re now calling them. 

Why do you think it is that data centers have such a public relations issue in this country right now?

There’s a variety of factors, but before even jumping into those, I do think it’s worth noting and worth emphasizing that we have roughly six of these projects up and running in the country. They’re in different stages of being built out and developed, but each and every one of them is moving forward. I do think that there is a right way to build these and perhaps a wrong way and we can get into that.

Do you think that you guys were doing it the wrong way before?

This goes to why I think we’ve actually been able to get approvals for each of the projects that we are doing. 

I think each of the individual projects themselves have been some version of a laboratory of democracy, where you actually learn from each project and apply those learnings to the next project. But I do think we got the fundamental insight right at the beginning, which is to actually go on the ground, listen, learn, hold yourself accountable and take the feedback and build your facility with the community.

I think that for a lot of communities, folks were coming in, they were building data centers, they were then transferring the electricity costs to the public, they were potentially impacting their water, they weren’t necessarily doing the type of community investments that you should do if you’re going to be building with a community. 

Where we’ve really tried to differ ourselves — and again, we’re not perfect, we’re learning every step of the way — but I do think that we have successfully applied the baseline as we’ve gone through this, which is, we make sure we’re paying for our own electricity, our own energy.

Point two is that we make sure we’re preserving water. We have something called closed water loops. I know this is getting a little bit technical, but think of these as sort of large radiators. You fill it up once and therefore you’re able to preserve the water.

One thing that seems clear from the election results is that there’s just not a lot of trust. Now there’s going to be a new Congress, and various components of said Congress are pledging to do more to regulate AI and tech. 

It wasn’t so long ago that the head of your company, Sam Altman, was calling for Congress to get more involved. Does that call still stand now that it’s a different Congress that might be more inclined to come down hard on AI?

When it comes to data centers, these are typically state or local issues. We envisioned that as state legislation that would actually make these requirements for folks who are building data centers to help give the public confidence that there’s going to be a real material benefit for them.

I think what you’re referring to was our call as OpenAI for there to be national-level mandatory safety requirements for the frontier labs who are building AI. We thought about that and called for it before the election. We think it’s more important than ever. 

Back in early September, I had a blog post out there that talked about this idea that the policy window was opening up to create a real opportunity to pass those mandatory safety requirements. And the reason I talked about the policy window being opened up is that you could clearly see where the politics were going, what was likely to happen with the election. 

You’re in Washington, DC. At some level, you have to be a romanticist to believe that you can actually get legislation passed. But what is happening is the politics are coming into alignment with the policy. I actually think both parties do recognize the importance of having mandatory national safety standards that would be good for the country. It would also put us in a position to be able to create international standards, which we also think is very important.

It’s funny, because we just had New York [state] assemblyman Alex Bores on the show. He was trying to be a congressperson, but a super PAC partly funded by OpenAI co-founders and some other Silicon Valley tech types spent a lot of money — millions — to defeat him. 

We asked him, if Democrats in Congress could do one thing to regulate AI, what would it be? And he said banning full recursive self-improvement, ban the practice of letting AIs build the next AIs without any human in the loop. Would OpenAI be open to that kind of regulation immediately?

The version that we have talked about is some version of broadly defined speed limits. I’ll use an analogy: As we were building out the automobile, ultimately we built out speed limits. Now, those speed limits changed over time, but the idea was to make sure that humans could actually have both hands on the wheel and be able to control the car and the car should not be able to go at a speed where a human would not be able to control it. 

Our north star in everything when it comes to AI is that people should be in control of this technology. The technology itself is accelerating, the capabilities are becoming stronger. And so I think there is a world here where we do need to build out a framework, potentially a regulatory framework, through legislation that effectively imposes some version of a speed limit.

If you think of speed limits being applied in the context of your question about recursive self-improvement, that’s a place where you could see the speed of the technology getting so strong that actually humans do lose control over it. 

I’m not sure it’s quite as binary as saying you do or do not do RSI. But I think spiritually, a similar concept, which is making sure that at the end of the day we have a lot of confidence that humans are actually in control of this, able to monitor it, able to make sure that it is not getting out of their control.

Before you worked with companies like OpenAI or Coinbase or Airbnb, you worked in government and you worked specifically in [the] Clinton White House.

I wonder, in the wake of this election — which people are calling the first big American AI election, and are saying that AI is going to be an even bigger issue for the presidential election in 2028 — what do you think companies like yours and all the other big-frontier AI companies need to be doing to flip the script in the United States, maybe around the world?

I think of 2026 as the trailer to 2028. AI was an issue. It wasn’t a top issue, but it was certainly an issue and an issue that was moving up the charts as we got closer and closer to the election. I think there is a decent chance, maybe even a strong chance, that AI is the issue in 2028. 

First and foremost, how do we make sure that people are actually in control of this technology? Who’s actually putting out an idea and a vision and approach to give people confidence that they’re going to actually be able to control this? 

I do think the 2026 election now sets up 2028, frankly for both parties, to have a conversation that I just don’t think we’ve had in this country for a long, long, long time. And that is, what does this social contract look like? Who actually has a big idea about how we’re going to make sure that the American dream actually exists in this country? And as part of that big idea, what is the role of AI going to be in that?

I just don’t think it’s going to be good enough for a candidate from either party to emerge from their primary by simply being the person who’s against things. I think they’re actually going to have to have some real ideas of what they are for. And at the core of that is, how are they going to address this anxiety that the American people have? And at the center of that anxiety is their ability to control their lives and make decisions about their lives.

title: Gestapo 2.0? Germany grants spy agencies sweeping new powers
content:
The controversial reform allows intelligence services to carry out sabotage, secretly enter homes and expand surveillance

The German parliament has passed sweeping legislation granting the country’s intelligence agencies unprecedented powers to conduct sabotage, secretly enter homes, and expand surveillance. The controversial law has prompted comparisons with the Gestapo and Stasi, the notorious secret police organizations of Nazi Germany and Communist East Germany.

The legislation, championed by Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s governing coalition, was approved on Friday by 300 votes to 190, with 71 abstentions. Only the ruling CDU/CSU bloc and Social Democrats backed the reform. The right-wing Alternative for Germany (AfD) and The Left opposed it, while the Greens abstained.

Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt hailed the overhaul as a “reform of the century,” declaring a “new era” for German intelligence agencies that would put them on an “equal footing with our European partners.”

He defended the measures by citing alleged threats from espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks and other hostile activities aimed at destabilizing Germany.

From surveillance to sabotage

The legislation fundamentally changes the role of Germany’s two principal intelligence agencies: the foreign intelligence service (BND) and the domestic Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV).

Read more

Previously focused primarily on gathering and analyzing intelligence, both agencies would gain powers to actively intervene against perceived threats.

The BND would be authorized to penetrate foreign computer networks, disable servers used by suspected hackers and delete data. Its new powers could extend to sabotaging foreign chemical laboratories and drone production facilities or disrupting supply chains by introducing defective components into shipments linked to potential threats.

The domestic intelligence agency would gain extensive surveillance and intervention powers, including covert access to smartphones and computers, interception of encrypted communications and examination of stored data.

BfV operatives could also secretly enter private homes to install surveillance software or neutralize suspected weapons.

The agency would additionally be able to obtain information from payment providers, online platforms, and vehicle manufacturers, while deploying AI-assisted facial recognition and biometric searches to identify potential suspects.

Oversight of the expanded powers would be consolidated under the Independent Oversight Council, a 12-member body established in 2021 and appointed by the Bundestag’s Parliamentary Oversight Panel.

Read more

Previously focused largely on the legality of BND surveillance, the council would gain authority to approve intervention operations by both agencies, including proactive sabotage abroad.

It would also be required to report to parliamentary overseers at least annually and publish public reports excluding classified information.

Return of the secret police?

The overhaul has triggered fierce criticism from opposition lawmakers, who warn that it threatens constitutional protections and dismantles safeguards established after the fall of Nazi Germany.

AfD lawmaker Christian Wirth condemned the reform as an “attack on the rule of law with truly totalitarian characteristics.”

He particularly criticized provisions allowing the BfV to exclude regional intelligence offices from information-sharing networks, warning that they could be used against politically “undesirable” state authorities.

In September, fellow AfD lawmaker Gottfried Curio accused Merz’s government of preparing to systematically violate fundamental rights, invoking Germany’s history under the Gestapo and East Germany’s Stasi.

“Manipulating, sabotaging, deceiving – with these subversive measures, the [BfV] is being transformed into Stasi 2.0,” he warned.

Read more

The criticism has extended beyond the AfD.

Green lawmaker Konstantin von Notz supported strengthening the BND but accused the government of lacking “any sensitivity to civil rights” in its domestic intelligence overhaul. He warned that the legislation could face “serious problems” before Germany’s Constitutional Court.

The Left’s Clara Buenger went further, accusing Dobrindt of undermining democracy through nationwide AI-powered mass surveillance and laying the groundwork for a “new German secret police.”

At the heart of the controversy is Germany’s longstanding separation principle, designed to prevent intelligence agencies from acquiring police powers.

The safeguard traces its origins to the Allied powers’ 1949 ‘Police Letter,’ which sought to prevent the re-emergence of an organization resembling the Gestapo. The distinction between intelligence gathering and law enforcement was subsequently incorporated into legislation governing Germany’s security services.

Critics argue that allowing intelligence operatives to secretly enter homes, interfere with property and conduct sabotage erodes that historical barrier.

Dobrindt has dismissed accusations that the reform threatens democracy as “madness.”

Russian threat narrative

The intelligence overhaul comes as Berlin accelerates its military buildup, with Merz’s government repeatedly invoking an alleged Russian threat to justify increased defense spending and expanded security capabilities.

German officials have increasingly warned of a possible military confrontation with Moscow, while accusing Russia of conducting espionage, sabotage, and other hostile operations across Europe.

Read more

Last month, BND chief Martin Jaeger warned that Germany could become “embroiled in a violent conflict with Russia,” accusing Moscow of waging a “shadow war” against Berlin.

Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and senior-most military commander General Christian Freuding have likewise warned that Russia could attack NATO before the end of the decade.

Moscow has repeatedly rejected claims that it intends to attack NATO members, dismissing such speculation as “nonsense” and “political schizophrenia.” Russian officials have instead accused Berlin of pursuing further escalation.

The controversy also has a domestic political dimension.

Merz has described the AfD as “Russia-backed” without publicly substantiating the allegation, while his Social Democratic coalition partners have pushed for a ban on the opposition party.

The AfD, which advocates stricter immigration controls and opposes German military assistance to Ukraine and sanctions against Russia, has become a major target of political scrutiny.

Defending the intelligence overhaul on Friday, Chancellor’s Office official Nina Warken argued that Germany faces daily threats from foreign powers that “disguise sabotage as an accident, espionage as business dealings, and propaganda as an opinion.”

title: Do the Dems need new leadership?
content:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.

Hi readers, happy Friday! Today, we’re saying farewell — for now — to “Democrats in array.” Not quite two weeks after winning the 2026 midterms by a historic margin, the party has a leadership fight on its hands. 

On Thursday evening, Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat from Maryland, made it official: He’s challenging current Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer for the title of majority leader next year, promising a bolder and more aggressive agenda for the party. 

“It is about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen told MS NOW host Jen Psaki when he announced his candidacy on her show. “The call was really to reject the status quo and to reject business as usual. And to do that, I think we need new leadership.”

Newly elected Democrats Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) and Peggy Flanagan (D-MN), each of whom defeated more leadership-aligned Democrats in their Senate primaries, are backing his bid. But Van Hollen will have an uphill climb to win the job, which is set to be decided in a closed-door vote early next month. Schumer, 75, has led Senate Democrats for nearly a decade, starting in 2017, and says he’s confident he will have the votes to be reelected in December.

Searching for “fighters”

The Senate is the only chamber currently dealing with an active leadership fight, but it’s not the only one with some leadership angst. In the House, current Democratic minority leader Hakeem Jeffries is the overwhelming favorite to become the new speaker in January (he currently lacks any Democratic challengers). But not everyone is happy about it, as my colleague Astead Herndon reported on Thursday. 

The divide, he argues — both in the Schumer-Van Hollen showdown and frustrations with Jeffries — is not really about progressive versus moderate. Instead, he says, it’s about an energized, angry Democratic base looking for fighters to lead the party into what’s almost certain to be a combative final two years of the Trump administration, and a sense that neither Schumer nor Jeffries are ready to meet the moment. 

It’s not just a problem for this cycle, either: Democrats won so widely last week that they’re very likely to hang onto their majorities at least through the 2028 election, Eric Levitz points out. 

There’s nothing to say that Democrats will have the same leaders in two years (particularly Schumer, who’s up for reelection in 2028 but may either retire or face a serious primary challenge). 

But the intra-party debate that we’re watching play out right now is effectively a preview of the higher-stakes fight to come in 2028, when Democrats could also have control of the presidency — and their freest legislative hand since the 2008 election. 

As Eric writes, that will come with some real challenges, not least that Democrats currently appear to be facing an impossible trio of economic promises, one of which they’ll likely need to break. But it will also be a moment of opportunity — if the party’s leaders are ready for it.

title: Why the left and right are both cheering Jensen Huang’s downfall
content:
Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s sudden downfall is in a sense shocking, considering his wealth, global fame, and role leading what was until recently the world’s most valuable company.

But Huang’s immense influence in Washington — and particularly in President Donald Trump’s Washington — has long been intensely controversial among a surprisingly diverse cross-section of the political, business, and tech advocacy world. And his ouster not only drives a wedge through Trump’s second-term coalition, it could usher in a major change in how the US steers the AI revolution.

Huang — who resigned this week after allegations he’d had affairs with two Nvidia employees and one Chinese businesswoman who some US officials claim was spying on him for the Chinese government — has been crucial in helping shape the Trump administration’s AI policies. That’s perhaps no surprise, given that Nvidia’s advanced chips are crucial to the AI revolution.

His many critics, however, say Huang’s influence has been deeply harmful. Their main objection? They believe the Trump administration hasn’t been doing enough to stop China from getting or accessing advanced AI chips — in part because of Huang’s lobbying and sway with the president.

This coalition of Huang critics spans the political spectrum. It includes right-wing China hawks and the bipartisan foreign policy establishment, who want to win an AI race against China. It includes economic populists in both parties, who resent China’s economic sway. It even includes some leading members of the Trump administration itself — Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent have reportedly pushed for tighter chip restrictions.

It also contains some even odder bedfellows. The coalition includes people who want to slow down the AI race, like the tech safety advocates who warn that advanced AI could cause human extinction. Yet it also includes two major US frontier AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, who hope to impede the growth of Chinese competitors by limiting their access to chips. 

All of these disparate groups come together around the core idea that the US urgently needs to do more to stop advanced chips from getting to China. Selling AI chips to China is like “selling nuclear weapons to North Korea,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has said.

Standing against them all — and often getting his way with Trump — has been Jensen Huang.

Beyond the obvious — Nvidia’s business is selling chips, and Huang wants to be able to sell more chips in more places — Huang is associated with a camp in the AI policy debate that some have dubbed with “let it rip.” Along with former White House AI czar David Sacks, Huang has scoffed at warnings that AI could cause human extinction, calling them “irresponsible” and “doomsday narratives.” He’s also dismissed some national security concerns, saying that being a “China hawk” was a “badge of shame” and said that the bigger risk to American influence over AI would be US companies losing market share around the world.

So Huang’s ouster and the claims of Chinese espionage around it have opened up an opportunity for a shakeup in US policy — and a rare chance for those China hawks to potentially investigate, undermine, and push out their rivals, while seizing the policy reins around chip exports. 

Trump administration officials who want tougher restrictions have their knives out for Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, a frequent ally of Huang’s. There’s a bipartisan push in Congress for new export controls legislation before the end of the year. Congressional Republican committee chairs are demanding Huang and Lutnick come in and testify in the coming weeks, before Democrats take over Congress.

Plus, there are the partisan incentives for Democrats to dig into the question of what Trump knew about all this (he was reportedly briefed on the spy concerns last fall). And there are political incentives for ambitious Republicans to find an issue on which they can distance themselves from an unpopular administration without antagonizing their conservative base. 

With so many different forces invested in the outcome, you can bet this topic will continue to dominate headlines for months to come — with unpredictable results for both the new Democratic Congress, the future of the GOP, and the AI boom.

The many critics of Jensen Huang’s influence on the Trump administration

In Washington itself, the most influential faction opposed to Huang is the bipartisan national security establishment, most of whom strongly believe in the necessity of competing with China for global influence. 

These “China hawks” were influential in the Biden administration and have historically been dominant in GOP administrations and on GOP-controlled congressional committees. And many of them have been flabbergasted at Trump’s policies toward China and Chips this term.

“I don’t think we should be using any American technology to uplift China’s capabilities in AI given how era-defining this technology will be in national security and in our economy,” Vivek Chilukuri of the Center for a New American Security, a center-left think tank, told me. “A company’s going to argue for this, that’s what companies do. But the interest of any one company should not be trumping the national security of the United States.

Moving further right, there’s a MAGA-aligned faction that is skeptical of foreign wars such as Trump’s conflict in Iran — but even some of them are still quite antagonistic to China.

Take, for instance, Trump’s onetime campaign manager and White House adviser Steve Bannon. He’s been furiously protesting Huang’s influence on the administration for more than a year — in September 2025, he argued that Huang should be arrested for being “an agent of influence of the Chinese Communist Party,” and argued we needed to “shut down” China’s “access to technology, chips, and training.”

Advocates and politicians focused on economic issues and reining in corporate power also have long criticized Nvidia. Oren Cass of the center-right group American Compass wrote an article titled “Break up Nvidia” last year, arguing that “its excessive concentration of power is exactly what antitrust law intends to combat.” 

Meanwhile, the left, Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-MA), a longtime critic of Big Tech, has frequently suggested Huang was corruptly influencing the Trump administration. At a hearing in June, she mentioned that Huang or his company had donated to Trump’s inauguration and his White House ballroom project. “If it’s not plain old-fashioned bribery, it sure smells like it,” she said.

Many in the AI safety advocacy world have also long criticized — and feared — Nvidia. That’s in part because they hope slowing down sales of AI chips abroad could slow what they view as a dangerous race to superintelligence. Additionally, after AI safety fears hit the mainstream in September due to Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon’s resignation and viral warnings, Huang took an increasingly public role in dismissing such fears.

Other AI safety advocates cite the company as having a chilling effect on public debate. “For months now, I’ve heard about widespread fear among think tank researchers and policy experts who publish work against Nvidia’s interests,” AI safety researcher Steven Adler wrote last year. “If you speak with people in-the-know at AI companies, fear of retaliation from Nvidia is a major concern when staking out policy positions.”

Indeed, OpenAI and Anthropic are highly dependent on Nvidia for its chips, so open criticism of the company is not common. Yet those big two US AI labs have been at odds with Nvidia in urging the Trump administration to do more to crack down on Chinese access to advanced chips, and to more heavily scrutinize Chinese “open source” AI models.

But to Huang and others in his camp, the growth of Chinese AI is a feature, not a bug. Sacks, for instance, has repeatedly argued that “open weight” or “open source” models — which make their parameters publicly available, in contrast to the proprietary models of OpenAI and Anthropic — would help avert “an unsafe and dystopian future where advanced AI capabilities are centralized and controlled by only a few hands.” The leading open weight models are currently from Chinese companies.

Huang has also used a more straightforward argument: that what’s good for Nvidia is good for the United States of America.

“American technology has to win across the world at every single layer,” he said in May. “If we can export chips, we should.”

Now it will be left to Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress, to carry that message, instead of a rock-star founder with a global cult following that’s drawn comparisons to Steve Jobs at his peak at Apple. Her first task: taking stock of all the powerful actors across the political, advocacy, and business world rooting for her to fail. Perhaps DeepSeek could help make a list?

title: Hope in Abu Dhabi, fighting in Europe, ‘hell’ in the Persian Gulf: RT stories that shaped the week
content:
In the past seven days we also watched Jensen Huang’s career crumble and saw how EU money finances the luxurious lives of the Ukrainian elite

Peace progress in Abu Dhabi

Read more

To follow the headlines this week, one needed simply to follow the movements of Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The two American envoys arrived in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday for the fourth round of trilateral talks between Washington, Moscow, and Kiev, bringing with them a plan to “create the conditions for a sovereign, secure, and prosperous Ukraine within a more stable European security environment,” according to Kushner at least.

The mere mention of a broader European security architecture represents progress, Russian analyst Fyodor Lukyanov wrote for RT, pointing out that Moscow’s calls to rethink European security were previously dismissed by Washington. Although the idea is still in its infancy, the trilateral talks ended positively, with Russia and Ukraine agreeing to a large-scale prisoner swap

Conspicuous in their absence were the Europeans themselves, who at this point had yet to decide whether they should even speak to Russian President Vladimir Putin in the first place. At a meeting with Putin in Moscow on Thursday, Witkoff and Kushner managed to secure the EU a seat at the table in the next round of discussions. However, as RT explained, ‘Europe’ is split into squabbling camps of realists, maximalists, and fantasists, all vying for control of the peace process.

EU deadlock in Dublin

Witkoff and Kushner left Moscow for Dublin on Thursday, where Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and his European backers were meeting for the European Political Community (EPC) and EU leaders’ summits. Their arrival at Baldonnel Aerodrome in the Irish capital was a more stripped-back affair than the welcome they received at the Kremlin, but Zelensky was likely unbothered: he had already bilked tens of millions of euros worth of energy-related aid from his patrons, who used the Dublin gathering to reaffirm their unconditional loyalty to Kiev. 

None dared ask where the money would end up, but a corruption case unfolding back in Ukraine offered a potential answer: in the pockets of oligarchs happy to spend it on sports cars, marble apartments, and, bizarrely, live crocodiles.

Some locals weren’t as happy to receive Zelensky, however, and his car was pelted with eggs after he left the meeting.

Sky News correspondent Stephen Murphy shows one of Zelensky’s convoy cars beign attacked by eggs in Dublin. What a warm welcome. https://t.co/uOgjIjReNy

— Margarita Simonyan (@M_Simonyan) November 13, 2026

Witkoff, Kushner, and now Zelensky are losing their patience with the Europeans. “We need to choose who will represent Europe in the negotiations,” he said on Wednesday, before issuing his ultimatum. This decision, he demanded, must be made “no later than the end of November.”

READ MORE: Dublin summit: European leaders double down on the Zelensky disaster

In true Brussels fashion, EU leaders decided on Friday that the continent will be represented at future talks by national security advisers from France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK, and by the European Commission and Council at leader-level discussions. With all three European factions – realists, maximalists, and fantasists – represented, and seven voices in the mix, European Council President Antonio Costa dismissed questions about potential clashes among the group.

“It is essential to have a team,” he said, yet “to speak with one voice.”

Jensen Huang gets honeypotted

Read more

Jensen Huang’s position at the helm of US chipmaking giant Nvidia made him one of the world’s most powerful billionaires. His weakness for the opposite sex, however, apparently made him a target for foreign intelligence agencies. Huang admitted on Sunday to an extramarital affair with an unnamed woman, who was quickly named in the media as Alice Huang, a Chinese tech executive and no relation to Jensen. US spies reportedly believe that Ms. Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to gather information about Nvidia and influence over its CEO.

Beijing has dismissed the allegations as “a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” and US President Donald Trump has stuck by the embattled executive, describing Huang as “an amazing guy” and “a high-quality person.”

Trump’s endorsement couldn’t stop the scandal from snowballing. As memes about the “honeypot” allegations flooded the internet, a second affair was revealed on Wednesday, and Huang resigned on Thursday, right after he was summoned to testify before Congress.

Iran threatens ‘hell’

The Republican Party’s devastating midterm election loss and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s shrinking odds of staying in power have placed the two principal antagonists of the war on Iran in limbo. If White House leaks are to be believed, Netanyahu wants Trump to restart attacks, and a conversation between the two descended into a “shouting match from hell” over the weekend.

Read more

Trump has acknowledged that the war cost his party the midterms, but the US president has rejected a deal with Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and instructed Vice President J.D. Vance – a moderate on Iran – to cease negotiations and focus on domestic issues. Whether these moves represent preparations for renewed conflict remains unclear, but Iran is taking no chances.

This week, Tehran lifted its self-imposed 2,000km limit on the range of its ballistic missiles and threatened to unveil “surprises… on the battlefield” if a new round of military confrontation erupts. Should the US and Israel “choose war,” they will “see our alert and battle-hardened Warriors rain down hell,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi warned in a social media post.

Iran and the US have traded tit-for-tat strikes, with Iranian forces claiming an attack on a US early-warning radar installation in Bahrain on Friday. Yemen’s Houthis have struck Saudi oil infrastructure and the headquarters of Saudi Arabia’s state-owned oil giant Aramco in Riyadh. For all parties involved, the cost of miscalculation could be huge.

Biden gets milked

Trump’s war on Iran may have dealt a generational defeat to the Republican Party, but he is not the only American president paying a price for siding with Israel. Joe Biden’s trip to Ireland was interrupted when pro-Palestinian protesters lobbed cartons of milk at the former president outside Dublin’s Trinity College on Tuesday.

Biden, whose son Hunter had just received an honorary award from the university, was met with chants of “blood on your hands” and “Genocide Joe” as he left the campus. Irish police were seen wrestling activists to the ground, and two people were pepper-sprayed and arrested.

Biden was in office when Hamas militants attacked Israel in October 2023, prompting the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) to launch a full-scale assault on Gaza. Biden vetoed multiple UN Security Council resolutions calling for a ceasefire, expedited the sale of military equipment to the IDF, and transferred just under $18 billion in military aid to Israel, on top of the $3.8 billion sent annually since 2016.

Biden’s “role in the genocide of the Palestinian people is well-documented,” Trinity College Dublin Students’ Union said in a statement after Tuesday’s protest. The union also called on Trinity to revoke the honorary doctorate awarded to Biden in 2016.

Read more

What we’re watching

Heading into the weekend, we’re preparing for further unrest across Europe, with protests planned in France, Germany, Italy and the Czech Republic, and strikes next week in France and Spain – all over the rising cost of living across a rapidly militarizing continent.

We’ll also be keeping an eye on the so-called Multinational Force-Ukraine (MNF-U) drills in Poland, which have been running since Monday and conclude next Friday. Held by 11 nations, including France, the UK, and Poland, in preparation for a potential deployment to post-conflict Ukraine, the drills look like an exercise in wishful thinking – Putin has already warned that the presence of foreign troops on Ukrainian soil would be “a recipe for an endless war.” Moreover, they could imperil the EU’s newfound plans to take part in talks with the US, Russia, and Ukraine.

Putin will travel to the Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum on Tuesday, where an historic trilateral meeting between him, Trump, and Chinese President Xi Jinping is expected to take place. Ukraine will be high on the agenda when the three heavyweights meet, and we’ll be bringing you live updates and analysis as it happens.

For more on these stories, and on everything else, stick with RT.

title: US grounds departing flights nationwide
content:
The FAA has ordered an emergency halt to all departures across the country, citing unspecified safety concerns

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has ordered a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights across the United States, citing unspecified safety concerns.

The emergency directive took effect at 3:54pm Eastern Time on Friday, with all departing aircraft instructed to remain on the ground until further notice.

According to the advisory, international flights arriving in the US are being handled on a case-by-case basis. The FAA has not specified how long the restrictions will remain in effect.

US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the nationwide ground stop was prompted by a “communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”

“FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them,” he wrote on X.

Preliminary reports suggest the disruption was not caused by a cyberattack, CNN reported, citing two law enforcement officials.

Read more

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the grounding was caused by a “telecommunications outage,” which authorities do not believe was the result of foul play.

The National Weather Service also reported nationwide internet and communications problems, warning that some weather information on its websites could be unavailable or outdated. The agency said technicians were working to restore services.

The last nationwide ground stop was ordered in January 2023 following a failure of the system that provides safety notices to pilots. The previous such shutdown occurred in the immediate aftermath of the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

The outage came just days after the FAA announced the nationwide rollout of SMART, a new AI-powered system designed to optimize flight routes and reduce delays. The technology was deployed across all 22 regional air traffic control centers, although authorities have not established whether it played any role in Friday’s disruption.

Similar technical failures have disrupted air travel worldwide this year. In September, a communications outage halted flights at major airports in the northeastern US, while a software malfunction caused widespread flight cancellations across Britain. Greece temporarily closed its airspace in January, and Italy halved its air traffic capacity following a technical failure in October.

title: Starshield speed limits return in Ukraine as senators demand to know who ordered them
content:
Ukraine's military is once again facing speed limits on Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk's Starlink.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Thursday that military units had detected restrictions that cut off drones moving faster than 161 kph (100 mph), along the entire front line and in Russian-occupied territory. He said a military investigation found the limits were not random errors.

On Friday, he said there are still "no clear explanations."

Trump admin offers mixed messages on limits to Ukraine's Starshield access

The cap matters most against Russia's jet-powered drones, the targets Ukraine's interceptor drones are built to chase.

"Without the speed we need, shooting down these Shaheds becomes much harder, and this means more Russian strikes get through and more of our people are killed," Zelenskyy said in a video posted Thursday.

Russia launched 117 drones at Ukraine overnight into Friday, killing at least two people, including a 17-year-old, Ukrainian authorities said. In Kyiv, a strike hit a medical facility of Ukraine's National Academy of Medical Sciences around 3 a.m., injuring one person and forcing staff to evacuate 30 patients. One person was killed in Odesa. In Zaporizhzhia, a single attack hit two apartment blocks and wounded 30 people, including six children, officials said.

Ukrainian officials are asking the U.S. State Department, the Pentagon and SpaceX to explain and fix the restrictions, Zelenskyy said. SpaceX has denied making any change. "This is false," a SpaceX official said Thursday. "There has been no change."

RELATED STORY | Ukraine disputes Elon Musk's claim that its military violated Starlink's terms of service

In Washington, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina are expressing outrage.

"Congress must determine who ordered or approved these disruptions and hold those responsible accountable," the senators said in a joint statement Thursday. "The Pentagon and SpaceX must preserve all records, turn over the contracts and communications that Congress needs to establish the facts and put safeguards in place so this never happens again."

It remains unclear who is calling the shots: the Pentagon or Elon Musk.

It has happened before. Last month, Musk acknowledged that SpaceX had throttled Starlink service in Ukraine for about a week. He had earlier written on X that limits on Starshield are "decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS." In late October, the Pentagon's inspector general turned down a bipartisan request from senators to investigate those disruptions.

RELATED STORY | Trump admin offers mixed messages on limits to Ukraine's Starshield access

Meanwhile, President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and with Zelenskyy in Dublin this week. More talks are planned, and the envoys say European negotiators will join the next round.

The talks have yet to stop the strikes.

title: UN chief says 'immediate and drastic' emissions cuts needed to avert climate change catastrophe
content:
The world must immediately and drastically cut fossil fuel emissions to avert the most catastrophic effects of climate change, United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said Friday at his final climate summit, urging the world to “follow the science” and face hard facts.

“You cannot build peace on a burning planet," Guterres told reporters, stressing that climate change is central to the U.N.'s work because it contributes to geopolitical instability by driving hunger and displacement, pushing countries into debt and fueling competition for land and water.

“You cannot eradicate poverty when climate disasters keep throwing people back into it,” he added. “You cannot promise young people a better future while destroying the natural systems on which that future depends. And you cannot speak seriously about justice when those who did least to cause this crisis suffer first and worst.”

World leaders meeting in Turkey for the annual U.N. climate talks are trying to reach consensus on concrete actions to address climate change — which is fueling more intense and deadly heat waves, droughts, floods and other disasters — and help countries at greatest risk, including island nations that also are losing land to rising seas.

Electrification goals emerge as point of contention

Achieving reductions in emissions is setting up a point of contention at the climate talks, especially around electrification. A goal introduced this year would increase the share of electricity in total global energy consumption from roughly 21% to 35% by 2035, preferably from renewable energy such as solar and wind.

But it does not require that electricity be generated by renewable sources — something Guterres said is essential — meaning coal and other fossil fuels could be used, at least initially. Climate TRACE, which tracks global emissions via satellites, found that prioritizing clean energy would cut global emissions 14% compared to 7% if fossil fuels also are used for electrification.

International Energy Agency Executive Director Fatih Birol said it's more important that as many countries as possible sign on to the pledge, which works best without a clean energy requirement.

But environmental groups say that electrification will only have a real impact if fossil fuels are omitted.

“Electrification must end fossil fuel dependence, not be an end in itself,” said Jasmin Duregger, from Greenpeace's Global Gas Campaign.

Vulnerable nations seek more compensation as warming takes a toll

Leaders from countries ravaged by climate change — mostly poorer, vulnerable countries that contributed little to the problem — also are calling for more money to deal with climate disasters and adapt to a warming world. Leaders of small island nations, who say climate change is a life-or-death matter for their people because rising seas are engulfing their lands, have been the most vocal at this year’s summit, COP31, saying a U.N. fund created for compensating vulnerable nations must be urgently strengthened.

Guterres said wealthier countries that have contributed most to climate change “must deliver the finance they have promised” at past summits — but also contribute much more.

“Let us be clear about the scale of the gap,” he said. “Even tripling adaptation finance would meet less than 30 percent of what is needed.”

Progress stalls, top-emitting countries skip summit

Progress is difficult without the cooperation of all nations, “particularly the biggest emitters,” Guterres said.

A report released Thursday by the independent Climate Action Tracker found that progress in slowing global warming has essentially stalled for the past five years. That means the world is sure to overshoot the goal set in the 2015 Paris Agreement of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial temperatures.

Climate change is caused primarily by greenhouse gases emitted by burning gas, oil and coal, and countries have established plans to reduce those emissions. But even if they fulfill all their promises — a big if — the globe will end the century 2.6 degrees Celsius (4.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than pre-industrial times, the report said.

“Our responsibility is to keep it as small as possible, for as short a time as possible and bring temperatures back below 1.5 degrees as quickly as we can,” by cutting emissions about 6% per year for several years, Guterres said, calling the overshoot “a recipe for catastrophe.”

But some of the top-polluting countries stayed away from this year's summit, most notably the United States — the world’s second-largest polluter after China and the largest historical polluter.

It's the second year in a row the U.S. skipped the summit, after President Donald Trump withdrew the U.S. from climate negotiations.

“Facts are facts,” Guterres said. “No country can protect itself from climate change alone. We share one planet, and whether we like it or not, we share one fate.”

Webber reported from Fenton, Michigan; Borenstein from Kensington, Maryland; and Delgado from Bangkok.

title: Israeli strike on Gaza hospital kills 6 people, including a doctor and a child, Health Ministry says
content:
An Israeli airstrike hit one of the main hospitals still operating in the Gaza Strip on Thursday, killing six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old boy, Gaza's Health Ministry said.

The Israeli military said the strike on Nasser Hospital in southern Gaza was targeting a Hamas commander and other militants. The commander it identified was not among the dead.

The strike hit the hospital's surgical wing, the ministry and witnesses said. Footage showed several wards and operating rooms heavily damaged or destroyed, with debris scattered across hospital beds and equipment and rebar dangling from holes in the ceiling. At least 28 people were wounded.

Israels president gives Eisenkot the first chance to form the next government

Among the dead were Dr. Rizk Abu Shaira, a general surgeon, and at least two patients, one of them the 13-year-old, according to the ministry.

Gaza's healthcare infrastructure has been decimated by a yearslong war whose trajectory is not expected to be altered by the outcome of Israel's recent election. The Israeli military has raided or laid siege to hospitals across the territory, accusing Hamas of using them as command centers and to hide fighters. Israel has also destroyed medical equipment and supplies and killed or detained hundreds of healthcare workers.

In armed conflict, hospitals and their staff are protected under international humanitarian law. A hospital can lose its protected status, however, if it is used for military purposes.

Work is halted in several areas of the hospital after the strike

British surgeon Goher Rahbour, who is volunteering at Nasser Hospital, said that the strike occurred just after midnight and shook the whole building.

"It was extremely smoky," said Rahbour, who was on the fourth floor of the surgical department at the time. The recovery area on the same floor was reduced to rubble, he said.

He said he had been operating alongside Abu Shaira just hours before the strike. "Lovely guy, happy and smiling," Rahbour said.

Ahmed al-Farra, a doctor and the general director of the hospital, said no warning came before the attack, but the Israeli army said it had warned "on several occasions, including recently, that the military activity at the hospital be halted."

Trump reverses course on Israel aid amid Tuesday's midterm election

Al-Farra said surgeries and other services had been suspended because of damage to the building where medical personnel were already struggling to provide care due to supply shortages and "miserable" conditions.

He said other nearby medical facilities were not equipped to do the type of "specialized surgeries" that Nasser Hospital had been providing, leaving patients in need of them to "face an unknown fate."

He said an attack on a hospital should be met with a forceful response from the international community. "Imagine if this event happened in another country in the world. Would the world fall silent about it? No, by God, no."

"No one's safe here," he added, switching from Arabic to English.

Israel has targeted Nasser before

A report from the United Nations, World Bank and European Union said in April that more than 1,800 medical facilities in Gaza have been partially or completely destroyed since the conflict began.

Israeli forces have previously attacked Nasser Hospital. In 2025, the military killed 22 people when it struck a gathering point for local reporters at the complex. Among the dead were five journalists, including Mariam Dagga, who worked for The Associated Press.

Hamas security men have been seen in hospitals during the war, controlling access to certain areas. In a statement on Thursday, the Israeli military said Hamas had "established a presence within the hospital complex" and that the commander had turned it "into a headquarters."

The World Health Organization said Gaza's health facilities should never be militarized or attacked. "Health needs remain immense in Gaza and will only grow as winter sets in," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said.

The Trump administration-backed Board of Peace said similar attacks are inevitable unless both Israel and Hamas honor commitments made under a stalled ceasefire plan the board has struggled to move forward.

The war in Gaza started on Oct. 7, 2023, when Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 others hostage. Since then, Israel's retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,600 people, according to the Gaza Health Ministry. The ministry, part of the Hamas-run government, maintains detailed records, and its figures are seen as generally reliable by U.N. agencies and independent experts. It does not distinguish between civilians and militants in its toll but says women and children make up around half the dead.

Israel has continued to strike Gaza despite a U.S.-backed ceasefire and controls at least 60% of the enclave. Since the truce went into effect in October 2025, Israeli strikes and gunfire have killed 1,622 people, health authorities say. Five Israeli soldiers have also been killed during that period.

title: Why online gamblers are obsessed with table tennis
content:
If you were living in Colorado in May and bet on sports online, you’d statistically have been most likely to bet on professional basketball. Next on the list was baseball. The third-most wagered sport?

Table tennis. 

Colorado is almost certainly not an outlier. Table tennis occupies a similarly high ranking in Oregon, the only other state to provide sport-by-sport breakdowns of gambling revenue. And it’s likely true in every other state that allows sports gambling. This is a strange fact, one that’s been reported by a few local and national outlets. And beyond the bets involved, it’s also a window into where sports gambling is going, and how sports betting is morphing into something stranger and more destructive than dropping $100 on the New York Yankees to cover the spread on Saturday.

There’s the old quip that the Holy Roman Empire was neither holy, nor Roman, nor an empire. In some sense, this is sports betting that involves neither sports nor betting. The gambling on table tennis isn’t really on the game of table tennis. It’s on a strange simulacrum of table tennis created solely for the purpose of creating more ways to gamble on it. For many of the people involved, it’s a kind of mindless, by-the-second slot machine rather than an informed wager on a player they might think can win. Ping-pong, in other words, has been reengineered into an addictive technology.

The story of how table tennis came to occupy this outsized role in sports betting — and what it really looks like now — offers an unsettling peek at how fast all of this is moving, and how much the business of gambling can distort the real world around it.

First, there’s a recent historical quirk. When most professional sports leagues shut down during the early stages of the Covid-19 pandemic, low-level, peculiar table tennis leagues in Eastern Europe popped up and were often the only game in town when it came to being able to place bets on sports. In May 2020 in Colorado, $6.5 million was wagered on table tennis, more than 25 percent of the statewide total — making it the most popular sport to bet on, simply because it was available. 

But even after other sports came back, table tennis stuck around. In Colorado this past May, with every other sport back and operating, table tennis was bringing in $33.9 million, five times what it had been. The same pattern held in Oregon: In May 2020, table tennis was the most bet sport in Oregon, with $3.7 million wagered. By this past February, it was still the second-most bet sport, but now with $9.5 million wagered.

LSports, a company that collects and provides the real-time data that sportsbooks use to take and pay out bets, has a report intended for gambling operators that provides some of the starkest information on this. Its advice: “Table tennis is no longer sports betting’s dark horse; it has become an essential asset for sportsbooks seeking 24/7 bettor engagement.” And a main reason for the appeal is the intense, constant flow of matches, so betting companies have “minimal gaps in their live offerings.”

How is table tennis producing this much betting content? Sports aren’t on 24/7, and they have leagues, tournaments, offseasons, and training camps. But table tennis is different. The matches being bet on are not real leagues. 

They have players that true fans of the sport would not recognize. They are played in strange, unmarked basements in Eastern Europe, with players whose names, if searched, reveal nothing beyond profiles on sports betting websites. The players’ abilities are clearly not at a professional level. Real, professional table tennis like World Table Tennis has packed arenas, high production value, professional announcers, and trophies for winners. Top athletes are elite physical specimens, able to hit small plastic balls 50 miles an hour at 150 rotations a second, with unfathomable hand-eye coordination. Players are national celebrities in their home countries. 

When I logged on to DraftKings in Maryland and saw the “TT Elite” league available to bet on, the livestream of the match showed a single table in a bare, windowless, dark-gray room with no evident spectators, coaches, or even windows.

It is the gambling tail wagging the sports dog; the sports exist solely to provide fodder to be bet on.

How sports betting became an addictive product

For those who don’t gamble on sports, there may still be a misunderstanding that what people are doing on DraftKings or FanDuel is dropping a basically simple bet or two a week, gambling on this or that team to cover the spread, or maybe betting a favorite player will win an end-of-season award. It isn’t.

These apps, however, are now a labyrinth of parlays (combining multiple bets into one, all of which must win to pay out), prop bets (bets on some individual event, like a single point), and invitations to bet on the next quarter, the next point, the next five seconds. The betting dashboard gives an impression of nothing so much as a casino floor: overwhelming and constantly changing, giving the impression that skilled play is possible, whether or not that’s the case. Most of all, there are hundreds upon hundreds of ways to bet, a salami that can be sliced infinitely thin.

This is very much how these companies intended it. Simple sports bets, like who will win a game, are actually not terribly profitable for bookmakers, who in fact can lose if betting lines are set incorrectly. This made companies actively seek to reengineer sports betting into slot machines, where bets come close to becoming totally abstracted button pushing. With prediction markets entering every nook and cranny of culture and politics, and casinos pushing states extraordinarily hard to get their products on our phones, it’s difficult to see where this stops.

The Public Health Advocacy Institute (PHAI) filed a lawsuit against FanDuel, DraftKings, and the NFL, among others, for selling a “known addictive product.” The organization’s complaint filed on March 24 specifically notes of one of their client’s betting behavior that “if there were no U.S. games happening at a certain time, he would bet on international table tennis, again wagering repeatedly on every single point.” FanDuel did not respond to a request for comment on the allegations in the suit. DraftKings referred Vox to its trade group, the Sports Betting Alliance.

I reached out to Harry Levant, PHAI’s director of gambling policy, and while he declined to expand on the facts in the complaint, he spoke generally about how someone might end up betting hundreds of times on table tennis a day. “By the time a person reaches pathological betting on ping-pong, they have often experienced many other forms of gambling, but more importantly, betting on ping-pong…is not a product built for recreation,” Levant said. “It’s a product built to deliver constant action.” 

Joe Maloney, the president of the Sports Betting Alliance, a trade advocacy organization representing online sportsbooks, told me on the question of addictiveness that “the existence of any market doesn’t make it more or less addictive.” He went on to say that “the vast majority of people that enjoy these products, that walk into casinos, that download legal apps…overwhelmingly these are people that are able to enjoy these products responsibly, but there are some people that demonstrate problematic behavior, and those people need all the support.”

One reason for the rise in table tennis betting is, frankly, its fakeness allows it to provide that action during otherwise barren hours. These are not prexisting and longstanding sports leagues that an interested consumer can decide they enjoy and place a bet on — they are ad hoc “leagues” created solely for the purpose of allowing sports betting for consumers at hours and during dates when more “normal” bets are not available, like PHAI’s client.

So, availability is one reason for table tennis’s continued success on sportsbooks — the fact that one can find a bet at almost any time, any day of the year. 

The second is the betting itself. By now, the concept of a proposition (prop) bet has become well-known: Will the first touchdown be from a pass or a run? Will the first pitch be a ball or a strike? 

Prop bets have come under fire from critics who say they push sports betting into dangerous territory. Two MLB pitchers were indicted for altering pitches in order to rig specific prop bets they could then profit on. Similarly, two NBA players pled guilty to federal charges after manipulating their performances to ensure certain prop-bet outcomes. One of them, according to a story in the New Yorker, was an avid table-tennis bettor. (In October, the NBA directed sportsbooks it has partnerships with to remove certain kinds of prop bets.)

But those scandals aside, online, mobile technology that allows live, in-game betting has fundamentally warped how sports gambling now takes place. In those TT Elite games and many other sports, you have the ability to make individual bets point by single point, which means many gamblers end up with dozens, even hundreds of bets laid an hour, with a constant stream of wins and losses. This is what led one gambling researcher to refer to it as “the crack cocaine of sports gambling.” 

Tennis is a sport I play poorly but follow reasonably seriously. On DraftKings, betting on tennis is completely inscrutable to me. I can barely interpret the odds it offers for point-by-point betting, or the numbers and statistics flashing and disappearing on the screen constantly. But there’s a reason it’s all there: As with ping-pong, tennis has a reasonably fast pace of point play, which fits the need for a gambler who wants the ability to push a button incessantly to gamble.

It isn’t about winning and losing bets

You may ask: Why? What does a gambler get out of this? It seems to defeat the purpose of sports betting as one sees it in pop culture, even degenerate gambling like in Uncut Gems: the immense bet on an outcome that will either make you a zillionaire or bankrupt you. What satisfaction is someone getting out of a steady stream of $30 bets on individual points of table tennis, which doesn’t even dangle the prospect of making you rich? 

The answer brings us to slot-machine design, which is what in-game betting has in essence devolved into. 

Natasha Dow Schull, who wrote Addiction by Design on casino gambling and specifically slot machines, explained why players end up searching for this experience. She interviewed many users of slot machines, who explicitly stated they were not searching for excitement or a prospective “big win” but a kind of flow state or sedating “zone” through high-speed action.

Dow Schull writes, “Speed is a critical element of the zone experience,” and gives several stark quotes from her interviewees.

“The speed is relaxing. It’s not exactly excitement; it’s calm, like a tranquilizer. It gets me into the zone,” says one. “In a very paradoxical way, the speed of it slows me down,” says another. Schull expands, “As he [the interviewee] recognizes, a mechanically mediated tempo functions as a form of predictability that structures and regulates his play, transforming risk into rhythm. As long as gamblers hold their speed steady, it suspends them into the holding pattern of the zone.”

As a matter of fact, problem gamblers sometimes even actively dislike winning a jackpot. Schull describes gamblers telling her, “It’s so weird, but when I win a jackpot, I get really frustrated and angry and irritated. … I think it’s because it interrupted the zone, and really why I’m sitting there is to stay in the zone. And when I win a jackpot, the lights start flashing, the machine freezes up. … Suddenly I’m back in the world where I don’t want to be.” Levant echoed this to me. He said, noting that winning money is not the point, really, “Gambling disorder has nothing to do with money, full stop. … It’s being in action, and that is what all of these products, including every serve in a ping-pong [match] that you can’t even see, is delivering.”

This is how one can mindlessly bet on two men playing mediocre table tennis in an empty gymnasium. No, there’s no inherent meaning — but does a slot machine have any inherent meaning? 

This was discovered by casino management consultants decades ago, long before the same phenomenon started infecting sports betting. Schull cites one consultant as writing, they designed the machinery of slot machines to “harness technology for continuous gaming productivity.” Long play durations and a slow bleed definitively take more money than single, high-stakes bets. (As a side point, this is actually why traditional slot machine arms were replaced with digital buttons: They were easier and faster to push, and fatigued users less to allow for longer play durations. Phones have the same benefits versus, say, traveling to a physical sportsbook.)

This language is echoed in that LSports report on table tennis, where they note specifically that the game’s strength is that its “extraordinary fixture volume enables fast cycles, encouraging bettors to reinvest their winnings quickly and fueling repeat engagement.” 

I was struck listening to Schull in an interview describe modern slot machines as fundamentally inscrutable in a way similar to what I experienced looking at tennis bets. Unlike an old-fashioned one-armed bandit, that you pulled once and hoped you won by a single line of three cherries, modern slot machines have hundreds of possible ways to win, with diagonal lines, criss-crossing lines, and so on.

A player might “bet 100 pennies on 100 lines,” which “creates more of a sense of flow. Instead of losing everything, winning everything, which can be very jarring…today, people are lounging back with glazed-over eyes in these ergonomic chairs spending a huge amount of time…slowly chipping away at their money…if you put in $100 and you win back $20, that’s a loss…it feels the same as a win. Lights flash, ding ding ding ding, and you kind of relax into the flow of the machine.” 

This is remarkably similar to the kinds of same-day parlays, bet hedging, and in-game live point-by-point betting that saturates modern sports gambling. In the same way it sounds a bit off to say you’re “betting” on a slot machine, this is the second part of that fork: The sports aren’t real, and neither is the betting. 

If you were asked to look at two players you’d never heard of, in a sport you neither watched nor played, and decide who would win this point, then the next, then the next, you would have created a certain kind of slot machine. A button is being pushed and a result is coming back. A single DraftKings page might have rows of bets, “Game 3 – Point 9,” “Game 3 – Point 10,” “Game 3 – Point 11,” each a spin of the proverbial slots.

What you’re gambling on becomes rapidly irrelevant to someone deep into problem gambling; there simply has to be something available and preferably fast. In the podcast Nothing Off the Table, a recovering problem gambler explained simply: “When you don’t have anything to gamble, you find a way, no matter what.” Which is why he also states at night he’d gamble on “Chinese ping-pong, Japanese tennis, anything I could get my hands on.”

The bleak future of sports betting

Companies are well aware of this phenomenon, which is why even legitimate niche sports are quickly taking sponsorship deals to collate and provide their data to betting platforms hoping that they can be the next table tennis. 

In many states you can now bet on the Disc Golf Pro Tour, the World Surf League, and the Grand Slam of Curling. For those not deep into the weeds of this kind of gambling, seeing maps of where gambling on “Street League Skateboarding” is legal, FAQs answering: “Why can’t I bet on BKB Bareknuckle Boxing in my area?” and headlines like “How to Get Started with Power Slap Betting?” might be jarring.

If the legitimate version of these sports are not available, they can simply be created ex nihilo, like the basement table tennis leagues. A reporting collaboration between Bellingcat and Josimar found similar “leagues” of school gymnasium soccer, sometimes with actual children as the players being bet on, along with glorified lawn games and literal arcade games, all taking place in gymnasiums and warehouses in Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus solely to provide something to bet on. 

The scale is breathtaking: Bellingcat’s reporter, Ross Higgins, estimated that they “played” and streamed 1,000 games in a 24-hour period: “It’s like watching sport with all the fun and competitive element taken out. You’re watching it to gamble on. … There’s no commentary…there’s no referee, there’s nothing that you’d enjoy from sports.”

Because these are filmed with cheap webcams, they have the appearance of “watching Squid Game through a camcorder.” The images are frankly difficult to fathom.

While this may seem like a seedy underbelly of the sports betting industry, it has to be emphasized that there are only a couple jumps between these sham competitions and the most successful multinational sports betting companies, along with professional sports. 

These fake school gym matches were being streamed and bet on 1xBet, which is an official sponsor of FC Barcelona, one of the top soccer clubs in the world, and sponsors many legitimate sports, like the ATP Challenger Tour, professional tennis’s “minor league.” LSports lists “TT Elite,” the warehouse table tennis I watched on Draftkings, as the second-most popular table tennis league to bet on. The seedy underbelly is just the creature itself.  (I also contacted 1xBet and TT Elite for their comments on steps they take to ensure match integrity, but they didn’t respond.)

It’s unsurprising that many of these matches have turned out to be rigged. This was a serious enough problem in the early days of Covid that New Jersey, Colorado, and Indiana suspended betting on these kinds of leagues, that is, those “not sanctioned by the sport’s top governing bodies.” And in 2023, an Australian table tennis player pleaded guilty of having inside information and placing over a thousand bets on matches he knew were rigged.

As real sports leagues like the NBA and MLB desperately try to control the damage to their brands by having platforms like DraftKings and FanDuel limit prop bets, problem gamblers will simply flow downstream to platforms and sports that allow the behavior they’re now in thrall to. Table tennis, for the time being, has a unique and powerful alchemy of speed of play and constant availability, but the devolution will likely continue.

Indeed, by the time you read this, this piece of writing may itself be out of date. Companies from multiple sectors are pushing extraordinarily hard to open up new venues to exploit potential profit centers. Eight states have already legalized so-called iGaming, which allows casino games and slot machines themselves to be played on one’s phone, removing the need for a fake sport to be played at all. 

Prediction markets, widely talked about as they enter into sports, politics, and current events also have bets on things like “Lowest temperature in Denver on November 5” and “# of views of next MrBeast video on day 4.” States have resisted legalization and in some cases sued prediction markets as being de facto gambling operators. But when they are legalized, the evolutionary process here escalates rapidly. 

As The Upshot found, Pennsylvania allowed mobile casino gambling in 2017, and within seven years, it was generating more than five times the revenue than all of sports betting. (They also rocketed up as the reason for calls to problem gambling hotlines.)

A moderate’s commonsense position might be to decide that if sports betting is to be legal, then the activity should consist of, well, betting on the sport. Not betting on whether a first pitch of a game is a strike, or the 14th point of the third game of a table tennis league in a warehouse basement will be won by player A or B, but a bet about an event at least one hour into the future, on the final outcome of a sport overseen by a top governing body. What’s wrong with “$100 on the Yankees to cover the spread tomorrow”?

Various countries have versions of these kinds of limits. Australia prohibits betting on live games online. Germany has intervals between live bets to prevent compulsive by-the-second bets. Norway has monthly limits on losses imposed on every resident. Nebraska voters on Election Day rejected a referendum supported by DraftKings and FanDuel to allow mobile gaming, in what Nate Grasz, the executive director of the Nebraska Family Alliance, a conservative organization, told me was “an effort by out-of-state gambling companies to make money off addiction.” That result means that residents will continue to need to go to a physical racetrack casino to bet.

Each of these restrictions share the same goal of increasing friction on betting. Meanwhile, we’ve let companies do the opposite — remove every last form of friction, whether physical, financial, or psychological. Even if we can’t return to the days of $100 on the Yankees, we don’t need to allow $5,000 to be spent in seconds on the 27th, 28th, 29th, and 30th point of YouTube gymnasium table tennis.
