title: Who wanted Nvidia’s Huang out? ‘Honeypot’ scandal raises questions over AI power struggle
content:
Jensen Huang’s exit removes a powerful opponent of US chip restrictions, exposing divisions in Washington over how to preserve America’s technological dominance

The downfall of Nvidia founder Jensen Huang in a scandal involving a suspected Chinese spy has raised a politically explosive question: who benefits from the removal of one of Washington’s most influential critics of chip restrictions on China?

Huang resigned on Thursday following revelations of extramarital affairs, including one with Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, former head of Nvidia customer, Singapore-based Megaspeed International. Anonymous US intelligence officials reportedly suspect that she was recruited by Beijing to potentially influence the Nvidia CEO to push Washington to ease AI chip export restrictions.

Read more

The scandal came at a pivotal moment in the US-China technology war, just days before a planned summit between Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping. With congressional hawks already pushing for tougher restrictions, the timing of Huang’s downfall has fueled questions about the political interests served by his resignation.

RT examines the intrigue surrounding Huang’s exit and the struggle for control of the global AI industry.

So who benefits from Huang’s departure?

Huang’s resignation removes one of Washington’s most prominent advocates of keeping China connected to American AI technology, potentially handing China hawks a major political advantage. The Nvidia founder repeatedly warned that cutting Beijing off from American technology would accelerate China’s push for independence. In a May interview with Fox Business, he pointed to Huawei’s growing influence: “They’re flourishing in our absence.”

His exit has immediately intensified congressional demands for tighter export controls and investigations into Nvidia’s China dealings.

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

Republican Representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, has seized on the scandal to question whether whether Chinese intelligence had obtained sensitive information through Huang or influenced US technology policy.

“[Huang has] been one of the strongest proponents for not having export controls,” Moolenaar said. “This shines a whole new light on that discussion.”

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast has also pushed for stronger safeguards, including measures to prevent chip smuggling and restrict access to advanced semiconductor equipment.

Despite Jensen Huang’s resignation, Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk.

The Trump administration must also answer for what it did once it learned about Mr. Huang’s relationship with a…

— Chuck Schumer (@SenSchumer) November 12, 2026

Trump defended Huang as a “very honorable guy” and said he believed the executive’s denial that he knew Alice Huang was allegedly involved in espionage. However, the controversy appears to have given advocates of tougher restrictions on China fresh ammunition against one of their most influential opponents.

Who benefits more – China hawks or AI rivals?

Huang’s abrupt exit has also raised questions over whether rival American technology firms could benefit from his downfall.

Independent journalist Lee Fang suggested rival US AI companies could gain, pointing to Huang’s support for cheaper Chinese open-source models that threaten established American competitors. He drew parallels with earlier campaigns targeting Huawei and TikTok.

What are the odds American AI firms are playing some role in the Huang ouster? In the same way Cisco paid PR firms to spread fears about Huawei and Meta paid PR firms to stir demands for banning competitor TikTok? Huang singularly pushed cheaper Chinese open source models.

— Lee Fang (@lhfang) November 12, 2026

Venice AI founder Erik Voorhees went further, calling Huang’s removal a “coup.”

Journalist Glenn Greenwald questioned whether extramarital affairs alone explained the removal of one of America’s most powerful technology executives.

“I don’t know who wanted Jensen Huang out but I know that whoever it was wields extreme levels of power,” he wrote on X.

The resignation also provoked a backlash across Silicon Valley. Binance founder Changpeng Zhao called it “a mistake,” Epic Games chief Tim Sweeney described it as “a sad day,” and Elon Musk said hiring Huang would be “an honor.”

A sad day for NVIDIA, developers, America, and all humanity. Jensen founded and ran one of the few companies to reach a massive scale while driving massive continued innovation and ubiquity, while others fell into the trap of ever-increasing extraction. https://t.co/AkS5XT9HF8

— Tim Sweeney (@TimSweeneyEpic) November 12, 2026

“Dark, dark day. Horrible decision for the US and the western world,” wrote Andreessen Horowitz partner Martin Casado.

The media has some questions to answer

Questions have emerged over how the story reached the press. New York Times reporter Tripp Mickle, who helped break the story of Huang’s affair, revealed on The Daily podcast that he and colleague Ana Swanson began investigating Megaspeed after receiving a tip from an unnamed technology industry contact.

The disclosure reinforces suspicions that journalists may have been deliberately steered toward Megaspeed, raising questions about who supplied the tip – and why.

What did Washington know – and when?

The intrigue deepened following reports that senior US officials knew about Huang’s relationship with Alice Huang months before the scandal erupted.

Read more

According to Axios, a highly classified intelligence memorandum overseen by Secretary of State Marco Rubio circulated before Trump’s May visit to China. Based on surveillance of Alice Huang and an investigation into suspected chip smuggling involving Singapore-based Nvidia customer Megaspeed, the warning reportedly reached Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Rubio also reportedly briefed Trump.

Megaspeed operates AI computing infrastructure, allowing customers to rent access to powerful Nvidia processors outside China – a potential route around restrictions on shipping advanced chips directly to the country.

Washington was also approving direct sales to Chinese buyers. In May Reuters reported that around ten Chinese companies had been cleared to purchase Nvidia’s H200 processors, although deliveries had not begun. The approvals were separate from the Megaspeed investigation, and their precise timing relative to the intelligence warning remains unclear.

The dispute reportedly reached the highest levels of the Trump administration. Axios reported that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick over his failure to blacklist Megaspeed despite repeated warnings. The Commerce Department denied the confrontation ever happened and Lutnick now faces congressional scrutiny over his department’s handling of chip exports and suspected diversion to China.

Read more

If Washington had been warned months earlier, why did the allegations become a public crisis only now?

How did Singapore become entangled in the scandal

Singaporean authorities had been investigating Alice Huang’s former company, Megaspeed International, long before her alleged ties to Chinese intelligence became central to the scandal surrounding Nvidia’s founder.

In a statement Thursday, Singapore’s Home Affairs Ministry said police began investigating Megaspeed in February 2025 over suspected false declarations involving servers shipped through Singapore to Malaysia.

Alice Huang was questioned and had her passport seized in June 2025. By February 2026, however, investigators found insufficient evidence that she had committed the suspected offenses. She received a warning for knowingly providing inaccurate information about her role at Megaspeed and was barred from re-entering Singapore.

Notably, Singapore stressed that she had never been investigated for espionage.

Meanwhile, the alleged Chinese spy narrative has come under growing scrutiny in Washington itself.

Bombshell story. The spy narrative is collapsing already.

Is there clear & convincing evidence that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy?

- AG says no. (“no conclusions reached”).
- CIA says no. (“not yet convinced”).
- DNI says no (“not entirely accurate and over-torqued”).
- Ranking… https://t.co/9Pt1W2zjVX

— David Sacks (@DavidSacks) November 13, 2026

According to CNN, US intelligence officials remain divided over whether the evidence establishes that Alice Huang worked for Beijing. Attorney General Todd Blanche said that the Justice Department had reached “no conclusions” about her alleged intelligence ties.

The assessments leave a fundamental question unanswered: how did an unproven espionage allegation gain such traction despite the lack of conclusive evidence?

Read more

Why is Nvidia central to US technological dominance?

Founded by Huang in 1993, Nvidia has become the leading supplier of advanced processors powering the global AI boom.

Its chips and software underpin data centers and AI systems worldwide, making the company a strategic asset in Washington’s competition with Beijing.

By controlling exports of advanced processors and semiconductor technology, the US can influence which countries gain access to the computing power needed to develop cutting-edge AI.

Washington argues the restrictions are necessary to prevent China from strengthening its military and intelligence capabilities. Critics see a broader strategy of technological containment aimed at preserving American economic and geopolitical dominance.

That is what made Huang’s position so consequential: he challenged a central instrument of Washington’s effort to maintain its lead over China.

Could US chip restrictions hand China the advantage?

Washington’s campaign to contain China’s technological rise risks achieving the opposite: accelerating Beijing’s drive to build an AI industry beyond American control.

Read more

Chinese firms, including Huawei, are developing domestic alternatives to US processors, while Beijing is pushing for technological self-reliance.

In an August regulatory filing, Nvidia warned that US export controls, combined with Chinese restrictions, had effectively excluded it from China’s data-center computing market.

The company argued that its exclusion was allowing competitors to expand their developer and customer networks, potentially challenging American technology worldwide.

That was the central contradiction Huang repeatedly highlighted: cutting China off from Nvidia could weaken American influence while strengthening Chinese competitors.

Washington’s national security hawks argue the opposite – that selling powerful processors to Beijing risks advancing its military and technological capabilities.

Huang’s departure removes a prominent voice from that debate, but not the dilemma: could Washington’s efforts to preserve its technological supremacy ultimately help China escape American dominance?

Read more

Who will take control of Nvidia now?

Huang’s resignation has triggered a leadership crisis at Nvidia. According to Wired, an internal post urging the board to consider employee sentiment attracted more than 1,600 comments, many supporting Huang’s return.

Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO while Nvidia searches for a permanent successor.

According to Reuters, Kress and Nvidia veteran Ian Buck, a key figure behind its CUDA computing platform, are among the possibilities. Other names floated include Arm CEO Rene Haas and AMD chief Lisa Su. On Polymarket, Buck has also emerged among the leading contenders, alongside Jensen Huang’s daughter, Madison Huang, who serves at Nvidia as senior marketing director, and Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji, although betting odds offer no indication of the board’s intentions.

BREAKING: Jensen Huang's daughter, Madison Huang, emerges as the leading candidate to become Nvidia's next CEO.

See all candidates: https://t.co/Ijsq636OPo pic.twitter.com/597e31lFlw

— Polymarket (@Polymarket) November 11, 2026

Trump has also weighed in, endorsing former Apple CEO Tim Cook, now executive chairman, declaring on Truth Social that “a Legend replaces a Legend.”

President Trump proposes Tim Cook to run Nvidia and says Apple would never be what it is today if Steve Jobs were still around

“Well, you know the expression, anybody can be replaced. So it’s very hard to replace him, but I had an idea this morning that I sort of just released.… https://t.co/uxJNkLoMW2 pic.twitter.com/ylwksgXenR

— Fireside Alpha (@firesidealpha) November 13, 2026

The succession debate has extended to Israel, where media have floated Nvidia technology chief Michael Kagan, Mellanox founder Eyal Waldman, and Apple‘s Srouji. All three have strong ties to the Israeli technology sector.

Whoever succeeds Huang will inherit a company caught in the escalating US-China technology confrontation, with the stakes extending far beyond the boardroom. Huang’s replacement will have to choose whether to continue advocating for keeping China within the American technology ecosystem or bring Nvidia closer to Washington’s advocates of tougher restrictions.

The broader question, meanwhile, is not simply who replaces Huang, but whether his departure will also mark a fundamental shift in America’s AI strategy.

content: Highway 1, or the Ring Road, connects Afghanistan's major cities. After September 11, 2001, it became a hotspot for crime and fighting, particularly between the capital Kabul and Kandahar, the Taliban's birthplace. People taking it had to navigate extortions, kidnappings and suicide bombings. What has become of the road after the US-led war and five years of Taliban rule? title: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
content:
Kurt Gödel left 1,009 pages of densely written text – much of it in an obsolete shorthand – which is now said to contain hundreds of proved theorems

The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.

After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

title: Deadly floods swamp tens of thousands in Gaza (VIDEOS)
content:
The enclave’s sewage infrastructure lies in ruins after Israeli attacks, and the UN accuses the country of obstructing vital aid

At least four people have been killed after heavy rain flooded camps sheltering tens of thousands in Gaza, according to UN agencies. Much of the enclave, including its sewage system, has been reduced to rubble by Israeli bombardment.

Heavy rain and strong winds, which are unusually intense for early November, battered the coastal territory for several days, the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) said. Floodwaters swept through makeshift camps and tents, soaking mattresses, washing away belongings, and collapsing shelters.

At Al Berka Reservoir, west of Deir al-Balah, a rain-soaked sandy embankment collapsed onto tents, reportedly killing five people, including three children and two women, with an infant feared drowned, according to local rescuers cited by OCHA. UNICEF, however, reported four deaths in the collapse.

At least 5 people are dead and thousands more without shelter after heavy rains hit Gaza. While Israeli authorities are not responsible for the rain, they are responsible for the displacement of 1.9 million Palestinians and obstructing entry of humanitarian aid. https://t.co/sVTTpc5g7n

— Human Rights Watch (@hrw) November 12, 2026

According to Gaza’s Government Media Office, around 70,000 tents were flooded within 12 hours. The UN separately recorded more than 6,000 family shelters destroyed and 17,400 damaged. UNICEF reported that around 950,000 displaced Palestinians live in flood-exposed areas, including 400,000 at extremely high risk.

The scale of the devastation is exacerbated by the aftermath of more than three years of Israeli bombardment, which destroyed or damaged 82% of structures, forcing vast numbers of Palestinians into flimsy tents, according to the UN.

Israeli attacks also ruined drainage and sanitation infrastructure, which was neglected before the conflict. According to UNICEF, not a single wastewater treatment plant in Gaza is operational, and just two out of six pumps at the Sheikh Radwan stormwater basin still function, raising the risk of sewage-contaminated floodwater overflowing into nearby neighborhoods.

The agency also stressed that it sought Israeli approval to bring in repair equipment for more than a year.

Even the US-backed Board of Peace, established under President Donald Trump’s Gaza peace plan, criticized Israel’s handling of the crisis, warning that delays in approving shelter, sanitation, and drainage equipment “exacerbated the consequences of a foreseeable humanitarian challenge.”

title: Bessent blames Lutnick's Commerce Department for not restricting Nvidia chip exports
content:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Friday he was frustrated with the Commerce Department’s delay in placing restrictions on Nvidia chip exports to a company led by an alleged Chinese spy.

Bessent said on CNBC that his department, along with the departments of State and Defense and the U.S. Trade Representative, were in favor of adding Singapore-based Megaspeed International to an export control list for months but that the Commerce Department was in charge of the matter.

“Commerce has the pen, and you will have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent said. “My deputy has been pushing this for months.”

Bessent's comments were an unusually public rebuke of a fellow Cabinet member, in this case Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Commerce oversees U.S. government controls over exports of sensitive, high-tech goods. The comments come as Nvidia’s ties to Megaspeed are prominent in the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. Huang allegedly had an affair with the CEO of Megaspeed, Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence suspects is a Chinese spy, The New York Times has reported. China has denied allegations of spying.

Lutnick has come under increasing scrutiny because of his reportedly close relationship with Huang. The ex-Nvidia CEO is also close to President Donald Trump and recently visited the White House Sept. 29 to discuss AI safety. The Times reported Thursday that Lutnick resisted placing greater limits on the sale of Nvidia's more advanced chips to China. Chinese firms have accessed Nvidia's chips through companies like Megaspeed, which has reportedly purchased more than $4 billion worth of Nvidia's advanced semiconductors.

The split in Trump's Cabinet reflects the widespread fallout from the scandal that has engulfed Nvidia, one of the most valuable publicly-traded companies in the world. Nvidia's computer chips play a central role in the buildout of artificial intelligence, powering AI models such as those developed by OpenAI and Anthropic.

Just last month, Trump awarded the then-Nvidia CEO a National Medal of Science. Earlier this week, Trump defended Huang, noting that “he said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

The U.S. government has, since the Biden administration, sought to restrict the sale of the most advanced AI computer chips to China in an effort to protect U.S. technology companies' lead. Yet China has at times retaliated, creating controversy over how far the U.S. should push its restrictions.

The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to messages seeking comment.

Bessent declined to comment Friday on the Times report that he confronted Lutnick last week in the White House's situation room about Megaspeed.

Separately, Axios reported this week that Lutnick received a classified memo this spring warning about Jensen Huang's relationship with a suspected spy.

Last year, Megaspeed was accused of illicitly shipping advanced Nvidia computer chips into China, but in December the company said there was “no evidence” of such exports.

The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security began investigating Megaspeed International in 2024. The bureau later handed off the investigation to the Justice Department.

A person familiar with the bureau’s investigation denied any intervention from Nvidia. The person wasn’t authorized to discuss the matter publicly and spoke on condition of anonymity.

The Justice Department’s national security division is investigating whether Megaspeed violated export control laws in an inquiry that will also include scrutiny of Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the matter, The Associated Press reported Wednesday.

On Thursday, Megaspeed maintained it takes its obligation to comply with American export control laws “extremely seriously” — and that it was committed to working “constructively and transparently” with the U.S. government.

Numerous members of Congress have said they will investigate Lutnick's actions and called for him to testify on Capitol Hill.

On Thursday, Oregon Sen. Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Rep. Richard Neal, both Democrats, wrote Lutnick a letter demanding that he preserve all records related to decisions about Nvidia chip exports, pending an investigation. Wyden and Neal are the top Democrats on the Senate Finance and House Ways and Means committees, respectively.

Trump's approval of advanced Nvidia chip exports to China “raises critical questions about whether and to what extent political considerations are improperly influencing policy decisions made by the Administration,” Wyden and Neal wrote.

And the chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee wants Nvidia’s general counsel, Tim Teter, and a senior Commerce Department official to appear before Congress.

Rep. Brian Mast, a Republican from Florida and the panel chair, sent a letter this week to Jeff Kessler, undersecretary of commerce for industry and security, seeking a Dec. 2 hearing on computer chip smuggling and “reported interference by private companies into export control policies and enforcement investigations.”

Republican Sen. John Kennedy of Louisiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, urged Lutnick to hold a press conference to explain what he knew.

“The Commerce Department greenlit $4 billion of sales of advanced chips to the company of the spy that Mr. Huang was having an affair with and I want to know why," Kennedy said. "I want to know why the Commerce Department did it in light of the export controls, and everything I read indicates that this was a decision by the secretary himself."

Kennedy added that Lutnick should testify before the Senate and should be subpoenaed if necessary.

___

AP writers Didi Tang and Kevin Freking contributed to this report.

title: UK approves controversial migrant center near ‘breakaway’ village
content:
The Home Office has used an emergency planning procedure to sidestep the local council’s decision-making opposition

The UK government has approved controversial plans to house up to 1,256 male migrants near a tiny Oxfordshire village of around 350 residents, Sky News reported on Thursday. To protest the plans, Piddington symbolically seceded from the UK in September.

Residents of the village, which had a population of just 358 in 2021, have fiercely opposed the proposed asylum center at a nearby former military site, raising concerns about its impact on their small community. Despite 285 residents voting in favor of secession in the symbolic referendum, the government has refused to cancel the plans.

British Housing Secretary Angela Rayner personally approved the project on Thursday, according to Sky News. A letter from her department to the Home Office said the facility would “provide a flexible and operationally resilient” response to housing demand and reduce reliance on migrant hotels, the news outlet reported, citing the correspondence.

Although the facility was intended for temporary use, Rayner assessed the project “as if it was for a permanent development,” according to Sky News.

The Home Office used the Urgent Crown Development procedure, allowing ministers to decide the application instead of the local planning authority, which would normally have the power to reject such projects following objections from residents.

Read more

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage blamed Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s government for the expansion of asylum accommodations, arguing that the policy endangered women and girls.

“Burnham is determined to flood towns and villages across the country with fighting-age male illegal migrants,” Farage wrote on X on Thursday.

“Burnham and his government are putting women and girls at risk,” he added.

The decision comes as the UK deals with an ongoing migrant crisis and continued illegal crossings via the English Channel.

Read more

More than 23,500 migrants have arrived in the UK aboard small boats so far this year, according to Home Office data published Wednesday.

Anti-immigration protests and riots have also erupted in the UK in recent years following multiple high-profile rape, murder, and assault cases involving migrants and people with migrant backgrounds.

Immigration topped the list of concerns among Britons, with 40% naming it as one of the country’s most important issues, according to an Ipsos poll published in late October. Nearly two-thirds of Britons expected the country's economic situation to worsen over the following year, according to the survey.

title: COP31 talks face resistance over any deal that would limit or shift away from fossil fuels
How science informs author Emily St. John Mandel’s fiction
content:
The world is full of unanswered questions and strange ideas. Do parallel universes exist? What would it look like if a pandemic wiped out life as we know it? Is time travel possible? 

I host the science podcast Unexplainable, where we often speak to scientists about their attempts to puzzle through life’s greatest mysteries, but academic researchers aren’t the only people wrestling with these concepts.

On the latest episode of the show, I spoke with Emily St. John Mandel, the award-winning author of Station Eleven, about her new book, Exit Party, which grapples with the question of the multiverse. We talked about how she approaches science in her fiction, and how, even if we never get clear answers to some of these strange ideas, they can still help us think deeply about ourselves and our world. 

Below is an excerpt from our conversation, edited for clarity and length. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Unexplainable wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts and Spotify, or watch us on Netflix.

Emily, you are often writing about really interesting scientific ideas. Why do you put these scientific concepts at the heart of the books that you write?

Because they’re so interesting. I don’t have an educational background in science. I didn’t study it in school. I did work in a cancer research lab for years, so I’ve definitely hung out with scientists. I was great with grant budgets. But I could not actually tell you the mechanisms by which microRNA 335 impacts breast cancer metastasis. 

Neither can I.

But you know what? Science is interesting to me. I like reading about ideas in the fringes of science. But my understanding is that physicists are more or less evenly split on the question of whether we’re living in a multiverse.

Where do you start with exploring these concepts?

It’s really book by book. Sea of Tranquility was the first book I wrote that had more of a hard sci-fi component, because I do have a time-traveling detective in that book.

And what that came out of was it was the spring of 2020. The pandemic hit. I was promoting The Glass Hotel on Zoom, and I thought that for my own sanity, it might be nice to be immersed in the grand project of a book. That can be good for you sometimes when everything is chaos, like in the early days of a pandemic. 

I’ve always loved time travel novels as a reader and a fan. The problem with the time travel narrative, though, is that it falls apart instantly.

What do you mean? 

If you think about it for a second, it’s like, if I walk out of this podcast studio and I’m transported back to 1812, was I not always going to walk out of the studio and be transported back to 1812? And doesn’t reality break upon my arrival? That raises other questions like immortality — am I always going round and round in time? The causation gets really complicated and weird.

But I felt like, you know what? I’m going to write whatever I want. So I start writing about my time-traveling detective, and then I run into the time travel narrative problem, the loops and the paradoxes and all the rest of it. 

And my solve for that, I thought, “What if I added a whole other layer of science fictional weirdness to try to make that work?” Enter the simulation hypothesis, which is the hypothesis that all of our reality is a simulation. And something I love about that is you can find really smart people convincingly arguing either side. 

I thought it was a cool idea, and I realized that I could use that to make time travel work. And so that’s what got me into that little branch of science for Sea of Tranquility. 

And then Exit Party, I had an idea about writing about doppelgängers. I’d been thinking about it for years — the idea of a counter life.

Counter life?

The life you did not live, where you moved to a different city or took a different job or married a different person — any of those inflection points. I wondered if doppelgängers could be thought of as a sort of embodiment of a counter life. It’s another you who has lived a different life in a different version of reality. That’s what got me to the multiverse idea. But then I was also thinking, “Okay, well, I’ve thought about the counter life of the individual. What is the counter life of the state?”

And that can be a really interesting thought experiment. There are some very obvious inflection points in our recent history, but every country has them. You know, the election that went a different way or the decision made to go to war or not. A policy that was enacted or not enacted and the fallout from that, and any of those inflection points create a somewhat different country. It was thinking about counter lives and doubling, and that’s what got me to this idea of the multiverse.

You’re talking about these ideas almost like, “It’s a fix to this problem that I created.” 

It often is. Exit Party opens with a woman going to a party, two doppelgängers show up, and somebody else disappears. I realized pretty early on, wait a minute, at some point I am going to have to account for where the doppelgängers came from, so in that case, it was definitely a fix. But it was also thinking about the double life of a state — the state that you could live in if things had gone a different direction at some inflection point.

Something that interested me as a thought experiment in writing this book is: How might the tropes of science fiction map onto actual lives? Doppelgängers are very science fictional. But we all have counter lives, so imagine those as the embodiment of the counter life. Or later in the novel, there’s a conversation about time travel. And the character says something to the effect of, “I think if you live long enough, you become a time traveler. It’s like you’re a migrant from another timeline.”

There’s nothing more science fictional than a time traveler. That is the definition of a trope, basically. But that is how adulthood works, or how time works. You learn to navigate the world as an adult, and then you look up one day and realize that world is long gone. 

If you’re lucky enough to get to live for a while, if you live into your 80s or potentially even older, that world that you learned is really gone. 

You get to a certain point in your life, you look back, and you realize you’re not really looking back at a life singular. It’s really one life after another, isn’t it? 

I wanted to express that. You were a different person 10 years ago and living a different life, and I wanted to follow a character, Ari in this case, from one life into another.

I don’t think it’s a spoiler to say, you drop us into a fairly dystopian world.

I mean, I collapse the United States in the first sentence…

I was almost expecting that we were going to enter into another world where we made different choices and everything worked out so wonderfully.

I mean, my wife wishes I would write a utopia.

No, it’s true. I do then present an equally dark vision. I think the key, though, and where I find hope personally in my life, but also in this book, is in transience — this idea that nothing lasts forever and everything ends. 

There’s such obvious grief and loss attached to that idea, but I think there’s also a lot of hope. Because if I look at it through the lens of my personal life, the worst moments of my life did not last forever. You move through them, and there’s something else after that. Or if you look at it at a larger scale, the worst moments in your country’s life don’t last forever either. 

In the second universe of the book, the authoritarian state, I was thinking in terms of modern-day surveillance states, but I was also thinking about East Germany and the Stasi system of citizen informants.

And you know, here’s where transience and hope intersect. A lot of what I know about them I learned in the DDR Museum in Berlin, because the Stasi are gone. We make museums about them. They’re both fairly dark visions, but in both sides of the book, we are moving through them toward something else.

You won’t always be in a terrible situation. You also won’t always be in a good situation. That’s where the loss comes in.

How did you go about trying to think through what the fractal parallel universes would look like?

I was thinking about that with the character Ari. She’s got this character defect. She’s pulled toward criminality. It’s this deep, fundamental proclivity that she has, and there’s a world where somebody like that just goes toward criminality and becomes a criminal, as she did in a previous part of her life.

But what if that same person were growing up in a much more repressive state where the consequences were much worse for breaking the rules? Maybe that interest in criminality pulls a person toward law enforcement, and it was interesting to think of that as almost two sides of the same coin.

When you’re borrowing these scientific concepts, do you feel trapped by the science of it all? Do you feel like you have to stay within certain boundaries?

I don’t, which may annoy some readers of sci-fi, but I think there’s a really interesting choice that you have to make if you’re writing speculative fiction, and that’s how accurate do you want to be, or how deep into the weeds do you want to go with your science fictional technology?

On one end of the spectrum, you’ve got an author like Cixin Liu, who wrote The Three-Body Problem. I really love his work. He gets so granular about those technologies. When I first started working on Sea of Tranquility, I thought, “I want to figure out how the time machine works.” I guess it was a bit of insecurity on my part. So I spent some time reading about current ideas and technologies that I imagine eventually evolving into time traveling. I was reading about the quantum blockchain, and then after I’d spent a bit of time in that rabbit hole, I realized I don’t actually care.

I had this realization: If I’m not describing how a car engine works in the 2020 section, why do I care about the mechanics of the time machine? It’s literally just transport.

And that was kind of liberating, realizing that I care more about the characters. I want to focus on how people respond in these interesting scenarios I’m putting them in. So honestly, the level of scientific detail I’m aiming for is “plausible within the context of a literary novel,” which is a low bar. 

For this parallel universe stuff, did you look into some of the physics debates about this? 

A little bit. Like the simulation hypothesis, you can find smart people on either side. I feel very unqualified to participate in the debates.

title: EU leaders prolonging Ukraine conflict to stay in power – Swiss journalist (VIDEO)
content:
Western officials would only obstruct peace efforts if allowed a seat at the negotiating table, Peter Hansler has told RT

EU leaders want to prolong the Ukraine conflict because they stand to lose their jobs if peace is achieved, Swiss journalist and Forum Geopolitica founder Peter Hansler has told RT.

During the two-day Russia-Ukraine-US talks in Abu Dhabi earlier this week, European officials held separate consultations with the US and Ukrainian delegations but were not included in the main negotiations. On Thursday, US President Donald Trump’s envoy Jared Kushner said Moscow agreed to expand the next round of negotiations to include “our European partners.”

Russia has not, however, confirmed that it agreed to direct European participation. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has accused European governments of sending mixed signals, with their calls for peace contrasting with plans to deploy troops to Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire. Moscow has consistently said it would oppose any such move.

“All the leaders in Europe, they will lose their job if there is peace. So does [Ukraine’s Vladimir] Zelensky,” Hansler told RT, arguing that the involvement of European governments in negotiations would be “highly problematic.”

Read more

“They will block any peace. This is my personal opinion,” the journalist added.

Hansler claimed that European leaders are not interested in negotiating an end to the conflict. “They will prolong the war. That’s their interest. Because all the European leaders, they are dependent on this war,” he said.

He also pointed to divisions within the EU over further financial support for Kiev, saying European governments are “running out of money” and lack unity on whether to continue financing Ukraine.

Hansler argued that there would be no meaningful negotiations or prospect of peace if German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, French President Emmanuel Macron, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham took part, accusing them of being “pro-war against Russia.” He also noted that European governments have thus far failed to name a negotiator to represent them in any potential talks.

title: Trump outlines Cuba plan
content:
The US president has not ruled out a military invasion of the island, which is already struggling under an American oil blockade

US President Donald Trump has said he wants to “get Cuba done” before leaving office in two years, adding that he is open to ordering a military operation against the island.

Speaking to conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump made clear that he “would certainly consider” a week-long campaign against Cuba, which the US has kept under a de facto blockade while openly advocating for regime change.

“I want to get Cuba done before I leave. And we have a very good, talented guy for Cuba named Marco,” he said, referring to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, whose parents emigrated from Cuba and who has been particularly critical of the government in Havana.

Read more

Last month, Rubio urged Cuban dissidents seeking “positive change” to establish a “discrete partnership with the CIA.” He has also defended US sanctions, blaming Cuba’s leadership rather than the six-decade-old American embargo for the country’s worsening economic crisis.

Cuban Deputy Foreign Minister Carlos Fernandez de Cossio mocked Rubio’s comments, saying “there must be a great deal of desperation or misery within the agency for it to be forced to sell its services like a tube of toothpaste.”

Read more

The US escalated pressure on Cuba after the kidnapping of Venezuelan leader Nicolas Maduro in January. Washington essentially cut Cuba off from crucial Venezuelan oil, while also threatening tariffs against other countries supplying the island.

The resulting fuel shortages have aggravated an already severe humanitarian crisis, bringing repeated nationwide blackouts and disrupting water supplies, transport, and healthcare. Russia, one of Cuba’s long-time close partners, sent hundreds of thousands of barrels of oil to the island as humanitarian aid, although the shipment provided only temporary relief.

In July, CBS News reported that Pentagon planners had considered an air assault against Cuba involving thousands of US troops from the elite 101st Airborne Division. In September, the network reported an Army Reserve inquiry about support units, including police forces and medical personnel, which might be needed within 90 to 120 days as part of potential Cuba-related planning. Neither report indicated that Trump had ordered a military operation.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodriguez has accused Washington of seeking to create a “humanitarian catastrophe” through its fuel restrictions. President Miguel Diaz-Canel has also insisted that Cuba’s future would never be decided in Washington, warning that Havana would fight back against any US invasion.

title: Berlin’s military spending spree risks debt surge – experts
content:
Berlin’s public debt is on track to reach nearly 100% of GDP by 2040, government economic advisers have warned

Germany’s continued military buildup, financed largely through government borrowing, could push public debt to nearly 100% of GDP by 2040, an independent government advisory body has warned, urging Berlin to promptly rein in spending.

The country’s deeply ingrained cultural and political aversion to debt has been slipping under the weight of an eroding economy and rearmament program aimed at confronting the supposed threat from Russia.

Germany launched a €100 billion ($122 billion) military buildup and restructuring program in the wake of the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022 under then-Chancellor Olaf Scholz. His successor, Friedrich Merz, has doubled down on this policy, vowing to turn the German military into Europe’s strongest conventional force while maintaining military support for Kiev.

“Public finances in Germany are coming under growing pressure. In the federal budget, projected revenue will not be sufficient to cover the planned spending in the longer term,” the German Council of Economic Experts (GCEE) warned in its annual report released on Wednesday.

According to the German Taxpayers Federation, the nation’s debt burden is currently increasing by €7,052 per second, with every citizen being effectively €34,046 in debt on behalf of the state.

Read more

Although a debt-to-GDP ratio of 100% is not in itself fatal – the US currently sits at just over 125%, while Japan has long been above 200% – it is a much more troubling proposition for a Eurozone country. Because the members of the single-currency bloc share the euro, they are limited in the tools they can deploy to manage monetary policy or monetize their own debt independently of the wider monetary union.

For the Eurozone itself, a more deeply indebted Germany removes an important buffer. Germany has historically maintained the financial space to act as the fiscal anchor during Europe’s recurrent debt crises.

German Bunds also serve as the primary risk-free benchmark and safe asset for the entire Eurozone. Because other members price their debt against Bunds, any significant loss of fiscal discipline in Germany, with a resulting rise in Bund yields, could trigger instability across the whole bloc. At the very least, the baseline borrowing cost for every country in the Eurozone would come under upward pressure.

Berlin appears to be shying away from its traditional role as fiscal anchor. The government ignored warnings in late 2025 from the Bundesbank that Germany was on course to record its largest budget deficit since reunification by 2028. Merz’s government amended the constitutional debt brake to fund the military buildup and passed a 2026 budget allocating a record €108.2 billion for defense and €11.5 billion in military aid for Ukraine.

Read more

The GCEE advises the government to gradually phase out the exemptions to the debt brake that have allowed for the debt-fueled rearmament drive.

“Above all, it is defense spending that is rising sharply and is financed by borrowing,” a council member, Achim Truger, told AFP. “From an economic point of view, it’s simply not rational to finance defense spending of this scale permanently through debt.”

Merz has so far refused to change course and has repeatedly reaffirmed his determination to continue the military buildup and provide funding for Ukraine despite what he himself called a “structural crisis” in the German economy.

“I will not deviate by a single millimeter from my fundamental conviction that, especially now, we must defend our freedom against Russia,” he stated in September, advocating for increased military spending and continued aid to Kiev.

Moscow has consistently dismissed the notion that it poses a threat to Europe as “nonsense” and believes the hostile rhetoric emanating from EU capitals is intended to distract populaces from mounting domestic problems.

title: Ukraine launches nearly 1,200 drones at Russia as US-led talks will consider wider European security
content:
Ukraine fired almost 1,200 drones at Russian targets overnight in one of its biggest aerial attacks since Moscow’s full-scale invasion nearly five years ago.

Meanwhile, U.S. and Russian negotiators raised the stakes in talks to stop the fighting by including for discussion wider European security arrangements that have been in place since the end of the Cold War. That change, long sought by Moscow, has alarmed European leaders and placed a question mark on NATO’s future role.

“Russia wants to talk about questions of European security architecture. We don’t need to talk about that. There is one,” German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said, referring to NATO.

After two days of talks with Russian and Ukrainian delegations in Abu Dhabi this week, U.S. envoys briefed Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Kremlin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who was in Dublin, Ireland, to meet European leaders.

More talks are planned as negotiators seek a breakthrough in peace efforts, according to U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.

A team of diplomats from the U.K., France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the European Union will be sent to the talks, said European Council President Antonio Costa after a meeting in Dublin. The session was dominated by European efforts to avoid being sidelined in the U.S.-led negotiations.

Kushner, who is also President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Russia had agreed to include Europe in upcoming talks, after Moscow's long insistence that the continent’s governments should be excluded because they supported Ukraine.

Europe’s presence at the table will allow negotiators “to address the broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia,” Kushner said on X.

European leaders remain wary of Russian moves

European leaders are wary of Russian maneuvering, as well as Trump’s praise for Putin and his administration’s sharp criticism of Europe.

The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said Europe must insist on a ceasefire before taking the negotiations further — the opposite of what Putin demands.

“If we start to talk about what Russia is asking regarding the security architecture, we actually walk into the traps that Russia is setting us,” she said in Dublin.

Luxembourg Prime Minister Luc Frieden insisted that Europe must take its fate into its own hands. “We cannot let neither the Americans nor the Russians decide about our future,” Frieden said.

Moscow is aiming “to dismantle NATO and the post-Cold War European security architecture,” the Institute for the Study of War said in an assessment Thursday.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov reaffirmed that Russia is open for contacts with the Europeans.

“Once we understand (Europe’s) true intentions and their readiness to facilitate the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding a dialogue regarding a settlement in Ukraine in an expanded format,” he said.

Ukraine raises Starlink problems again

Zelenskyy on Friday repeated his complaints about drone speed limits on the U.S. Starshield system — SpaceX’s military-grade version of the Starlink satellite internet service — that Ukraine needs for its defense.

The speed restrictions are limiting Ukrainian drones to 161 kph (100 mph) on the entire front line and in Russian-occupied territory, he said, making it impossible for Kyiv to deploy its interceptors effectively against Moscow's fast-moving jet-powered drones.

“We still have no clear explanations,” he said of the unannounced restrictions, after first raising the issue on Thursday.

Ukrainian officials are asking the U.S. State Department, the Pentagon and SpaceX to clarify and resolve the situation, he said.

Last month, similar SpaceX limits on Ukrainian drone speeds severely disrupted operations, alarming officials in Kyiv who fear a drop in U.S. support.

Elon Musk acknowledged in October that his company SpaceX had throttled the Starlink internet service in Ukraine for about a week, saying the system couldn’t be used for offensive strikes against Russia.

Ukraine deploys drones and robots against Russia

Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 1,198 Ukrainian long-range drones between late Thursday and early Friday. However, strikes on three Russian regions killed seven people, including a 12-year-old, and wounded 17, local officials said.

Ukraine’s General Staff said it hit an oil refinery in the Russian city of Volgograd, starting a fire. The refinery has a capacity of about 110 million barrels per year, it said.

The massive Ukrainian drone barrage appeared designed to show that Kyiv is holding its own in the war, countering Moscow’s insistence that a Russian victory is inevitable. Ukraine has repeatedly hit Russian refineries, claiming last month it neutralized more than half of Russia’s refining capacity.

Kyiv’s forces are using drones and ground robots to help defend against Russia’s army along the about 1,200-kilometer (750-mile) front line snaking down eastern and southeastern Ukraine.

With its troops largely bogged down on the battlefield, Moscow has used strategic bombardment of civilian areas to hurt Ukraine.

Attacks bring power outages in 12 Ukrainian regions

Russia launched 117 drones against Ukraine overnight, killing at least two people, including a 17-year-old, authorities said.

A single Russian attack Friday on southern Zaporizhzhia hit two five-story apartment blocks and wounded 30 people, including six children, officials said.

The war has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians, analysts and humanitarian organizations say.

Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure caused widespread power outages across about half of the country's regions Friday, said First Deputy Minister of Energy Artem Nekrasov.

Moscow has battered Ukraine’s power grid each winter during the war, hoping to weaken public morale.

___

AP reporters Sam McNeil in Dublin, Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed.

___

title: Merz echoing Goebbels with ‘guns or butter’ choice – former Spanish diplomat to RT (VIDEO)
content:
Jose Antonio Zorrilla has mocked the German chancellor’s claims of a Russian threat as EU leaders ramp up military spending and Ukraine aid at the expense of domestic needs

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s approach to military spending is comparable to the rhetoric used by Nazi propaganda chief Joseph Goebbels, former Spanish diplomat Jose Antonio Zorrilla has told RT.

Earlier this week, Merz described long-term support for Ukraine as “a common European task” at a joint press conference with Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar in Berlin, saying continued funding for Kiev should be reflected in the EU’s next budget. European governments have also been pushing to increase military spending, citing what they claim is a growing threat from Russia.

Commenting on the remarks, Zorrilla told RT: “Well, they have a very old tradition of that in Germany. If you remember a certain Goebbels, he said something like cannons and butter […] We have to make a choice between the cannons and the butter, so I think Merz is doing more or less the same.”

Read more

The reference was to a 1936 speech in which Goebbels argued that Germany could do without butter but not guns, prioritizing military rearmament over civilian needs.

Zorrilla also mocked claims that Russia poses an imminent threat to Europe, asking: “Who can believe that Russia is about to invade us?” He argued that invoking the alleged threat was being used to justify militarization rather than address pressing domestic problems.

The former diplomat also criticized European support for Ukraine, saying that Spain had allocated €13 billion ($14.3 billion) for Kiev last year while failing to properly maintain its own infrastructure. He cited a recent high-speed train derailment as an example of domestic shortcomings that, in his view, should take priority over foreign military commitments.

title: Pope says it's a 'joy' to be home as Peru's Chiclayo welcomes back its former shepherd
content:
Pope Leo XIV returned Friday to his beloved former diocese of Chiclayo and said it was a “joy” to be home, an emotional return underscoring his love for his Peruvian flock and their pride that their shepherd now runs the Catholic Church.

The pontiff, known here as “Padre Roberto,” arrived at Chiclayo’s airport on the Pacific coast and immediately headed to a vast, dusty field outside Chiclayo for his first Mass on Peruvian soil. The Vatican estimated 1 million people had lined his motorcade route to the Mass and that 500,000 attended.

They cheered wildly when Leo arrived and looped through the crowd in his popemobile, under a scorching sun and temperatures of 31 degrees Celsius (88 degrees Fahrenheit).

“What a joy it is to return to Chiclayo!” Leo said. “It is a blessing for me to be with you once again,” he said, thanking the faithful especially for their prayers during his recent hospitalization for lung cancer. He declared that “with God’s help, I am overcoming” the health scare.

Chiclayo, population 700,000, is the commercial hub of Peru’s northern Pacific coast. But much of the world heard about it on the night of Leo’s election, May 8, 2025, when he gave Chiclayo a shoutout, in Spanish, from the loggia of St. Peter’s Basilica.

And on Friday, Chiclayo welcomed its former shepherd home.

"I’m elated. He has decided to return to Chiclayo and we have him here, with us -- home,” said Julie Albujar, who woke before dawn with her sister to travel to the Mass site, where they were tasked with taking the collection. “This is a party and it’s a sign of our faith and our love for the pope.”

Beloved for being close to the poor

The former Robert Prevost spent two decades as a missionary priest and bishop in Peru and credits the place and its people with teaching him how to be a shepherd. Pope Francis sent the Chicago-born Augustinian to take over as bishop of Chiclayo in 2014 and he stayed until Francis summoned him to Rome in 2023 to run the Vatican's bishops' office.

In hindsight, the 2023 transfer to Rome signaled that Francis saw in Prevost a potential successor, since the job is one of the most important in the church and would give Prevost the Vatican experience that many consider necessary to be a viable contender for the papacy.

But Prevost's heart is in Chiclayo, where he remains beloved for championing social justice issues and for his closeness to the people, especially poor people, during times of crisis. And he had quite a few during his tenure: COVID-19, devastating floods, and a surge of Venezuelan migrants as the humanitarian situation worsened there in 2018.

“I’m so glad he’s returning,” said Rolando Antonio Mendoza, who was selling posters bearing the pope’s image in front of the cathedral where Leo used to celebrate Mass. “Even though he’s now Pope Leo XIV, he hasn’t forgotten about his homeland.”

Nearby, the El Trébol proudly calls itself the pope's restaurant, and his image is displayed in framed photos of Prevost riding a horse, wading through the mud in rubber boots and celebrating his birthday with a cake.

A sign on his favorite table — No. 3 — with a view of the cathedral reads: “mesa bendita” – Spanish for blessed table. Like many other places around the city, the restaurant sells “Papaletas” or “Pop(e)sicles" with Leo's image in white chocolate.

Just a few steps from the restaurant, a life-size cardboard cutout of the pope now welcomes visitors to his former residence at the diocese, where an exhibit displays the amaranth purple, scarlet and white zucchettos, or skullcaps, that he wore as bishop, cardinal and now pope.

A giddy pope on his home turf

Ever since Leo touched down on Peruvian soil on Wednesday, the world has seen a very different pope.

Normally reserved and placid, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed at turns positively giddy and overwhelmed with emotion to the point of tears, as was the case on Friday.

Chiclayo seminarian Darwin Sánchez, who carried the pope’s miter during the Mass, said Leo greeted all the servers before Mass and was “very moved.”

“It was truly touching; thank God everything went well,” he said.

It wasn't Sánchez's first run-in with Leo. He recalled a Mass when, as a young altar boy, he mishandled the censer and passed it onto the man who was then bishop of Chiclayo.

After the service, Prevost took him aside and affectionately told him to be a bit more careful: Prevost had burned his hand when the chain fell into the hot charcoal, but he kept carrying it and didn’t complain or reprimand Sánchez in front of others.

“He’s approachable, happy and he gave me the strength and courage to follow my vocation,” Sánchez said.

As the Mass ended, the crowd erupted into a chant that reaffirmed their pride in calling the spiritual leader of more than 1.4 billion Catholics their own:

“El papa es Chiclayano!” they joyously yelled in Spanish: “The pope is Chiclayano.”

A prayer at a chapel dedicated to Romero

After Mass, Leo went to pray in a chapel dedicated to St. Oscar Romero, beloved among the working class and poor for defending them against repression by El Salvador’s army.

The chapel’s construction was spearheaded during Leo’s time as bishop, and its renovation was achieved through the efforts of the Rev. Edgar Rimaycuna, the pope’s personal secretary.

Leo’s decision to go there was perhaps symbolically significant.

When Prevost first arrived in Chiclayo, priests from the conservative Opus Dei movement had long had something of a monopoly on the diocese's parishes, alienating the faithful who had a more social justice bent and who were particularly devoted to Romero, according to the new biography “American Pope,” by NPR reporters Daniel Burke and Scott Detrow.

While careful not to alienate the Opus priests, Prevost worked hard to try to bring about change in the diocese to make it less the clerical model used by Opus and more a model that empowers lay people and looks out especially for the poorest, they wrote.

It was a dynamic that Prevost had embraced in the diocese of Trujillo, Peru, where he worked as a young missionary priest, said the Rev. John Lydon, a fellow Augustinian who lived with Prevost in Trujillo in those years from 1990-1999.

He said many of the Augustinians in Peru at the time had a devotion to Romero, Prevost included.

“This was before he was canonized by Pope Francis, but we always referred to him in the house in Trujillo as Santo Oscar de las Americas,” Lydon said in an interview. “So we canonized him before the church.”

___

AP writer Mauricio Savarese contributed from Lima.

title: Southeast Asian leaders, with US and Chinese counterparts, will renew alarm over online scams
content:
Southeast Asian leaders and their key counterparts, including from the United States and China, will renew their alarm over the escalating threat of online scams, according to a draft statement seen by The Associated Press on Friday.

Such transnational crimes, which have swindled billions of dollars from people in Asia to the United States and elsewhere, will be high in the agenda when leaders of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations gather in an annual summit with their Asian and Western counterparts on Tuesday in the Philippine capital.

The Philippines currently holds the rotating leadership of ASEAN, an 11-nation bloc in a poverty-stricken region where criminal groups have used technology and resorted to human trafficking to expand their illicit and lucrative operations to other parts of the world.

The leaders of the expanded ASEAN bloc, called the East Asia Summit, will express their “grave concern over the escalating threat posed by transnational criminal organizations inflicting harm through online scams, including those originating from scam center operations and associated criminal conduct such as human trafficking,” according to a draft of their joint statement to be issued after their summit.

They acknowledged “the exploitation of digital and other advanced technologies and digital financial platforms, by increasingly sophisticated criminal actors and the need to strengthen financial and digital systems, as well as the severe human consequences associated with scam centers.”

Authorities in Southeast Asia have reported in recent years how large numbers of workers, who were lured by recruitment syndicates into working in online scam centers, including in the Philippines and Cambodia, have been subjected to threats and even torture when they tried to escape or defy orders.

Aside from sharing of information and strengthening law enforcement coordination, the leaders will encourage “the sharing of threat assessments and best practices" as well as strengthening cooperation between relevant authorities in dismantling scam centers, the leaders said in their draft statement, without elaborating.

In July, the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime reported how Southeast Asia-based criminal groups have increasingly used integrated networks and technology to expand to other regions. The scams caused estimated combined losses of $88.3 billion to $114.1 billion in 2025, according to the report.

Criminals are using new technologies to launder money through global financial systems and using artificial intelligence to steal from victims worldwide, the U.N. report said.

East Asian crime syndicates are running businesses that use malware, generative AI and deepfakes for sexual extortion and exploitation in a trend that increases the risks of in-person as well as livestreamed abuse. Apart from outright trafficking for the sex industry, victims can be sold into domestic servitude, forced begging and forced labor, among other forms of exploitation, the report said.

The East Asia Summit leaders meeting in Manila will underscore “the need to address underlying drivers and other related factors of online scams," such as poverty, lack of social protection interventions, outdated domestic laws, private and public coordination gaps, corruption and limited economic opportunities.

They will stress that government responses to online scams must be consistent with international law and respect human rights.

title: Why Moscow’s Taliban outreach unnerves Pakistan
content:
The latest Moscow Format on Afghanistan failed to deliver a joint statement, but the deeper problem is the widening perception gap between Moscow and Islamabad

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, speaking at the Minsk International Conference on Eurasian Security last week, called the Moscow Format consultations on Afghanistan “the most representative platform for developing a region-wide consensus.”

It is hard to argue with the central point of the foreign minister’s remark. The Moscow Format really is broad-based, bringing together not only Afghanistan and the Central Asian states, but also India, Iran, China, and Pakistan, as well as guest delegations such as Belarus and Egypt.

Yet while few doubt the forum’s representative character, the question of whether it can actually produce a region-wide consensus is much more complicated. At its anniversary meeting last month (the format has been in place since 2016) the participants could not even agree on a joint final statement.

Moscow still appears to believe that the platform remains effective. The consultations are held regularly, and there is an exchange of views. As for the communique, in the view of Russian officials, while adoption of a final document is desirable from a protocol standpoint, it is not an absolute requirement for such a format. However one looks at it, the host side can hardly be blamed for the lack of a final communique. The real issues lie deeper.

Read more

The failure to come up with a statement stems from disagreement between Kabul and Islamabad over how to describe terrorist activity emanating from Afghan territory. At the previous meeting, the same wording was agreed upon without objections. But this year circumstances worked against Moscow. As armed tensions between Afghanistan and Pakistan escalated, both sides were far more sensitive to any phrasing that in current circumstances might be interpreted as an attack on their position in the bilateral standoff.The absence of a joint statement is unlikely to have a major impact on the future of the forum itself. The Moscow Format will continue to function as one of the recognized frameworks for discussing Afghanistan-related issues.

However, the fact that the recent meeting ended without a communique could have a bigger impact on Russia-Pakistan bilateral ties. Until recently, concerns within Pakistan’s ruling circles about Moscow’s growing closeness with Kabul were largely confined to tight-lipped diplomats and a narrow circle of experts. In October, however, dissatisfaction with the outcome of the Moscow Format spilled into the public domain with a number of leading Pakistani outlets publishing critical commentary. 

An editorial by influential newspaper The Dawn, for example, noted that while many other third parties, including Qatar, Türkiye, Saudi Arabia, and China – have tried to mediate between Pakistan and Afghanistan, “Russia is the only state that recognizes the Taliban regime” and hence could “be engaged” to “try and give the peace process another chance.”

The Tribune newspaper went even further, suggesting in its report on the talks in Moscow that “what raised eyebrows in diplomatic circles was Moscow’s apparent effort to play down the regime’s links with terrorist activities, prompting speculation that changing regional dynamics may be pushing Russia closer to Kabul.” 

The roots of such reactions in Islamabad, of course, go back not months or years, but decades.

Old narratives, ground realities

The idea of the ‘Great Game’ inevitably resurfaces whenever discussion turns to Moscow’s dealings with Kabul and the wider region. Repeated use of the term in historical, geopolitical, and geoeconomic debates has diluted its meaning, turning it into something of a buzzword. Yet it remains essential for understanding Pakistan’s reaction to Russia’s policy toward Afghanistan.

To say that Pakistan’s elites have simply inherited the British colonial idea of Russia as an inherently expansionist power would be an oversimplification. Islamabad and Rawalpindi have their own strategic culture and their own worldview, in which Moscow is seen both as an important power center and as a potentially useful partner. But when it comes to Afghanistan, old colonial notions still tend to surface – particularly the belief that Russia seeks to expand its influence in Kabul in order to gain access to the ‘warm waters’ of the Indian Ocean (even though this myth conveniently ignores the fact that Russia already has maritime access).

Read more

This narrative shaped perceptions throughout much of the second half of the 20th century, especially during the Soviet military presence in Afghanistan, and it has resurfaced in recent years, particularly after the Taliban was recognized as the official Afghan government.

One can point out endlessly that such assumptions bear little relation to reality. Yet century-old narratives are often more durable than arguments grounded in facts. The persistence of this perception is directly linked to the depth of the problems Pakistan faces in its relationship with Afghanistan.

First, Islamabad has never been able to reconcile itself to the refusal of every Afghan government to recognize the Durand Line, dating back to 1893, the time of British colonial rule in the region, as the official border. (Pakistan does recognize it.)

Second, from the point of view of Islamabad, the porous nature of that border is the main source of terrorist activity in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan provinces, which remains the core national security challenge for Pakistan. According to Islamabad’s official line, militants from Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan and Baluch separatist movements are able to operate only because they can find sanctuary inside Afghanistan. (The Taliban authorities deny harboring the TTP, arguing that the insurgency is a homegrown domestic issue for Pakistan.) 

Finally, and most importantly, Pakistan fears that some third power might aggravate these two problems — by encouraging Afghan claims on the border and by indirectly supporting anti-Islamabad elements. In Pakistan’s strategic imagination, that role is usually assigned to New Delhi, but in moments of acute crisis – as in the 1970s and 1980s – Moscow can also be cast in the same role.

Breaching the differences

Allowing the situation to drift to that point is hardly in Moscow’s interests – or in the interests of anyone else in the region. That is why Russian officials and experts continue trying to explain their own reading of events to their Pakistani counterparts.

Read more

At the official level, Moscow defends its rapidly expanding engagement with the Taliban on two main grounds. First, the current authorities in Kabul are seen as the most reliable partner for counterterrorism. The Taliban have consolidated enough coercive power to prevent a return to full-scale civil war and to establish a relatively stable grip over the country. For the Russian leadership, that makes them a necessary interlocutor in coordinating efforts against ISIS-Khorasan, whose activities threaten not only Russia but also its partners in Central Asia. Second, the authorities in Kabul have shown a willingness to curb drug trafficking, something reflected in data pointing to a decline in opiate production.

The difficulty is that neither argument carries much weight in Pakistan. On the contrary, Islamabad has long had ready-made counterarguments to both. Hance, the conversations end with a counter-question: “Why are our concerns not being taken into account?”

The answer, once again, seems to lie in differing perceptions – this time on the Russian side. In Moscow’s strategic worldview, the development of ties with Kabul and the problems between Pakistan and Afghanistan are seen as two different tracks.

The clearest illustration of this is Russia’s own geographical mindset. In Moscow’s view, Afghanistan belongs to Central Asia and is typically treated only as an actor or object affecting the dynamics north of its borders. The Taliban’s policy toward Pakistan is barely discussed. Kabul’s ties with other South Asian countries are also largely ignored. As a result, Afghanistan plays almost no role in Russia’s broader foreign policy planning for South Asia. For observers from the subcontinent, this is surprising, but it reflects a long-established pattern in Russia’s foreign policy theory as well as practice.

Broader vision

None of this means that Russia-Pakistan relations are doomed to crash against a wall of mutual misunderstanding and distrust over Afghanistan. Admittedly, Moscow and Islamabad are currently moving in different directions. Russia’s cooperation with Kabul is likely to continue and may well expand into new areas, while the military standoff between Afghanistan and Pakistan is likely to persist for the foreseeable future, with harmful effects on the lives of people along the border.

READ MORE: This is what the post-Western world looks like

Even so, divergent approaches to Kabul need not lead inevitably to hostility between Russia and Pakistan. Such an outcome would run counter not only to Moscow’s and Islamabad’s own interests but also to those of other regional actors. It could deprive both countries of the benefits of bilateral cooperation and even paralyze the work of the Moscow Format and other regional mechanisms, including the SCO. That would benefit no one.

The first step toward avoiding such a scenario could be to let old, familiar narratives give way to new ways of thinking – ones that recognize how fundamentally differently the parties can perceive the same problem, and that are ready to accept development and peace as indispensable for global progress.

title: Trump envoy touts new approach to Ukraine peace talks
content:
The Russia-Ukraine territorial dispute and the wider European security order will be discussed in parallel, Jared Kushner has said

This week’s efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict yielded “meaningful progress,” US President Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law Jared Kushner has said. He announced plans to address the Russia-Ukraine territorial dispute and wider European security order in parallel.

In a statement on X on Friday, Kushner summarized three days of intensive diplomacy that began with trilateral Russia-Ukraine-US negotiations in Abu Dhabi. He and fellow Trump envoy Steve Witkoff subsequently met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky in Dublin, before consulting with security advisers from Ukraine and European countries.

“We have made meaningful progress in understanding both sides’ concerns, identifying possible solutions, and establishing a path forward,” Kushner wrote, while acknowledging that “significant differences remain.”

Read more

He went on to say that both Russia and Ukraine “have now agreed to expand the next round of negotiations to include our European partners,” adding that the expanded format will allow discussions on “broader postwar European security arrangements alongside the territorial issues between Ukraine and Russia.”

Kushner stressed that a settlement will require credible security guarantees, mechanisms to prevent renewed confrontation, and mutual commitments to de-escalation. “We will begin discussing these interconnected issues in parallel, with the understanding that, apart from humanitarian measures, nothing will be finalized until a comprehensive agreement is reached.” 

Read more

Despite the announcement, Moscow has not confirmed that it agreed to direct European participation. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has argued that European governments are sending contradictory signals, claiming to support peace while preparing to deploy troops to Ukraine in case of a ceasefire, which Moscow has rejected.

“They are moving toward an expansion of the war, but they talk about peace. A vicious circle,” he said on Thursday.

Peskov noted that European governments are struggling to decide on an envoy, likening their infighting to “spiders in a jar.” He also suggested that politicians who seek contact with Moscow face ostracism from their European counterparts.

Kushner said on Wednesday: “if Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

During the two-day Russia-Ukraine-US talks in Abu Dhabi, European officials held separate consultations with the US and Ukrainian delegations, but were not included in the main negotiations. Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov mocked the situation, saying: “Well, they flew to Abu Dhabi. Let them sit there in the hotel.”

According to Politico, the EU is divided into at least three camps over who should represent it in talks. One favors European Council President Antonio Costa, who the paper describes as the most broadly acceptable candidate due to his institutional role. Another includes France and Germany, “both of which are reluctant to surrender their own places at the negotiating table to Brussels.” 

The third and “loneliest” group reportedly backs EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, who is hawkish on Russia. According to Politico, some EU diplomats believe she “could put off the Kremlin and make her a liability.”
