title: The Ukraine peace process has a Western European problem
content:
A lasting Ukraine settlement needs Western Europe. Bringing it into negotiations too soon, however, could derail fragile progress.

Two days of negotiations in Abu Dhabi have ended without a breakthrough. This was predictable because the Ukraine conflict is too complex, and too many interested parties still believe they can improve their positions at somebody else’s expense, but the absence of a dramatic announcement shouldn’t be mistaken for the absence of progress.

The delegations were experienced, the discussions lengthy, and judging by the accounts, substantive, so this wasn’t another diplomatic performance designed merely to buy time or lull the opponent into complacency. For once, the parties appear to have discussed the issues that might eventually make peace possible.

An agreement on a prisoner exchange is the most visible result. These exchanges aren’t unprecedented, but they demonstrate a willingness to keep channels open, while US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner have since traveled to Moscow to brief President Vladimir Putin, before continuing consultations with the Ukrainian leadership in Ireland. However, for now, decisive political commitments remain beyond the authority of the negotiators.

The delegations can assess battlefield developments, the state of the opposing economies, and the costs of continuing the war, but they can’t resolve the most difficult questions without instructions from their leaders, which means Abu Dhabi was an important stage in the process, not the conclusion.

Still, there is a sense of approaching a crossroads. Either the parties find some basis for reducing tensions, or the fighting enters another period of escalation, which may actually depend on actors who were not seated at the trilateral negotiating table: the Europeans.

Read more

The EU was conceived as a framework for economic cooperation and integration, not as a military-political organization, and its founding generation could hardly have imagined a continent in which industrial policy would be increasingly shaped by weapons production and military mobilization.

Yet that is the direction the EU has moved, and this isn’t merely a matter of acquiring new powers, because its political character is changing, and an organization established to overcome Europe’s historic divisions now risks defining itself through confrontation, which for Europe and its peoples is a tragedy.

In fairness, Russian analysts underestimated the Europeans. For years, the prevailing assumption in Moscow was that Brussels would follow Washington without serious resistance, but President Donald Trump’s return to the White House demonstrated otherwise.

Once the Trump administration altered the approach to Ukraine, European governments displayed an unexpected determination to chart their own course. They may still dream of the Democrats returning to power in Washington, but in the meantime, they have developed a degree of strategic autonomy, above all in their policy toward Russia.

Europe has become Kiev’s principal sponsor, supplying economic assistance, intelligence, political backing, and military equipment. At times, the conflict has looked less like a confrontation between Russia and Ukraine than one between Russia and the EU fought through Ukrainian forces.

Read more

Brussels has also acted as Kiev’s advocate in Washington as European leaders have repeatedly sought to steer American decisions towards stronger support for Ukraine, including after the Anchorage summit, and their influence is substantial, even if they aren’t party to the current negotiations.

European officials were present in Abu Dhabi, but Russia opposed their participation in the trilateral discussions and that position reflects Moscow’s view that the EU is neither impartial nor particularly interested in compromise. Individual European governments, meanwhile, are pressing Washington to secure them a direct role.

This is becoming one of the central dilemmas of the peace process, given that excluding Europe indefinitely would be unrealistic because any durable settlement must address the wider security order on the continent, not merely the line of contact in Ukraine, and Russia has raised this issue for years.

As one Russian formulation has it, the whole body is ill – Ukraine is simply where the abscess has burst. A lasting solution will require more than treating the wound. It will require a comprehensive European security arrangement that takes account of Russian interests as well.

But timing is key here, because giving European governments a seat before the principal parties have identified common ground could extinguish the diplomatic initiative at the outset. Their involvement may become necessary later, once negotiations advance beyond technical exchanges and a workable framework begins to emerge, but we aren’t there yet.

Read more

Another complication is the political upheaval in the US. The Republican defeat in the midterm elections has strengthened forces determined to oppose Trump’s Russia policy. The president remains in office, but he now faces a more hostile Congress and a domestic struggle that will consume political energy.

Those in Europe and Kiev who favor continuing the military confrontation will see an opportunity. They hope Washington’s room for maneuver will narrow and pressure on Moscow will intensify, while Trump, the principal sponsor of the present diplomatic effort, may find it increasingly difficult to sustain his course.

There are powerful interests in Europe, Ukraine, and the US that consider continued confrontation preferable to a settlement on terms Moscow would accept, and their influence can’t be wished away.

Nevertheless, Abu Dhabi is important because it has shown that serious discussion is possible and that the agenda is gradually widening beyond immediate battlefield questions. A prisoner exchange is modest progress, but progress all the same.

The choice ahead is stark: further escalation or the difficult work of constructing a peace that acknowledges the security interests of all the principal parties. Neither outcome is inevitable, but for the first time in some while, there is at least reason for cautious hope.

This article was first published by the online newspaper Gazeta.ru and was translated and edited by the RT team

title: Ex-Nvidia boss faces Congress grilling over ‘Chinese honeypot’ scandal
content:
Jensen Huang’s alleged affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset has triggered scrutiny of US chip exports to Beijing

Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been called to testify before Congress alongside US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over national security concerns sparked by an alleged affair between Huang and a suspected Chinese spy.

Senator Tim Scott sent letters to both men on Thursday, seeking their testimony before the Senate Banking Committee in early December.

“Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive US technology,” Scott wrote on social media. “The American people deserve answers.”

Huang’s appearance is voluntary, but the committee warned it is prepared to use “all tools” at its disposal, including subpoenas, if he refuses to testify.

Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology.

I am requesting that NVIDIA CEO Jensen Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify before the Senate Banking Committee.

The American people deserve… pic.twitter.com/Xu1kiNzkhW

— Senator Tim Scott (@SenatorTimScott) November 13, 2026

The scandal erupted earlier this month following reports linking the CEO to Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a businesswoman formerly associated with Singapore-based Nvidia chip buyer Megaspeed International.

Read more

The New York Times and Financial Times claimed US intelligence officials suspected her of gathering information for Beijing and attempting to influence Huang to loosen restrictions on chip exports to China.

The FBI opened an investigation, while Nvidia’s board launched its own probe. On Thursday, the company announced Huang’s resignation as CEO, president, and board member “effective immediately,” ending his 33-year tenure without offering an explanation. Finance chief Colette Kress was named interim CEO.

Huang admitted on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife but did not identify the woman involved. Subsequent media reports alleged further affairs involving Nvidia healthcare executive Kimberly Powell and another employee. The New York Times reported on Thursday that Huang had hired lawyers experienced in government investigations to handle the fallout.

Read more

US Attorney General Todd Blanche said Thursday that the Justice Department had reached no conclusions about whether Alice Huang had spied for Beijing. China strongly rejected the allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun dismissing them as “a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear.”

Lutnick, meanwhile, faces scrutiny over his department’s approval of Nvidia chip exports to China. Despite fierce technological rivalry and lingering trade tensions, Washington cleared sales of H20 processors in July 2025, then authorized exports of more powerful H200 chips in December under an arrangement giving the US a 25% cut through tariffs. Lawmakers are questioning whether the Commerce Department adequately assessed national security risks before approving the sales. Lutnick’s spokesperson, Kristen Eichamer, told NBC News he has agreed to testify.

title: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
content:
Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week

Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.

title: Military helicopter crash kills four soldiers in Türkiye (VIDEO)
content:
The incident occurred in the province of Malatya, the National Defense Ministry has said

Four Turkish military personnel were killed when an S-70-type helicopter crashed in the country’s eastern province of Malatya, the National Defense Ministry said on Thursday.

The ministry did not provide details about the aircraft’s mission or the number of personnel on board. There was no immediate official information on casualties or on the causes of the crash.

“As a result of an accident involving our S-70 helicopter in Malatya, for a reason not yet determined, four of our heroic comrades-in-arms aboard the helicopter were martyred,” the ministry said in a statement, extending condolences to the families of the soldiers.

The helicopter went down in the Samankoy neighborhood of Malatya’s Yesilyurt district around 6:45 PM local time, according to reports by local media. A fire reportedly broke out at the crash site and spread to a nearby house.

Video footage circulating online shows the helicopter’s burning wreckage near a cluster of buildings in an otherwise open area.

The S-70 belongs to the Black Hawk family of military utility helicopters manufactured by US defense manufacturer Sikorsky Aircraft Corporation. Variants of the aircraft are operated by armed forces in several countries. The Black Hawk is able to carry up to 11 soldiers plus its air crew.

The Turkish Air Force operates a large base – the 7th Main Jet Base – to the north of Malatya.

title: US military downs 2 Iranian attack drones as Iran claims a strike on a US radar in Bahrain
content:
The U.S. military said it intercepted two Iranian attack drones headed toward Bahrain, as Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed it struck a U.S. early warning radar system in the kingdom. Iran also said a tanker struck a naval mine while attempting to sail through the Strait of Hormuz.

Here is the latest news from the Middle East on Friday. Read our full coverage here.

US says it intercepted Iranian drones after Iran claims strike in Bahrain

The U.S. military said Friday it shot down two Iranian attack drones headed toward Bahrain, denying Iran’s claim that it had struck a U.S. radar system in the kingdom. CENTCOM, the U.S. command center covering the region, said there were no injuries or damage.

Iran's official IRNA news agency cited a Revolutionary Guard statement that said the attack on the radar system followed a U.S. strike on a telecommunications pole in the southern Iranian port of Sirik. It was Iran's first report of targeting a facility in Bahrain since September.

Bahrain's Ministry of Information did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Iran says a tanker struck a mine in the Strait of Hormuz

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said Friday that a liquefied petroleum gas tanker struck a mine, causing an explosion, while trying to sail through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the state-run IRNA news agency.

The Guard said the vessel ignored repeated warnings while transiting the eastern part of the strait. The claim could not be independently verified.

In a related development, the United Nations said October had the highest number of incidents against commercial ships in the contested waters since February, when the Iran war began.

The UN's International Maritime Organization said 25 seafarers died and many others were injured or remain missing following some 134 incidents in the Strait of Hormuz and the wider Middle East maritime area as of Nov. 11.

Iran: Nuclear monitoring cannot proceed while under threat

Iran told the United Nations' nuclear watchdog that discussions on nuclear monitoring cannot proceed while the country is facing military threats.

According to a confidential report by the International Atomic Energy Agency, Iran insists inspections cannot resume amid threats from the U.S. to target its nuclear facilities. Iran hasn’t given inspectors access to sites affected by Israeli and U.S. strikes during the June 2025 war.

Israeli fire kills 3 in Gaza, including a 12-year-old, health officials say

Israeli tank shelling on Friday in central Gaza killed three people — a woman, a father and his 12-year-old son, according to health officials at Al-Aqsa Martyrs hospital.

The tank shelling in the eastern part of Deir al-Balah city also wounded 20 others, most of them children, the hospital said.

Israel’s military said it had opened fire to drive away suspects whom it claimed had approached troops near the Yellow Line, which delineates the part of the Gaza Strip that the Israeli military controls.

Near-daily Israeli fire and airstrikes have continued more than one year after a ceasefire deal was reached between Israel and Hamas.

Infant's hypothermia death raises worries about winter in Gaza

A 9-month-old infant in Gaza died from hypothermia, becoming the first reported cold-related death of the winter season, health officials said Friday.

Kanan Ahmed Arqiq was living with his family in a tent that provided little protection from the cold and was flooded by rains earlier this week, family members said. Outside the hospital, Ahmed Arqiq, the infant’s father, held up the baby's tiny body and a certificate attributing his death to severe cold.

The majority of Gaza’s roughly 2 million people now live in tents and makeshift shelters because of the war. The United Nations and other agencies have accused Israel of blocking the entry of needed aid, but the Israeli military denies the claims.

Turkey and Qatar reach a mutual defense agreement

Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani signed a mutual defense agreement Friday in Istanbul, according to Erdogan’s office.

In a statement posted on X, the office said the two sides, which already share deep military ties, would continue working together to prevent war from resuming in the Gulf region and to encourage diplomacy.

The deal follows a joint defense agreement signed between Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia in August.

Iranians mourn 350 unidentified soldiers from Iran-Iraq war

More than 38 years after the Iran-Iraq war ended, the remains of hundreds of unidentified soldiers were carried through Iranian cities Friday in one of the largest such funerals in recent years.

In Tehran, thousands joined a procession for the remains of 110 soldiers. Funerals for another 240 were held in other cities. The remains were recently recovered from former battlefields.

Trucks carrying flag-draped coffins passed near Tehran University as mourners dressed in black wept.

UN calls for attacks on civilians in Yemen to stop

U.N. deputy spokesman Farhan Haq said Friday that civilians across Yemen are increasingly being hit by drones, missiles, airstrikes and shelling in their homes, markets and other places once considered safe.

In one of the deadliest attacks since fighting resumed between Iran-backed Houthi rebels and Saudi-backed government forces, at least 30 people died in airstrikes on a market in Taiz province on Nov. 6, according to the Houthis.

___

This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Microsoft outage shows the risks of relying on a single technology provider for essential services
content:
A global Microsoft outage this week disrupted email and other workplace tools, plunging business chatter and everyday services into disarray worldwide and highlighting the risks of depending on one of just a few major providers of essential technology.

Microsoft 365 services, including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot, were interrupted. As the outage entered its second day Friday, Microsoft said it saw “encouraging recovery progress.” But the company also warned that “intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery" may persist for some users.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us," Microsoft wrote in a social media update.

The disruptions offer the latest example of the cascading problems that can erupt when so many communications and technology platforms depend on the same provider. Some lawmakers outside the U.S. have also argued that the outage shows the consequences of overreliance on American tech.

“With no emails coming or going, many office workers feel like they are having a virtual snow day,” said Jeremy Singer, a professor at the University of Glasgow’s School of Computing Science.

Still, he added, “this problem serves to emphasize the dependence we have built on one company’s digital infrastructure, and may lead us to question whether we need more resilience in our IT ecosystem.”

The global reach of the outage was swift. After problems first emerged midday Thursday in the U.S., online tracker Downdetector said it received outage reports from 74 countries and territories within an hour.

The total number of people affected was not clear, but Microsoft said in January it had more than 450 million paid commercial subscriptions to its 365 services.

Microsoft has scrambled to recover services

A series of posts by Microsoft 365 on X suggested its engineers struggled to get the problem under control for some time, drawing teasing from other companies and users alike. But the tech giant has said there is “no indication” that the disruptions were caused by malicious activity, specifically noting Friday that the outage was not related to a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

Microsoft said a technical issue arose during an upgrade that followed “a recent network change.” The company added that it restored services gradually, which took longer.

As Microsoft addressed issues affecting its Exchange Online mailboxes, it earlier cited a failure that it said caused a number of its servers to be “unexpectedly unavailable” during automated checks.

For Outlook, many users said they couldn't send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether. Those problems piled up across much of the world into Friday.

By Friday morning in the U.S., Microsoft said email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels.” Still, it warned of potential intermittent access and ongoing delays.

On Thursday, the company said it had “successfully restored” Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

Disruptions piled up from the courtroom to the pharmacy

In Britain, the outage brought a halt to a trial in Manchester. Judge Maurice Greene sent jurors home because of delays that he said illustrated the danger of the court’s reliance on technology.

The British government said it was “working closely” with Microsoft to assess any impact on public services but that “robust contingency plans” were in place to minimize disruption.

British police said they were unable to receive crime reports online and urged people to phone in urgent requests. The outage also affected some law enforcement in the U.S. The sheriff's office in Colorado's Arapahoe County, for example, noted that online bond payments were affected.

Also in Britain, the National Pharmacy Association warned customers of delays in getting medication. The outage affected the National Health Service and threatened to prevent doctors from emailing prescriptions to pharmacies.

“Please bear with your pharmacy teams today, where waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions,” a spokesperson said.

Governments in Singapore, Japan, Greece and Norway said the outage affected some of their operations, including email communications for certain ministries or agencies.

And of course, businesses were wracked with disruptions. Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum company, said his business couldn’t receive updates from its U.S. customers through Outlook. If the situation dragged on, the trouble could “impact the production timeline,” he said.

Some banks in Hong Kong, an Asian financial hub, also saw disruptions.

OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies’ software.

Outage has parallels with 2024 shutdown

Some have drawn parallels to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, which stemmed from a faulty update to computers running Microsoft Windows. That outage grounded flights and disrupted hospitals, banks and retailers.

Governments and institutions in Western Europe, in particular, have been trying to reduce their reliance on services provided by a few big U.S. tech services in their continuing push for “digital sovereignty.” This week's outage renewed some of those calls.

British lawmaker Chi Onwurah, who chairs the Science and Technology Committee in Parliament, said the Microsoft outage “only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the U.K.’s digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services.”

She said her committee has previously warned that the U.K. is “hugely dependent” on a small number of U.S.-based technology providers, preventing homegrown alternatives from developing.

Florian Druckenthaner, a spokesperson for Germany’s digitization ministry, said the government’s IT security agency believes German business was widely affected, but there were no reports of major disruption at the government level.

Regardless, Druckenthaner said, the outage shows “the significance of building up redundancies and alternatives. We are working on that.”

___

Associated Press journalists Adam Schreck in Bangkok; Eileen Ng in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia; Rod McGuirk in Melbourne, Australia; Sheikh Saaliq in New Delhi; Mayuko Ono in Tokyo; Geir Moulson in Berlin; Menalaos Hadjicostis in Nicosia, Cyprus; and Pan Pylas and Brian Melley in London contributed.

title: The Independent accelerates its multimedia content strategy
content:
By Chris Sutcliffe

That approach accelerated in 2020 with the launch of a standalone Independent TV section, and a monetisation-first approach to commissioning video content.

At the time, Christian Broughton, then managing director and now CEO of The Independent, said the ambition was to offer a “full-on TV experience,” with the video content sitting across a variety of platforms, devices, and destinations.

Since then, the team has continued to invest in multimedia capabilities. This investment spans tech, talent, and internal ambition. It is, says Broughton, driven by a recognition that content consumption habits in 2026 favour creators, and that all media is to some extent part of the “creator economy.”

He cites the team’s investment in personality-led podcasts as an example of how The Independent is developing a multimedia strategy that rides that trend, with podcasts like “In The Room” that live and die on the personalities that host them.

Notably, Broughton explains that the videos and podcasts being put out by the brand tend to highlight those personalities first and foremost, and the newsbrand itself second: “If you look at something like the World Cup, [we had] Adam Clery out there. Adam’s channel is really interesting: it’s Britain’s fastest-growing football analysis channel [and], it’s called ACFC. It’s the Adam Clery Football Channel, from Independent Studio.”

The Independent’s podcasts like ‘In The Room’ live and die on the personalities that host them.

Investment in multimedia capabilities

To achieve its aims around multimedia audience growth, The Independent has invested in the tech – including AI – that allows for a greater production capability. As a result of the investment in professional-grade studios and hardware, Broughton says that much of the actual editing process can be automated. This then allows for a wider proportion of staff in the newsroom to create audio and video that meets standards without necessarily having to be experts in editing or production.

Broughton is keen to stress, however, that while he estimates around 80% of the process can be automated, the remaining 20% is vital, and that human oversight is necessary.

“There’s a very accessible production route now in here as well, which means you can focus more on what you’re doing and why you’re doing it, rather than exactly how you’re doing it,” he said.

Broughton explains that the focus on multimedia – set to see “a really substantial acceleration in this area for the next three years” – is also impacting roles within the organisation. While he highlights that much of the on-camera talent is drawn from the pool of reporters and correspondents, he also states that new skillsets, and new employees, are needed for multimedia content.

He cites Clery again, who, as “originally a YouTuber,” brought a sensibility around how to present on that platform that was not necessarily present within Independent Studio’s existing team.

“You do need a good balance of external talent that you bring in, because the roles are different. But then it works most powerfully when you’ve got a good strong link to the journalism of The Independent and the Standard and HuffPost and the content teams on BuzzFeed and Tasty, so having that link is important. You can see people move between teams, but bringing in expertise is vital.”

Specificity and generalisms

As a result of the overall growth in audience and revenue across its multimedia offering, Broughton says Independent Studio represents “20% of our revenue this year.”

That growth is predicated on its audio and video working as hard as possible on every third-party platform, which make up a large part of the mix for The Independent’s programming.

Broughton points out that, to some extent, many of those third-parties can effectively dictate the success of a podcast or series by promoting or deprecating them in recommendation feeds. He cites the different podcasts that rise to the top of the charts across Apple Podcasts and Spotify as an example of how content does not necessarily succeed based on its quality or provenance.

However, he says that tailoring audio and video to relevant platforms can mitigate that issue: “You can do worse than think first and foremost about YouTube, and then clip that into other platforms. You can’t do it the other way around. You can’t say, ‘Hey, we’re great on TikTok, therefore we’ll put it on YouTube,’ but it kind of does work the other way around.”

It speaks to The Independent’s creator-led approach to its multimedia offering. By emulating the type of personality-led work that succeeds on platforms like YouTube and TikTok, the brand is riding the wave of a particular digital trend in order to expand its audiences on those platforms.

AI and investments

Beyond personality-led multimedia content, the news brand is also leveraging AI tech to develop new consumer facing products. Last year the paper launched its Bulletin section, an AI-powered news section “for seriously busy people.”

Developed using Google’s Gemini and trained on The Independent’s own content, Broughton says Bulletin represents a fact of modern journalism – that AI will comprise part of production: “About a year and a half ago, we built an app called Bulletin, which has been absolutely flying.”

See also: Independent CEO Broughton urges publishers to get excited about AI

“We’re just in development with our second business that would be launched off the back of using AI for great journalistic reasons, so we believe in kind of incubating new businesses that would be impossible without leveraging AI, so you can’t just kind of hope it goes away and ignore it.”

Nevertheless, as has been stressed since Bulletin was first announced, there is human oversight at the very top level of the product, and it has been trained on The Independent’s journalism to ensure quality: “We created our own tool for it, because we wanted to know exactly how it works, and we wanted to know [it] was only getting this information from our own trusted journalism.”

The Independent, then, is developing its multimedia strategy based on a proactive sense of how audiences are choosing to consume content online. By bringing personality to the forefront it is ensuring that multimedia content lives and dies on its terms, on the most relevant platforms, rather than simply branding it as being from The Independent and hoping it coasts on that recognition.

This interview is extracted from Measuring Multimedia Readiness in Newsrooms, a new report from WAN-IFRA and Base Media Cloud that gauges the realities of creating, managing and distributing multimedia content. WAN-IFRA members can download the full report from our Knowledge Hub here. Non-members can download the report here. 

The discussion continues on Wednesday, 25 November, with a webinar, Multimedia Readiness of Newsrooms: Turning Investment into Execution, that focuses on the current challenge: executing on that ambition and investment. 

About the author: Chris Sutcliffe is a freelance journalist specialising in the intersection of technology and media. He is the founder of Media Voices, co-founder of The Publisher Podcast & Newsletter Awards and Summits, and has written for a variety of international and specialist news titles.

title: Thailand bets on local AI as Chinese drones dominate its skies

title: Iran Rejects Transfer of Enriched Uranium Abroad
content:
By Evgenia Filimianova

Iran has ruled out transferring its enriched uranium abroad, as senior officials have said the material is needed for domestic nuclear projects.

Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran had informed Russia that all enriched nuclear material would remain inside Iran for domestic use. Russia has previously offered to remove uranium ‌from ⁠Iran.

“We need enriched materials to design ships and submarines powered by nuclear energy,” Rezaei told Lebanon’s Al Mayadeen television network in an interview published on Nov. 10.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly said it aims to prevent Iran from rebuilding its nuclear program after U.S. forces struck the Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan nuclear sites during Operation Midnight Hammer on June 22, 2025.

Trump said in September that the United States had detected activity at Iran’s Pickaxe Mountain and warned that the site could become a military target.

International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi told Bloomberg Television in September that there were some indications of movement around the site.

“We don’t have any concrete information as to activities that may be taking place there,” Grossi said. “Of course, we need to go there. When we regain access, we need to go back to Fordow, as we need to go back to Isfahan, and so on.”

Tehran has rejected U.S. allegations surrounding its nuclear activities and outlined seven conditions for ending the conflict with Washington, including sanctions relief, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and war reparations.

Nuclear Facility Inspections

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) recently inspected the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant, the country’s sole operating commercial nuclear reactor.

The plant began commercial operation in 2013 and generated nearly 1.3 percent of Iran’s electricity in 2025, according to the IAEA.

Baghaei said in an interview published by Al Mayadeen on Nov. 9 that IAEA inspectors visited Iran about 10 days earlier to conduct routine inspections at Bushehr and other facilities that remain accessible.

He said other nuclear sites had sustained damage and that no inspection mechanism currently exists for damaged facilities.

Baghaei also rejected any proposal to transfer enriched uranium outside Iran, saying the option was “off the table” and there was no justification for such a move.

The Epoch Times contacted the IAEA for comment but did not receive a response.

The IAEA said in a February report that Iran had almost 22,000 pounds of enriched uranium in June 2025. That amount included about 1000 pounds enriched to 60 percent, about 400 pounds enriched to 20 percent, and about 13,000 pounds enriched to 5 percent.

Grossi said last month that Iran had not provided the access and information needed for the agency to verify previously declared nuclear material at its safeguarded nuclear facilities, including sites damaged in military attacks.

He said the exception was the Bushehr plant, where inspectors continue verification activities.

Iran has engaged with the IAEA to “arrange for the delivery of safeguards equipment required for the verification of spent fuel prior to its transfer to a new dry storage facility,” Grossi said.

He said that the transfer is expected to take place early next year.

“While communications between the IAEA and Iran continue at a technical level, normal inspection activities have not resumed,” he said.

US Maintains Pressure

The United States has continued efforts to gather intelligence on Iran’s nuclear program.

The U.S. State Department’s Rewards for Justice program is offering up to $20 million and possible relocation for information about the program, including its nuclear facilities, its equipment, associated scientific personnel, and the movement of related materials.

“The regime’s lack of compliance with the IAEA on safeguards obligations has led to the agency’s loss of ‘continuity of knowledge’ regarding Iran’s production and inventory of key components like centrifuges,” the U.S. State Department said earlier this month when announcing the reward.

On Nov. 9, Trump said that additional U.S. military action against Iran was unlikely, while warning that the United States remained “locked and loaded” should circumstances change.

Trump made the remarks after meeting Qatari Prime Minister Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani at the White House. Qatar has served as an intermediary between Washington and Tehran.

title: New York City Investigating Brooklyn Building Collapse That Killed 8, Injured 18
content:
By Nicholas Zifcak

NEW YORK CITY—Mayor Zohran Mamdani said city officials are investigating the sudden collapse of an apartment building in the borough of Brooklyn on Nov. 11 that killed eight and left 18 injured, as well as an adjacent active construction site, to determine the cause of the tragedy.

“If there is anyone or any entity operating in this city that bears responsibility for what happened, we will hold them fully accountable,” Mamdani said at a Nov. 12 news conference at the site of the collapse on Flatbush Avenue and Bedford Avenue.

The three-story building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. collapsed on the afternoon of Nov. 11, taking with it the exterior wall of 1323 Flatbush Ave., leaving the interior staircase and neighboring apartments exposed.

James Williams, 60, who works at the Chelsea Deli Grocery across the street and knew some of the building residents, said the adjacent construction site was often active from the early morning hours late into the night.

On Nov. 11, Williams said he came to work at 6:30 a.m. and heard what sounded like construction workers hitting the foundation of the structure. Then came a big bang as loud as a gunshot and the smell of burning metal, he said. He said he later saw a few bricks fall from the building but never imagined the situation was so dangerous that the entire building could collapse.

At about 4 p.m., Williams said he heard and saw the building crumble, and that a woman on the interior staircase of the neighboring structure also slid into the construction site.

“The lady that I saw trying to climb up that staircase, I don’t know if she got out alive or not,” Williams said. “It was devastating. Who wants to see a building collapse that people live in?”

Mamdani confirmed on Nov. 12 that eight people died in the collapse, with six declared dead at the site and two in the hospital. Two of the victims were children who lived in the building, and two were construction workers at the 2625 Bedford Ave. site.

There are 18 still in the hospital, including one who is in critical condition. Four of the 18 are firefighters who arrived to help with search and rescue.

New York City Fire Department firefighters responded to the 911 call for help within one minute of the call coming in.

On the morning of Nov. 12, search-and-rescue efforts continued with grapplers removing large debris items from the site. New York City Fire Commissioner Lillian Bonsignore said firefighters are removing the larger items and will not stop searching until all debris is cleared. Heavy rain hindered site clearing efforts on the afternoon of Nov. 12 as the dusty site turned to mud.

“We always assume there are more people there until we can access the ground,” Bonsignore said.

Mamdani said five entities were involved in the work at the construction site, and those five are connected to 100 construction sites across the city. The Department of Buildings is conducting sweeps of all sites to make sure they are safe.

title: Trump Administration Approves $480 Million Loan for Gulf of America Oil and Gas Project
content:
By Naveen Athrappully

The Department of Energy (DOE) announced the closing of a $480 million project loan to increase oil and natural gas production across the Gulf of America shelf.

The DOE will provide the loan to Arena Energy’s Project Elkhorn, which will “modernize 22 offshore platforms off the coast of Louisiana and, at peak production, is expected to add up to 38,600 barrels of oil per day and up to 77 million cubic feet of natural gas per day to U.S. energy production,” the department said in a Nov. 10 statement.

Arena Energy currently produces roughly 30,000 barrels of oil per day offshore in the Gulf of America region. The latest modernization effort is estimated to increase production capacity by more than 129 percent.

This is the first loan closed by the DOE in support of domestic oil and gas production. The loan underscores the DOE’s commitment to deliver reliable, affordable energy to families and businesses, the department said.

Project Elkhorn is expected to provide roughly 250 billion cubic feet of natural gas and 125 million barrels of oil over its lifetime. It is projected to create 400 operational jobs and 2,400 construction-related jobs.

“The United States is the world’s largest producer and exporter of oil and natural gas, and thanks to President Trump, American energy production will continue to grow,” Secretary of Energy Chris Wright said in the statement.

“By providing financing for projects like Project Elkhorn, the Energy Department is expanding domestic production and strengthening our energy security to power American prosperity for decades to come,” Wright said.

The loan closure comes after the completion of all environmental, legal, financial, and technical requirements by the DOE, Arena Energy said in a Nov. 10 statement.

The increased production resulting from the $480 million in funding for Project Elkhorn is estimated to result in $1.6 billion in additional royalties for the federal government, which is more than three times the federal loan amount, the company said.

“Arena was founded on the belief that the mature fields of the Gulf Shelf still hold vast potential, and Project Elkhorn is a critical part of that strategy,” Mike Minarovic, CEO of Arena Energy, said in the statement.

The DOE financing “lets us put existing infrastructure back to work, develop proved reserves, and keep producing some of the most reliable barrels in the world,” Minarovic said.

EDF Loans

The $480 million loan is being provided by the DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF), the department said, adding that the Project Elkhorn loan was made possible by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act signed into law by President Donald Trump last year.

The bill removed the requirement that financed energy infrastructure under energy dominance financing reduce, use, or sequester greenhouse gases and air pollutants, according to an April 2026 report from the Energy Information Administration.

The EDF program guarantees loans to projects that add energy or enhance reliability of the power grid. It funds projects seeking to retool, repurpose, or replace energy infrastructure that has stopped operation.

The EDF can provide funding for projects involving nuclear power, coal, and power lines in addition to oil and gas.

The EDF office has issued a conditional loan commitment worth $17.5 billion to rebuild America’s commercial nuclear supply chain, the DOE said in a June 23 statement. The funding was aimed at helping speed up the deployment of commercial nuclear reactors.

EDF previously closed a $26.5 billion loan package to support constructing or upgrading more than 16 gigawatts of power infrastructure, according to a Feb. 25 DOE statement. The funding is projected to deliver more than $7 billion in electricity cost savings to residents in Alabama and Georgia.

title: Trump Proposes Tim Cook as New Nvidia CEO
content:
By Andrew Moran

President Donald Trump has proposed former Apple chief Tim Cook as a replacement for Jensen Huang as CEO of chipmaking giant Nvidia.

Huang resigned as president, CEO, and board member, effective immediately, at the $4 trillion company on Nov. 12. Colette Kress, Nvidia’s chief financial officer, was selected as his interim replacement.

In his first public statement since Huang’s departure, the president on Thursday suggested Cook become the next permanent head of Nvidia.

“Now that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, who has done a fantastic job, has resigned, there is only one man to take his place – Tim Cook of Apple. A Legend replaces a Legend!” Trump said in a Truth Social post.

After 15 years as Apple CEO, Cooked stepped down to become the iPhone maker’s executive chairman. He was succeeded by John Ternus, who had previously served as senior vice president of hardware engineering.

Trump has been complimentary of Cook in the past, calling him an “incredible guy.”

“Tim Cook had an amazing career, almost incomparable, and will go on and continue to do great work for Apple, and whatever else he chooses to work on,” the president said in an April post on Truth Social.

When Cook took over from Steve Jobs in 2011, he inherited a roughly $350 billion company. Fifteen years later, it briefly crossed the $5 trillion milestone.

Hiring Cook would be a terrific opportunity for investors, said Ken Mahoney, president and CEO of Mahoney Asset Management.

“If he were to take the helm, well that is probably a mega long,” Mahoney said in a note emailed to The Epoch Times.

Prediction markets favor Ian Buck, a high-level executive at Nvidia, to become the new CEO, with 38 percent odds as of 2:30 p.m. EST on Nov. 12. This is followed by Kress (15 percent) and Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas (10 percent).

“Nvidia’s succession remains far from settled,” Ben Mendelowitz, prediction markets analyst at The Action Network, said in a statement to The Epoch Times.

“The odds highlight the uncertainty between technical expertise and leadership continuity, while external contenders Rene Haas and Lisa Su remain in the picture.”

Su, currently the CEO of Advanced Micro Devices (AMD), was named Yahoo Finance CEO of the Year this week.

‘That Would Be an Honor’

Huang’s professional future is unclear, but he might have an easy time finding new work.

SpaceX and Tesla CEO Elon Musk suggested he would give Huang a job.

“That would be an honor,” Musk said in a Nov. 11 post on X in response to financial blog Zerohedge, which stated, “Elon please hire Jensen.”

If hired, Huang would not have a hard time navigating SpaceX operations. The company is largely centered on Nvidia hardware, and the chipmaker maintains a $21 billion stake in SpaceX.

Musk, in the company’s debut earnings call in August, said SpaceX has been built “exclusively on Nvidia,” and it would continue to absorb a greater percentage of its graphics processing units—or GPUs—the chips that train and run artificial intelligence (AI) models.

As Nvidia Turns

Nvidia’s short-term prospects could remain intact as many of the deals for 2027 and 2028 have likely been arranged.

Its long-term fundamentals may also be sound, according to Siebert Financial CIO Mark Malek.

“Nvidia’s competitive position extends beyond its founder,” Malek told The Epoch Times in an emailed note, pointing to its software ecosystem, established customer relationships, and enormous demand for AI infrastructure.

While there are still risks ahead, markets could be confusing Jensen Huang’s value with the company value.

“Jensen Huang was arguably more indispensable five years ago than he is today. Back then, investors were buying his vision; today, they are buying an established business with substantial demand and a formidable competitive moat,” Malek said.

Shares of Nvidia tumbled as much as 13 percent after Huang’s resignation. They pared their losses as investors bought the dip in one of the world’s richest companies. The stock slumped about 6 percent near the closing bell.

title: Astros’ Alvarez, Cubs’ Crow-Armstrong Take Home MVP Honors, and It’s Unanimous
content:
By Ross Kelly

For just the third time in the history of Major League Baseball, there are a pair of unanimous winners of the Most Valuable Player awards. Yordan Alvarez of the Houston Astros claimed the AL MVP, while Pete Crow-Armstrong of the Chicago Cubs took home the NL award.

The duo running away with the votes indicates just how dominant their seasons were, albeit in far different ways. Alvarez was the best hitter in the sport and almost single-handedly carried an injury-plagued Astros team to an AL West crown and the MLB playoffs. As for Crow-Armstrong, he was the best all-around player in baseball and the catalyst to the Cubs making the postseason.

Alvarez had a little extra motivation entering the year, considering how last season played out. He missed over 100 games due to injuries in 2025 and was unproductive when he did play, posting the lowest OPS of his career. However, he rebounded in 2026 by leading the AL with his entire slash line of .316/.432/.601. He went from his career-worst OPS+ to a career best, as his 190 mark led all of MLB.

Additionally, the 29-year-old designated hitter led the AL with 341 total bases, which is almost unfathomable considering all of the free passes he was offered. Alvarez had limited opportunities to even swing the bat as he also topped MLB with 109 walks. For the season, the slugger hit 42 homers, drove in 106 runs, and scored 105 runs himself. He also came through when it mattered most, posting a .355 batting average with runners in scoring position.

Logging just 25 games in the field, Alvarez becomes the second primarily designated hitter to be named MVP, joining Shohei Ohtani when he won the award but didn’t pitch during the 2024 season. Alvarez is also the third Astro to take home the honor, alongside current teammate Jose Altuve (2017) as well as Hall of Famer Jeff Bagwell (1994). The Cuban-born Alvarez is the fourth from his country to become Most Valuable Player, joining Zoilo Versalles (1965), Jose Canseco (1988), and Jose Abreu (2020).

Alvarez received all 30 first-place votes, with Junior Caminero of the Tampa Bay Rays finishing as runner-up. Bobby Witt Jr. of the Kansas City Royals finished third, and AL Cy Young winner Cam Schlittler of the New York Yankees was fourth.

In the Senior Circuit, Crow-Armstrong also received all 30 first-place votes, with Ohtani the runner-up, which ended the latter’s three-year streak of winning MVP awards. Third in NL voting was Brice Turang of the World Series champion Milwaukee Brewers.

Crow-Armstrong, nicknamed PCA, became the seventh member of the 40/40 club by slugging an MLB-leading 45 home runs (tied with Kyle Schwarber) and also swiping 41 bases. Both his slugging (.570) and OPS (.943) topped the National League, and like Alvarez, PCA also led the league in total bases (357). However, his exploits at the plate and on the basepaths tell only part of the story.

He was also, per nearly every metric, the best defensive outfielder in baseball, and he wasn’t hiding out at a corner spot—he played center field. He led all NL outfielders in putouts as he played all 162 games, with 158 of them as a center fielder.

With his five-tool abilities, Crow-Armstrong ran away with the WAR title, and his margin of victory was one of the greatest in MLB history. His fWAR (FanGraphs WAR) was 10.6, while the player with the second most was Witt at 7.0. That difference of 3.6 fWAR between first and second marked the first time since 1954 that the top two players were separated by at least 3.0 fWAR.

Crow-Armstrong becomes the 11th Chicago Cub to notch an MVP award, for a total of 12 wins in franchise history, as Ernie Banks won twice. He’s the first since Kris Bryant (2016) to win for Chicago, and the franchise’s dozen MVP awards ties them for sixth most among all franchises.

The only previous years in which there were unanimous MVP winners in both leagues were 2023 and 2024. Alvarez and Crow-Armstrong getting all of the first-place votes comes just one day after unanimous Cy Young awards were also handed out in both leagues, with Schlittler winning in the AL and Jacob Misiorowski of the Milwaukee Brewers winning in the NL.

That makes the 2026 MLB season a historic one, as this marks the first season that both MVP winners and both Cy Young victors won unanimously, dating back to when the pitching awards were first handed out in 1956.

All of the major awards have now been handed out, save for the Silver Slugger awards, which will be announced on Nov. 17. Both Alvarez and Crow-Armstrong are locks to get recognized and add to their respective trophy cases.

title: ‘Wild Horse Nine’: John Malkovich Leads a Brilliant Ensemble Cast
content:
By Michael Clark

In the course of over three decades, Irish scribe Martin McDonagh has penned 10 stage plays and written and directed five feature films. He won his lone Oscar in 2006 for the short film “Six Shooter.” McDonagh has a storytelling style that harkens back to Elmore Leonard, Dashiell Hammett, Carl Hiaasen, and especially Quentin Tarantino.

With films that are dialogue-heavy and low on action, McDonagh’s greatest strength is creating immensely appealing and entertaining characters who are instantly engaging (even the bad guys). His understanding of the human condition is virtually unparalleled and, for lack of a better word, endearing. He has yet to make a bad or even an average movie, and his latest film, “Wild Horse Nine,” is another easy winner.

Appearing in his third McDonagh production, Sam Rockwell (“Seven Psychopaths” and “Three Billboards Outside Ebbing, Missouri”) takes on another supporting role as Lee Chesterfield, a CIA operative. He’s the underling and protege of Chris Carlisle (John Malkovich), a grizzled vet in every sense of the word. Depending on the time of day, Chris is either contemplating retirement, suicide, or slow death by cancer.

Fourth Time’s the Charm

Also enjoying a repeat career achievement, this is the fourth time that Malkovich has played a CIA agent. His gonzo turn in “Burn After Reading” (2008) was followed by the excellent “RED” (2010), the incredibly average “RED 2” (2013), and now the career-capping “Wild Horse Nine.”

Despite the perpetual gray cloud following him everywhere, Chris is surprisingly jovial and upbeat. He’s sometimes even flippant, with a major disregard for authority as he laughs in the face of impending doom. The authority here is in the form of MJ (Steve Buscemi), the CIA chief based in Santiago, Chile. From what’s presented, Chris and MJ have a long-running, mutual disdain for each other.

MJ would be fine with Chris experiencing a nasty death while in the field. Chris would delight in accommodating this wish as long as it brought MJ some degree of red tape paperwork and the need to explain himself to his indifferent superiors. The plot of this film is an accidental extension of “Burn After Reading.”

Big Head Statues

The bulk of the story is set on Easter Island off the coast of Chile. It’s the home of nearly 1,000 ancient stone statues. Known as “moai,” they were created by the Rapa Nui people and date back to the 13th century. Any internet search of Easter Island will pull up images of the moai structures, for which the area is best known.

In 1973, MJ temporarily stations Chris and Lee on Easter Island, where they await an impending overthrow of the Chilean government. To McDonagh’s immense credit, the details of the coup are only alluded to; it’s made clear early on that the coup’s actual nature is something of a non-factor.

Reflecting the plots of “In Bruges” (2008), “The Banshees of Inisherin” (2022), and essentially every other McDonagh film, “Wild Horse Nine” uses the backdrop of a bigger event or locale to highlight the finer points of conflicting interpersonal relationships between the two leads.

Forced Alliance

It’s made clear early on that Chris and Lee get along not so much because they want to but because they have to. One has yet to reach the peak of his career, while the other has long passed it. The tension of waiting on an anticipated event to act while in hiding, or at least while trying to keep a low profile, only adds to the tension and their forced air of camaraderie.

While waiting to start their mystery mission in Santiago, Chris and Lee are halfheartedly ordered to remain in their borderline fleabag hotel rooms, something Chris totally ignores. By default, this forces Lee to shadow him and try to minimize any trouble he can get into by running his mouth too much.

Of the half dozen or so times this happens, the most interesting scenario is when the men cross paths with two younger women, who might be Chilean college students. As both Alicia (Ailín Salas) and in particular Monica (Mariana di Girolamo) appear to be in their mid-30s, this seems unlikely. Repeated chance meetings indicate that there’s more to them than initially indicated.

Malkovich for the Win?

McDonagh’s last two features (“Three Billboards” and “The Banshees”) received a combined 16 Oscar nominations. The early buzz is that this picture will get at least six nominations, with Malkovich the heavy favorite to nab the Best Actor prize.

This would be Malkovich’s third Academy Award nomination, and he’s never been predicted to win. Nevertheless, this year is different. He’s at the age (73 in December) to easily get the “lifetime achievement” edge, although he’ll be facing stiff competition from Matt Damon in “The Odyssey.” The results of the Critics Choice Awards, BAFTAs, Golden Globes, and Actor Awards ceremonies will provide the most accurate final tea leaves.

As of right now, Malkovich is the slight front-runner and sentimental favorite.

“Wild Horse Nine” is now playing in theaters.

‘Wild Horse Nine’ Director: Martin McDonagh Stars: John Malkovich, Sam Rockwell, Steve Buscemi Running Time: 1 hour, 56 minutes MPAA Rating: R Release Date: Nov. 6, 2026 Rating: 4 1/2 out of 5 stars

title: FTC Reaches $63 Million Settlement With Family Dollar Over Pricing Complaints
content:
By Craig Shoup

Family Dollar has agreed to pay $63 million as part of a settlement with the Federal Trade Commission and 17 states over allegedly deceptive pricing.

The company was alleged to have charged customers higher prices at checkout for goods priced lower on store shelves, the FTC said in a Nov. 12 statement. The FTC said that Family Dollar continued making false pricing statements, despite consumer complaints and thousands of failed regulatory inspections.

Family Dollar did not respond to a request for comment.

Under a proposed order subject to approval by a federal judge in Virginia, the company would pay $40 million in relief to eligible shoppers, and $20 million in discounts mandated across stores that would apply a fixed 15 percent reduction for two consecutive days, excluding certain products. Another $3 million would be paid directly to the 17 states that participated in the complaint.

The filing also states that, within 90 days, Family Dollar must establish and maintain a pricing accuracy program that will be independently assessed and certified annually. The company must also train staff to identify price discrepancies and to correct errors so that displayed prices match register totals.

“The FTC is committed to ensuring price transparency and fairness so consumers can make informed choices,” Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in the Nov. 12 statement. “Today’s order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices.”

The complaint said thousands of the discount retailer’s stores across the country were overcharging shoppers, including in low-income communities with limited access to full-service grocery stores. The company allegedly failed to correct the pricing issues despite being warned about the problem after customers reported pricing disparities. Regulatory inspections purportedly confirmed price labels across stores in America were inaccurate.

In one instance cited in the 85-page complaint, a customer reported that a Family Dollar employee admitted that false pricing was due to failures to put up new pricing labels at the store due to a lack of time to change them.

The company was also accused of charging higher prices at the register than those listed on its website and mobile app, and not accepting discount prices and coupons at checkout, the FTC said.

Federal, state, and local regulators reported Family Dollar for thousands of pricing violations, resulting in more than $3 million in fines.

The settlement announced Nov. 12 is the latest in a string of settlements and penalties Family Dollar has paid out in the past three years. Since 2024, the company has paid more than $800,000 to state attorneys general for inaccurate pricing, according to the complaint.

In February 2024, Family Dollar reached a $400,000 settlement with Ohio. In January 2025, the company paid $113,960 to Wisconsin, and in May 2025, the chain paid $300,000 to Arizona.

The state settlements each require Family Dollar to post a sign in each store stating that in the event of a price charged at the register being higher than the price posted on the shelf, the customer is entitled to pay the lower price, or receive a refund for the price difference.

A January 2026 internal Family Dollar presentation indicated that Ohio stores were not following the signage agreement, the FTC said in the 85-page complaint.

“In general, stores were not aware of and following the Consent Agreement. For example: No signage on stores or POS; Store managers were mostly unaware of monthly pricing audit obligation; District Managers were not doing full pricing audit every eight weeks,” the complaint said.

Internal audits in April found that 64 Ohio stores still lacked the proper pricing policy signage.

title: Spain’s leader wanted a campaign focused on housing. A deadly train crash has complicated that
content:
Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez hoped to leverage widespread discontent over unaffordable housing when he called snap elections in October. Then a high-speed train rammed into another, killing 69 people and casting a pall over the nation.

It was Spain's second deadly rail collision this year and couldn't have come at a worse time for Sánchez.

With the campaign officially underway, the 54-year-old progressive is working to keep the tragedy from derailing his message to voters. Instead, he has projected his administration as willing to assume responsibility for errors on its watch. More than that, he has folded the disaster into his campaign's main message: that a right-wing government would be worse for Spaniards, who need government help for housing, healthcare, infrastructure and more.

“If there is one lesson to be drawn from the Urda rail tragedy, it is that public services matter,” Sánchez wrote on X after the collision. “This is what is at stake.”

It may be a tough sell. Until this year, there had never been a fatal crash on Spain’s dedicated high-speed lines, and analysts told The Associated Press that the lethal crashes won't be so easy to downplay.

Sánchez draws inspiration from the left’s victories in Brazil and US

On the morning of Oct. 28, Sánchez was putting a message of positivity onto social media:

“There are so many reasons to be optimistic in this country. We respond to the haters with data, intelligence and humor.”

Minutes earlier, as he would soon learn, a high-speed train south of Madrid slammed into a stationary one, leaving authorities searching for dozens of bodies in the wreckage.

Even so, in recent weeks he has kept an uplifting tone, especially in his speeches while sporting red T-shirts emblazoned with aspirational slogans: “The Strength of Love,” “The Strength of the People,” and “Vote with Strength.” He spoke at his campaign kick-off event Thursday night in Seville, hours before the official midnight start.

The Spanish leader has also tried to invigorate his campaign by pointing to recent elections in Brazil, where leftist President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva secured reelection with a come-from-behind victory in a runoff, and in the U.S. where Democrats seized control of the Senate and the House.

“It has happened in Brazil, it has happened in the United States, and it will happen in Spain too. The key is mobilization,” he said in an interview with newspaper La Vanguardia this week.

A Spanish prime minister is elected by Parliament, needing an absolute majority in the first vote or a simple majority in the second, often relying on coalition agreements or support from other parties.

Sánchez’s strategy is to “instill a sense of hope, the idea that things can be reversed, that change is possible — and, by doing so, to launch a campaign of optimism and foster a positive outlook,” said Alejandro Quiroga, a professor of political science at Madrid’s Complutense University.

On Monday, the Brazilian president will visit Spain and lend his support to the Socialist’s campaign. It’s unclear how much the Spanish leader will benefit from basking in the reflected glory of a foreign leader; analysts including Quiroga and Sánchez’s party officials themselves acknowledge that the 2 1/2-week campaign will be dominated by domestic concerns, such as housing, immigration and corruption — and last month’s deadly crash.

Turning the transport minister’s resignation into a campaign strength

Six days after the rail accident, Sánchez’s transport minister Óscar Puente stepped down. He did so at the tail-end of a parliamentary grilling about his administration of the country's high-speed rail network, the second largest in the world after China's.

At every turn since, Sánchez and his top officials have pointed to the minister's resignation as proof that the government is accountable.

“We have stepped forward with absolute transparency,” Sánchez wrote soon after on X, calling the minister's move an “act of dignity.”

Sánchez himself was notably absent at a state funeral held this week in central Spain for the crash's victims, perhaps due to the potential for volatile scenes at the service attended by mourning family members of the dead.

But ordinary Spanish voters have shorter memories, and Sánchez appears to be counting on that, according to Quiroga. Still, his right-wing opponents are sure to make the two crashes a central topic of their campaigns and debates, as they undercut Sánchez's arguments about his record.

“There is a sense of public shock, compounded by the nature of these accidents,” said Montserrat Nebrera, a former conservative politician and political analyst. “It points to a failure in management over the last eight years.”

Several opinion polls conducted before and after the Oct. 28 train crash showed Sánchez’s Socialist Party behind the combined support of the conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox.

Focus back on housing after a general strike and nationwide protests

On Wednesday, a nationwide protest over soaring rents and home costs drew over 100,000 people to the streets of Spain's major cities. It was well-timed for Sánchez, bringing the national conversation back to Spain’s housing woes on the eve of the campaign.

The demonstration was part of a general strike — the first in 14 years in Spain — and the first whose main driver was born from frustrations over housing.

While Sánchez’s Socialist Party did not organize or participate in the strike, his government praised the effort. Affordability issues are traditionally more favorable to left-wing politics and he has sought to appease housing activists who, since the dramatic eviction of an 87-year-old woman, have been protesting regularly.

Right-wing parties' rejection of Sánchez's two proposed emergency housing decrees served as the trigger for him to call the early general election, on Nov. 29. His government on Thursday passed one of them through a smaller interim parliament.

Sánchez and his allies hope the move shows Spanish people that he's working on their behalf, and that the Popular Party's promise to repeal the decree if it takes power will help motivate voters.

“Yesterday, the right to housing won on the street and in workplaces, and I hope it will win again at the ballot box,” Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez told lawmakers after its passage.

title: Iran claims strike on US radar
content:
Tehran says it destroyed an American early-warning installation in Bahrain in retaliation for an alleged airstrike

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claims that it struck a US early-warning radar installation in Bahrain.

In a statement carried by Iranian media on Friday, the IRGC said the attack was in retaliation for an alleged enemy airstrike on a telecommunications tower in Sirik, in Iran’s southern Hormozgan Province. The IRGC claimed that it destroyed the radar, although neither the strike nor the reported damage has been independently verified.

There was no immediate confirmation from the US military or Bahrain.

The incident comes amid continued tensions between Washington and Tehran, with peace negotiations stalled and fears persisting over a possible resumption of major US military operations.

Read more

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that further military action against Iran does not appear to be necessary. He expressed hope for a diplomatic breakthrough amid calls for restraint from Arab allies. However, he warned that US forces are “locked and loaded” and ready to resume strikes if the circumstances change.

In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump declared that the US no longer needs a peace deal with Iran, claiming that Washington controls Iranian funds and the Strait of Hormuz.

The US carried out limited airstrikes against Iranian air-defense positions on Qeshm Island on November 2 and 6. Trump described the latest operation as “minor.” Media reports have said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pressed Trump to launch a new offensive against Iran following the November 3 US midterm elections, but the president declined.

Speaking to conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt on Thursday, Trump warned that Iran will “not exist very long” if it kills a senior US official. The remarks followed reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent moved to a military base over alleged Iranian threats, which Tehran denied.

Mohsen Rezaei, the secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, warned on Thursday that US military bases involved in a renewed attack on Iran, including those in Europe, would be considered legitimate targets. “No safe distance. No safe haven. No immunity,” he wrote on X.

title: Mamdani moves to disband NYPD protest-control unit – Politico
content:
The New York mayor is reportedly considering a civilian-led replacement for the police unit, which has faced accusations of excessive force

New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, is finalizing plans to disband a specialized police unit responsible for counterterrorism and crowd control, Politico reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.

Mamdani pledged to dismantle the NYPD’s Strategic Response Group (SRG) during his 2025 mayoral campaign following accusations that its officers used excessive force against protesters.

According to Politico, the mayor is considering replacing the SRG’s protest-response function with a civilian-led unit focused on de-escalation, which could assist police in making arrests when necessary. The new unit could operate under Mamdani’s Office of Community Safety, established earlier this year. The plan could be announced as early as this week and formalized through an executive order.

Read more

“As the mayor has said, our administration will disband the Strategic Response Group and separate protest response from counterterrorism,” Mamdani’s spokeswoman, Dora Pekec, said, promising further details soon.

Established in 2015, the SRG came under increased scrutiny over its handling of the nationwide unrest sparked by the killing of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer in 2020. In 2023, the NYPD agreed to restrict the unit’s deployment at peaceful demonstrations and prohibit the practice of surrounding and trapping protesters without grounds for arrest.

New York City Public Advocate Jumaane Williams has called for the SRG to be removed from protest policing, arguing that its aggressive tactics escalated peaceful demonstrations into violent confrontations. He also accused the NYPD of obstructing misconduct investigations.

Mamdani has argued that counterterrorism operations should be separated from policing demonstrations to protect constitutional rights while maintaining public safety. Last month, the mayor ordered the first comprehensive review of the NYPD’s use-of-force policies in a decade, aiming to “strengthen accountability when police officers are accused of serious misconduct.”

Mamdani’s broader police reform agenda has drawn criticism from police unions. In October, Police Benevolent Association President Patrick Hendry accused the mayor of appeasing his “radical base,” warning that the proposed overhaul would not make New Yorkers safer.

Scott Munro, the president of the Detectives Endowment Association, accused Mamdani of seeking to dismantle vital police units rather than support officers, warning that “New Yorkers should be worried.”

title: Israel bars French presidential hopeful over Gaza flotilla pledge
content:
Jean-Luc Melenchon vowed to send French warships to escort pro-Palestinian activists

Israel has banned French left-wing presidential candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon from entering the country after he vowed to deploy warships to escort activist flotillas seeking to break the blockade of Gaza.

The Israeli Foreign Ministry also imposed an entry ban on Mathilde Panot, the parliamentary leader of Melenchon’s La France Insoumise (LFI) party.

“Both have made statements spreading blood libels against Israel, while Jean-Luc Melenchon has also called for French naval vessels to escort illegal flotillas to Gaza,” the ministry said in a statement on Thursday.

“The State of Israel will respond firmly to those who seek to harm it.”

French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot called the move “a demagogic decision made by a government that has repeatedly violated international law.” He argued that the ban will only help LFI to “thrive on exploiting the Israeli-Palestinian conflict for political gain.”

According to recent opinion polls, Melenchon ranks second behind Marine Le Pen of the right-wing National Rally (RN) in voting intentions for the 2027 presidential election. LFI is one of the largest opposition parties in the French parliament.

Read more

A vocal critic of Israel, Melenchon has pledged to “take direct action” to support Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank if elected president.

“French naval vessels will, if necessary, escort flotillas of citizens mobilized to assert their rights,” he said on Saturday, referring to civilian boats attempting to reach Gaza. Israel has repeatedly intercepted the flotillas at sea and deported foreign activists.

Melenchon said on Thursday that he has never sought to enter Israel and reiterated his accusations of “genocide in Gaza,” as well as his opposition to the expansion of Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, and what he described as the gradual annexation of southern Lebanon and the Golan Heights.

The entry bans came shortly after France refused entry to Israeli settlement leader Yossi Dagan, who heads the Samaria Regional Council in the West Bank. The UN considers Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank illegal under international law and a major obstacle to the establishment of an independent Palestinian state.

Israel previously barred foreign politicians, journalists, and activists who are critical of its policies toward Palestinians. In 2019, it denied entry to US Representatives Ilhan Omar and Rashida Tlaib. In 2025, French-Palestinian European Parliament member Rima Hassan, who represents LFI, was also denied entry.

Israel has dismissed accusations of genocide and blamed Hamas for the devastation in Gaza, where more than 74,600 Palestinians have been killed and over 176,000 wounded since October 2023, according to the enclave’s Health Ministry.

Two in three Germans are dissatisfied with how democracy functions in their country, according to the latest Leipzig Authoritarianism Study conducted by researchers at Leipzig University in cooperation with the Heinrich Boll Foundation and the Otto Brenner Foundation.

The findings, published on Wednesday, show that satisfaction with democracy as experienced in everyday life has fallen to just 33.3%, down from 42.3% in 2024. It is the lowest level recorded since researchers began measuring the indicator in 2006.

Discontent is particularly pronounced in the former East Germany, where only 22.8% of respondents expressed satisfaction, compared with around 36% in the west.

More than half of Germans expressed at least some sympathy for either “nostalgic idealization of the past” or “apocalyptic expectations of the future,” according to the study.

The survey involved 2,507 respondents interviewed from March 16 to June 3.

Read more

The findings follow an INSA poll showing that 82% of Germans are dissatisfied with Chancellor Friedrich Merz and his government. Around 60% said their personal circumstances have worsened since he took office.

Merz became chancellor following snap elections in February 2025, after promising to revive the struggling economy. However, economic difficulties have persisted, while his government has increased military spending, maintained financial and military support for Ukraine, and advocated for reforms to Germany’s welfare system.

The chancellor urged Germans to work more, saying the “welfare state as we have it today can no longer be financed.”

Merz refused to change course after his Christian Democratic Union (CDU) suffered crushing defeats to the anti-immigration, Euroskeptic Alternative for Germany (AfD) in September’s regional elections in the eastern states of Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. Merz described the latter result as a “disaster.”

The CDU’s coalition partners, the Social Democrats, have called for a formal review that could pave the way for a ban on the AfD following its sweeping victories in both eastern states. The party denounced the move as an attempt to suppress political opposition and undermine democracy.
