title: Jensen Huang is out. What now?
content:
The first big sex scandal of the AI era has taken down Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s co-founder and longtime CEO. Nvidia’s board of directors announced his resignation on Thursday morning and named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO.

Huang has been making headlines all week after news broke Friday that he had an affair with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singaporean tech firm Megaspeed who the US government alleges was also a Chinese spy.

The revelation Wednesday of a second extramarital affair, this time with an Nvidia employee reporting to Huang directly, added to the pressure, and another affair came to light later on Thursday after Huang’s ouster.

The scandal has implications far beyond one company: Huang’s central role in the AI race can’t be overstated. It was his vision of an AI future that led him to pivot Nvidia from a small company making video game chips into the dominant player in making the chips that serve OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google’s computing needs.

Huang is close friends with President Donald Trump’s and a leading voice in resisting efforts to slow AI progress. And he has pushed for the US to take a less hawkish position toward China’s own AI goals, a stance now called into question by his relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. Among its other impacts, the news has revived efforts on Capitol Hill to further restrict chip exports to China.

To break down the national security implications of Huang’s departure, how the Trump administration is involved, and what it says about US AI industry writ large, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Garret De Vynck, a technology reporter at the Washington Post.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get your podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.

Nvidia has been called the central bank of AI, which is why it’s so important that we figure out what Jensen Huang may have disclosed to this alleged spy. How long has the president known about this, as far as we know?

As far as we know, the president has known about the fact that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with someone that the US government thought was a spy for about a year. This circulated within the administration, and the decision was made not to tell Jensen.

That doesn’t necessarily mean that it was automatically some kind of corrupt decision of President Trump protecting Jensen Huang. There’s all sorts of reasons why you might not want to tell someone they’re being spied on, the number one being that they might blow up the operation. Maybe you want to learn more. Maybe you suspect that the person themselves knows that they’re being spied on and is willingly sharing information and you need some more time to gather that. It’s unclear why the US government specifically chose not to pull in Jensen Huang. 

It’s also a little bit unclear whether he knows he was being spied on, or whether maybe he was told through some kind of back channel. He has said that he did not know that she was a spy and he is admitting to the affair, to the infidelity. He’s admitting to essentially breaking Nvidia’s code of conduct by sleeping with one of its customers, but he is not admitting at all to knowing that she was a spy and definitely not admitting to sharing any information willfully.

It feels like this is the kind of thing that the government would investigate. There’s been reporting that the Commerce Department was involved with some kind of investigation, but that investigation came to an end and no one really knows why.

The context here is that the United States and China are in an AI race. Going back to the first Trump administration, there’s been pretty aggressive export controls saying, “We don’t want China to get our tech so that they can develop AI.” And the Biden administration continued that. He increased the export controls on China. China was complaining very loudly about this. They said, ‘We don’t care. We want to win AI and we need to slow you guys down.’

When Trump came in, he actually lifted his foot off the gas a little bit. They didn’t throw the gates open and say, “You can have whatever you want. All American companies can sell whatever they want to China.” But he said, “Some AI chips that are less powerful than the state of the art. We can send those to Chinese companies.“

The other thing that national security experts have pointed out is that the Trump administration could theoretically have been doing more to stop the smuggling of computer chips to China. And that’s where this story gets so important for national security.

Megaspeed is accused of essentially being a front for Chinese companies to get access to computer chips. Journalists have gone to Megaspeed’s office in Singapore where it’s based, and there were only a couple of people working there. It didn’t really seem like there was a lot going on. Nvidia has said all through this process over the last couple of years that, “No, we’ve checked it out, Megaspeed is a legitimate company and we’re not breaking the law when it comes to this.”

There are a lot of questions and what everyone is focused on finding out, both journalists and I would say congressional Democrats when they come into office in the new year is, is there something more going on here? Is there something where the Chinese either convinced Jensen Huang to sell more chips to them or Jensen Huang himself, who has been advocating for selling more chips to China, essentially did this himself? 

He’s been pressuring the president, he’s been donating to him, he’s been glad-handing with the president and the president has been listening more to this corporate executive who is his friend and who donated him a bunch of money rather than listening to China hawks or national security experts who say we should be limiting what China is able to access.

That’s really where the locus of this investigation is going to be. It’s not so much that Jensen Huang had an affair. It’s more the fact that he himself is someone who has said we need to sell more computer chips to China and he was involved with an alleged Chinese spy, and he’s very close to the president and had influence on the president.

You mentioned the Democrats. Have they said anything? Are they going to call him in front of Congress for an investigation?

Going forward, there are two big things here. One of them is these investigations into Jensen Huang and this whole situation. The company is likely going to continue to investigate. Maybe more information will come out there. Jensen Huang has been called to speak later this month in Congress. And congressional Democrats have also said that when they come into power in January, they will be asking him. 

The second big thing that comes out of this is, what does America do when it comes to China and AI? Now that one of the biggest advocates for being a bit more friendly towards China when it comes to selling them things that they need for AI is out of the room and completely discredited, I think that the China hawks, those who say we need to crack down more aggressively, we need to limit China’s access to AI computer chips, they’re really coming into ascendance here and they’re in the Republican Party, they’re in the Democratic Party, some of them, people like Marco Rubio, are even in the Cabinet. 

I think there’s this real question of: Do we see a much stronger push to actually ramp up controls on China and how does Trump respond? There’s all sorts of geopolitical things that could sort of spin out of this CEO affair.

I’m old enough to remember when a board tried to get rid of Sam Altman and then he was just back a week later. Elon Musk is already offering Jensen Huang a job. Is there a fair chance that he just goes somewhere that’s not that concerned about espionage affairs or getting with your VP of health or whatever it is? Is he just going to go work for China?

I don’t think he’s going to go work for China. This is definitely the wildest corporate story since Sam Altman was fired as CEO and brought back three or four days later. It’s a very different situation. That was a startup where you essentially have five or six investors who get to make the call about who the CEO is, and the employees at that company overwhelmingly wanted to bring Sam Altman back. I think they wanted more continuity of the company, but they also wanted to make sure that their company didn’t go under and go bankrupt and get disappeared, which was sort of on the table at that point in time. 

Nvidia’s not going anywhere. Obviously employees have lost a lot of money in terms of the stock value already coming down due to the situation. So employees are probably shocked. They’re probably upset. Jensen Huang is broadly loved at Nvidia, and so I can definitely see that employees would be doing petitions, asking for him to return. 

But this is a giant public company and the board makes a decision here. Jensen Huang was untruthful publicly and I think that also will make other public companies hesitant before rushing to bring him on as CEO.

As we’ve talked about many times in the show, half of our economy is staked on AI at this point. How concerned should we be that one of the most important people in this industry was so easily duped in this honeypot situation? Are these the people we should be trusting with the future of our society?

It’s a really good reminder that people are people. I think that we like to lionize individuals and say that they are the ones who are going to take us into the future and they are inventing the future and it’s so incredible. And I do think Jensen Huang gets a lot of credit for making sure that the companies kept up in AI, but at the end of the day, it was also a lucky break for them that the computer chips they were making just happened to work well for the math that is required by artificial intelligence. 

I do think that this speaks to something that a lot of people across the country and maybe even the world really feel. They do not want to sign off the future to a dozen dudes in Silicon Valley and their collaborators in the Trump White House. I think that is a view that a lot of people increasingly have. I think it was one of the factors in the midterms, maybe not the most important one, but people are concerned about concentration of power. They’re concerned about AI and they don’t see it as something that they themselves have control over. 

I think that this is just going to be another thing that sort of adds skepticism to the idea that people like Jensen Huang should be the ones making the final decision when it comes to artificial intelligence.

title: How the 7 healthcare workers who just got elected to Congress plan to fix our broken system
content:
Last week’s blue tsunami carried a lot of white coats: At least seven newly elected Democrats have medical degrees or nursing careers. Pediatrician Annie Andrews of South Carolina scored one of the most shocking Senate victories of election night for Democrats, while Abdul El-Sayed (who earned a medical degree before working in public health) won the all-important Michigan Senate race. In the House, Democrats will soon welcome pediatrician Richard Pan of California, emergency room physician Amish Shah of Arizona, surgeon Adam Hamawy of New Jersey, emergency nurse Mitchell Berman of Wisconsin, and oncology nurse practitioner Kristina Knickerbocker of Ohio.

Like many Democrats, these candidates campaigned on lowering costs, expanding health coverage, and confronting the drugmakers and healthcare corporations that they accuse of putting profits ahead of patients. They have endorsed big ideas to make healthcare better, from a public insurance option to Medicare-for-all, alongside targeted changes to drug prices and health insurance denials.

With President Donald Trump still in the White House, Democrats’ healthcare agenda faces obvious obstacles in the short term. But I spoke with Pan and Shah this week to learn how they hope to influence the healthcare conversation in Washington going forward. 

They may be politicians, but they have seen America’s broken healthcare up close. They’re hoping to help some of their new colleagues, who may not have those same experiences and may be prone to thinking of policy issues in abstract terms, understand the urgency and the human toll of our messed-up medical system. And as lawmakers try to come up with solutions to fix those problems, they’ll be there to make sure those policies actually make sense in practice.

“For us, these policy discussions are not abstract,” Pan said. “As a practicing physician, I know what it’s like to be on the front lines and have to look a patient in the eye and even tell them that, well, these programs either exist or don’t exist, and we’re not going to be able to get you help. And those are the types of things I have to deal with each time I see a patient.”

What practicing medicine teaches you about politics

The new members will join a small but notable group of providers-turned-politicians: The Congressional Doctors Caucus, founded last year, had six Democratic members before last week’s midterms. Shah, who previously served in the Arizona legislature, told me that he believed his medical career had given him a valuable outlook for thinking about how to serve in political office.

“The core function of practicing medicine is to care for people,” Shah said. “The same should really be true about politics.”

He’s experienced the shocking inequities of US healthcare, and seen its impact on people’s well-being, firsthand. Earlier this year, Shah said, an uninsured woman came into his emergency room department with an allergic reaction. His team treated her successfully. But she was worried about the bill, asking if she might have to pay a $10,000 charge after she was discharged. And Shah told me that he had to be honest with her that she might.

That’s when he learned that his patient was her family’s breadwinner — and that she actually worked in a nearby emergency department. Somebody who helped provide emergency care to others couldn’t afford it herself.

“It’s a tragedy that those of us who actually go out to help others and be part of the team that saves lives can be left without insurance,” Shah said.

Pan, a former California state senator, described a similar experience while treating kids in primary care. He has seen all the ways US health care is lacking: children who don’t get the mental health support they need to excel in school, families that struggle to afford stable housing or find healthy food. His ability to help depended on decisions made well outside his examination room.

Sign up for the Good Medicine newsletter

Our political wellness landscape has shifted: new leaders, shady science, contradictory advice, broken trust, and overwhelming systems. How is anyone supposed to make sense of it all? Vox’s senior correspondent Dylan Scott has been on the health beat for a long time, and every week, he’ll wade into sticky debates, answer fair questions, and contextualize what’s happening in American health care policy. Sign up here.

“These are all things that certainly have potential policy solutions, but it’s not just theoretical,” he told me. “It is very real and tied to very specific patients that I’ve seen.”

But while these experiences have made them eager to change things, the newly elected physicians are also mindful about how proposed changes could disrupt ongoing patient care. Pan said he wants to push his colleagues about both the intended and unintended consequences or new policies: Who will get help? What happens to people whose needs don’t fit neatly into boxes? As any doctor will tell you, every patient is unique.

That’s especially true for people with chronic conditions, he said, who may have spent years finding the right doctors and treatments. Lawmakers have to strike a balance: identifying ideas that will improve the health system in the long term, without jeopardizing the care that people need right now.

Shah said he hopes his experience as a physician can help Congress find a middle ground between the patients demanding reform and the providers who are wary of big changes. After decades in medicine and a stint in the state legislature, he knows the different players and their concerns.

“I speak the language of healthcare,” he said. “I’ve earned the trust of a lot of those stakeholders that I will not take an axe to the system, but rather reform it in a way that really improves it and centers the patient. So that gives me a unique ability to improve this at the congressional level.”

What the new doctors and nurses want to change

These Democratic doctors, like their party’s leaders, have a clear No. 1 priority when they take office next year: reversing the $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts that Republicans passed as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act in 2025.

“Given all the damage the Republicans did in the past two years, first we got to triage to stop the bleeding,” Pan told me. He wants to repeal the OBBBA’s Medicaid work requirements, restore the lapsed Affordable Care Act tax credits that helped reduce premiums for millions of Americans, and protect Medicare payments. Those were common themes across these physician-politicians: Andrews, Berman, and El-Sayed endorsed the same policies as part of their campaign platform, while Knickerbocker likewise pledged to protect Medicaid, Medicare, the ACA, and children’s health coverage.

Beyond reversing the Republican cuts, the newcomers want to cover more people, though they have different ideas about how to do it.

Shah said he supports letting people buy into Medicare. Andrews, Berman, Knickerbocker, and Shah have also endorsed a public option: a government-backed health insurance plan that would compete with private plans. El-Sayed and Hamawy, meanwhile, say they favor Medicare-for-all, guaranteeing comprehensive coverage without premiums or out-of-pocket costs.

“I want to see every United States citizen covered, and I’d like to see the premiums drop,” Shah said.

But even the people who have health insurance often struggle to pay for medical care. Andrews, Berman, El-Sayed, and Hamawy have all proposed expanding the government’s negotiation of prescription drug prices. Andrews and Berman want to extend Medicare’s $35 insulin cap to private insurance. Andrews, Berman, and Hamawy also want to crack down on private equity ownership and consolidation among healthcare providers.

Perhaps unsurprisingly, these doctors were not afraid to get into the weeds of healthcare policy on the campaign trail. Andrews’s detailed plans include limits on some hospital prices and changing Medicare payments so the same service costs the same regardless of where it is performed. Berman’s agenda draws on his own nursing experience: He wants nurses to help set staffing standards, more funding for nursing education, and enhance workplace safety for medical workers, a goal he shares with Shah. In Arizona, Shah worked on protections for healthcare workers, and he wants Congress to focus on the problem too.

Pan also wants to figure out how to restore trust in public health after two years of US Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. undermining faith in vaccinations and other medical science. He helped write California laws tightening exemptions from school vaccination requirements; in Congress, he wants stronger oversight of the administration’s healthcare agencies, including probing any possible corruption, and stronger protections for scientific decision-making. He told me that lawmakers may want to consider creating new safeguards into law so future administrations have less latitude to overhaul public health policy.

“The American people need accurate information from their government,” Pan said. “We might want to rethink how to put better guardrails so that someone like an RFK Jr. in the future couldn’t…basically upend everything.”

Andrews and Shah have also placed a lot of emphasis on fixing prior authorizations, one of the most common frustrations for patients and providers alike.

Shah recalled that he once met a Republican constituent who said he was completing prior authorization paperwork on behalf of the doctor treating his son, who had muscular dystrophy, because the doctor’s office was overwhelmed. He was shouldering an absurd administrative burden as a layperson, just so his child could get the care he needed. 

And so, Shah worked on legislation to streamline the prior authorization process. A 2021 law standardized prior authorization forms and limited their length to two pages, excluding supporting medical documentation. He sees his state work as a possible model for federal legislation.

“We really need to start looking at these denials,” he said. He wants more scrutiny of decisions that are later overturned and of automated and increasing AI-driven systems that reject people’s claims without meaningful review.

It’s another example of how these freshman members will be ready to dive into the weeds of fixing healthcare. The question will be whether the new lawmakers can translate their direct experience with patients’ frustrations into changes that make getting healthcare care easier.

“You have these real stories that then drive the legislation,” Shah said, “and give you the ideas to solve the problems for people.”

Democrats made shocking gains with religious voters — but not everywhere
content:
One of the most eye-opening aspects of last week’s midterms was the new cohort of religious politicians it sent to Congress — many of them part of a wave of Democratic-leaning Christians.

Another striking feature was the dramatic shift among many religious voters.

For years, American politics has seemed stuck on a partisan track, with religious-identified voters shifting more firmly to the right, and the nonreligious tacking to the left. There are a few exceptions, of course — Jewish voters, Latino Catholics, and Black Protestants, who have stayed firmly Democratic — but the broader tide has flowed clearly one way.

Key takeaways

  • This year’s blue tsunami carried voters everywhere to the left; it also scrambled voting trends in America’s religious electorate.
  • Catholics shifted hard to the left after Donald Trump won their vote by a double-digit margin in 2024.
  • Jewish voters were still strongly Democratic, though there are clear signs of lower support than in previous electoral cycles.
  • Other religious groups, mainline Protestants and Muslims, contributed to a diverse Democratic coalition — while evangelicals appeared less enthusiastic to turn out.

The 2026 vote, for the first time in a while, makes that picture look less certain. Based on exit polls, county-level data, and some post-election analysis, we already have a handful of intriguing signs of change. The data is still early and patchy, but it appears that Catholic voters around the country moved left, evangelical Christians stayed home, and some Jewish voters dug in against the anti-Israel rhetoric and moved rightward. And in Utah, generational differences, particularly among Mormons, may be starting to change the political makeup of a rock-ribbed conservative state.

There are caveats: Wave elections, especially when they’re of the historic proportions of last week’s Democratic tsunami, can obscure and cloud these changes. When everyone moves in one direction, it can be hard to distinguish specific storylines. And with religion, as with any single voter attribute, it can be difficult to tease out just how much faith and religious identity influenced vote choice, as opposed to working in combination with race, class, and concerns about issues like affordability and immigration.

And better data is still to come; the gold standard of voter roll-validated studies, like the Pew Research Center’s, won’t be available until next year.

Yet that combination of factors also suggests a new possibility for our politics: that religious voters of all creeds can come to function as swing voters too, cracking up old alliances, like on the religious right, and offering the hint of new winning coalitions, as Catholics and mainline Protestant Christians seem to have done for the Democrats.

The largest shift: Catholic voters swung against the GOP

Catholics play a special role in American politics. They spent much of the last century operating as a solid Democratic bloc, reaching a peak in the 1960s when John F. Kennedy, the first Catholic president, won about 80 percent of their vote. Since then, they’ve gradually become more Republican, due to assimilation of former European Catholic immigrants, the rise of conservative activism over abortion and social issues, and the rise of the religious right.

In the last two decades, Catholics have tended to reflect the views of the median American voter, evenly split in the 2012, 2016, and 2020 presidential elections. But that changed in 2024. Across different polls and surveys, Catholics shifted decisively to the right: backing Trump 59-39 according to exit polls, and 55-43, according to the Pew Research Center.

Now, in a year in which Trump and Republicans frequently clashed with Pope Leo XIV and his bishops — over the Iran war, mass deportations, and immigration policy — Catholic voters again turned into a wild card.

This year, according to exit polls, they swung left, with the margin shifting by more than 20 points. Democrats narrowly won the Catholic vote this time, 50-49. As a subgroup, that put Catholics up there with Asian voters, Latinos, urban and suburban voters, Gen Z and millennials as being the top groups that swung to the left this year.

View Link

Other estimates from the religion and politics scholar Ryan Burge show particularly noticeable shifts among white Catholics, swinging about 9 points toward Democrats, even if a majority of them still voted for Republican congressional candidates. In Texas, his analysis showed that counties with higher shares of Latino Catholics were much more likely to support the winning Democratic Senate candidate, James Talarico.

The results were even more dramatic in the most Catholic House districts. Of the 12 districts with the highest share of Catholics, the average swing in the vote was about 15 points, and Democrats won eight of these seats, while gaining in all 12.

Catholics have tended to basically operate like the median voter — swinging in the same direction as the overall popular vote. That makes it harder to pinpoint any unique motivators that caused Catholics to move against the GOP: Trump’s fights with Catholic leaders, the lack of a mobilized anti-abortion movement this year, or the affordability concerns that moved all voters.

One notable exception here are Latino Catholics, who tend to be the most Democratic of the Catholic electorate, and most opposed to Trump’s immigration and deportation policies this cycle. It’s no coincidence that they’re concentrated in the Southwest, including those parts of Texas that swung toward Talarico and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa over both economic stress and anger over immigration enforcement.

Does this all suggest the rise of a new Catholic swing vote? Potentially — combined with the decline in abortion politics in the US, and a more active Vatican. For the first time, the Church has an American pope, one who isn’t afraid to get involved with current affairs and push harder on Catholic social teachings (which align more with the Democratic Party’s views of society and the economy). That could have meaningful repercussions heading into 2028.

Though still very blue, some Jewish voters broke with the Democrats

Jewish Americans, though they only make up about 2 percent of the American population, became a huge focus of political attention this year — in large part because of how central they are to Democratic coalitions (along with Black Americans, they are some of the most loyal Democratic voters), and because Israel became a flashpoint in American politics. 

As Democrats made a dramatic shift in the last two years in how they talk about Israel and AIPAC, with increasingly open criticism of the Israeli government’s actions, some Jewish Democrats and Republicans responded with charges of antisemitism — and some Republicans started leaning into overt Islamophobia, particularly in Michigan. In turn, Republicans made bold predictions that Democrats would see a large drop in support this year, especially in Michigan (with an anti-Israel Senate candidate) and New York, where they counted on Jewish voters to rally to the more pro-Israel party.

In the end, there was no mass exodus of Jewish voters — but the exit polls did report a slight shift toward the GOP this year: 68-31, compared to 78-22 in 2024. Other post-election surveys show similar dynamics. (The numbers can vary, in part because different pollsters use different metrics for measuring Jewish support and identity, and also because exit polls can be imprecise.) The Jewish Electorate Institute’s polling from the Mellman Group, for example, shows that while Democrats still held a large, 44-point advantage at the end of the day, (69 percent to the 25 percent that backed the GOP) that was smaller than the margin in 2024, and nearly 20 points smaller than their margin in 2018’s blue wave. That’s an anomaly, given the scale of the tsunami this year.

Even the most Democratic-friendly poll, from GBAO Strategies, had a kind of rightward signal, though a longer-horizon one: It showed nearly identical levels of Democratic support among Jewish voters this year as in 2024 — but both those figures, about 70 percent, are lower than Jewish Democratic support in 2022 (74 percent) and 2020 (77 percent), noted The Forward.

This shift away from Democrats looked especially dramatic in Michigan, where The Forward also noted last week that the winning Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed underperformed other Democratic candidates in precincts with large Jewish populations. In another piece of data, a Michigan exit poll from the NORC-Civic Health and Elections Project, there was a more dramatic result, albeit with a tiny sample size of about 100 people: Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers winning a majority of Jewish voters, 52-47, a much worse result than it found for House Democratic candidates, who won the demographic by more than 30 points. Though small, it adds to other evidence of Democratic underperformance with Jewish voters in the Senate contest.

In surveys about their views, Jewish voters are sending signals that should put both parties on notice. A quarter of Republican Jews in the Mellman Group’s poll reported being concerned their party is “too accepting of antisemitic rhetoric within the Party” while a third said it’s “becoming too much of a home for White nationalists and the far right.”

More than a third of Jewish Democrats, similarly, said they worry the party is becoming “too accepting of antisemitic rhetoric within the Party,” while a quarter think it’s “becoming too much of a home for socialists and the far left.” Given how much larger the Jewish Democratic base is than the Republican one, and how central it is to winning coalitions in battlegrounds, these concerns pose a bigger electoral risk for the Democrats, particularly if the anti-Israel left grows into an even larger and more vocal wing of the party.

Protestants, and evangelicals, showed weaker Republican support

When it comes to evangelical Christians, the data suggests there was a different change afoot in the electorate.

They are perhaps the most important, or at least influential, religious group in American politics, given their strong and stable support for the Republican Party for the last 50 years. That loyalty has delivered them tremendous influence within party politics, while Trump, in particular, seems to have had a unique ability to turn these voters out during presidential elections. And at least in this year’s elections, that level of support for the GOP did not drop: they backed Republicans 82-16, consistent with their support for Trump in 2024.

What they didn’t do in 2026 is show up.

Exit polls suggest they made up a smaller share of the electorate when compared to 2026. That suggests a combination of lower turnout and lower enthusiasm may have contributed to Republican losses — even if those who did vote remained firmly Republican.

Still, the national results obscure one other notable trend that Burge, the religion scholar, noted from the 10 congressional districts with the highest share of evangelical voters — notably concentrated in the South (Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana, Oklahoma, and Tennessee). Each of these districts swung left, by an average of 23 points — more than in Catholic or nonevangelical mainline Protestant districts. This suggests stronger turnout and enthusiasm from the non-evangelical portion of these local electorates, which skews more Democratic — and in turn a weaker ability by Republican candidates to turn out evangelical voters in the way that Trump seems like he uniquely can.

In sharp contrast to evangelicals, the oldest but least-healthy strain of American Christianity — the mainline Protestant denominations like Episcopalians, Presbyterians, and Methodists — seems to have delivered a more politically interesting result this year. Many of the House and Senate seats that flipped for the Democrats this year were won by mainline Protestants in Iowa, Kansas, and Texas. They represent what used to be the dominant Christian electorate — which this year demonstrated it could still be a decisive part of a winning Democratic majority.

Heavily mainline districts swung by an average of 15 points toward Democrats, and each of the top eight districts ended up flipping to the Democratic column. The exit polls showed a Democratic gain among Protestants and nonevangelical Christians in general — moving from backing Republicans 63-36 in 2024 to 60-39 this year, a 6-point swing on the margins that can explain these flips.

As these numbers suggest, this is a demographic that seems more ripe for moderate Democratic appeals in the future — though they have been neglected by the establishment left over the last few decades.

We have less data and reliable post-election polling so far on what happened with other parts of the electorate, like Muslim voters, Hindus, and Mormons. What data we do have suggests they all played a part in forming the tidal wave that carried Democrats to their stunning victory last week. But above it all, this year’s results suggest that religious voters can function as swing voters in the post-Trump future, play an influential role in forming winning coalitions, and are not solely the domain of the Republican Party.

title: Denmark ‘moving towards dictatorship’ – MP to RT (VIDEO)
content:
Jacob Harris snubbed Zelensky and accused Copenhagen of prioritizing Ukraine over its own citizens

Denmark is “moving towards a dictatorship,” independent MP Jacob Harris has told RT in an exclusive interview. The Citizen’s Party lawmaker defended his refusal to stand and applaud Vladimir Zelensky during the Ukrainian leader’s controversial address to the Danish parliament.

Harris sat with his arms crossed as other lawmakers gave Zelensky, who openly mocked US President Donald Trump during his speech, a standing ovation on Wednesday. He later posted photos of his protest on X.

His protest was condemned by Danish politicians. Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen called it a provocation, while opposition leader Inger Stojberg accused Harris of “doing [Russian President Vladimir] Putin’s bidding.” 

Et diktatur kommer ikke fra den ene dag til den anden. Det vokser frem gennem tavshed, når befolkningen holder op med at sige fra. Demokratiet kræver, at vi tør stille spørgsmål – også når det er ubelejligt for magthaverne. https://t.co/nl8pinTdEG

— Jacob Harris - Folketingsmedlem (@JParti91252) November 11, 2026

Speaking to RT on Thursday, Harris accused the Danish government of undermining democratic rules by allowing a foreign leader to address parliament from its main podium.

“According to our democratic laws, you have to be elected to the Danish parliament before you are allowed to speak there,” he said.

Harris accused Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of setting aside parliamentary rules for political reasons, calling the decision a move towards dictatorship.

Read more

The Danish parliament has rejected his interpretation, explaining that Zelensky’s address was not a formal parliamentary sitting.

Harris also criticized Copenhagen’s financial support for Kiev, arguing that spending billions on Ukraine while ordinary Danes struggle with rising living costs is “wrong.” 

“People can no longer afford the same standard of living they enjoyed three years ago, and then they see Zelensky come to Denmark and leave with billions,” he told RT.

His remarks came two days after Copenhagen announced another 4.8 billion Danish kroner ($710 million) in military aid for Kiev.

Denmark has committed more than $12.2 billion in military and civilian assistance to Ukraine since 2022, according to its Foreign Ministry. During Zelensky’s visit, Frederiksen reaffirmed Copenhagen’s support, vowing to back Ukraine until the end of the conflict.

Harris met Russian Ambassador to Denmark Vladimir Barbin in Copenhagen on Tuesday, describing their talks as “respectful” and that the two called for a more neutral Danish policy towards the Ukraine conflict. He had also met Ukraine’s ambassador the previous week.

title: Is this the end of the Electoral College?
content:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.

I don’t know how much time you spend in the more feverish right-wing corners of the internet, but some conservative commentators are growing very alarmed about a specific Democratic policy proposal that could be nearing fruition.

It’s not abolishing ICE. It’s not nationalizing grocery stores. It’s not even investigating President Donald Trump over his reported failure to act on intelligence about his newly jobless/disgraced pal, Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang.

Instead, they’re concerned about a wonky electoral workaround called the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, which would essentially sidestep the Electoral College. (And in the words of one right-wing commentator, “effectively [rig] the system so Democrats could never lose again.”) 

NPV isn’t quite as nefarious as that (Trump won the popular vote just two years ago!), though it would revolutionize how the United States conducts presidential elections. The compact is basically an agreement between states to award their electors to the winner of the national popular vote, regardless of how their own state voted. Once enough states sign on, their combined electoral votes would guarantee the presidency to whoever wins the national popular vote.

The compact has laid dormant for two decades, however, while its backers lobby to sign on more states and their electoral votes. Eighteen states and Washington, DC, have signed on thus far, representing 222 votes. 

But with Democrats soon controlling state governments in Arizona, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, NPV could finally gain the critical mass to become reality. Politico reported on Tuesday that lawmakers in several states, including Pennsylvania, are already discussing the possibility.

There’s just one problem: Conservative influencers aren’t the only ones worried about the plan. In fact, even one of its architects has come to regard NPV as a “doomsday machine” that could trigger gigantic constitutional problems.

Go a little deeper

View Link

My colleague Andrew Prokop called up this conflicted architect, the Yale University professor Akhil Amar, earlier this week. Andrew has been writing and thinking about NPV for years. But Amar has been thinking about it even longer — since the aftermath of the 2000 election that made George W. Bush president. 

Famously, Bush was elected even though he lost the popular vote, which Al Gore won by roughly half a percentage point. Amar thought the Electoral College was historically and inherently flawed, but only a constitutional amendment could abolish it. 

Recognizing the long odds there, Amar and his brother instead sketched out a quick thought experiment — the broad strokes of what is now the NPV compact. The concept was later picked up and championed by the computer scientist John Koza and his group National Popular Vote Inc.

Koza has had quite a lot of success getting states to sign on to this workaround. But all the signees so far have leaned Democratic, which concerns Amar. The institution of the Electoral College doesn’t inherently favor one party over the other (in fact, both parties nearly got rid of it after the 1968 election), and the NPV wasn’t designed to tilt the scales, either. But as the discourse on right-wing social media suggests, Trump’s 2016 victory with a popular vote minority has only further hardened views on each side, and all the Democratic signatories have made it look like a partisan proposition. 

There’s another problem too, Amar says. The compact leaves each participating state to calculate the national total, without a centralized body to oversee a nationwide count or recount. A very close election could leave states disagreeing over who won. But in the current environment, it’s actually hard to imagine a centralized body that both parties would find credible: People just don’t trust institutions the way they did in, say, 2000. 

That puts NPV advocates in a tricky spot: The political process may finally favor the compact, but it faces significant cultural problems that could undermine its legitimacy. 

Amar, for his part, thinks that even the small risk of electoral disruption outweighs the benefits of NPV. Especially since the Electoral College does actually work, whatever its shortcomings. 

“The one thing we really do need to avoid as the stabilizing superpower in the world is constitutional chaos,” he told Vox. “And because this is sort of a new plan, even if it’s in principle likely to be better in all sorts of scenarios, if in a certain small percentage of cases it would lead to chaos, that’s something we need [to] seriously consider.”

One link for later

➨ Stop subway scrolling. If social media feels exhausting and overwhelming to you — which it does to me, often — try to stop logging on from public places. “People feel more lonely when they use social media while in transit, around people they have close relationships with, and when they are in nature,” says Vox contributor Shayla Love. “In contrast, when people use social media for shorter periods when they are alone at home or in study locations, it doesn’t have as much of a negative effect.”

Before you go…

  • Did you know…that the invention of fabrics like Spandex and Lycra changed not only what we wear — but when and how we wear it? With the advent of stretchy fabrics, Parisian fashion houses and the silhouettes they designed lost some of their influence. 
  • Today’s trivia: What type of nymphs live in trees, as opposed to water, caves or clouds? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword. Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.)
  • Yesterday’s trivia: Yesterday we asked you what type of music Leontyne Price performed. That would be opera: Price, now 99, was among the first Black American opera singers to achieve acclaim around the world.

title: Fantasy vs. reality: The confusion of the willing and Ukraine peace talks
content:
‘Europe’ now has a seat at the negotiating table, now the challenge will be to speak with one voice

In their most recent talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner apparently secured a place for ‘Europe’ at the negotiating table with Russia. European leaders will have to overcome deep factional divides and square away their most ideologically-driven fantasists to have any influence over the talks.

“The Europeans will join at the next meeting, which we consider to be a very important moment,” Witkoff told reporters in Moscow on Thursday, before he and Kushner departed for Ireland to brief Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky and his EU backers. 

The Kremlin has not set a date for the next round of talks, nor has Moscow confirmed the precise extent of European participation. However, as Kushner pointed out the previous day, Europe has a more immediate problem on its hands : “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf,” he said, “that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiation.”

The US president’s son-in-law is not the first American to express bewilderment at the absence of a common voice in Europe, and there will likely be much talk around this question now that the invitation has been secured by US President Donald Trump’s diplomatic team. So who is “Europe”? 

Rumsfeld’s “New Europe”

After Danish Foreign Minister Knud Borge Andersen met with US Secretary of State Henry Kissinger on behalf of the nine-member EEC in 1973, Kissinger complained that Andersen seemed to speak for Europe, but lacked any real authority to do so. “We seem to be talking to those who can’t negotiate and those who can negotiate won’t talk to us,” he remarked.

Three decades later, Donald Rumsfeld faced staunch opposition from Belgium, France, and Germany as he attempted to drum up European backing for the illegal invasion of Iraq. However, he received salivating support from Britain, Italy, Poland, and the so-called ‘Vilnius Ten’ – a Baltic and Eastern European bloc with a civil society throbbing with American cash – that enthusiastically signed up to combat “the nexus of terrorism and dictators with weapons of mass destruction.”

The newbies, Rumsfeld figured, were the only Europeans worth talking to. “You’re thinking of ‘Europe’ as Germany and France,” he told a reporter six weeks before the war. “I don’t. I think that’s old Europe. If you look at the entire NATO Europe today, the center of gravity is shifting to the east.”

Who is “Europe” now?

The fault lines identified by Rumsfeld are still visible, and there are three broad camps competing for the position of “voice of Europe.”

The realists

‘Europe’ and ‘foreign policy realism’ rarely appear in the same sentence these days, but among some of “old Europe’s” leaders, there is a realization that the continent will have to acknowledge the limits of its pro-Ukraine stance and take part in talks, before it is overtaken by them.

French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni could be considered figureheads, with Macron proposing last December that Europe find an envoy “in the coming weeks.” Meloni declared that the French president “is right on this,” and that “if Europe decides to take part in this phase of negotiations by talking only to one of the two sides, I fear that in the end the positive contribution it can make will be limited.”

Read more

Even German Chancellor Friedrich Merz – despite pivoting his economy into militarization mode and demanding the EU steal billions of Russian sovereign assets – has called on the bloc to “find a balance again with our largest European neighbor.”

Finnish President Alexander Stubb, floated in EU-funded media as a possible envoy to Moscow, along with Meloni, joined Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Store to call Putin last month.

“Realism” is a relative term here. All of the aforementioned leaders remain committed to arming Ukraine and pushing for peace on Kiev’s terms, while support for the theft of Russia’s assets remains strong across the EU. Stubb and Store offered “no change in Europe’s approach” to Ukraine during their phone call, according to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever has also placed himself in the realist camp, arguing that seizing the €210 billion ($236 billion) worth of Russian assets, a move he has blocked, would collapse trust in the European financial system.

The maximalists

The golden children of Rumsfeld’s “new Europe” are full-throttle maximalists. They consider any talks with Russia a betrayal of Ukraine, and remain determined to fight, as Putin has said, “to the last Ukrainian.”

Read more

Their poster boy, Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski, reacted with shock when Kushner announced last week that he and Trump were working on an agreement that would “address the security concerns of all sides” in Europe. He told reporters that “the last thing we want is Western Europe dealing with Russia, over the heads of the east Europeans.”

The belief that Ukraine can inflict a military defeat on Russia is a core tenet of European maximalism. Latvian President Edgars Rinkevics made this clear in 2024 when he openly stated “Russia must be destroyed.” Sikorski’s calls for “aggressive” NATO exercises to destabilize Russia’s exclave of Kaliningrad, former Lithuanian Foreign Minister Gabrielius Landsbergis’ demand that NATO leaders remove “all red lines and de-escalation policies” on Russia, and Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal’s likening of Putin to a “rat in a corner” are just three examples of the maximalist rhetoric radiating from Eastern Europe and the Baltics.

Moscow views these “new Europeans” as hysterical, reactionary, and paranoid. Even the US has told them to pipe down, with Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby reportedly ordering the Baltic states last month not to “make noise” and stop “poking” Russia.

To the maximalists, even symbolic outreach to Moscow is unconscionable. After Stubb and Store spoke to Putin last month, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen complained that the call had “not been coordinated with the rest of us,” referring to a group reportedly including her and Swedish Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, two of the most hardline anti-Russian voices in the EU.

The fantasists

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas wield significantly more power than their predecessors did when Rumsfeld toured Europe in 2003. Von der Leyen has no electorate to answer to, nor has she authority to dictate policy, however she likes to present herself in such a light.  

Read more

The commission still relies on unanimity among the EU’s member states to approve its loans, aid packages, and sanctions, and it has no military power to back up its diktats and proclamations. Brussels and NATO are, however, steadily coalescing in ever closer union.

What the commission has are appeals to fantasy. Von der Leyen has insisted that the EU have veto power over any potential peace deal negotiated between Moscow, Kiev, and Washington, that Ukraine be allowed to keep its pre-conflict borders, and that Moscow be forced to pay reparations to Kiev.

Kallas’ position is even more loosely tethered to reality, with her repeated calls for representation at the negotiating table interspersed with quotes from Marvel superhero movies – “Europeans, assemble!” – and suggestions to dismember Russia into “many smaller nations.”

Von der Leyen’s and Kallas’ hubris has ruled them out as negotiators – both in the eyes of the Kremlin and their fellow Europeans. “How can you discuss anything with Kaja Kallas?” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov remarked to reporters earlier this year. Brussels, he added, is full of “semi-literate, incompetent functionaries.”

A reckoning in Dublin

A compromise in Dublin

European Council President Antonio Costa followed through on his promise to discuss the creation of an envoy during talks at the EU’s summit in Dublin this week. However, the compromise he reached with EU leaders will leave nobody satisfied. Instead of a single envoy, ‘Europe’ will be represented by France, Germany, Italy, Poland and the UK at the national security adviser level, and by the European Commission and Council at leader-level discussions.

Despite selecting seven separate entities, which include all three European factions – realists, maximalists, and fantasists – Costa insisted that the panel of interlocutors will be able “to speak with one voice.”

Read more

Moscow on maximalists and fantasists

Russia maintains that it is open to serious discussions, but Peskov noted on Wednesday that “for the moment, the statements we hear from the Europeans do not indicate any desire on their part to contribute to progress along a peaceful path.”

“They [top European politicians] are engaged in a group deception of the Ukrainian people. They finance and supply one of the fighting sides with weapons… It contributes to the mass death of the civilian population. And therefore, we do not really understand what we can talk about with them,” Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky told journalists after the Abu Dhabi talks concluded on Wednesday.

title: Progress made in Ukraine peace talks – Russian deputy FM
content:
European involvement could derail diplomatic efforts, Sergey Ryabkov has told RT

The two-day trilateral talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi this week have brought progress toward settling the Ukraine conflict, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov has told RT in an exclusive interview. However, involving European governments in the process could undermine diplomatic efforts, he warned.

Ryabkov was among the Russian delegates at the negotiations, which concluded on Wednesday with an agreement in principle on a major prisoner exchange. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner subsequently traveled to Moscow, where they met Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday for talks lasting around two and a half hours.

Ryabkov noted that the latest round in Abu Dhabi differed from previous meetings, with American representatives seeking to make discussions more concrete. Much of the attention focused on a future European security architecture that could support a lasting settlement and prevent “uncontrolled escalation,” he said.

“We have made progress. That is an indisputable fact,” Ryabkov said, while cautioning that previous diplomatic advances had been followed by setbacks and attempts to derail the process.

“Bringing the Europeans into the negotiating process could mean a reversal and the disruption of efforts,” the diplomat warned.

He pointed to a fundamental divide between European governments and both Moscow and Washington, adding that they rejected Russia’s approach and appeared equally opposed to proposals advanced by the US administration.

Read more

Ryabkov said that European governments had shown “not the slightest desire to exercise common sense” while continuing to recklessly support Kiev. He described the gap between their declared support for a settlement and their actual policies as one rooted in “hypocrisy and lies.”

Those who had previously sought to derail diplomatic efforts should recognize that the situation is changing “not in Kiev’s favor” and draw lessons from past setbacks, the Russian diplomat said.

Western European representatives were not part of the trilateral negotiations, although they held separate consultations with the American and Ukrainian teams. On Wednesday, Vladimir Zelensky demanded that European countries agree on a representative to join the peace process by the end of November.

Moscow has repeatedly questioned Europe’s credibility, citing its continued military and financial support for Kiev and calls for Russia’s strategic defeat. It has also rejected calls for an unconditional ceasefire coming from Brussels, arguing that such a pause would allow Ukrainian forces to regroup and rearm.

Putin also addressed the issue on Thursday, telling Witkoff and Kushner that Russia wanted Washington to work with European governments to establish whether they sought peace or war. He also reiterated Moscow’s opposition to foreign troops in Ukraine, warning that their presence would threaten Russian national security and make them legitimate military targets.

title: The disturbing reality behind America’s milk and cheese — and the fight to end it
content:
This story is part of a series supported by Animal Charity Evaluators, which received a grant from EarthShare.

Deep-blue, regulation-happy California is not usually imagined as factory farm country. But the state leads the US in agricultural output, and it is, by a wide margin, America’s top producer of dairy, one of the most brutal sectors in our food system. And it turns out that one of the most foundational, most disturbing practices found in modern dairy farming may already be illegal under a California animal cruelty law — but state officials have shown little inclination to look into it. 

At any given time, 9 million to 10 million dairy cows populate farms across the US, and California is home to 1.7 million of them, the vast majority of whom are raised on mega dairies. Because cows, like other mammals, must give birth to produce milk, dairy farming is organized around continuous cycles of pregnancy, birth, and lactation. Dairy cows typically give birth around once a year; their calves are then promptly taken from them. Depending on their sex, the calves will eventually join a milking herd or be raised for beef. 

But whatever their ultimate market destination, the overwhelming majority of baby cows born in the dairy industry, in California and nationwide, spend their first few months of life housed alone, in individual crates or enclosures. Many of them look like this: 

Earlier this year, I wrote at length about that practice. These wooden crates provide each calf about 13 square feet of living space, less than one-tenth the size of a typical parking spot. “We’re talking roughly the size of a coffin,” Vanessa Shakib, a lawyer and co-founder of the Los Angeles-area nonprofit Advancing Law for Animals, told me. Confining calves in this manner is not dissimilar to the use of gestation crates in the pork industry — tiny metal enclosures where pigs barely have room to move. Gestation crates have sparked intense national controversy that’s reached the halls of Congress and the US Supreme Court. But the extreme confinement of dairy calves has not received anywhere close to as much legal and political scrutiny. 

In California, there’s an obvious legal problem with calf crates. The state has a plain-English law, Section 597t of its criminal code, that mandates that confined animals be provided an “adequate exercise area.” Though it doesn’t define what constitutes such an area, Shakib and other farm animal advocates argue that it strains credulity to believe the minuscule, barren crates provide one. The practice “is squarely at odds with the plain meaning of the words,” Shakib said. 

But California has never enforced that law against calf crates in the state’s powerful dairy industry, where millions of newborn calves have been kept in extreme confinement (nor, apparently, has the law been enforced against any factory farm). It’s a prime example of agricultural exceptionalism — the doctrine running through American legal and political culture, as Vox’s Kenny Torrella has written, that effectively absolves agribusiness from having to play by the same rules as everyone else. 

Shakib and her organization are now hoping to change that. 

They’re leading a lawsuit against Hettinga Dairy, a Southern California farm that has kept thousands of calves in individual crates, alleging that it’s violating Section 597t. If the case succeeds, it could create a blueprint for similar challenges statewide, and even spark a broader reckoning within America’s dairy industry. 

The case that could transform how dairy calves are treated

Advancing Law for Animals just filed suit on behalf of the Caru Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, a California animal protection nonprofit seeking a court ruling that the calf crates violate state law. The case names Hettinga Dairy and related defendants in connection with a  San Jacinto, California, facility that specializes in raising calves. The most recent available records from California’s State Water Resources Control Board report the farm’s animal population as 4,200 calves. 

Such facilities, often known as “calf ranches” or “calf nurseries,” have become increasingly central to the US dairy business — as we wrote earlier this year, they “raise calves on dairy farms’ behalf during the fragile infant stage in which they’re too young to bring in any revenue.” 

Caru SPCA (which is formerly known as the Animal Legal Defense Fund Cruelty Prevention Unit) flew drone cameras over the Hettinga facility earlier this year to document the calf housing there, filming the small wooden crates that are common in California and the Southwest, typically providing less than 15 square feet of space per calf. Many dairy farms and calf ranches use a different, plastic hutch design that provides more space, but the smaller wooden hutches remain widespread. 

Calves typically spend about two months in these hutches before being moved into larger group pens; the lawsuit alleges that Hettinga keeps them in crates for around nine weeks. 

“Calves are trapped for months, even in summer heat, unable to stretch their limbs or move freely,” the lawsuit alleges. Under 597t, “animals have a statutory right to minimal movement, and Defendants systematically violate that right daily, creating immense and ongoing suffering.”

That San Jacinto farm is part of a broader network of dairy farms and calf-raising facilities linked to the Hettingas, a prominent dairy family whose farms collectively confine thousands of calves and cows across California, according to state public records. Most consumers have never heard of Hettinga, nor of the hundreds of other industrial dairies and calf-raising farms across California that operate largely out of public view. But the Hettingas also have a presence on grocery store shelves: According to the brand’s website, the family also owns Sarah Farms, a mass-market milk label in the Southwestern US.

Vox emailed a list of questions about the allegations in the lawsuit to multiple contacts associated with Hettinga businesses. An employee at GH Processing, a Hettinga family-associated dairy plant in Arizona, confirmed receiving the email and said she would pass it on to colleagues in California. No one responded to Vox’s questions by publication time. 

A representative from the California water board told Vox that the 2024 annual report for the San Jacinto calf facility identified Hein and Ellen Hettinga as the farm’s operators. But state regulators have not received the 2025 report, which was due in January 2026, and could not verify the facility’s current ownership. Hein Hettinga, who built the family’s dairy empire, died in 2023; Ellen, his wife, is one of the defendants named in the lawsuit. 

Dairy industry trade groups often defend calf crates, arguing that they allow farmers to provide each animal with individualized care and reduce their exposure to pathogens. Whether that’s true is contested — some industry veterinarians endorse that view, while others maintain that it’s based on a narrow view of calves’ well-being and that properly managed social housing need not harm their physical health. Even within the industry, there’s growing acknowledgement that isolation is harmful to calves, and that it would be better for dairy farms to transition to a different system. 

A 2023 assessment of calf welfare from the European Food Safety Authority — the EU agency that provides scientific guidance on animal welfare — found “no locomotor play behavior possible” for calves given a space allowance of about 16 square feet each. A calf in such confinement “is expected to spend most of its time lying down because no other activities can be performed,” the review states. To fully express natural behaviors like galloping, jumping, and kicking, it recommends that calves housed alone be allotted 318 square feet each, and calves housed in groups be allotted 215 square feet each, though it notes that even smaller increases in space could meaningfully improve their welfare. 

Guidelines from Calf Care and Quality Assurance, a US industry-created animal care program, state that “individually housed calves have a harder time coping with changes in housing and diet and may have cognitive and developmental disadvantages, including poor learning skills and deficient social skills.” Temple Grandin, the famed livestock scientist at Colorado State University, has written that “calves should be raised with other calves, not in isolation.” They are, after all, intensely social herd animals. 

Regardless of the industry’s opinion on the practice, though, 597t makes no exception for livestock industry standard practices, the way some states’ animal cruelty laws do. “It doesn’t matter whether this defendant or whether the dairy industry believes solitary confinement of baby animals serves a useful purpose,” Shakib said. “California law here is crystal clear — it requires an adequate exercise area. Industry custom or convenience does not erase that requirement.”

California’s animal cruelty double standard

The ubiquitous confinement of dairy calves in tiny crates remains poorly understood by the general public, and even, to some extent, within the animal protection movement. That is because, for many years, animal advocates focused their campaigning against extreme confinement in the dairy industry on veal, the notorious specialty meat made from male dairy calves.

Those efforts helped bring about California’s Proposition 12, a landmark law passed in 2018 that bans certain forms of extreme confinement, including tiny crates that used to be the norm in veal production. Any veal raised or sold in California must now come from calves allotted at least 43 square feet of living space each. But the overwhelming share of California’s dairy calves are not raised for veal and thus get no protection under Prop 12, even as many members of the public may assume the problem of extreme confinement of calves has been solved. 

In the last few years, however, a small wave of animal advocates have been drawing attention to the continued plight of dairy calves. The animal rights group Direct Action Everywhere (DxE) over the last year has documented and mapped calf confinement across California, including at Grimmius Cattle Company, the largest calf raiser in the state and the subject of Vox’s earlier reporting. This fall, DxE investigator Lewis Bernier obtained footage showing calves from a dairy farm that the group said supplies to Land O’Lakes being transported to Grimmius, where the newborn animals are raised in the same standard, approximately 13-square-foot wooden hutches. Land O’Lakes did not respond to requests for comment. 

The crates aren’t the only problem

Beyond extreme confinement in crates,  DxE’s investigations have surfaced allegations of overt abuse of calves — including animals being kicked, punched, and pulled by their ears and tails — at calf ranches and dairy farms throughout California.

Drone footage taken earlier this year at a dairy farm that DxE linked to Leprino Foods — a major cheese supplier that reportedly sells to Domino’s, Papa John’s, and Pizza Hut, among others — shows calves being kicked, pushed, pulled by their ears, and thrown to the ground. In one clip, a calf appears to be kicked in the face. One of DxE’s investigators followed a milk truck from that farm to a Leprino plant, the group said. Leprino Foods did not respond to requests for comment. 

DxE has also captured drone footage of calf and dairy facilities that California records list as operated by members of the Hettinga family, separate from the one that is being sued by Advancing Law for Animals. At one of the calf ranches, in San Bernardino County, Robert Drummond, a member of DxE’s Los Angeles chapter, filmed handlers who appear to be whipping frightened calves and pulling them by their tails. Hitting calves and pulling them this way are both considered “unacceptable” handling practices by the industry’s own calf-raising guidelines. DxE reported those findings to the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department, which did not provide comment for this story. 

An annual report filed with the California water board identifies Gerben Hettinga as the operator of that farm, a representative from the agency told Vox. Vox attempted to reach Hettinga using the email addresses and phone number listed for him in state records but received no response.

Advancing Law for Animals’ lawsuit is not the first time animal advocates have accused California’s dairy industry of violating 597t. “There’s a long history of animal activists and organizations trying unsuccessfully to enforce this law,” Will Lowrey, founder and legal counsel at animal advocacy legal nonprofit Animal Partisan, told me in an email. His organization has also sought enforcement of 597t in the dairy industry. 

DxE has sent criminal complaints about calf crates, citing 597t, to eight law enforcement agencies throughout California; the group says that none of them have taken enforcement action. In March, the sheriff’s office of Tulare County, in the heart of the Central Valley’s dairy industry, rejected one of these complaints and stated in its reply to DxE that calf confinement did not violate the law because “the facilities reviewed do not raise calves for veal production.” But 597t doesn’t exclusively apply to veal; it applies to all confined animals. The sheriff’s office may have confused it with Prop 12. The office did not respond to a request for comment.

DxE has also met with California Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office about calf confinement, and office staff asked the group questions about its investigative findings, DxE director of communications Cassie King told me. Responding to Vox’s request for comment about whether 13-square-foot crates are permissible under 597t, the attorney general’s press office said, “we cannot provide a comment at this time.” DxE plans to rally outside Bonta’s office in Sacramento this week calling for enforcement of that law against Grimmius Cattle Company. The group submitted a packet of documents to the attorney general, including a statement from more than a dozen veterinarians about the animal welfare harms of small calf crates.   

“The California dairy industry seems inclined to act like [597t] doesn’t exist and no law enforcement officer, prosecutor, or judge that I have come across seems inclined to enforce the law as written,” Lowrey wrote to me. “It’s hard to imagine that this is for any other reason than deference to the state agriculture industry.” 

The law enforcement officials that have rejected these complaints haven’t explained how calf crates could satisfy 597t’s requirement for an adequate exercise area; they largely sidestep the question altogether. For non-livestock animals, meanwhile, California has enforced the law more readily. A state appeals court recently upheld 597t convictions against two people who had continuously kept German shepherds in kennels measuring 48 to 50 square feet. For hundreds of thousands of calves kept in cages one-quarter of that size, though, the protections offered by California’s animal cruelty laws have proven illusory. 

Police and prosecutors have broad discretion to decline to pursue criminal complaints, but a lawsuit like Caru SPCA’s may be harder to brush aside. The question will now be addressed by a judge, and California’s dairy industry could finally face an on-the-merits ruling on whether these crates are legal. “At some point, I believe a judge will find that the law says what it says and will decide that a California dairy keeping calves in hutches [is] in violation of Penal Code 597t,” Lowrey wrote. “It’s just a matter of time and maybe—hopefully—Caru v. Hettinga is that case.”   

It’s understandable that state officials may hesitate to enforce a law that could upend a linchpin of the dairy industry, whose products are consumed by nearly every American and woven into virtually every corner of our food system. But animal agriculture has a long history of warning that animal welfare regulations will devastate its business, only to adapt when regulation takes effect. 

And although California has earned its reputation for overly burdensome regulation in other domains, giving newborn calves enough room to move hardly seems like an unreasonable imposition (especially considering that dairy farming makes up only a tiny share of the state’s massive economy). Freeing them from this form of solitary confinement would amount to one of the most consequential animal welfare advances in California’s history. And it need not require passing any new laws — the state merely needs to hold the dairy industry to a standard already in place.

title: Dublin summit: European leaders double down on the Zelensky disaster
content:
With Moscow absent and peace efforts elsewhere advancing, the gathering was just a show of stubborn loyalty to a failing proxy war

Let’s start with the obvious, which, oddly enough, remains largely unnoticed: If the summit of the European Political Community (EPC), a formally informal gathering that brings together the high and mighty of NATO-EU Europe plus friends, was serious about reflecting Europe, then Russia (and, by the way, Belarus, too) would have been invited.

The fact that Moscow is not present is, once you think about it, a striking anomaly, even if Western mainstream media framing has been quite effective at making the obviously strange appear to be the new normal.

Russia’s longstanding exclusion is, of course, also very telling. At the risk of re-stating the obvious, it reflects NATO-EU Europe’s fundamentally flawed, catastrophically costly (including for Ukraine), and very obstinate policy of waging a proxy war against Russia, while using up Ukraine and Ukrainians.

It’s a shame: Europe could have been the ideal framework for preventing, or at least quickly ending, the Ukraine War by offering honest mediation, facilitating real compromise, and, last but not least, helping review and revise a continental security structure destabilized and, in effect, ruined by a reckless NATO expansion based on brazen Western cheating.

Yet, unsurprisingly, NATO-EU Europe has always done the opposite: from being too arrogant to listen to Russian President Vladimir Putin’s clear warning in Munich in 2007, through the foul compromise of the Bucharest summit one year later and the perfectly misguided EU Association Agreement designed to force Kiev to make an impossible choice between the EU and Russia, to taking over from Washington as the main proxy war promoter and key obstacle to peace – NATO-EU Europe has a consistent record of making things go awfully wrong and then making them worse and worse again.

Read more

In that sense, the great Dublin let’s-all-hate-on-Russia-some-more fest is simply very boring. But there are aspects to it that – notwithstanding its makers’ and participants’ worst intentions – merit attention.

Take, for instance, French President Emmanuel Macron’s open announcement that the US has left its European vassals (not Macron’s words, of course, but let’s make him a little more honest) holding the Ukraine War bag all on their own. Strictly speaking, Macron, as is so often the case, is not factually correct: Zelensky’s recurring complaints about Starlink/Starshield slowdowns are only possible because these massive US resources, for instance, are still – wrongly – made available to his regime, hellbent as it is on escalating open warfare far beyond Ukraine.

If only Washington had really fully retreated from the proxy war! Perhaps the war would be over already, and many Ukrainians and Russians would still be alive.

Yet Macron’s slightly hysterical misreading of US behavior does betray something very real, namely an acute and deep sense of abandonment among Washington’s vassals. One day, probably far in the future, some of them may even begin to draw the correct conclusions from it.

But today is not that day. Instead, it seems that the Dublin summit’s main message regarding its proxy war and the authoritarian, man-hunting, ultra-corrupt Zelensky regime deployed to manage it on the ground is “stay the course.”

Halfway self-respecting proxy war sponsors would long have refused to touch Zelensky with a bargepole – “here’s the money but we really can’t be seen with you” – due to his regime’s outrageous and essentially open embezzlement of their funds (they do not care about his massive brutalization of ordinary Ukrainians, it goes without saying). Not a week goes by without another “Mindich,” “Carthage,” “Khimprom,” or “Sokolov” mega-scandal.

Read more

And yet, the opposite is happening. In Dublin, too, the boss of bosses of the rapacious and quite murderous crime syndicate that the Zelensky regime really is gets the VIP treatment. And, of course, also license to lecture anyone in sight on what they must do and owe “Ukraine,” that is, him and his cronies. Nothing has changed.

What may be even worse, Zelensky is also permitted – or, most likely, encouraged, for instance by his most submissive fan, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz – to publicly gripe at a recent key shift in serious diplomacy about ending the Ukraine War: alert to dangers to his income streams, power, and political survival, Ukraine’s de facto dictator has used Dublin to complain about, in essence, Washington’s apparent willingness to finally take seriously Russia’s demand for a comprehensive review of security structures. And yet without that, peace won’t come.

Zelensky’s unshaken – at least in public – permission to play dissatisfied-consumer-from-hell and berate his sponsors is even more remarkable as the Dublin summit is being held against an international context with which it clashes profoundly. Consider a few places and what they stand for regarding the Ukraine War: Abu Dhabi, Moscow, and, soon probably, Shenzhen. Different as the specific formats are or will be, what they all have in common is that real if not yet successful work is done or likely to be done there to bring peace about.

And yet, quite like their creature Zelensky, the NATO-EU establishments resist precisely that outcome. It is true that we are seeing signs of – auspicious – disunity. Norway and Finland, for instance, have emitted weak but intriguing signals of rediscovering a sense of reality.

Yet, overall and as of now, Dublin shows us another, still dominant side of NATO-EU Europe: too weak and too submissive to Washington to be a power on its own in the emerging multipolar order, but hellbent to use all its resources to be a spoiler. It is sad to have to say this as a genuine European, but NATO-EU Europe is a caricature of our common identity. If there’s hope, it lies in its weakness.
