title: US no longer needs Iran deal – Trump
content:
The president has redirected J.D. Vance toward domestic issues after the vice president blamed the conflict for Republicans’ midterm defeat

Washington no longer needs a deal with Iran, US President Donald Trump has declared. He has directed Vice President J.D. Vance to focus instead on alleged corruption and crime in Democrat-run states and cities.

The announcement follows Vance’s criticism of the US-Israeli war on Iran, which he blamed for Republicans’ defeat in last week’s midterm elections. On Wednesday, the vice president questioned whether the conflict had been worth its cost. Vance had previously pursued diplomatic efforts to end the war and reportedly favored reaching an agreement with Tehran over continued military pressure.

In a Truth Social post on Thursday, Trump ordered Vance to devote his “complete and total attention” to tackling the domestic issue, arguing that a sweeping corruption crackdown could help balance the federal budget.

“We don’t need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed,” Trump wrote. “We’ve got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we’ve got their Strait!”

Read more

Trump offered no explanation for his claim about Iranian money, which some media outlets have interpreted as a reference to frozen Iranian assets. Tehran estimates the funds at more than $100 billion, largely consisting of oil and gas revenues held in foreign banks under US sanctions.

His assertion of control over the Strait of Hormuz appears to refer to the US naval blockade, which restricts shipping to and from Iranian ports while allowing vessels serving other Gulf countries to pass.

On Monday, Trump said he would hold off on further strikes against Iran after Gulf states urged Washington to avoid another escalation.

Iran, however, has also asserted its authority over the strategic waterway.

Iran’s parliament speaker and chief negotiator, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, told Al Jazeera on Wednesday that Tehran had reached an understanding with Oman on managing the strait as part of its seven-point peace proposal.

Read more

Ghalibaf insisted that Hormuz would “never return” to its pre-war status, when foreign vessels could transit without Iranian permission. Tehran is now seeking greater control over shipping through the vital oil trade route.

The Iranian official said Tehran had submitted its peace terms through Qatari mediators but had yet to receive a formal response from Washington.

The proposal calls for lifting US sanctions and the naval blockade, releasing frozen Iranian assets and ending hostilities across the region.

“The ball is now in the American court,” Ghalibaf said.

title: 5 People Shot in Washington D.C. Before Shooter Turned Gun on Himself
content:
By Savannah Hulsey Pointer

A gunman on Nov. 12 shot five people, killing one, in Washington’s Logan Circle neighborhood before turning the gun on himself.

Police told reporters at around 10.30 a.m. that officers discovered the gunman suffering from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

The neighborhood is within walking distance of the White House.

At around 11 a.m., a barricade around the scene was lifted, but the Metropolitan Police Department (MPD) asked the public to avoid the area for the time being.

One victim, who was shot at a gym, died from his injuries.

Jeffery W. Carroll, the Interim Chief of Police of the MPD, told reporters that of the four surviving victims, only one had life-threatening injuries.

The suspect was barricaded in the vicinity of the initial shooting, and a SWAT team responded to the area.

A witness, James Spellman, said he heard shots fired shortly after 8 a.m. at the gym, which held about 50 people.

“Within seconds, there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” he said. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”

According to Spellman, he and others at the gym ran outside, where they heard more gunfire in the area of 15th Street.

Police said the gunman is a white male, and they believe they know who he is and that he had a conflict with the homeowner’s association of the apartment building in which he had barricaded himself.

“They’ve been talking to him for over the past hour again, attempting to try to resolve the situation,” Carroll said.

“Just moments ago, while communicating with that individual, officers heard a gunshot … officers forced entry, and located the suspect suffering from a gunshot wound.”

“We do believe that the suspect is now contained in that location,” the police chief said.

Carroll said that investigation is still ongoing, but that officers have cleared the apartment where the shooter was barricaded.

D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser said she was “devastated” by news of the shooting, saying “someone was killed in our city this morning in a senseless act of gun violence.”

She also confirmed that the White House has been briefed. In response to a question, she said she “praised MPD for bringing down crime in the city, and I praise our prosecutors.”

“I am very grateful to MPD and fire and EMS who responded immediately, quickly, and contained this situation,” Bowser said.

title: US Condo Sellers Far Outnumber Buyers in September: Redfin
content:
By Mary Prenon

Potential homeowners seeking to purchase a condo could have the strongest negotiating power in more than a decade.

A Nov. 9 Redfin report showed that sellers in the condo market outnumbered buyers by an estimated 123 percent in September, up from 95.5 percent in the same month last year and marking the biggest seller surplus since 2013.

This is a significant reversal from the COVID-19 pandemic years when there were 25.1 percent fewer sellers than buyers in September 2021, according to the report.

The estimated number of condo buyers was about 88,460 in September—a 2.5 percent decline from August and the lowest level in at least 13 years. Meanwhile, there were 197,248 condo sellers—an uptick of 0.9 percent from August.

The report said rising insurance premiums, homeowners’ association (HOA) fees, and special assessments are eroding the affordability advantages condos have over single-family homes for first-time homebuyers, particularly in hurricane-prone states such as Florida and Texas.

An Oct. 16 report from Hippo Insurance estimated that, nationally, condo owners typically pay lower insurance premiums than a standard homeowner’s policy for single-family homes because the HOA master policy covers the building structure.

However, condo owners in Florida pay annual insurance premiums of $600 to $1,400, the highest in the country, compared with $200 to $380 in Arizona, the lowest nationwide.

“The factors that move your price most are location risk, how much personal property coverage you choose, and how much interior dwelling coverage you carry based on your HOA’s policy type,” the report noted.

According to HOAFeeCalculator.com, an online financial tool, HOA fees can vary substantially across states, depending on weather conditions, structure type, state mandates, and regional labor rates.

Hawaii had some of the highest HOA fees, averaging $790 per month, followed by New York at $480 and California at $450. Mississippi and Arkansas had the lowest average fees, at $140 and $145 per month, respectively.

“Although condo prices and HOA fees remain relatively high, buyers have more room to negotiate price cuts, and condos are still generally more affordable than single-family homes,” Redfin senior economist Asad Khan said.

“For renters who have saved for a down payment and are ready to build equity, these buyer-friendly conditions are an opportunity.”

The report noted the national median sales price for condos declined by 0.8 percent to about $339,000 in September—the first annual decrease in five months.

It also indicated that sellers were lowering asking prices to attract more buyers. Nearly 37 percent of condos sold in September had price reductions, compared with just 16 percent during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Regionally, San Antonio, Texas, had the widest gap between sellers and buyers, with an estimated 459 percent more sellers than buyers. Houston, Miami, and Austin followed with 322 percent, 273.6 percent, and 258 percent more sellers than buyers, respectively.

Miami, Florida, also has a significant seller surplus in the condo market, with about 274 percent more sellers than buyers.

Meanwhile, Nassau County, New York, was the only metro area considered a seller’s market among the 50 analyzed. The Long Island county had 32 percent fewer sellers than buyers.

Redfin also noted that the single-family market mirrored the condo trend in September, with sellers outnumbering buyers by 53.7 percent, although the gap was much narrower.

title: Trump floats Tim Cook as Nvidia chief after ‘Chinese honeypot’ scandal
content:
The US president has suggested the former Apple CEO as a successor to Jensen Huang, who resigned following reports of two affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for Beijing

US President Donald Trump has suggested that former Apple CEO Tim Cook take over Nvidia following the resignation of its longtime chief Jensen Huang, who stepped down after reports of two extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China

“A legend replaces a legend!” Trump wrote, floating Cook, who now chairs Apple’s board, as a potential successor to Huang. The American president had previously defended Huang as “an amazing guy,” saying he believed that the executive had been unaware of the alleged espionage.

Trump and Cook have maintained ties for years, with the president previously claiming that the Apple executive had called him to “kiss my ass” while seeking help during his first term. In August 2025, Cook visited Trump in the Oval Office, presenting him with a plaque featuring a 24-karat gold base as Apple announced plans to increase its US investment commitment to $600 billion over four years. Trump later praised Cook as an “incredible guy,” describing their relationship as “long and very nice.”

Nvidia announced on Thursday that Huang had stepped down as president, chief executive, and board member “effective immediately,” ending his 33-year tenure. Finance chief Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while Nvidia seeks a permanent replacement.

The crisis erupted over reports linking Huang to Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a businesswoman formerly associated with Singapore-based Nvidia chip buyer Megaspeed International. The New York Times and Financial Times reported that US intelligence officials suspected her of gathering information for Beijing and influencing Huang to seek looser chip export restrictions.

Beijing has rejected the espionage allegations, with Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun calling the Chinese spy narrative “a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear.”

Read more

Huang admitted on Sunday that he had been unfaithful to his wife, without identifying the woman. 

On Wednesday, the New York Times wrote that Huang also had an affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, who reported directly to him. 

Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into the affair on November 8. It initially backed Huang and said it had no reason to believe company secrets or US national security had been compromised. 

The subsequent resignation announcement gave no specific reason or explanation for his departure.

Nvidia and Huang also face a proposed shareholder class action alleging that they deliberately concealed the relationship and misled investors about the risks.

Following the announcement, Nvidia shares plunged more than 13% in early trading on Thursday, wiping over $575 billion off its market value and leaving the stock down roughly 17% over the past year. On Wednesday, its valuation had already fallen below $4 trillion for the first time in over a year.

READ MORE: Trump backs ‘honeypot-hit’ Nvidia boss

The turmoil has spread across the AI sector and weighed on the broader US market, erasing hundreds of billions of dollars in share value. Nvidia-linked cloud computing provider CoreWeave fell about 11% at the opening, while the S&P 500 and Nasdaq also declined.

Polymarket traders, meanwhile, were pricing a roughly 12% chance of an “AI bubble burst” by year-end.

Peltola’s Lead Shrinks as Alaska Processes More Votes
content:
By Zachary Stieber

Democrat Mary Peltola’s lead in the race for Alaska’s U.S. Senate seat has shrunk in the latest update from the Alaska Division of Elections.

Peltola now has 121,487 first-place votes, or 48.9 percent, in the Nov. 11 update.

Sen. Dan S. Sullivan (R-Alaska) has 117,512 first-place votes, or 47.3 percent. Peltola had been ahead by 4,250 votes, and is now 3,975 votes ahead.

The gap between the candidates—which had exceeded the number of votes for Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whom Republicans and others allege entered the race at Democrats’ behest to draw votes away from the sitting senator—is now smaller than Sullivan Jr.’s total.

Sullivan Jr., in last place, has received 4,100 votes. Gerald Heikes, a Republican, is currently in third with 5,426 votes.

The Alaska Division of Elections and the campaigns for Peltola and Sen. Sullivan did not return requests for comment by the time of publication. Peltola’s campaign has said it is confident she will ultimately prevail in the race.

The Associated Press estimates that with the new update, 86 percent of the votes cast have been counted.

Alaska is one of a handful of states that use ranked-choice voting, in which voters rank candidates by placing their preferred candidate as their first choice, their next preference as second choice, and so on.

If no candidate receives a majority of first-place votes, then all ballots listing the last-place candidate as the top choice will be checked to see who voters placed second. That would add votes to the count for the other three candidates.

If a candidate still did not have a majority after that, another round will be completed for the third-place candidate.

A preliminary analysis by the organization FairVote of the ranked-choice voting record of some ballots released by the state on Nov. 11 shows Peltola with 50.15 percent of the vote, or 710 votes ahead of Sen. Sullivan, after the final round of counting.

President Donald Trump has called for all votes cast for Sullivan Jr. and Heikes to be awarded to Sen. Sullivan, and the Department of Justice has asked a federal court to enjoin certification of the race until an investigation determines whether voters for Sullivan Jr. meant to vote for the senator. The court dismissed the case, but an appeal is ongoing.

The race for the seat is the only uncalled Senate race in the country. Prosecutor Scott Colom, a Democrat, was declared the winner of a close race to represent Mississippi in the Senate on Wednesday.

Democrats flipped control of the upper chamber in the midterms and will have 55 or 56 seats in the next Congress, depending on the outcome of the Alaska race.

Peltola, 53, represented Alaska’s at-large congressional district from 2022 to 2025. She lost in the 2024 election to Republican Nick Begich III.

Peltola said she ran for the Senate because she’s “seen firsthand how government is failing Alaskans.” Her platform included promises to make life more affordable for Alaska residents and fix what she described as a rigged system.

Sen. Sullivan, 61, a Marine Corps veteran and former Alaska attorney general, was first elected to the Senate in 2014. He won reelection in 2020 with 53.9 percent of the vote.

Sen. Sullivan’s campaign website says he has brought together a broad coalition of supporters. He’s sponsored legislation that has been signed into law, including bills that required studies on ocean-related pollution.

title: WAN-IFRA stands with AMI Colombia as threats against the press escalate
content:
According to our member association AMI, security alerts led to the evacuation of Caracol Televisión, Caracol Radio, RCN and Semana in Bogotá. AMI also reports continuing threats and acts of violence against journalists in different regions of Colombia, and public statements targeting media outlets and reporters. As AMI points out, these are separate events, but they raise a common question: what place does Colombia give its press?

AMI notes that public stigmatisation of journalism and violence against it, particularly in the regions, have reached alarming levels in recent years, and that the IAPA’s Chapultepec Index places Colombia among the countries where press freedom indicators have deteriorated the most. AMI’s figures show that more than 2,000 attacks were recorded against hundreds of journalists between August 2022 and July 2026, including ten murders, four of them in 2026. On average, according to AMI, a journalist is threatened every two days.

Press freedom and the right to information are not privileges of the people who report the news. They are guarantees that belong to citizens, who need a diversity of voices to understand what is happening and form their own opinions. When threats against journalists and media outlets create a climate of intimidation that leads to censorship and self-censorship, society as a whole has the most to lose.

WAN-IFRA joins AMI in calling on the Colombian authorities to:

  • adopt concrete public policies that protect the practice of journalism, with protection mechanisms and guarantees that outlast any single government;
  • reconsider the language they use about media outlets and journalists. The words of people in positions of authority carry more weight than those of any other public actor. They can build a climate of respect for those who inform society, or one of contempt.

Pluralism cannot be imposed by decree. It grows when criticism is accepted as a normal part of democracy and a diversity of voices is understood to strengthen both those who govern and those who are governed. A society that respects differing opinions, promotes media pluralism and guarantees the free exercise of journalism is a safer society.

title: EU member jails woman over pro-Russia TikTok posts
content:
A Latvian court imposed a three-year prison sentence over alleged glorification of war crimes in Ukraine

A court in Riga, Latvia has sentenced a woman to three years in prison over TikTok posts deemed to glorify alleged war crimes committed by Russian forces in Ukraine, LETA news agency reported on Wednesday.

The case is the latest in a series of prosecutions in Latvia over statements deemed supportive of Moscow or critical of Kiev. Since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022, the Baltic state has tightened restrictions on Russian-language media, cultural activities, and public expressions of pro-Russian sentiment.

According to LETA, the case involved around 20 videos and comments posted by Latvian citizen Tatyana Masenko from April to July 2024. The agency cited several examples of content that prosecutors considered criminal.

One video reportedly showed a Ukrainian serviceman with a prosthetic limb standing in front of a cemetery lined with Ukrainian flags. Masenko captioned it: “Forward, to the gay-European future.”

Another video included a similar message: “Soon, all of you from across gay Europe will be gathered together and sent to defend Ukraine with bags of sunflower seeds and packets.”

Read more

Masenko’s defense argued that the three-year sentence is excessively harsh, noting that she had already spent four months in custody. Her lawyer said the verdict would be appealed.

This comes after a series of similar cases in Latvia. In January, a court sentenced 72-year-old professor Aleksandr Gaponenko to ten years in prison over his participation in an academic roundtable, where he gave a ten-minute speech on discrimination against Russian speakers in Latvia.

The Baltic state, which has a substantial Russian-speaking population, has restricted Russian-language education, removed Soviet-era monuments, and tightened the rules governing the public use of Russian symbols.

Russia has accused Latvia and its Baltic neighbors, Estonia and Lithuania, of pursuing a policy of “extreme Russophobia” and systematically discriminating against Russian-speaking residents under the pretext of national security.

Moscow downgraded diplomatic relations with all three Baltic states in 2023, citing their hostile policies.

Putin-US envoy talks conclude: Latest reactions (Updates, VIDEOS)
content:
The Kremlin has described the meeting as constructive and said Moscow and Washington had agreed to continue diplomatic efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict

Russian President Vladimir Putin has concluded talks with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner in Moscow. The Kremlin described the meeting as constructive and confirmed that diplomatic efforts to resolve the Ukraine conflict will continue. 

The talks followed two days of US-mediated negotiations between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, which focused on a potential settlement of the conflict and the future European security architecture. 

Senior officials, including Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov, and Witkoff, have been speaking to reporters following the meeting. 

RT brings you the key statements and latest developments.

“Constructive” talks

Putin’s negotiations with the US envoys were “substantive, constructive, frank and useful,” Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov told reporters following the meeting.

He said the discussions followed a similar pattern to previous exchanges between the Russian president and American negotiators. 

Read more

Kushner also described the talks with Putin as “very fulsome and detailed,” saying they covered all major issues and would help shape the next round of multilateral negotiations and upcoming discussions with Zelensky.

“Very productive time,” he said.

Witkoff hails progress in peace efforts 

The US special envoy welcomed the resumption of trilateral negotiations between Russia, Ukraine, and the US, pointing to plans for another round of talks. 

“I think progress was made today, yes,” Witkoff told reporters before departing Moscow following his meeting with Putin. 

He noted that few had expected the trilateral format to resume in Abu Dhabi, but the negotiations did restart and another meeting has already been scheduled. “This is what President Trump wants to see,” he added.

Key positions on European security 

Putin reaffirmed Moscow’s proposals for a new European security architecture, including an end to NATO expansion, restrictions on the deployment of weapons systems threatening Russia near its borders, and a return to the military bloc’s force configuration at the time of the 1997 Russia-NATO Founding Act, Ushakov said. 

Moscow considers the existing European security system ineffective and is ready to begin talks with Washington on a new long-term arrangement, which it hopes European countries will also support, he added. 

Read more

European governments have been seeking to join the negotiations but should decide whether they want peace or a continuation of the conflict, according to the Kremlin aide, who said that their actions so far suggest the latter. 

Foreign troops in Ukraine would mean ‘endless war’  

Plans by the European “coalition of the willing” to deploy foreign troops in Ukraine after the conflict would risk prolonging the fighting indefinitely, Ushakov said. 

“This is a recipe for an endless war,” he said. 

Zelensky unwilling to end conflict

Putin and the US envoys also discussed Vladimir Zelensky’s recent remarks about President Donald Trump. 

According to Ushakov, Kiev is reluctant to end the conflict because a settlement would require new elections, potentially threatening Zelensky’s hold on power. 

Major prisoner exchange 

Moscow and Washington backed a proposal discussed during the Abu Dhabi negotiations for what could become a major prisoner exchange between Russia and Ukraine.

The terms are still being negotiated, Ushakov said, expressing hope that Kiev would honor the agreement reached in principle.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters that further work was needed to finalize the exchange, with the Russian Defense Ministry expected to provide details. 

Russia and Ukraine have conducted 35 prisoner exchanges since 2025, involving approximately 5,000 people from each side, according to Ushakov.

Witkoff also commented on the planned prisoner exchange, telling reporters it would be completed “in short order” and describing it as the “largest in history.”

He added that European representatives would join the next round of negotiations, calling their participation “a very big deal.”  

Putin-Trump talks in China

The Russian president and his US counterpart are expected to discuss the Ukraine settlement during the upcoming APEC summit in Shenzhen, according to Ushakov.

Read more

He said that Trump was personally involved in efforts to reach a lasting resolution to the conflict. 

Both Moscow and Washington view the planned trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping as an important step, Ushakov said. Preparations are underway, with Moscow hoping the first meeting in this format will have a positive impact on international relations. 

Europe’s actions contradict its calls for peace  

European countries are pursuing policies that could prolong the Ukraine conflict despite their stated desire for peace, Peskov said. “They are moving towards continuing the war, expanding the war, but talking about peace.”  

European leaders have yet to agree on who should represent them in negotiations, Peskov added, noting that those seeking direct contact with Moscow risked being ostracized by their counterparts. 

What’s next? 

Witkoff and Kushner are expected to meet Ukrainian and European representatives in Dublin following their talks in Moscow. 

The Kremlin hopes the American negotiators will fully convey Moscow’s position to their Ukrainian and European counterparts, Ushakov said.

title: America’s Constitutional Crossroads: When Political Lawfare Threatens the Liberties of a Free People
content:
By Stephen Zogopoulos, USNN World News

The Great American Distraction

There comes a moment in the history of every free nation when its citizens must ask a question that transcends political affiliation:

Are we still governing ourselves, or are we slowly surrendering that responsibility to those who have learned to manipulate the institutions entrusted with protecting our freedom?

Following the November 3, 2026, midterm elections, the United States finds itself confronting that question once again.

Democrats have secured congressional victories. Republicans are questioning their political future. Legal battles continue. Congressional investigations loom. Accusations and counteraccusations dominate the headlines.

But while politicians fight over who controls Washington, Americans should be asking a more consequential question.

Who is protecting the Constitution?

For decades, the American people have been conditioned to view political conflict as a contest between Democrats and Republicans. One party wins, the other loses, and the cycle begins again.

Yet elections are not the ultimate purpose of our republic.

Liberty is.

The Constitution was not written to protect political parties. It was written to establish a government whose authority would remain limited, accountable, and subordinate to the people.

When political institutions become instruments of intimidation, when litigation becomes a substitute for democratic persuasion, and when governmental power is exercised selectively, the constitutional foundation begins to weaken.

And the greatest danger arises when Americans become so consumed by the spectacle that they stop watching what government actually does.

Lawfare: When the Courtroom Becomes a Political Battlefield

There is a profound difference between the legitimate enforcement of law and the political exploitation of legal authority.

One seeks justice.

The other seeks advantage.

In recent years, Americans have witnessed increasingly aggressive attempts to resolve political disputes through investigations, litigation, executive directives, and administrative action.

The 2026 midterm elections were no exception.

According to the Election Reformers Network’s November 10 litigation assessment, significant pre-election legal disputes involved federal intervention in state elections, voter-registration information, mail-in voting procedures, and congressional redistricting.

These are not insignificant disagreements.

They concern who can vote, how ballots are counted, who controls election administration, and how political representation is determined.

When such questions are resolved through the courts, constitutional review may be necessary. But when political leaders use legal institutions primarily to weaken their adversaries, Americans have every reason to challenge their motives.

The distinction matters.

A congressional investigation supported by evidence and conducted with due process is legitimate oversight.

An investigation designed primarily to humiliate political opponents, manufacture damaging headlines, or intimidate dissenters is something entirely different.

And that standard must apply whether the target is Donald Trump, a Democratic governor, a Republican senator, or an ordinary American citizen.

Justice cannot survive when the identity of the accused matters more than the evidence against them.

The Democratic Investigation Offensive: Accountability or Political Retaliation?

The Democratic Party’s victories in the 2026 midterms have positioned it to assume control of Congress in January 2027.

Already, Democratic leaders are preparing investigations into President Donald Trump, his administration, and associated officials.

The political confrontation has escalated to the point that the White House has warned that certain investigative tactics could cross into criminal misconduct. Democrats, in response, maintain that their inquiries are legitimate constitutional oversight and accuse the administration of attempting to intimidate Congress.

These developments deserve far greater scrutiny than partisan headlines alone.

Americans should insist on answers to several questions.

Are these investigations directed toward demonstrable violations of law, or toward inflicting maximum political damage?

Will congressional investigators examine evidence that contradicts their preferred conclusions?

Will individuals under investigation receive appropriate due process?

Will findings be made transparent to the public?

And perhaps most importantly, will Congress devote equal seriousness to the economic, security, and constitutional concerns of the American people?

Democrats have a constitutional responsibility to investigate legitimate wrongdoing.

They do not possess an unlimited mandate to use the machinery of government against political opponents.

Republicans, equally, have no authority to shield themselves from lawful oversight simply because an investigation is politically inconvenient.

The Constitution demands accountability, not revenge.

Americans should judge the incoming Democratic Congress not by the number of investigations it announces, but by the evidence those investigations produce, the fairness of their procedures, and the tangible benefits delivered to the nation.

The Election Integrity Question That Cannot Be Ignored

Every legitimate vote must count.

Every unlawful vote must be rejected.

Every election official must be held accountable.

And every candidate, regardless of political affiliation, must respect a lawful election result.

These principles should be universally accepted.

Unfortunately, public trust in American elections has become dangerously entangled with partisan expectations.

When a political party wins, its supporters frequently praise the electoral system.

When that party loses, some begin questioning the process.

This cannot become the permanent condition of American democracy.

Following the 2026 midterms, allegations of election misconduct circulated across social media. Some claims proved false, including allegations of a supposed FBI operation that uncovered thousands of fraudulent ballots in Houston. The FBI publicly rejected that account.

That does not mean election systems should be immune from examination.

It means allegations must be investigated using verifiable evidence rather than political assumption.

If illegal voting, ballot manipulation, obstruction, or misconduct occurred, those responsible should face consequences under applicable law.

But allegations of a nationwide coordinated operation cannot responsibly be declared proven without supporting evidence.

The American people deserve more than assurances that everything worked properly.

They deserve transparent procedures, lawful audits, documented chains of custody, accurate voter-registration records, and accessible explanations when irregularities occur.

Election integrity should never be considered a Republican issue or a Democratic issue. It is an American constitutional obligation.

The correct response to legitimate concerns is neither automatic dismissal nor unsupported accusation.

It is independent examination, transparency, and accountability.

The Sleight of Hand: Watch What Government Does While Everyone Else Is Arguing

Political distraction does not require a secret conspiracy.

Sometimes, it requires nothing more than an endless succession of controversies.

A congressional subpoena dominates the news.

A political figure faces another investigation.

A heated exchange erupts over an executive order.

Social media explodes with partisan outrage.

Meanwhile, the ordinary work of government continues.

Regulations are proposed.

Budgets are negotiated.

Federal agencies exercise their authority.

Surveillance policies are debated.

Administrative decisions affect businesses, families, and individual liberties.

And constitutional questions that should dominate public discussion receive comparatively little attention.

This is the danger of political spectacle.

Americans become consumed by personalities rather than policies, accusations rather than evidence, and political victories rather than constitutional principles.

The public must examine whether politicians are using legal conflicts to divert attention from unpopular decisions.

That is a legitimate question.

It becomes a provable accusation only when documents, communications, testimony, or other credible evidence establish deliberate coordination.

But citizens do not need evidence of a secret master plan to recognize a dangerous pattern.

A government that constantly demands the public’s attention for political warfare may escape the scrutiny its everyday exercise of power deserves.

That possibility should concern every American.

The Constitution Is Not a Political Suggestion

The framers of the United States Constitution understood something that modern political leaders occasionally appear determined to forget.

Power must be restrained because power can be abused.

The First Amendment protects speech, religion, the press, peaceful assembly, and the right to petition government.

The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable searches and seizures.

The Fifth Amendment establishes essential protections involving due process and the deprivation of life, liberty, or property.

The Sixth Amendment guarantees important protections to individuals accused of crimes.

The Tenth Amendment reserves powers not delegated to the federal government to the states or the people.

And the constitutional separation of powers establishes a system designed to prevent any single institution from exercising unlimited authority.

These safeguards are not ceremonial language.

They are enforceable limitations on government.

A political administration cannot legitimately suppress lawful criticism merely because it finds that criticism offensive.

A government agency cannot disregard due process because an individual holds unpopular political beliefs.

Congress cannot exercise investigative authority without constitutional limitations.

And executive officials cannot unilaterally rewrite election law outside the authority granted to them.

Nevertheless, constitutional boundaries remain subjects of intense litigation.

An October 2026 Brennan Center analysis documented numerous judicial decisions addressing the Trump administration’s election-related executive actions and demands for state voter information.

That record demonstrates something important: the struggle over constitutional power is not confined to one political party.

Citizens who oppose excessive Democratic authority must be equally willing to oppose excessive Republican authority.

Otherwise, constitutional arguments become little more than partisan conveniences.

A constitutional right that exists only when one’s preferred party governs is not a right at all. It is a temporary political privilege.

The Dangerous Normalization of Political Intimidation

Perhaps the most troubling development in contemporary American politics is the growing acceptance of intimidation as an ordinary tool of government.

Political leaders increasingly discuss investigations and legal consequences in language that resembles political combat.

Opponents are portrayed not merely as wrong, but as enemies.

Government institutions become symbols of partisan conflict.

And public officials may find themselves pressured to demonstrate loyalty to a political agenda rather than fidelity to constitutional obligations.

This creates an environment in which citizens understandably begin questioning whether the law will protect them equally.

That question should alarm every elected official.

The rule of law requires that similar conduct be judged by similar standards.

Evidence must matter more than political affiliation.

Procedural rights must extend to unpopular defendants.

And public officials should never receive immunity from scrutiny simply because they serve a favored political cause.

Americans should reject the argument that extraordinary political circumstances justify abandoning ordinary constitutional protections.

History repeatedly demonstrates that powers expanded during moments of fear or political emergency rarely disappear automatically when the emergency passes.

A government that can circumvent constitutional safeguards against one political faction may eventually use the same mechanisms against another.

The precedent outlives the politician.

The power survives the administration.

And the American people inherit the consequences.

The Silent Erosion of American Sovereignty

The greatest threat to a constitutional republic is not necessarily a dramatic overthrow of its government.

It can be a gradual erosion of the principles that make self-government possible.

When citizens accept selective enforcement of laws, equal protection weakens.

When government secrecy replaces transparency, accountability diminishes.

When political loyalty becomes more important than constitutional duty, public service deteriorates.

When Americans surrender their willingness to question authority, representative government becomes less responsive.

And when constitutional protections are viewed as obstacles to political objectives, liberty itself becomes negotiable.

This danger extends beyond elections.

It reaches into the government’s power over speech, property, taxation, commerce, privacy, and the administration of justice.

The federal government possesses considerable lawful authority.

But that authority has boundaries.

Those boundaries do not vanish because politicians claim their objectives are necessary, popular, or morally justified.

The American people created the government.

The government did not create the American people.

That distinction is fundamental.

What the American People Must Demand

The American people should demand a standard of governance that neither political party can evade.

Transparent elections

Lawful audits, verifiable ballot handling, accurate records, independent oversight, and evidence-based investigation of credible irregularities.

Equal application of the law

No preferential treatment for powerful political figures, and no targeting of individuals because of protected speech or partisan affiliation.

Constitutional accountability

Genuine oversight of Congress, the executive branch, federal agencies, and the exercise of governmental authority.

Public access to evidence

Release of legally disclosable government records, defensible findings, documented expenditures, and meaningful explanations of official decisions.

Public service over partisan warfare

Government that addresses affordability, economic opportunity, public safety, national security, and the protection of individual rights.

These are not extraordinary demands.

They are the minimum expectations of a functioning constitutional republic.

And they should apply to every administration, every Congress, and every political party.

A Warning to Washington: The American People Are Not Your Subjects

Let me be unequivocal.

I do not believe Americans should be expected to surrender their constitutional freedoms in exchange for promises of political security.

I do not believe government officials should be allowed to exploit their positions to punish lawful disagreement.

I do not believe elections should become exercises in political theater where transparency is sacrificed to protect institutional reputations.

And I do not believe either major political party possesses a monopoly on patriotism, integrity, or constitutional authority.

The Democratic Party should understand that gaining control of Congress does not confer unlimited power.

The Republican Party should understand that executive authority does not supersede the Constitution.

Both parties should remember that their political power is temporary.

The rights of the American people are not.

As a citizen, I reserve the right to question the conduct of my government.

As a journalist, I believe public institutions must withstand scrutiny.

And as an American, I refuse to accept the proposition that constitutional liberties should be compromised for political convenience.

I walk without fear because the Constitution does not require me to kneel before political power.

Nor should it require any other American to do so.

The Final Question: Will America Defend What It Inherited?

Our nation was not founded on the belief that government should be trusted without question.

It was founded on the recognition that liberty requires limits on governmental authority.

The Declaration of Independence established the revolutionary proposition that legitimate governments derive their just powers from the consent of the governed.

The Constitution translated that principle into a framework of limited government, divided power, enforceable rights, and public accountability.

Generation after generation of Americans has fought, sacrificed, served, and died to preserve those principles.

Their sacrifice must never be reduced to a historical footnote.

The 2026 midterm elections will eventually become another chapter in our political history.

But the constitutional issues confronting this nation will remain long after the electoral celebrations and political grievances have faded.

Americans must refuse to become passive spectators while political leaders compete for control over institutions that exist to serve the public.

We must question government actions.

We must demand evidence.

We must protect due process.

We must defend free expression.

We must insist on election integrity.

And above all, we must remember that freedom does not belong to a political party.

It belongs to the people.

The greatest victory for those who would abuse governmental power is not winning an election.

It is convincing the American people to stop paying attention.

Let Washington understand something that should never need repeating:

The United States Constitution is not a campaign platform.

It is not a political bargaining chip.

It is not a document that becomes optional when those in power find its restrictions inconvenient.

It is the foundation of the American republic.

And it belongs to every American.

Our freedoms were not granted by Democrats.

Our freedoms were not granted by Republicans.

Our freedoms are secured by constitutional principles that both parties are obligated to respect.

The question before America is no longer simply who won the midterm elections.

The question is whether Americans will insist that whoever governs remains accountable to the Constitution.

Because once a free people accept that constitutional protections can be selectively applied, the danger is no longer merely political.

It becomes generational.

America, pay attention.

Not to the political spectacle.

To the power being exercised behind it.

And never forget:

The government answers to the American people. Not the other way around.

Stephen Zogopoulos, USNN World News

Editorial Disclaimer

This article is an opinion and commentary piece authored under the byline of Stephen Zogopoulos for USNN World News. The views and interpretations expressed represent the author’s editorial perspective and should not be construed as established findings of criminal wrongdoing, election fraud, or unlawful coordination by any individual or political party.

References to alleged election irregularities, political lawfare, and potential abuses of authority are intended to encourage lawful scrutiny, transparency, public accountability, and constitutional debate. No coordinated nationwide Democratic election-fraud operation has been substantiated by the sources reviewed for this article.

title: Pope Leo returns to beloved former home of Chiclayo, Peru
content:
Pope Leo XIV seems omnipresent in Chiclayo. His image is painted in colorful murals, emblazoned on baseball hats and bobbleheads, and celebrated with signs across this city in northern Peru that read: "Welcome home."

Lima is the culinary epicenter of South America. Cusco is the historic capital of the Inca empire and the gateway to Machu Picchu. But Chiclayo has a special claim as home to the Peruvian American pope, who returns there on Friday.

The first U.S.-born pontiff, Leo spent about two decades in Peru as a missionary and church leader, obtaining Peruvian citizenship shortly before he served as bishop of Chiclayo from 2015 to 2023. He remains beloved here for championing social justice issues and for his closeness to the people, especially the poor.

Many remember how the bishop then known as Robert Prevost led the life-saving purchase of oxygen production plants during the COVID-19 pandemic; how he waded through mud after torrential rains to bring help to the needy; how he celebrated Mass at the local prison. Others recall how he'd drive his pickup truck to remote villages to hand out blankets and sing Christmas songs, and his love of regional dishes like duck with rice and goat stew.

The love is reciprocal

In his first words as the leader of 1.4 billion Catholics, Pope Leo gave a special shoutout in Spanish to his "beloved Diocese of Chiclayo" from the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica. His return reaffirms his affection for Chiclayo's churches, schools and sanctuaries and is widely viewed as the emotional highlight of his South American trip.

"People aren't saying: 'The pope is Peruvian.' They're saying, 'The pope is Chiclayano!'" said the Rev. Jasson Sempertegui, who was his secretary when he led the diocese. "In Chiclayo we like to say: 'The pope is returning home.'"

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Pope Leo XIV casts mail-in ballot, becoming first pope to vote in US election

It is, Sempertegui said, the most important moment in Chiclayo's history since it was settled in the 16th century by Spanish Franciscan priests as an Indigenous village about 13 kilometers (8 miles) from the Pacific Ocean.

Chiclayo and its people, he said, might have been more influential to the pope than his native Chicago and the Vatican.

The torrent of crises he confronted in Chiclayo including the COVID pandemic, assisting newly arrived Venezuelan migrants, and the devastating floods helped form his pastoral identity.

"He's Chiclayano because he faced the biggest challenges of his pastoral life here," Sempertegui said. "This helped him to connect with people's pain."

From Chicago to Chiclayo

During his time in the city, Leo often repeated a joke: "Chicago, Chiclayo, what difference is there? Only one letter."

A city of about 700,000 people, Chiclayo is the commercial hub of Peru's northern Pacific coast, with highways linking it to the Andes and the Amazon region. Chiclayanos take pride in the city's nickname, "Capital of Friendship," and its proximity to major archeological sites.

"Before, we were an unnoticed, low-profile city," said Zuly Castillo, who worked for Leo when he was bishop. Across from her office, a life-size cardboard cutout of the pope now welcomes visitors to his former residence. "Now we see that he has given us so much and we have become known worldwide."

In Chiclayo, the pope would wake before dawn to pray, then walk to the cathedral in the city center. He listened to confession and was moved by stories of adversity in a city where 20% of residents live in poverty.

He became known as an efficient problem solver, even fixing diocesan cars with YouTube tutorials. He learned local jargon and humor, and sometimes invited priests to join him for a lunch of his lomo saltado (Peru's classic beef and tomato stir-fry) or ceviche (raw fish marinated in lime juice).

A pope who binge-watched 'Prison Break'

In the breaks between prayers, theology classes and chores, the aspiring priests at the city's seminary of Santo Toribio de Mogrovejo remembered how Leo would visit them offering encouragement, sharing a meal, playing tennis.

The Rev. Marcos Ballena, a seminary leader, recalled the glee of seminarians watching TV in the common room when Cardinal Prevost was elected pope. "Everyone jumped as if they had won a World Cup!"

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Pope wraps up Uruguay visit and heads to most fraught stop of his tour in Milei's Argentina

Seminarian Jose Miguel Teran agreed: "There are some funny videos where we're all euphoric ... and even more when he said, 'My beloved diocese of Chiclayo', we understood very clearly that this is his home, and we feel him as part of our family."

Darwin Sanchez first met Leo while serving as an altar boy. Soon, he'll have the honor to carry the miter that Leo will wear when celebrating Masses.

"In our youth ministries, with the altar boys there's a surging interest in the vocation because the pope is deemed to be Chiclayano," Sanchez said.

On his breaks in Chiclayo, he liked to watch his beloved Chicago White Sox' baseball games and binge-watch American TV series, like "24" and "Prison Break."

In the working-class neighborhood of San Antonio, people remember him sharing a meal with the needy at a soup kitchen that he inaugurated.

"He told immigrants at the time that we welcomed vulnerable people," said Daria Chavarry, a volunteer at a soup kitchen that has been renamed "Papa Leon XIV."

After a meal near a large poster of the pope, 78-year-old Maria Teresa Santa Cruz said she paid 25 soles (about $3) in three installments to buy a T-shirt of Leo.

"I bought it because we have one more representative here on Earth," she said about Leo's mission to protect the dignity of the poor.

A pope who waded through mud in rubber boots

Leo helped deliver donations in 2017 when hundreds lost their homes as rivers overflooded. He also welcomed Venezuelan migrants escaping their country's political and economic crises and oversaw construction of a temporary shelter and 13 homes.

"This is the place that he gave us for us to build a home again," said Betania Marina Rodriguez, who worked closely with Leo on projects and lives in one of the homes.

She recalled how Leo delivered live chickens to her home during the COVID pandemic, to share with other migrants.

"In him we saw the feeling of hope," Rodriguez said. "He always said that human dignity has no borders."

Rocio Zea lost her home to flooding in 2023 and remembers fondly how Leo took off his priestly robes and waded through the mud in rubber boots to reach the needy.

"He was the first person who came with help and cared about us when everything was flooded and the water reached our necks," said Zea. "It's surreal to think that the person who's been there for you is now the pope the most important person on Earth after God."

He grew so fond of Chiclayo that he hoped to stay put "and even to be buried alongside the diocese's other bishops," Daniel Burke and Scott Detrow write in their book, "American Pope."

But then Pope Francis asked him to return to Rome for an important Vatican job. He teared up in his final Mass with his parishioners.

Prisoners at Chiclayo penitentiary gathered at the carpentry workshop to carve a papal staff before his visit their gift to the missionary who visited them to celebrate Mass and who became the pope.

"There's so much joy over his visit," said the Rev. Elmer Uchofen, the prison chaplain. "We knew he'd come back; Chiclayo is in his heart."

Democrats Planning Probe of US Intelligence Community
content:
By Ryan Morgan

WASHINGTON—Democrats in the House of Representatives are preparing to lead expansive probes into the U.S. intelligence community’s operations under President Donald Trump when they take the majority in January, House Intelligence Committee Ranking Member Jim Himes (D-Conn.) has announced.

In an interview with The New York Times published on Nov. 11, Himes said Democrats plan to investigate an “extremely aggressive” use of covert operations by the CIA during the second Trump presidency.

Covert operations by the U.S. intelligence community may include secretive lethal strikes and other paramilitary actions meant to advance foreign policy objectives.

Himes told the newspaper that he also intends to probe donations that defense and intelligence community contractors have made to various construction projects the president has pursued in office, including a new ballroom for the White House and a triumphal arch. Himes said this line of inquiry will focus on whether contractors were threatened or promised anything in return for donations to these construction projects.

The House and Senate intelligence committees typically hold hearings behind closed doors. Oversight of U.S. covert operations abroad would likely require such secretive proceedings.

Himes told the paper that a congressional probe into contractor donations to Trump’s Washington construction projects could involve public hearings.

In a Nov. 10 interview with Reuters, Himes said Democrats also intend to scrutinize intelligence community staff reductions under the Trump administration.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which coordinates the intelligence-gathering operations of the various U.S. intelligence agencies, has cut hundreds of jobs under the Trump administration.

Himes suggested that these staff cuts entailed retaliatory firings.

“We’re going to tell the story of the patriots who were fired because they said something that was inconsistent with what the president wanted to be true,” Himes told Reuters.

The congressman said remaining intelligence community employees feel pressured to self-censor and withhold analyses that break with the Trump administration’s policy objectives.

“There’s absolutely evidence that analysts are hesitant to write on topics that they think might be controversial,” Himes told Reuters. “There’s absolutely evidence of a decline in morale in the analytic community because of the pressures that they are under.”

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence did not respond to a request for comment by publication time.

Other Democratic Party leaders in the House have previewed similar oversight plans for when they take the majority in January.

Last week, House Armed Services Committee Ranking Member Adam Smith (D-Wash.) announced plans for expansive scrutiny of the U.S. military under Trump’s leadership. Among the oversight topics, Smith said Democrats would review the war with Iran, strikes on suspected drug smuggling boats in the Western Hemisphere, and the process by which contracts have been awarded for military projects.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) forced a vote on articles of impeachment against Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, asserting that he has committed high crimes and misdemeanors in his handling of issues such as the Iran war and the boat strikes. The House, which is currently controlled by Republicans, voted on Nov. 10 to send Massie’s impeachment articles to committee, where they’re unlikely to progress with the time remaining in this session of Congress.

Democratic lawmakers have also signaled plans to scrutinize Homeland Security Secretary Mark Wayne Mullin, former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, and Tesla CEO Elon Musk in his capacity as an adviser on government efficiency policies.

White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) on Nov. 9, warning that certain Democrat-led efforts to scrutinize the administration could constitute an effort to “abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government.”

Garcia, in response, asserted that Congress has a broad authority to conduct oversight.

title: How ‘Honey Traps’ Can Exploit Emotion and Ensnare Western Leaders
content:
By Daniel Y. Teng

Meticulous planning and a deep understanding of a target’s emotions and weaknesses are some of the ingredients that go into a successful honey trap, says one security commentator.

Paul Johnstone, a security expert and former agent of the Australian Federal Police, lifts the lid on how CCP spies deploy “sexploitation” or honey traps (also called honeypots) to ensnare Western leaders.

His comments come in the wake of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s admission of an affair with alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang (of no relation), who supposedly worked in tech, finance, and media—although Johnstone suspects these are just cover stories.

The issue has brought the tactic of “honey trapping” into the global spotlight and elevated concerns about what kind of technology or intelligence Jensen Huang’s affair may have leaked to the Chinese Communist Party (CCP). Nvidia is the world’s leading developer and producer of advanced computer chips.

His case comes after the high profile incident involving suspected spy Christine Fang and former lawmaker Eric Swalwell (D-Calif.), as well as a 2025 warning from the British MI5 about CCP recruiters, particularly attractive women, targeting parliamentary workers.

Johnstone is currently authoring a book on the strategy called “Red Honey,” which details his own encounters with attempted honey pots.

He says the Nvidia case reveals just how meticulous the CCP is.

“When you think about it, if they had put a young 27 or 30-year-old attractive woman to be the actual honey trap, that would have set off alarm bells,” Johnstone told The Epoch Times.

“Huang may have had advisers close to him say, ‘Hey, think about the impact. It’s a young woman. You’re an older man,’” Johnstone said.

The Afghanistan War veteran said the lady was closer to Jensen Huang’s age, meaning she would have been better able to connect with him on a personal level. It also suggests long-term planning before Alice Huang got close to her target.

“When you think about the age of that lady, her looks, her appearance, her position, that would have been meticulously planned over a long period of time,” Johnstone said.

He reveals one of the key pressure points is loneliness.

“When I advise clients, I ask: ‘Are you happy in your home?’ And that’s where it all starts,” Johnstone said.

“CEOs, it’s a very lonely job. It’s a very lonely existence that these people have because they’re working long hours. They’re traveling a lot. They may have a wife and children at home,” Johnstone said.

“Maybe there’s no intimacy in that relationship. Maybe their relationship is kind of stale. Then all of a sudden, a very beautiful woman, maybe an articulate woman, a very intelligent woman, approaches that male,” he said.

Johnstone said the tech industry was a major target of the CCP with the analyst suspecting a “percentage” of workers have links to Beijing’s Ministry of State Security (MSS).

He also says countries like Australia should be wary.

“Even here in Australia, there will be people walking amongst us in the community who have been trained by Beijing and are here for a particular purpose,” Johnstone said. “Sometimes these assets, these spies, can be dormant for a long period of time before they’re activated.”

He says they wait until the right opportunity comes along to build a relationship with someone in politics or a high-value industry.

Jensen Huang is currently being investigated by the American FBI with three House committees asking the tech leader to provide testimony.

title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang Resigns After Affair With Alleged Chinese Spy
content:
By Troy Myers and Andrew Moran

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has resigned following intense scrutiny after admitting to an extramarital affair with an alleged Chinese spy, the company announced on Thursday.

Days earlier, the chip giant launched an investigation into Huang after he admitted on Nov. 8 to having an affair with a woman who was suspected of being a spy for the Chinese Ministry of State Security.

Alice Huang, who is not related to the CEO, allegedly had the task of gathering intelligence on Jensen Huang and U.S. artificial intelligence (AI) chips while trying to encourage Nvidia to make its most advanced chips available for China.

Before she became a top executive at a Singapore-based data center company called Megaspeed, one of Nvidia’s largest customers in Southeast Asia, Alice Huang had professional experience in broadcast journalism, banking, and securities in China.

Huang, one of the wealthiest men in the world, apologized in a message to Nvidia employees on Nov. 8.

“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Jensen Huang wrote. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.

“To my wife and family: I love you. I know an apology cannot undo what I have done. I hope our family will heal and that, over time, I can earn back your trust.”

The Nvidia board emphasized its commitment to U.S. national and economic security, as it named on Nov. 10 law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to lead the probe into whether Jensen Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort.

When announcing the internal investigation on Nov. 8, the board had said it had no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.

President Donald Trump stood behind Jensen Huang when questioned about what he thought about the investigation and suggested the Nvidia CEO could join him on his trip to China next week.

“I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what is going on. I hope everything’s fine,” he told reporters on Nov. 8, adding that the FBI is conducting its own investigation into Jensen Huang. “He’s a fine person, in my opinion.

“I think he’s an honorable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it. … He’s done an amazing job for our country.”

Nvidia and Jensen Huang were sued by shareholders on Nov. 9 who accused the company and CEO of defrauding them by concealing the CEO’s affair with the alleged spy.

Democratic House members have called for tightening restrictions on advanced-chip exports to China.

The scandal has also impacted relations between Washington and Beijing, which U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue described as “bumpy.”

“The situation with Nvidia is another reminder that we have to stay diligent,” Perdue told Bloomberg Television on Nov. 11.

“National security is part of this economic conversation because economic security is national security,” he said. “And so, what we’re doing with China is bumpy right now.”

title: Canada ignores court ruling to bar Russian hockey team
content:
Ottawa says it will not admit Russian players to the upcoming World Junior Championship, even with valid visas

Canada will bar Russian hockey players and officials from the upcoming World Junior Championship, even those with valid visas, the government has announced.

Canadian Secretary of State for Sport Adam van Koeverden sought to justify the ban, announced on Wednesday and defying a sports court ruling, by portraying Russian athletes’ participation as a vehicle for “state representation, political legitimacy and propaganda,” adding that immigration authorities will block their entry.
 
“Canada’s position is unequivocal: As long as Russia continues its war of aggression against Ukraine, there can be no return to business as usual,” he declared, echoing Prime Minister Mark Carney, who had ruled out Russian participation last week. The tournament runs from December 26 to January 5.
  
Ottawa’s move puts it at odds with the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), which last month overturned the International Ice Hockey Federation’s (IIHF) suspension of Russia over the Ukraine conflict and ordered its reinstatement for five championships in 2027, including the World Juniors in Canada and the men’s World Championship in Germany. The IIHF expressed disappointment but pledged to comply.

Read more

The ruling sparked boycott threats from several of Kiev's European backers, including Sweden, Finland, Norway, Denmark, Latvia, and the Czech Republic, while Germany has called for a fresh IIHF suspension of Russia.

Moscow has accused the boycotters of putting politics above sport. Russian Sports Minister Mikhail Degtyarev earlier warned that federations defying the CAS ruling could face lawsuits, lose hosting rights or suffer automatic 5-0 defeats under IIHF rules for refusing to play Russia.
 
The Russian Ice Hockey Federation has demanded that the IIHF either guarantee Russia’s participation in Canada or move the tournament elsewhere, according to Match TV.

READ MORE: Russia’s hockey comeback a ‘return to normality’ – German opposition 


Two-time Olympic hockey champion Boris Mikhailov has blasted Ottawa’s decision as politically motivated, joking that Carney might be jealous of Russian NHL star Alexander Ovechkin for smashing Canadian legend Wayne Gretzky’s long-standing record of 894 regular-season goals in April 2025.

Ovechkin himself argued that fans should get to see the world’s best players compete.

Read more

”I’m pretty sure if you ask the fans, the fans want to see the best players out there,” the Washington Capitals captain told reporters Tuesday. “The fans want to see young generation players who are going to be future stars, future NHLers. But you know it’s not up to us.”

Russia remains an ice hockey powerhouse and a member of the sport’s elite 'Big Six'. Soviet and Russian teams have claimed a record 27 World Championship titles and nine Olympic golds, with the legendary Soviet “Red Machine” dominating the sport for decades. The country also remains a major source of hockey talent, producing stars including Ovechkin, Nikita Kucherov, and Andrei Vasilevskiy.

title: One dead, four wounded after shooting near White House (VIDEOS)
content:
The incident occurred in Washington, DC’s Logan Circle neighborhood, about a mile north of the presidential residence

At least one person has been killed and four wounded by a gunman in Washington, DC, interim Metropolitan Police Chief Jeffery Carroll said at a press conference. The shooting occurred about a 15-minute walk from the White House.

Police said the suspect shot one person with a handgun inside a gym before returning to his apartment and shooting four others with a rifle from his balcony.

“Within seconds there was a man who fell to the ground, and a pool of blood came out,” a witness, who was at a gym when the shooting began, told AP. “One gym member rushed to help him. He was instantly dead. He had been shot in the neck.”

Videos and images circulating on social media purport to show heavily armed police stationed on rooftops around an apartment building. Other footage shows officers armed with ballistic shields closing in on what appears to be the same building.

Videos also show a heavy police presence on DC streets after the incident.

Huge police presence in Washington DC for an active shooter. Residents being warned to shelter in place. Am watching SWAT teams get ready to storm a building. 15th St NW at junction with P street. https://t.co/MEuFtcQdUR

— Richard Gaisford (@richardgaisford) November 12, 2026

The suspect, who was found with a self-inflicted gunshot wound and received medical assistance, has since died of his injuries, according to the police chief.

Read more

Of the four people injured in the shooting, one is in critical condition and the other three have non-life-threatening injuries, DC Fire and EMS Chief John Donnelly said at a press conference.

Police identified the suspect as 55-year-old Matt Lambert. “We do know there was a conflict between him and the homeowners association of that building. But at this point, we’re continuing to look into that,” Carroll told reporters.

On his personal website, Lambert described himself as “a seasoned clinician, consultant, and entrepreneur.” He also identified himself as the founder and CEO of MLEM, a healthcare and technology consultancy.

title: EU incapable of speaking with one voice on Ukraine – analyst to RT (VIDEO)
content:
Divisions between major powers have left the bloc without a credible representative for talks with Moscow, Xavier Moreau says

The European Union lacks a diplomatic heavyweight capable of negotiating with Russia, while disagreements between its largest member states have undermined its ability to speak with one voice on Ukraine, Stratpol director Xavier Moreau has told RT.

His comments follow two days of trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi, which concluded on Wednesday, marking the first formal three-way meeting since February. European representatives were excluded from the negotiations, although they held separate discussions with US and Ukrainian officials on Tuesday. Moscow has questioned Europe’s potential contribution to the peace process, accusing EU governments of undermining previous agreements and prolonging the conflict through continued weapons supplies.

“The European Union makes the big European countries weak,” Moreau said, arguing that the bloc’s diplomatic structure has left its most influential members unable to take the lead in potential negotiations with Moscow.

Read more

He questioned who could credibly represent the EU in talks with Russia, dismissing the bloc’s foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, as an unsuitable candidate.

“She’s not very known as a clever diplomat, so the Russians will never accept,” Moreau said, suggesting that any European representative should instead come from Germany, France, or Italy.

However, he argued that the EU’s overlapping national and supranational diplomatic structures have created confusion over who actually speaks for Europe.

“Who is in charge of the diplomacy in the European Union? Brussels, Paris, Germany, or Italy?” he asked.

Moreau also pointed to sharply differing positions among the bloc’s three largest economies. According to the analyst, France has exhausted its financial capacity to support Ukraine, while German Chancellor Friedrich Merz remains committed to continued assistance despite mounting difficulties.

Italy, meanwhile, is seeking to distance itself from the conflict, he claimed, while ultimately following Washington’s lead.

Moreau also cited disagreements between Germany and Eastern European countries, including Bulgaria, Czechia, and Romania, which he said are increasingly unwilling to fund Ukraine.

“So a common voice in Europe, it’s not possible,” he concluded.

title: White House warns Democrats over Trump probes
content:
The exchange of threats comes after House Democrats vowed to investigate alleged corruption during Trump’s second term

The White House’s top lawyer has warned the House Democrats that their plans to investigate the administration of US President Donald Trump “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The dispute follows a pledge by the Democrats to launch a broad series of investigations into the Trump administration after winning control of the House of Representatives in last week’s midterm elections. The probes are expected to focus on alleged corruption, conflicts of interest, and abuses of power.

In a three-page letter issued on Wednesday to incoming House Oversight Committee chairman Robert Garcia, White House counsel Will Scharf argued that congressional investigations must remain within constitutional limits, adding that Garcia and members of the new Congress have “evinced a clear intent to transgress” them. The letter accuses Democrats of “abusive and capricious threats” against Trump and members of his administration.

Garcia pushed back, saying Congress has the constitutional authority to conduct oversight independently of the White House and will not be deterred by “baseless threats” from the administration or the Justice Department. He argued that voters gave the Democrats a mandate “to root out corruption and abuse.”

The latest exchange comes a week after Garcia issued a blunt warning of his own. On election night, after projections showed Democrats would take control of the House, he addressed the incoming Congress with a two-word message: “Lawyer up.”

Read more

Last week, Garcia also outlined several areas Democrats intend to investigate, including what he described as corruption within the Trump family, corporate misconduct, alleged abuses by Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and the administration’s handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation. He also intends to examine the Trump family’s business dealings, including cryptocurrency and mineral deals, as well as construction projects at the White House.

Commenting on the plans at the time, White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said Trump is willing to work with Democrats to deliver results for Americans, but warned that pursuing “sham investigations” and “radical-left policies” would mean acting “against the American people.”

Outgoing Republican Representative Thomas Massie of Kentucky, a Trump critic, told AP on Wednesday that he hopes the Democrats focus on real issues rather than “stupid things” such as the Russiagate inquiry, an investigation based on debunked claims that Trump’s 2016 campaign colluded with Russia. Massie, who recently lost his primary to a Trump-backed Republican challenger, said he believes there is “real corruption” involving the president and the people around him.

title: Russia’s hockey comeback a ‘return to normality’ – German opposition
content:
The AfD and Left Party have urged respect for a court ruling reinstating Russian national teams despite European boycott threats

Russia’s return to international hockey would mark a “return to normality,” a senior Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmaker has said, as his party and the Left Party backed Russian participation in the 2027 Ice Hockey World Championship despite European boycott threats.  

The statements follow an October 30 ruling by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS), which overturned Russia’s exclusion from International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) competitions. The German government and hockey federation remain opposed to Russian participation, citing security, political and economic concerns.  

The right-wing AfD and the Left Party have urged Berlin to respect the CAS ruling, which restored Russian national teams’ right to compete internationally.  

“We see this as a return to normality. Of course, Russian athletes should also be issued visas,” Jorn Konig, the AfD parliamentary group’s sports spokesman, told ZDFheute.  

Read more

Russian and Belarusian athletes were barred from numerous international competitions following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in 2022. Since then, criticism of the bans as politically motivated and discriminatory has grown, with a number of sports federations easing restrictions.  

Konig, who has opposed the Ukraine conflict, accused sporting authorities of double standards, noting that the US had never been excluded from international competitions despite waging wars he described as violations of international law.  

The AfD won September’s regional election in Saxony-Anhalt, defeating Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s CDU.  

Christian Gorke, the Left Party’s sports spokesman, also urged respect for the CAS ruling, saying Germany could no longer ignore the “regrettable reality” of Russia’s return.  

The championship is scheduled for May 13-30, 2027, in Dusseldorf and Mannheim. The IIHF has expressed “disappointment” with the ruling but pledged to comply.  

The German Ice Hockey Federation (DEB) opposes Russia’s return, with its chairman, Frank Lutz, warning that the ruling “fundamentally changes the situation,” citing political, economic and security concerns.  

Days earlier, Finland, Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Latvia, and the Czech Republic announced boycotts of matches against Russia, while Austria indicated it would follow suit.  

The boycott threats have cast doubt on Germany’s ability to host the tournament. Berlin is consulting hockey officials, warning that the event could become impossible to organize for sporting and economic reasons.  

Read more

Russian officials have condemned the politicization of sport, arguing that athletes should not be punished over geopolitical disputes. Sports Minister and Olympic Committee chief Mikhail Degtyarev branded the threats “infantile” and warned that countries pressuring the IIHF could face legal action or lose hosting rights.  

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggested moving the championship elsewhere if Germany refuses to host it, noting that “there are plenty of countries” willing to stage the tournament.  

Earlier this year, the International Olympic Committee provisionally lifted its suspension of the Russian Olympic Committee, while several federations have readmitted Russian athletes, sometimes under their national flag and anthem.  

President Vladimir Putin has welcomed the trend, calling for a return to the principles of international sport, including “equality, justice, mutual respect and the unifying power of sport.”  

Meanwhile, Canada announced on Wednesday that Russian and Belarusian athletes and officials would be barred from December’s World Junior Ice Hockey Championship, even with valid visas.
