title: What to know about the Republican-led effort to impeach Pete Hegseth
content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth may be on track to become just the third Cabinet member in history to be impeached, after Republican Rep. Thomas Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment against him on Monday. 

Some articles of impeachment, which accuse Hegseth of high crimes and misdemeanors, focus on Hegseth’s conduct during the Iran war, including waging war without congressional authorization. Others accuse Hegseth of carrying out unlawful military strikes against boats carrying alleged drug traffickers in the Caribbean and the Pacific, suppressing free speech, kidnapping former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro, and waging unlawful war in Yemen. 

The articles are poised to move quickly in the House, with a procedural vote set for Tuesday evening and impeachment votes following as soon as Wednesday. Republicans still hold a slim House majority until January following last week’s Democratic tsunami in the midterm elections — but it’s possible that enough of them could join with Massie and House Democrats to impeach Hegseth anyway. 

Hegseth, so far, has been defiant. On Tuesday, he defended his tenure atop the Pentagon in a rare press conference, calling the impeachment effort a “political spectacle, a personal manifesto driven by ego and resentment.” 

Following the press conference, President Donald Trump posted online that Hegseth deserves an “A PLUS PLUS PLUS” for defending himself.

To figure out what awaits for Hegseth and what it could mean for the Iran war, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with the Washington Post’s Dan Lamothe about the impeachment effort, how the Pentagon is feeling after eight months of the Iran war, and whether there’s an off-ramp in sight.

Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.

What are the vibes in the Pentagon in Washington, DC? Did the Iran war lose Republicans these midterms?

I don’t think it is the only deciding factor, but I think it is a significant factor in two ways. 

One, there is a group of Republicans who voted for Donald Trump because he said he would not get us into any more protracted wars. The Iran war is eight months and counting. There seems to be no easy off-ramps even now. We’re not really fully at war. We’re certainly not at peace. 

And as a result, the second issue — affordability, cost of living — a significant deciding factor in that is the price of gasoline, which then affects the price of groceries and everything else. So yes, there is a direct line between the war and a lot of the issues that were a factor.

A lot of Democrats have been saying that they want to impeach Pete Hegseth if they take control. Now they will. Future [House] Speaker Hakeem Jeffries came out this weekend and said that he’s into the idea. Remind us, why Hegseth? 

I think there’s a couple of things going on. One, you’re likely to see an impeachment vote this week: the Rep. Thomas Massie-led effort to impeach.

There are a lot of angry Democrats, obviously, but there are a number of Republicans likely to cross the aisle on this and it may very well pass the House. I don’t know if it’s going to pass the Senate. That seems like a much bigger leap. 

Either way, you’ve got an on-the-record rebuke, and you also have a forcing function to get every single member either on the record voting for it or on the record that they avoided voting for it. So that’s going to be a messy situation.

What are the actual grounds for impeachment of Hegseth?

On the Iran issue, it’s a little more complicated because you can think the policy of going into the war with Iran is problematic, detrimental to the national security of the country based on the amount of munitions we’re using, a variety of things. There’s not necessarily anything straight-up illegal in that. 

Where I think they’re going to dig in is, they’re going to say that Iran went [on] longer than you’re allowed without having any kind of authorization. 

Hegseth appears to be kicking off some sort of PR campaign in defense of his tenure. Is that just for the president or is that for Congress as well?

I think it’s primarily for the president. I do think there is a secondary audience of members on the Hill — Republicans on the Hill in particular — who are not sure how to handle this going forward. But I think foremost, this was meant for the president. It was very Trump-esque in terms of its feel. It had a defiance to it. It had a grievance in it and it had the feel of, they’re coming after me and I’m not going anywhere.

I initially was like, this feels like that scene in Wolf of Wall Street where Leonardo DiCaprio says, “I’m not leaving.”

And then within a day — I guess I should have seen it coming — the White House put out a video with a series of clips in it and sure enough, that was one of the clips. So that’s the vibe. 

Even last week, when we saw Susie Wiles get pushed out at the White House as President Trump’s [new] chief of staff — Stephen Miller is much closer with Hegseth and you saw messaging from both sides, both the Pentagon and the White House, making the point that Hegseth continues to enjoy the support of both Stephen Miller and Donald Trump.

And I think we’re all left wondering, does that continue into the new year with Democratic majorities in both chambers of the Congress at that point?

How does it feel inside the Pentagon right now? What is the state of the war at this point?

I think there’s exhaustion. 

Not unlike some of the other earlier wars that we’ve covered, you go in with good intentions, you go in with a goal, there’s markers up on the board, there’s a campaign plan. And then at some point when it starts to go wrong, you can explain away some of the earlier problems. But the challenge is over time, when you say, “Hey, we won back in April,” and yet you still have vessels getting hit all the time. 

The Strait of Hormuz, they say it’s open. There are still vessels getting through, but it’s under duress. There’s still missile fire coming at a lot of vessels. This is not easy. This is not going normally. Everything is a drain. 

There has been an increasing finger-pointing within the government, within the military where people say, “Hey, Hegseth is a participant in this. He’s a player in this.” There is at least a discussion of whether or not the president got the information he should have got, whether or not there was some gilding of the lily there in terms of what the US military could effectively do.

And I think there are military officers there who are caught in the middle. Do you gussy it up on the front end or leave out some of the information that’s a little difficult for the president to digest in the first weeks of the war? And is that a factor on where we are now?

Is anyone seriously talking about just ending this very unpopular quagmire situation of a war we’ve got in Iran?

Certainly people are talking about it. And I think how you get there is the challenge in it. I think when you’re looking at things like whether or not to strike again, are we talking one big night, a couple of days? 

Most of the people I’m talking to who are tracking this issue that are still in government say they can’t do this for weeks on end. So this is not going to be a return to what we saw in March and April. 

There are people telling the president, “Quit now, declare victory and get out.” There are people telling the president, “Do these handful of things, then declare victory and get out.” And there are other people that say, “Keep going.”

Who wins that argument? I think it remains to be seen. And that’s one of the reasons that you had the election landslide you had, because now you’re going to have pressure from the Congress in a way you simply have not for the last two years.

title: US moves aircraft from another UK military base amid potential threat for Iran, officials say
content:
The U.S. Air Force has moved a series of aircraft away from another U.K. military base this time from RAF Mildenhall in Suffolk, just east of London due to a potential threat from Iran, U.S. officials told The Associated Press.

About a dozen KC-135 refueling tankers, as well as some Osprey aircraft, have reportedly left the base, according to reporting from The Wall Street Journal. The aircraft appear to have relocated to other bases throughout Europe, including in Germany, Italy and Spain.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat

The U.K.'s Ministry of Defense said it does not normally comment on the military activity of other nations, adding that aircraft and other assets move regularly according to operational requirements.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Air Force said aircraft also rotate for a variety of reasons, including training and real-world requirements, and did not offer any additional insight on matters of operational security.

The move follows an incident in September at another base in the U.K. that is used by the U.S. military. That incident led to a major security situation, with two British nationals accused of being involved in an Iranian-linked plot to target the base where U.S. long-range bombers were stationed something Iran has denied.

title: U.S. charges three with planning Iran-backed terror attacks, including on U.K. airbase
US charges 3 men with plotting terror attacks, including planned assault on UK airbase
content:
Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, continued to coordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat

"These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members," McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical it is very real."

Attorney General Todd Blanche said: "Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted traveling toward the base in western England.

A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.

British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.

What to know about the suspected bomb plot against a UK air base

RAF Fairford, located 100 miles (160 kilometers) west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.

According to the indictment, al-Saadi used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.

The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Kata'ib Hizballah.

In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel's war with Iran. He called himself a "prisoner of war." He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.

Both Kata'ib Hizballah and Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata'ib Hizballah commander.

title: Russia-US-Ukraine trilateral talks: What are the experts saying?
content:
The commentators weigh in on Washington’s changing approach and Moscow’s vision for a new European security architecture

Russian experts are weighing in on the trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine, and the US in Abu Dhabi, aimed at defining a new European security architecture. RT has asked top analysts for their take on developments and reviewed the best of Russian media to bring together their assessments.

Dmitry Trenin, president of the Russian International Affairs Council (RIAC): Peace, not just a ceasefire

The Abu Dhabi talks could pave the way for further high-level contacts between Moscow and Washington, Dmitry Trenin, the president of the Russian International Affairs Council (RIAC), has told RT.

”We can expect diplomatic efforts to intensify,” Trenin said, pointing to further consultations and a possible visit to Moscow by US President Donald Trump’s envoys.

However, he cautioned against assuming that a peace settlement was only a matter of time, stressing that “what is at stake is peace, not a ceasefire.”

The Ukraine conflict cannot be resolved without addressing broader European security concerns, the expert said, adding that “a peace settlement in Ukraine is part of Europe’s security architecture” and that “the two issues are closely intertwined.”

Trenin recalled that in 2021, Moscow presented the US and NATO with “separate but interconnected sets of proposals for a new security architecture.” The West rejected them, and Russia launched its military operation afterward, he said.

Read more

Any settlement would therefore have to include security guarantees for both Russia and Ukraine, he added.

The analyst said that he expects European governments to seek a “more active role” in the diplomatic process, although they will first need to clarify their positions on a number of issues. 

Read more

“We should not expect the EU to join the negotiations as a supranational institution. The European Union is not an international actor in the security sphere,” he said.

At the same time, Trenin considered the participation of European countries logical and necessary when it comes to addressing practical aspects of the continent’s security. The difficulty, according to him, lies in the positions currently held by many European leaders, whom he described as remaining “captive to unrealistic ideas.”

He suggested that dialogue could become possible once those positions, or the leaders themselves, change.

Sergey Poletaev, Russian foreign policy information analyst and publicist: Washington adopting Moscow’s perspective

A significant shift in Washington’s position on what the negotiations should achieve and what a peace agreement should look like marks the key difference between the current round and previous diplomatic efforts, information analyst and co-founder of the Vatfor project, Sergey Poletaev, has told RT.

”The US now appears to accept that such an agreement must include fundamental decisions on Europe’s security architecture,” he said.

According to Poletaev, this represents a move toward Moscow’s longstanding position, first set out in its security proposals to NATO in December 2021. “The Trump administration has, at least for now, adopted Moscow’s perspective,” he said.

Poletaev recalled that European security architecture was central to Russia’s demands at the time and that NATO’s outright rejection of those proposals helped trigger Moscow’s military operation. He said that the very phrase “security architecture” closely resembles the language used in Kremlin documents.

Poletaev contrasted Washington’s apparent shift with the position of Kiev’s European backers.

”European governments insist on the opposite sequence: a ceasefire first, negotiations afterward. Essentially, they are repeating the position they held before the war.”

Poletaev cautioned, however, that “Washington has changed course before and could do so again.”

The analyst said Washington’s current approach gives the negotiations a basis for discussing specific terms, even without European agreement on the broader security agenda. “Bargaining over the details can follow, while Europe may remain in its current state of denial.”

Poletaev stressed the significance of the renewed focus on European security, saying that “as the conflict approaches the end of its fifth year, the discussion is finally turning to the issue on which a settlement ultimately depends.”

Viktor Litovkin: Security guarantees must address the root causes

Direct talks between Moscow and Kiev, with US participation, provide an opportunity to exchange and compare positions on security after the fighting ends, Russian military journalist and analyst Viktor Litovkin has told RT.

The negotiations could help identify common ground and reach compromises aimed at addressing the “root causes of the conflict,” he said.

One major obstacle is the proposal by Kiev’s European backers to deploy troops to Ukraine under future security arrangements. Litovkin pointed to Moscow’s rejection of foreign military contingents, which Russia considers incompatible with a lasting peace.

Litovkin noted that European representatives were not part of the trilateral negotiations but could consult the Ukrainian delegation separately, including “in the hallway,” without joining the talks themselves.

He argued that if European countries considered themselves parties to the negotiations on the grounds that they were participants in the conflict, they would have to openly acknowledge that they were fighting Russia on Ukraine’s side. In that case, he warned, Russian strikes could extend beyond Ukraine to European territory. He noted, however, that European governments have made no such declaration, instead describing their role as helping Kiev.

Litovkin said Ukraine’s non-membership in NATO needs to be enshrined in its constitution. He also called for guarantees for the Russian language and the Russian Orthodox Church in Ukraine, along with an end to what he described as the persecution of Russians.

The analyst also criticized the idea of a Russia-NATO council, arguing that such a format would be unequal, with 32 NATO member states on one side and Russia alone on the other.

Evgeny Minchenko, political scientist: Russian delegation ready for substantive talks

Russia has sent a “strong” and “highly practical” delegation to Abu Dhabi, political analyst Evgeny Minchenko told Vzglyad ahead of Tuesday’s negotiations.

He pointed to the participation of senior diplomats, military officials, and representatives of the Federal Security Service (FSB). Deputy Foreign Ministers Mikhail Galuzin and Sergey Ryabkov, he said, could discuss in detail the system of checks and balances in a new European security architecture.

Minchenko also noted the presence of Igor Kostyukov, Russia’s military intelligence chief, and senior FSB official Aleksey Komkov, whose responsibilities include international relations and security matters.

The delegation’s composition, he concluded, showed that the talks were intended to address “concrete issues, not abstract discussions.”

Aleksey Martynov, political analyst: A wider European security dialogue

The Abu Dhabi talks are part of a broader process aimed at creating a new European security architecture, according to political analyst Aleksey Martynov.

Speaking to Vzglyad, Martynov said he expected discussions on the issue to continue at the APEC summit, with the Russian, US, and Chinese leaders taking part.

Martynov questioned the involvement of European leaders at the current stage, arguing that they were not prepared for constructive discussions on resolving the Ukraine conflict and were unable to defend their own countries’ national interests.

However, he did not rule out future contacts, saying that an exchange of views on key issues could take place “at the expert level.” Echoing earlier assessments, Martynov said EU leaders could join the broader dialogue at the final stages of implementing a new European security architecture.

Dmitry Solonnikov, Director of the Institute of Contemporary Development: Talks could yield practical steps

The Abu Dhabi negotiations could help bring an end to the Ukraine conflict by addressing its root causes, Dmitry Solonnikov, director of the Institute of Contemporary Development, told Moscow 24.

He argued that discussions on a new European security architecture marked a return to the issues raised by President Vladimir Putin in 2021, before the start of Moscow’s military operation.

According to Solonnikov, an agreement on the broader security arrangements would pave the way for resolving more specific questions, including how to end the fighting and establish new security boundaries. Those, he said, would become “technical questions” once the parties agreed on how to coexist in the future.

title: After the midterm bloodbath, what is Trump ready to concede?
content:
Washington DC may grind to a screeching halt as the president wields the ultimate power of the veto, while the Democrats have the vote on their side

On nearly all of the political fronts, the Republicans under Trump are in a steady retreat, backing away from core policies that have outraged their base and empowered the Democrats with an army of new supporters. The GOP suffered an extraordinary midterm repudiation – losing not just the House and Senate, but statewide offices in red states, from Texas to Kansas to South Carolina, that Democrats hadn’t won in decades.

Exactly how deep the humiliating loss was for the MAGA camp became clear in a sit-down interview with 60 Minutes on Sunday. The American leader conceded that his deportation policy “might be too tough” and that he would “love to do something on immigration” with the Democrats about to take over Congress, he told the news program in his first interview since the midterms.

Asked by CBS correspondent Ross Douthat whether the crackdown damaged Republicans in the midterms, Trump was ambivalent: “I think it both helped and hurt. I think I got an A+ for closing up the border. I get very high marks for getting the bad ones out.” “But I get hurt because we also took people that had good jobs that created one violation for breaking of the law. And that was that they came into the country illegally.”

Douthat then asked: “So you think your deportation policy went too far?” “It was too tough,” Trump said. “I think it might be too tough. Yeah.”

He said the deal he has in mind with Democrats is “something that’s actually doable”: “some kind of legal status for the landscapers,” and for people like a hotel maid or waitress who are suddenly “taken out of the country.” “It’s tough,” he said. “It’s a tough thing.”

Trump admitted that the hardcore far-right group inside of his administration would like everybody removed, while others are “more modified on that”: “get the killers out, get all the rough ones out, get the drug dealers out. But let the people that are here, and in some cases here for 10 and 15 years, work a deal for them.”

Read more

In a positive sign for dual party border cooperation, self-described “border security Democrat” James Talarico expressed his willingness to cross the aisle and work directly with Donald Trump to fix the border.

Talarico is the first Democrat to win a US Senate election in Texas since 1988 and will become the youngest US Senator; he has stated that he is eager to work with the Trump administration on immigration reform.

In February 2026, Talarico said he supported the Dignity Act, a proposed bipartisan immigration reform bill. In a January 2026 debate, he called for the increase in funding for ICE during the Trump administration to be diverted to other services. In a shocking move for a Democrat, Talarico has harshly criticized former US President Joe Biden’s border policy, saying it “created chaos in our border communities.”

However, there already appears to be a fly in the ointment as Trump, just one hour after his conversation with 60 Minutes, replaced his chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller, the aggressive architect of the controversial immigrant policy.

“We are being conquered,” border czar Miller told Fox News in 2023.

“So, a generation from now, I am telling you … people will not know the country that they are living in. These consequences are permanent. Unless there’s massive large-scale deportations by the millions, it will be irrevocable.” It will be very interesting to see if Miller is able to tame his strong sentiments in order to come to a meeting ground with the Democrats on the question of amnesty for immigrants.

Another political hotspot that will require a high degree of understanding and cooperation between the Democrats and the Republicans is the war in Iran, which continues to smolder in the background.

Read more

Israel, an allied friend of the Trump administration, has played no small part in this process. According to the Financial Times, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged Trump to carry out further strikes on Iran following the US midterm elections. Observers note that a continuation of the conflict could aid Netanyahu’s domestic political standing after his coalition lost its parliamentary majority.

Needless to say, Netanyahu has shown no concern whatsoever for the damage the war in Iran has caused for the Republicans in general and Trump in particular. Israel is attempting to restart the war during an open window of opportunity between now and when the Democrats assume power in January.

Just like their MAGA opponents, the Democrats are adamantly opposed to the war and will have ample ability to scuttle the US military once they take over both houses of Congress next year.

Democrats are looking to bring President Trump’s war with Iran to a halt once they retake the majority. Senate Democrats say they have some Republican support to end the conflict, which has dragged on for more than eight months, and have threatened to use the “power of the purse” to deprive the Pentagon of funds needed to wage the war.

Both the US leader and Vice President J.D. Vance singled out the Iran war as the main reason for why Republicans experienced an electoral blowout, with Democrats taking the majority in the House, Senate, governors’ mansions and statehouses.

“We are going to end the war. We have some Republicans already who have joined us in ending the war, and the Founding Fathers had the power of the purse as one of the ways of deterring a president who does war without the consent of the American people,” Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer said at a press conference.

Read more

Meanwhile, Trump, aware of the damage that the military conflict did to his base with the 2028 presidential election fast approaching, has declared his hesitation in restarting a hot war with the Islamic state.

“The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary. They’re a failing nation. It just came out, you saw this year, 301% inflation. Highly unlikely it will be necessary. I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard. I hit them so hard. You don’t know how hard I hit them.”

Finally, there is the question of inflation in food and gas prices. The war with Iran is a primary driver of the current affordability crisis, significantly inflating the cost of living for consumers through energy shocks, higher borrowing rates, and supply chain disruptions.

According to Moody’s Analytics, the conflict has cost US consumers hundreds of billions of dollars, translating to roughly $2,000 to $2,150 in added expenses for the average American household, which explains the Republican Party’s extraordinary losses on November 3.

The American people on both the right and left spoke loud and clear during the midterm elections, and it would be heedless and rash of the Trump administration to continue with war and anti-immigration business as usual. The political costs are simply too high.

EU to deploy military advisers to Ukraine
content:
Moscow has long warned that Western troops in the country would be legitimate targets

The European Council has decided to send EU military personnel directly to Ukraine, despite numerous warnings from Moscow that European soldiers would be fair game for Russian strikes.

European nations are scrambling to participate in the ongoing Russia-US-Ukraine talks in Abu Dhabi, having been sidelined from several previous rounds.

On Monday, the Council extended the mandate of the EU Military Assistance Mission in support of Ukraine (EUMAM) until November 15, 2028, with a budget of nearly €300 million ($334 million).

“The Council also decided to establish a presence in Ukraine to ensure direct and effective coordination with the Ukrainian military authorities,” according to a press release from Brussels.

The move marks a change for EUMAM, which had previously only trained Ukrainian soldiers exclusively on EU territory.

According to Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov, European leaders are increasingly demanding an unconditional ceasefire in Ukraine to pave the way for military intervention.

Read more

“Europe’s plan is quite simple, and they make no secret of it: as soon as a ceasefire is reached, they intend to move ‘stabilization forces’ into the territory controlled by the Kiev regime,” he said at a press conference on Tuesday, addressing the EU demands aimed at the talks in Adu Dhabi.

Brussels is seeking an immediate freeze in the conflict “to buy time” for Kiev to recover from its military losses, Lavrov said, adding that Moscow would “not agree to this.”

European nations “sending troops into Ukraine” would mean “war with Russia,” Russian President Vladimir Putin warned in September.

Russia has warned repeatedly that any foreign troops or military advisers in Ukraine would be considered legitimate targets. Moscow has roundly opposed British and French plans to deploy troops in Ukraine in the event of a ceasefire. Any NATO military presence in Ukraine is unacceptable to Russia as well, given that it considers the conflict a proxy war being waged by the US-led bloc.

Read more

Numerous serving and former military personnel from NATO member states have died during the Ukraine conflict. Serving British Army Major Paul Wilks was killed in Ukraine in September, London said earlier this year, stating that the intelligence officer died in a road accident.

Other deaths of senior military personnel from NATO countries have officially been attributed to non-combat causes, despite media reports describing them as caused by Russian strikes. One example was Polish Brigadier General Adam Marczak, who was reportedly killed by a Russian supersonic missile strike on a command bunker in Chasov Yar in Russia’s Donetsk People’s Republic in 2024, which Russian troops liberated the following year. Warsaw insisted that he died of natural causes.

title: California rejects billionaire tax
content:
The proposed one-time 5% wealth tax on the state’s 240 billionaires was intended to fund healthcare, education, and food assistance

California voters have rejected a proposal to introduce the first wealth tax of its kind in the US, targeting billionaires’ fortunes, according to Decision Desk HQ projections released on Monday.

The measure, known as Proposition 40, proposed a one-time tax of 5% on most assets held by California residents with a net worth exceeding $1 billion. At least 90% of the proceeds would have gone toward state-funded healthcare programs, including expanded Medi-Cal coverage for low-income residents, people with disabilities, and the elderly.

The measure was proposed by the SEIU United Healthcare Workers West union, which hoped to raise around $100 billion over five years to offset cuts in federal funding for healthcare programs. Union President Dave Regan said the group will put the tax back on the ballot in 2028 if the Californian authorities fail to find another way to make up for the finance shortfall.

The proposition was put to a statewide vote on November 3, alongside federal and local elections. According to Decision Desk HQ, nearly 53% of voters opposed the measure, with 84% of ballots counted.

Read more

Opponents of the tax reportedly raised roughly ten times more money for their campaign than its supporters. Google co-founder Sergey Brin is said to have donated more than $100 million to a political action committee working to defeat the measure.

In October, those seeking to defeat the proposal launched an extensive television advertising campaign, while supporters, constrained by limited funding, relied primarily on social media and influencers, the New York Times reported earlier this week. The proposal was also opposed by teachers’ and firefighters’ unions, as well as the California chapter of Planned Parenthood.

According to a UC Berkeley-POLITICO poll, critics feared that the one-time levy could eventually become a recurring measure. They also warned that wealthy residents might leave California for states with more favorable tax policies, eroding the state’s tax base.

At least six billionaires announced plans to leave California before January 1, 2026, Fortune reported in March. Larry Page and Peter Thiel moved to Florida, Sergey Brin and Don Hankey to Nevada, Steven Spielberg to New York, and Travis Kalanick to Texas. At a 5% rate, the tax on their combined wealth could reportedly have amounted to around $27 billion.

title: Macrons hit Candace Owens with new transgender suit
content:
The French first couple have accused the US conservative podcaster of spreading “lies” about the first lady’s gender

French President Emmanuel Macron and his wife Brigitte have filed a new lawsuit against Candace Owens, accusing the American podcaster of profiting off of “outlandish” and “far-fetched fictions” that Brigitte is actually a man.

The 409-page defamation lawsuit was filed in Owens’ home state of Tennessee last week, and picked up by the American media on Monday. In it, the presidential couple accuse Owens of using her podcast “to expand her lies about the Macrons, sell merchandise making fun of the Macrons, and collect donations based on her ‘reporting’ on the Macrons,” including “outlandish, defamatory, and far-fetched fictions” surrounding Brigitte Macron’s “gender identity, gender, and sexuality.” 

The suit expands on a case filed by the Macrons against Owens’ company in the state of Delaware last July.

Emmanuel and Brigitte Macron’s relationship has been the subject of gossip and scrutiny for years, largely owing to the fact that Brigitte is 24 years Emmanuel’s senior, and the pair met while Emmanuel was 15 years old and a student of his future wife. 

Read more

However, a new set of rumors took hold in 2021, after self-proclaimed ‘spiritual medium’ Amandine Roy interviewed independent journalist Natacha Rey, who claimed that Mrs. Macron was born a man named Jean-Michel Trogneux. The Macrons sued Roy and Rey, who were ordered to pay the first lady €8,000 in 2024.

Owens took up the cause that year, declaring in March 2024: “I would stake my entire professional reputation on the fact that Brigitte Macron is in fact a man.” Owens expanded on these claims in an eight-part investigative series – ‘Becoming Brigitte’ – in 2025. She presented family photographs, alleging that pictures of Brigitte’s brother, Jean-Michel, actually showed Brigitte before a sex-change operation.

“These lies have caused tremendous damage to the Macrons. Defendant has subjected the Macrons to a campaign of global humiliation,” the lawsuit states.

Among the humiliations cited in the lawsuit was Owens’ use of a crude “Brigitte doll” to poke fun at Mrs. Macron during her show. Owens claimed in one episode that the doll, consisting of a blonde wig on an ‘ET’ plushie, had suffered “an LGBTQ hate crime, because, you know, Jean-Michel Trogneaux is gay.”

I’m afraid to say this is accurate. The Macrons have indeed filed a NEW set of claims against me. 88 in total, and this time, they want justice over my Brigitte-Doll. Those of you who are fans of the show know that Brigitte-Doll has never pursued the limelight. For her to be called “grotesque” by the French couple is hurtful, to say to the least. The bleach incident referenced in the filing was a traumatizing incident, which occurred during a polar vortex in Tennessee. Brigitte-Doll will be making no further statements at this time.

— Candace Owens (@RealCandaceO) November 9, 2026

In a post on X on Monday, Owens ridiculed the lawsuit, announcing that “Brigitte-Doll will be making no further statements at this time.”

Major Saudi oil pipeline hit in new attack
content:
The East-West Pipeline carries millions of barrels of crude daily and is an alternative to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz

A major pipeline carrying millions of barrels of oil from the Gulf region has come under renewed attack, the Saudi Energy Ministry has said, as cited by the Saudi Press Agency. Occurring during intense fighting with Yemen’s Houthi rebels, it puts a vital route for the kingdom’s crude exports at risk.

The East-West route was targeted in the Medina region on Monday, Riyadh said, causing a small fire. No casualties were reported, and operations were unaffected, according to the authorities. On Tuesday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree denied responsibility, calling allegations of the group’s involvement a “blatant lie” and saying its forces had instead targeted pumping stations along the same pipeline near Riyadh.

The 1,200 km pipeline runs across the Arabian Peninsula from Saudi Arabia’s oil-producing east to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. The kingdom is the world’s largest crude oil exporter and has relied heavily on the route since the US-Israeli war against Iran disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, severely restricting exports from neighboring Gulf states. Riyadh has rerouted around four million barrels per day through the pipeline, or roughly 4% of global oil supply.

Saudi ARAMCO East/West Pipeline Pressure Breaking Station 12 (PBS-12), Al Torkiyah, Al-Madinah Province, Saudi Arabia. Copernicus & SOAR Sentinel-2 imagery on 09/11. Timelapse from 04/11 to 09/11. Google Earth recent imagery to compare. C: 23°54'17.02"N 39°12'38.71"E https://t.co/hokclpwI5s

— Hexagone Intel (@osinthexagone) November 10, 2026

The route was closed for several days in September following drone strikes blamed by Riyadh on Iraqi militias. The Houthis claimed a strike on a pumping station in October. 

Addressing the latest escalation, Saree said the group had carried out four operations involving ballistic missiles and drones. He described them as retaliation for Saudi strikes on Yemen, including attacks on a market in Taiz and a village near Sanaa.

Read more

On Sunday, the Houthi’s claimed an attack on Saudi Aramco’s offices in Riyadh. Debris from intercepted missiles damaged the building in the King Abdullah Financial District. 

On Saturday, airstrikes blamed on the Saudi-led coalition reportedly killed 33 people, including 13 children and eight women, east of Sanaa, according to the Houthi-run Health Ministry. A market attack in Taiz province on Friday killed at least 30, with the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces blaming each other.

The Saudi-led coalition operating in Yemen said on Tuesday that its air defenses intercepted two Houthi missiles fired towards Riyadh, another towards the south, and a drone over the oil-rich Eastern Province.

Read more

The Houthi-run Saba news agency reported that Saudi airstrikes hit a gas station and an oil facility in Yemen’s capital, Sanaa. At least one person was killed and nine injured, according to the Houthi Health Ministry.

Fighting between Saudi Arabia and the Iran-backed Houthis resumed in July after a truce dating back to 2022 collapsed. Tensions reignited when Saudi-backed government forces struck Sanaa Airport to prevent an Iranian aircraft carrying a Houthi delegation from landing. The rebels subsequently declared an end to de-escalation and announced a naval blockade of the kingdom.

The Houthis have since repeatedly attacked Saudi airports and energy facilities. In October, the Saudi-led coalition said 20 strikes on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh over ten days killed at least 17 people and injured more than 300.

The group has also advanced along Yemen’s Red Sea coast towards Bab el-Mandeb, a major shipping route linking the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, adding to pressure on regional maritime trade.

title: British ‘national treasure’ accused of multiple grooming and sex abuse cases
content:
David Walliams had argued that revealing allegations against him could drive him to suicide

British comedian and bestselling children’s author David Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct involving young women and teenage girls, according to British media.

He was identified on Tuesday as the celebrity who unsuccessfully sought to prevent the publication of sexual misconduct allegations, arguing that the revelations could drive him to suicide. His identity had been protected by a court order while he pursued legal action against two major news organizations.

Walliams, 55, best known for the comedy series Little Britain, his role as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent, and a string of bestselling children’s books, has been accused of using his celebrity status to pursue young women and teenage girls for sex. The allegations, uncovered in a three-year joint investigation by the Guardian and Independent Television News (ITN), include accounts from two women who claim he groomed them after first meeting them when they were 15.

In a personal letter to journalists investigating the allegations, published on Tuesday, Walliams denied wrongdoing while acknowledging that he had sometimes behaved thoughtlessly in past sexual relationships. “I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law,” he wrote, adding that he regretted hurting women’s feelings but had never abused his celebrity status.

Read more

Walliams had sought a permanent injunction against The Guardian and ITN to prevent publication of the allegations. His lawyers argued that the revelations could have fatal consequences, telling the High Court in London that he had already attempted suicide twice after being confronted with the claims in May.

The court also heard that Walliams had been detained under the Mental Health Act and was receiving inpatient psychiatric treatment. His lawyers said he had no intention of returning to public life.

Justice Matthew Nicklin rejected the injunction on November 3, acknowledging the serious risk to Walliams’ mental health but ruling that preventing publication would constitute an “exceptionally serious interference” with freedom of expression. The judge noted that psychiatric services were already taking measures to protect him and stressed that the court had not determined whether the allegations were true.

Read more

Walliams’ anonymity remained in place pending a possible appeal. His lawyers confirmed on Monday that he would not challenge the ruling, allowing the media to identify him.

The scandal has dealt another blow to one of Britain’s most recognizable entertainment figures, whose children’s books have sold more than 60 million copies worldwide.

His publisher, HarperCollins, dropped him in December 2025 following a separate investigation into allegations of inappropriate behavior toward young female employees, which he also denied. Earlier this month, Alton Towers, a major British theme park in Staffordshire, permanently closed its World of David Walliams attraction, which featured rides inspired by his books.

title: France’s ‘Cold War’: Paris blames Tehran for supermarket fridge hacks
content:
France now believes that Iran was behind a series of supermarket cyberattacks that were pinned on Russia less than a week ago

The French government has accused Iran of hacking refrigerators in hundreds of supermarkets, claiming that the “cyber campaign” was the work of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC).

The attack, which took place in October, affected fridges and freezers at nearly 700 distribution sites across France. Hackers reportedly targeted the fridges’ internet-connected control units and forced them to overheat, destroying tons of food and forcing several stores to temporarily close. A wave of similar attacks took place in Belgium, Ireland, Sweden, and at least six other EU countries three weeks later.

“This was a cyber campaign of unprecedented scale and aggression,” French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Monday. “Today, thanks to the work of government agencies, we know who is responsible: the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps of the Islamic Republic of Iran.”

Read more

Iran’s ambassador has been summoned, Barrot said, adding that France will “sanction those responsible and take all measures we deem necessary and proportionate to respond.”

Paris prosecutor Laure Beccuau said that investigators discovered the hackers used Farsi and IP addresses linked to Iran, and that three IRGC members are suspected of carrying out the operation “to serve the interests of a foreign power – in this case, Iran.” 

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi rejected the allegations, accusing Paris of shifting blame for its own failures. “Unable to manage fridges let alone addressing grievances of its people, French government is shifting blame for its failures onto others,” he wrote on X on Tuesday.

“Yes, Iran is powerful. But unlike France, we do not exercise power via support for massacres in Gaza or bombings of schools and hospitals,” Araghchi added.

Although Beccuau’s accusation is stronger than that of British Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who stated “we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran” was behind a bungled “terror plot” at an RAF airbase in September, it is still not entirely watertight. WikiLeaks’ 2017 ‘Vault 7’ disclosures confirmed that the CIA had developed sophisticated hacking tools capable of leaving behind false digital ‘fingerprints’ in foreign languages, including Russian, Chinese, and Farsi, to implicate other countries in cyberattacks.

The accusations mark a dramatic turnaround from the climate of mid-October. Then, despite it taking place at a time of daily riots and anti-government demonstrations, almost every commentator speaking to European media outlets accused Russia of committing the attack. “We strongly believe this activity could be attributed to a Russian state-sponsored threat actor,” cybersecurity executive Xavier Bellekens told Politico last week, in an article that portrayed the hack as something straight from the pages of “the Kremlin’s hybrid playbook.”

Read more

“When we pull on the thread it does look like it could well be Russia. So, that is basically where we’re at,” Bellekens told Euronews – which, like Politico, is funded by the EU – two days later. Russia is “looking into where the weaknesses in the systems lie,” former Dutch intelligence officer Tim Bosch told NU.nl. “Right now it concerns refrigeration, but next time it might be a hospital.”

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the claims as “baseless,” “absurd,” and “backed up by no reasoning.”

Neither Iran’s Foreign Ministry nor the IRGC has commented on Tuesday’s accusation. However, Iran’s state Mehr News agency has dismissed it as “baseless and unsupported by evidence.”

German World Cup winner placed on Ukrainian ‘kill list’
content:
Former Germany football star Mesut Ozil had criticized FIFA and UEFA for banning Russian teams while allowing Israelis to compete

Former German football star and 2014 World Cup winner Mesut Ozil has been added to a Ukrainian “kill list” after accusing FIFA and UEFA of double standards over their treatment of Russia and Israel, media have reported.

The notorious Mirotvorets website, which maintains the list, publishes personal information on people it considers “enemies” of Ukraine. The database, which claims to be a private research project but enjoys tacit backing from Kiev, has published data on over 180,000 people and marks the profiles of deceased individuals with a “liquidated” stamp.

Ozil came under fire after publicly criticizing FIFA and UEFA for suspending Russian teams from international competitions while allowing Israeli teams to continue participating. The website has accused him of supporting Russia’s military operation in Ukraine.

Read more

Ozil made the remarks during a veterans’ football match in Istanbul between his former Turkish club Istanbul Basaksehir and Russia’s Zenit St. Petersburg.

“Football has always brought people together,” Ozil said, arguing that sporting organizations should not discriminate on the basis of nationality or religion.

“As you know, FIFA has not imposed any sanctions on Israeli teams, but it has done so against Russian teams,” he said, urging football authorities to abandon double standards and treat all countries equally.

Russian national teams and clubs have been barred from FIFA and UEFA competitions since February 2022, following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict. Israeli teams, meanwhile, have continued to participate in international tournaments despite growing calls for their suspension over Israel’s military campaign in Gaza.

Ozil, 38, retired from professional football in 2023 after a career that included spells at Real Madrid, Arsenal, Fenerbahce and several German clubs. He made 92 appearances for Germany, scoring 23 goals, and helped the national team win the 2014 World Cup in Brazil.

Launched in August 2014 following the Western-backed change of government in Kiev, Mirotvorets claims to identify individuals it considers threats to Ukraine’s national security. Its database includes Western journalists who reported from Donbass and Crimea and Ukrainian writer Oles Buzina, who was murdered in 2015 after his personal details appeared on the website. His killing remains unsolved.

Read more

The list has also included prominent foreign politicians and athletes. In August, former Soviet and Russian footballer Akhrik Tsveiba, who won the 1990 Soviet championship with Dynamo Kiev, was added to the database.

More recently, Polish MEP Ewa Zajaczkowska-Hernik and Poland’s presidential chief of staff were reportedly added after criticizing Kiev’s commemoration of Ukrainian nationalist figures who collaborated with Nazi Germany.

The website has repeatedly faced international criticism for publishing personal information without consent. In 2016, the OSCE warned that the disclosure of journalists’ details could endanger their safety, while human rights organizations raised concerns about threats against those named on the platform.

title: Orban accuses Hungarian authorities of ‘witch hunt’ after brother’s arrest
content:
The government of Peter Magyar is trying to establish a one-party system, the former prime minister has said

Former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban has claimed the detention of his younger brother is part of a campaign by the government of Peter Magyar to eliminate political opposition in the country.

Aron Orban and three other people were arrested on Monday in a human trafficking case. The 49-year-old businessman, who owns the firearms company Multi Shot, was photographed arriving at a detention center in Budapest on the same day.

In September, reports emerged that the former prime minister’s sibling was part of a separate investigation into alleged falsification of paperwork to help Vietnamese workers enter Hungary.

In a post on X later on Monday, Viktor Orban, who left office after 16 years in power this May, accused Magyar’s government of going on a “witch hunt.”

“I am the real target. My younger brother is simply being used to get to me,” he insisted.

Read more

According to the former prime minister, the aim of the “dirty political game” played by the authorities is “to eliminate opponents and establish a one-party state.”

Orban also suggested that his brother’s detention was an attempt “to divert attention” from the scandal that erupted after Magyar’s government released the records from Hungary’s communist-era secret police last week.

Critics warned that the move could lead to public shaming, reputational damage, and painful family revelations. The historians stressed that the files, containing 50,000 to 60,000 names, were incomplete and unreliable, adding that being mentioned in them doesn’t necessarily serve as proof of collaboration with the agency.

After the pro-EU Tisza party’s election win, Magyar promised accountability for Orban-era politicians over alleged corruption and abuse of power.

Orban’s Fidesz party hosts “a list of political prisoners” on its website, which includes the names of its members who have been arrested since the change of leadership. On Tuesday, Aron Orban’s name became the sixth to be added to the list.

READ MORE: US wants Orban to be next UN chief – WSJ

Magyar’s cabinet has been actively dismantling the legal, media, and financial structures set up by the previous government. It also changed the constitution to impose a 12-year term limit on MPs, effectively banning Orban from running for office again. Fidesz has repeatedly labeled the conduct by its Tisza rivals as “authoritarian.”

High-stakes Ukraine talks resume as Europe pushes to be included
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of Seven developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia.

As three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States got underway in the United Arab Emirates, top G7 diplomats were meeting Tuesday with Ukraines foreign minister in France.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha started his day in Paris in talks with Rubio before heading to the French foreign ministry for a larger group meeting with the entire G7. Neither man spoke as they posed for photos ahead of their discussion.

The State Department said afterwards in a brief statement that the pair had discussed negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war, energy resilience, and defense cooperation.

The larger meeting was expected to cover defense and security assistance to Ukraine, which the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has reduced, causing consternation not only in Kyiv but in capitals across Europe, the largest of which Paris, Berlin, Rome and London are G7 members.

RELATED STORY | Trilateral talks between US, Ukraine and Russia to resume this week

It was not immediately clear if the U.S. or any of its G7 partners would announce any new assistance for Ukraine.

Meanwhile in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, Trumps envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner began talks with Russian and Ukrainian officials in part to persuade Moscow to agree to broader negotiations that would include key European officials on how to end nearly five years of war.

In Paris, Europeans have been clamoring for a seat at the table in Abu Dhabi, but two U.S. officials said Monday that representatives from Britain, Germany, France, NATO and the European Union would not join the main talks but rather discuss potential security guarantees and the long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe beforehand.

Russia has resisted European participation in negotiations and insisted the talks should proceed strictly as a trilateral format involving Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. The three last held talks in February.

But on Monday in Paris, German Foreign Minister Johan Wadephul, who met separately with Rubio on the sidelines of the G7, was emphatic that Europe must be included.

RELATED STORY | Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US

I am still very grateful to the United States of America for making every effort to get the parties to the conflict to the table, he said. But I made clear again here that Europe belongs at this table. There can be no solution without Europe, only with Europe.

Rubio said the U.S. has no objection to eventual European involvement in the direct talks, but that it wasnt yet time.

Ultimately, it would be a positive, but weve got a ways to go, he told reporters after a full day of group and bilateral meetings with G7 counterparts. But, no, its good that theyre talking, its good that the trilateral talks are on again. Its better than not having talks.

title: High-stakes Ukraine talks resume as Europe pushes to be included
content:
U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and his counterparts from the Group of Seven developed democracies are turning their attention toward Ukraine and how to support it in its struggle to defend itself from Russia.

As three-way talks between Russia, Ukraine and the United States got underway in the United Arab Emirates, top G7 diplomats were meeting Tuesday with Ukraines foreign minister in France.

Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha started his day in Paris in talks with Rubio before heading to the French foreign ministry for a larger group meeting with the entire G7. Neither man spoke as they posed for photos ahead of their discussion.

The State Department said afterwards in a brief statement that the pair had discussed negotiations to end the Russia-Ukraine war, energy resilience, and defense cooperation.

The larger meeting was expected to cover defense and security assistance to Ukraine, which the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has reduced, causing consternation not only in Kyiv but in capitals across Europe, the largest of which Paris, Berlin, Rome and London are G7 members.

RELATED STORY | Trilateral talks between US, Ukraine and Russia to resume this week

It was not immediately clear if the U.S. or any of its G7 partners would announce any new assistance for Ukraine.

Meanwhile in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, Trumps envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner began talks with Russian and Ukrainian officials in part to persuade Moscow to agree to broader negotiations that would include key European officials on how to end nearly five years of war.

In Paris, Europeans have been clamoring for a seat at the table in Abu Dhabi, but two U.S. officials said Monday that representatives from Britain, Germany, France, NATO and the European Union would not join the main talks but rather discuss potential security guarantees and the long-term security architecture between Russia and Europe beforehand.

Russia has resisted European participation in negotiations and insisted the talks should proceed strictly as a trilateral format involving Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. The three last held talks in February.

title: AFP builds a new funding model for investigative journalism
content:
By Maria Lisicka

With 1,700 journalists in 151 countries, Agence France-Presse documents events around the clock. But Karl Malakunas, its Head of Philanthropic Partnerships, described a different kind of experiment they have under way: “a completely new editorial and funding model for AFP” for in-depth and investigative journalism.

Malakunas, an Emmy-nominated and Walkley Award-winning journalist, joined AFP in Hong Kong 25 years ago. “Breaking news is in my veins,” he said. Yet, like a lot of journalists, he always wanted “to scratch that itch” of going deeper.

He did so in the Philippines, turning a 700-word article on environmental defenders in Palawan into a 90-minute feature documentary. The film took 10 years and was largely funded by foundations.

In March 2025, AFP’s global news director asked him to bring that approach inside the agency.

AFP gets about a third of its funding from the French state and two-thirds from its 4,000-plus clients. Philanthropy adds a third stream, focused on the “Future of the planet” and the “Future of societies.” Above all, editorial independence must remain “sacrosanct,” Malakunas said.

A global desk for environmental justice

The first project is AFP’s Environment and Climate Legal Desk, billed as the world’s first global newsroom unit dedicated to environmental and climate justice. Its specialist reporters will support AFP’s bureaus on cases too complex for busy news teams, such as SLAPP suits (lawsuits designed to silence critics) in the Philippines.

Raising the money proved to be the more difficult part.

“It’s definitely harder, the fundraising element than the editorial element,” Malakunas said. “We’re not going to sugarcoat that.” AFP bypassed traditional journalism funders to approach environmental foundations, “a long, slow process.”

The desk now has a founding editor to build and lead it, and is hiring reporters in Asia, Africa and Latin America.

Impact you can document

Working with The Gecko Project, which brought the story idea, AFP put its boots on the ground to reveal that an Indonesian mill supplying Asia Symbol, a Chinese maker of “so-called carbon-neutral packaging,” had processed wood from plantations where orangutan habitat had been cleared. Haleon, the British maker of Panadol, then dropped Asia Symbol as a packaging supplier for its China operations.

AFP now documents such outcomes.

Asked how impact is measured for funders, Malakunas said AFP is building its first impact tracker. Beyond distribution reach, it asks: “Is it cited by civil society? Is it cited by lawmakers? And did it lead to anything?” The results go back to funders. As AFP reaches audiences through its media clients, journalists will log impact themselves.

“It’s boots-on-the-ground journalism. That’s the differentiator … And it’s expensive and it’s hard to do.”
– Karl Malakunas, Head of Philanthropic Partnerships, AFP

Protecting independence

AFP published a code of ethics on day one. Once the desk is running, there is a firewall: “Foundations can speak to me,” Malakunas explained, but they “don’t have direct access to our journalists.” AFP is also not “foundation-led”: “We did spend a lot of time determining what we wanted to do, what our value was […] and not chasing what foundations wanted.”

Funding, he said on the panel, is “fickle” and the sector “opaque”, especially after last year’s USAID cuts sent many organisations to philanthropies. AFP’s answer: no more than 25 or 30% from any one funder.

Lessons for Asian newsrooms

In Southeast Asia, investigative journalists face harassment, rising costs, SLAPP suits and barriers to US and European foundations.

“It’s extremely difficult, but it is possible,” Malakunas noted. “There is big money in the US and Europe. It’s extremely hard to access, but it’s there.”

Established outlets have an edge, he argued: “Foundations do take confidence in the fact that you’re an established media organisation; you’re already doing good journalism.”

His advice for the next 12 months: commitment and training. “You’re going to have in your newsrooms people who are raring to go,” he said. “Even without the extra funding, if you are committed to this, allocate some space for one or two or whoever those people are.”

 About the author: Maria Lisicka is a young professional in PR and strategic communication, currently pursuing her studies at the University of Amsterdam and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.

title: Trump backs ‘honeypot-hit’ Nvidia boss
content:
Jensen Huang is “an amazing guy,” who is “suffering greatly” due to the scandal, the US president said

US President Donald Trump has said that the FBI has launched a probe into Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman accused of working for Chinese intelligence, but stressed that he believes in the Nvidia chief’s innocence. Beijing has vigorously denied the spying claims.

On Monday, Nvidia, a US company which dominates the market for chips used to power AI, said that it started its own investigation into allegations that its founder and CEO was targeted in a Chinese intelligence ‘honeypot’ operation. Earlier in the day, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife, but didn’t name the woman he had been dating.

The New York Times and Financial Times reported previously that the 63-year-old tech entrepreneur had developed a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a Chinese executive formerly associated with the Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed International, who had allegedly been gathering data on Nvidia for China’s Ministry of State Security.

Read more

When asked about the scandal around Jensen Huang during a media briefing at the White House later on Monday, Trump said that “we’ll look into it. I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else. I think he will be in good shape.”

“I just hope there’s no problem. If there is a problem, we’ll let you know about it. But I hope there’s no problem,” he added.

The US president said that he had already discussed the situation with the Nvidia CEO, whom he described as “an amazing guy” and “a high-quality person.”

“He said: ‘I had no idea that she was a spy,’ and I really believe him,” he stressed.

Trump noted that he believes that Huang is “suffering greatly” due to the whole ordeal after reading the tech entrepreneur’s statement, in which he said that he was “deeply sorry” for hurting his wife and children.

Huang is seen as one of Trump’s closest allies in Silicon Valley as the president insists on the US winning the AI race against China. The Nvidia CEO accompanied Trump on a state visit to Beijing in May and was awarded the National Medal of Science last month.

Read more

Trump contradicted claims by NYT that he had been briefed on Huang’s affair and the security risks posed by it before the Chinese trip, but decided not to take any action on the information.

“Well, I’ve been hearing about it, and I’ve been reading a little bit about it over a period of time. But, not too long ago,” he said.

The US president was also asked if he’ll raise the issue with Chinese President ‌Xi Jinping at an APEC leaders’ summit in Shenzhen next week. “No, I don’t think so. Maybe, I’m sure, President Xi will ask me about it,” he replied.

On Monday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun denied claims of Beijing collecting intelligence on Nvidia. “The so-called Chinese spy narrative is purely a groundless accusation, slander, and a smear,” he insisted.

Nvidia lost nearly $200 billion of market value after Huang acknowledged the affair and the company launched a probe against him.

title: Taiwan’s CommonWealth Magazine doubles down on data-driven investigative journalism
content:
By Maria Lisicka

Despite the challenges and costs of investigative journalism, pursuing it is paramount for news publishers: “The externality is much bigger than its cost,” Chen told participants at WAN-IFRA’s Asian Media Leaders Summit recently in Singapore.

Chen cited Reuters Institute research ranking original investigations and on-the-ground reporting as top priorities for news executives in the AI era.

“The reality is very simple,” Chen noted. “AI and video have already completely changed how people consume news.”

Breakthrough investigative reports, she argued, “send a powerful wake-up call to both society and our subscribers. They remind people the media are here and that we create value that AI can never replace.”

No investigative unit, but an investigative culture

Chen’s first takeaway was counterintuitive: CommonWealth’s most popular investigations did not come from a dedicated investigative unit.

“Every single beat has the potential for deep investigative work,” she pointed out. The key is “an open editorial culture where all journalists can pitch early leads [and] hold honest discussions.”

Once committed, the newsroom backs the work with proper, not excessive, resources, ensuring that “when we bet our resources, we deliver something significant.”

Reading China through unconventional data

As examples, Chen showed two projects built on “unconventional data from China.”

First, CommonWealth worked with scholars from Taiwan’s Academia Sinica, using AI to analyse more than 10 years of CCTV footage of Xi Jinping’s face, speech and gait. The finding: Xi looked noticeably thinner at the 2025 military parade, but his health was “actually quite stable for his age.”

The second project was personal. “I come from the most dangerous place on earth,” Chen noted. “It’s related to our life.” It began in 2020, when a CommonWealth reporter on holiday in Tainan kept hearing fighter jets scrambling overhead and asked herself: are we going to have a war?

The available data was terrible, Chen said: two static PDF images a day from Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense. A team of just three logged every flight path and aircraft type by hand, for a full year.

What emerged was striking. The sorties were not aimed at Taiwan at all.

Coordinated with the Chinese navy, they pushed southwest towards the South China Sea, a sign, Chen explained, that Beijing’s real goal was to break through the “first island chain” from Japan through Taiwan to the Philippines.

“It’s not only a Taiwan story,” she concluded. “It’s actually an Asia story.”

From three reporters to a live dashboard

In 2023, AI took over the mapping and data entry. By 2025, the project had become a fully automatic dashboard tracking Chinese military activity every day, later expanded with Japanese and Philippine data.

Then Beijing’s playbook shifted to “grey zone” warfare.

The team began tracing China Coast Guard ships day by day, using AI to scale up to more than 1.8 billion lines of ship-tracking data. Cross-matched with data from US think tank CSIS, Japan and the Philippines, the conclusion was stark: these operations target not only Taiwan, but Japan and the Philippines too.

Long-term projects, Chen observed, “give us historical depth” and keep the newsroom from “very sensational panic reporting.”

“With AI, we can process data at a scale we never could before. But the true secret sauce, I will not say it’s AI. I will say it’s still the editorial vision and the research methodology.”

– Yi-Shan Chen, Editor-in-Chief, CommonWealth Magazine

Asking the right questions and staying curious

During a panel discussion, Chen said that the hardest part is not the tools but “asking the right questions and keeping curiosity to discover the right topics.”

She also urged newsrooms to look beyond their walls, as data companies, white-hat hackers and NGOs are often willing to help. “We just need to spend some time to look around,” she added.

Her advice for smaller newsrooms: since covering every topic is rarely possible, choose one or two fields worth investing in and find the right people for them.

About the author: Maria Lisicka is a young professional in PR and strategic communication, currently pursuing her studies at the University of Amsterdam and Nanyang Technological University, Singapore.

title: Russia and Ukraine hold nearly 4 hours of US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi
content:
Russia and Ukraine on Tuesday held their first U.S.-mediated talks in nine months on ending the 4 1/2-year-old war, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio calling the meeting “very productive” and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy saying the session was “constructive and quite substantive.”

Hopes of ending Europe’s biggest conflict since World War II are tempered, however, by the absence of any significant breakthroughs in three previous rounds of talks earlier this year.

There's nothing to suggest a new posture that would lead to a breakthrough, but circumstances surrounding the talks have been changed by the outcome of the U.S. midterm elections as well as increased pressure on Russia’s wartime economy. Moscow also is seeking to break Ukrainians’ will as another winter sets in by ramping up its battering of the country’s power grid.

Neither Rubio nor Zelenskyy attended the talks in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. The session lasted four hours and another is scheduled for a second day Wednesday.

Delegations from Moscow and Kyiv met as Washington, represented by U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and envoy Steve Witkoff, renewed its push to stop the fighting.

“It looks like the talks in Abu Dhabi were very productive,” Rubio said in Paris at the Group of Seven meeting, although he urged patience. “There’s a lot of work to be done in that regard. It’s not like something that’s on the verge of being solved in the next 24 hours or anything like that.”

Zelenskyy said the talks were largely about humanitarian issues, including prisoner exchanges and returning Ukrainian civilians in captivity, as well as children taken from the country. Security guarantees also were discussed, he added during an appearance at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark.

A senior Ukrainian official who spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to comment publicly said Ukraine and Russia talked about a large scale prisoner swap, although the details will be discussed in the coming days.

The 3-way meeting was the first since February

The two-day session is the first such meeting since February on Russia's full-scale invasion, which analysts and humanitarian organizations say has killed hundreds of thousands of soldiers and thousands of civilians.

Kushner said he believed there were “some good ideas how to bridge” the differences between the two sides.

Trump, whose stance on the war has varied, must reckon with Democrats taking over the U.S. Congress in January following the U.S. elections. Democrats could demand more support for Ukraine.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz told ZDF television Monday night that “I don’t have overly high expectations” for the talks.

There are no signs the fighting is abating, and the talks come against a backdrop of new long-range strikes by both Russia and Ukraine. The two armies are largely deadlocked on the front line.

Russia launched 162 drones of various types and a ballistic missile at Ukraine overnight, Ukraine’s air force said.

Russia’s Defense Ministry said its forces downed 155 Ukrainian drones overnight in eight Russian regions, as well as over the Crimean Peninsula, which Moscow illegally annexed from Ukraine in 2014.

Kushner says the U.S. aims to build on past experience

Kushner said in opening remarks that the goal of the talks is to “create a new framework and a new understanding building upon the different institutions and understandings of the past.”

“We take what’s worked, we try to identify what’s failed, why we’re in this position and hopefully create a new framework that leads us for decades, if not centuries, of peace,” he said.

The commander of U.S. forces in Europe, Gen. Alexus Grynkewich, who was also present, said the U.S. delegation looked forward “to working with both sides as we seek to advance the progress we’ve made in the past and continue this pursuit to set the foundations for a lasting peace.”

Rustem Umerov, the head of Ukraine’s Foreign Intelligence Service who leads Kyiv’s delegation, thanked the U.S. for its peace efforts.

“Our people are waiting to end this war. And we hope that we will achieve the lasting peace for Ukraine,” he said.

Ukrainians meet first with European and NATO officials

The head of the Russian delegation, Vladimir Medinsky, expressed hope the meeting “will allow us to advance on the path towards peace in the interests of the people of Russia and the people of Ukraine.”

Umerov said the day began with a meeting between the Ukrainian team, the U.S. envoys and representatives from the United Kingdom, France, Germany, Italy, NATO and the European Commission.

Russia has objected to the Europeans’ involvement in the three-way talks, but said EU representatives could join at a later stage.

Russia and Ukraine hold to their demands

The Russian and Ukrainian governments remain far apart on key elements of any prospective deal.

Russian President Vladimir Putin wants Ukraine to pull its troops back from four regions of Ukraine that Moscow annexed in September 2022 but has never fully captured. He also demands that Ukraine abandon its bid to join NATO and accept strict limits on its military, among other issues.

Putin wants a comprehensive peace deal on those conditions and won’t agree to a general halt in hostilities, arguing that it would only allow Ukrainian troops to rest and replenish their weapons stockpiles.

Zelenskyy rejects Putin’s demands to voluntarily cede territory. He also rejects any limits on Ukraine's military or its arrangements with Western partners, which Kyiv sees as essential security guarantees to stop Moscow from invading again.

Ukraine argues an immediate ceasefire is the necessary first step toward negotiating a wider settlement and says a direct meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy is the only way territorial issues can be settled. Putin has spurned those suggestions.

Moscow and Kyiv sent experienced negotiators

The Russian and Ukrainian delegations include senior officials who have attended previous rounds of talks.

Russia’s chief negotiator is Medinsky, a Putin aide who has led Moscow’s team since the first full-fledged peace negotiations with Ukraine in Istanbul in March 2022, although exploratory talks took place earlier in neighboring Belarus. The Russian delegation also includes deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin and military intelligence chief Igor Kostyukov.

Ukraine's delegation includes Zelenskyy’s chief of staff, Kyrylo Budanov.

The US says a broader European security deal is in the works

Last week, Trump declared that some kind of grand deal about European security was in the works, describing it as “a big agreement” that is “going to involve more than Ukraine.”

Kushner said Monday on X that a “comprehensive and lasting settlement will also require direct engagement between Russia and our European partners on the broader security arrangements that affect them.”

Moscow has welcomed that approach. “The idea of ​​defining clear parameters for a future security architecture, and only then moving on to resolving the actual Russian-Ukrainian conflict, is quite sensible,” said Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov.

——

John Leicester in Paris, Geir Moulson in Berlin, Susie Blann in Kyiv, Ukraine, and Barry Hatton in Lisbon, Portugal, contributed.

___

This story was updated on Nov. 13, 2026 to correct that Grynkewich was attending the talks in Abu Dhabi in his capacity as the commander of U.S. forces in Europe.
