title: Polish MP mocks Tusk for ‘most spectacular self-castration in history’
content:
The prime minister moved Poland “from Central Europe to Central Africa” overnight by supporting a coup attempt, Lukasz Mejza said

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk subjected himself to the “most spectacular castration in history” by backing an attempt to oust the conservative-linked leadership of the country’s Constitutional Tribunal, lawmaker Lukasz Mejza has said.

Poland’s long-simmering constitutional crisis erupted into open confrontation last Friday, when Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, a judge elected by Tusk’s pro-EU governing majority, ordered the suspension of the tribunal’s president, Bogdan Swieczkowski, and his deputy, Bartlomiej Sochanski, both linked to the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party.

Korwin-Piotrowska claimed the role of acting head of the court, prompting accusations of an attempted coup, and resulting in street protests and a heavy police deployment around the courthouse. Both the court’s current leadership and right-wing President Karol Nawrocki, who later pushed past judges at the tribunal’s entrance, rejected her authority.

Read more

Tusk, who was president of the European Council from 2014 to 2019, said the showdown was necessary to restore judicial independence, criticizing earlier PiS reforms and Nawrocki’s refusal to administer the oath to five Constitutional Tribunal judges elected by the current parliamentary majority. He also accused an “army of Russian bots” of supporting his opponents, without providing evidence.

Addressing parliament on Thursday, Mejza, an independent MP who was previously part of the PiS faction, claimed Tusk tried to become a Soviet-style dictator but ended up as a “Ceausescu from Temu,” referring to Romania’s former communist leader and a Chinese online discounter.

Read more

“You have accomplished the greatest logistical feat in world history: Overnight, you moved Poland from Central Europe to Central Africa,” Mejza said.

He went on to call Tusk’s actions “the most spectacular castration in history, because you staged a coup d’état and simultaneously stripped yourself of your manhood and any shred of honor,” warning the prime minister that the “time of reckoning will come, sooner than you think.”

On Friday, Polish MPs unfurled a large ‘Tusk = Dictator’ banner during a visit by European Parliament President Roberta Metsola to the parliament. Lawmakers also displayed English-language placards accusing the prime minister of staging a coup. Tusk ridiculed the protest, saying his opponents “will start singing and selling watches in a moment,” in reference to previous demonstrations.

More than a week into the stand-off, the crisis remains unresolved, although Tusk’s coalition partners proposed a sweeping “constitutional reset,” which would see the termination of the terms of all current tribunal judges and the appointment of an entirely new bench through a constitutional amendment.

However, both Tusk’s Civic Coalition and PiS have expressed skepticism about the proposal, for opposing reasons. The Civic Coalition says there is no reason to dismiss judges recently elected by its parliamentary majority, while PiS refuses to negotiate with those it accuses of staging a coup.

title: Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US
content:
Drone and missile attacks struck across Ukraine on Saturday, wounding at least nine people, as Kyiv and Moscow prepared for new talks next week with the United States.

Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. are to meet on Tuesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. The new round of negotiations would be the fourth brokered by the Trump administration, the most recent having been in Geneva in February.

Western governments backing the peace initiative are seeking a new formula to break the impasse while acknowledging that territorial and security questions remain unresolved.

The Russian missiles that hit overnight across the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, damaged homes and commercial properties, triggering new power and water outages, national and city authorities said.

Melania Trump hosts Russian, Ukrainian officials to mark ceasefire she brokered

Kateryna Korniichuk, 64, was at home with her granddaughter when an attack hit.

"The first blast wave threw us against that wall and then against the other wall, because we were in the corridor. It's very hard. No sleep, no peace nothing. The children aren't sleeping, and neither are we," she told The Associated Press. "I'm old, I can handle it, but what have the children done wrong?"

Strikes also prompted officials to close Kyiv's 816-meter-long (892-yard-long) Northern Bridge, a major route connecting the city with large residential areas on the east bank of the Dnipro River.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that work was already underway to repair the city's Northern Bridge and that water pressure in Kyiv had been stabilized. Earlier Saturday, he had described the city's energy situation as "extremely difficult, affecting the city's heating and water supply systems."

Zelenskyy slams Russian attacks ahead of trilateral negotiations

In a statement Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia was preparing for trilateral talks by "launching ballistic missiles at Ukraine's critical infrastructure."

Later, he said that Moscow was stepping up strikes to build pressure on Ukraine ahead of the Abu Dhabi talks. "Russia perceives diplomacy in its own peculiar way as a form of aggression," he wrote in an online post.

The Ukrainian leader said that Russia fired 36 ballistic missiles at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight, of which only four were shot down due to a lack of Patriot interceptors.

Zelenskyy also said that Russia had used North Korean-made ballistic missiles to strike energy facilities, citing preliminary findings from investigations at impact sites.

The barrage involved 172 drones over Kyiv and 12 other regions, wounding nine people, including a child, he said.

"When Russia tries to plunge Kyiv a city of millions and the entire country into a blackout, Ukraine must not be left to face this alone," Zelenskyy said. He urged greater U.S. support and attention from Congress, calling for bipartisan backing for Ukraine and stronger sanctions on Russia.

Ukraine's Energy Ministry said Saturday's missile attacks damaged networks that carry electricity from nuclear power plants to Kyiv and central regions, as well as multiple other power facilities. It said outages were most widespread in the Kyiv and central Zhytomyr regions, as well as in the eastern regions of Kharkiv, Donetsk and Dnipropetrovsk.

The outages were separate from scheduled rolling blackouts imposed to protect the grid, which remain in effect across much of Ukraine.

Russia's Ministry of Defense confirmed Saturday that it had targeted the Northern Bridge, saying that it facilitated the transport of weaponry, military hardware and specialist equipment for Ukraine's armed forces.

It also said that it had targeted an industrial facility in the capital producing Flamingo missiles, as well as a power station, an electrical substation, and a plant producing ammunition, explosives and gunpowder in the wider Kyiv region. It also confirmed striking an electrical substation in the Zhytomyr region.

Kyiv's power now travels 200 miles, and Russia knows the weak point

Death toll rises to 55 after the strike on aid center in Komyshuvakha

Meanwhile, in southern Ukraine, a recovery operation continued into its sixth day in the village of Komyshuvakha, devastated on Monday when multiple Russian guided bombs slammed into a former school and nearby shelter as residents waited for humanitarian aid.

Emergency services said they had recovered nine more bodies in the previous 24 hours, bringing the death toll early Saturday morning to 55. Dozens of people remain missing.

Village resident Mykola Krasnov, 72, said he was still looking for his wife but had heard no word from rescuers.

"She went to get humanitarian aid, and a three-ton bomb was dropped there. Where is she?" he said. "She didn't come home, and they didn't find her body there. She isn't in the morgue, and she isn't here alive."

The village of Komyshuvakha is located near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Ukrainian attack on Russia's Belgorod region kills 1 person

A Ukrainian attack killed one person in Russia's Belgorod region when a drone hit a private home in the town of Grayvoron, local officials said Saturday.

Russia's Ministry of Defense said its forces shot down 411 Ukrainian drones overnight over 10 Russian regions, including Belgorod. Drones were also destroyed over the annexed Ukrainian peninsula of Crimea and the Black and Azov Seas, it said.

The head of Russia's southwestern Saratov region, Gov. Roman Busargin, wrote on social media that a drone attack damaged "civilian infrastructure" and several residential buildings in the area. Russian media outlets later reported that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and shared images of plumes of smoke over the city.

The head of Russia's Oryol region, Gov. Andrey Klychkov, also said Saturday that a Ukrainian attack had damaged commercial warehouse and production sites in the regional capital, as cited by state media.

Russian media outlets reported that a Ukrainian attack sparked a blaze at Oryol's Proton-Electrotex plant, which produces components for military equipment.

title: Crisis deepens in Ukraine as Russian official's White House visit draws scrutiny
content:
Russia is escalating its assault on the infrastructure that keeps Ukraines capital functioning, leaving residents facing repeated disruptions to electricity and water as temperatures fall.

Repeated Russian strikes have damaged the power network serving Kyiv and surrounding areas. Outages are stretching for hours, water service has been interrupted and parts of the citys electric transit system have also been affected. Ukrainian officials say the capital region is facing some of the countrys most severe energy disruptions.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko has warned that continued Russian attacks could push the capital toward a far more serious blackout, saying repeated strikes are putting critical energy facilities at risk.

The infrastructure campaign comes as Ukraine is also reeling from a mass-casualty Russian attack in the Zaporizhzhia region.

Ukrainian authorities now say at least 53 people were killed when Russian bombs struck a school compound being used to distribute humanitarian aid in Komyshuvakha. Search crews are still working through the wreckage, meaning the death toll could rise further.

The Nov. 2 attack has become the deadliest Russian strike in the Zaporizhzhia region since the full-scale invasion began. Authorities say roughly 50 people remain missing.

Another development, this one thousands of miles from the battlefield, is drawing anger from advocates for Ukrainian children taken by Russia.

First lady Melania Trump hosted Russian and Ukrainian representatives at the White House Thursday, highlighting a humanitarian operation in Russian-occupied Oleshky that allowed civilians to leave the area and humanitarian assistance to reach them.

But one member of the Russian delegation has a controversial history.

Yana Lantratova is Russias human rights commissioner. She is also under U.S. sanctions, and Ukraine accuses her of helping remove children from occupied Ukrainian territory and transfer them to Russia.

It is a story Scripps News has followed for nearly four years.

READ MORE | Scripps News Investigates: Ukraine's stolen orphans

One of the children tied to those allegations is Margarita Prokopenko, who was just 10 months old when she was taken from the Kherson Childrens Home in 2022. Ukrainian authorities accuse Lantratova of involvement in removing Margarita and another child from the region.

Margarita was later given a new Russian identity and adopted into the family of prominent Russian politician Sergey Mironov, according to Ukrainian authorities and records uncovered by subsequent investigations. Her Ukrainian family has spent years trying to bring her home.

For advocates trying to recover Ukraines stolen children, Lantratovas appearance at a White House event devoted to humanitarian cooperation presents a stark contradiction: The woman Russia now calls its human rights commissioner is someone Ukraine accuses of helping take its children.

title: Melania Trump accused of delivering Putin the victory he craved
content:
A Ukrainian researcher has said Melania Trump may have walked straight into the Kremlin’s trap.

Petro Andrushchenko, head of the Center for the Study of the Occupation, was livid following a Russian drone strike at a train station in Dnipro, about 160 miles from Oleshky, on October 29. The attack killed 14 civilians and injured at least 14 more as they were waiting on the platform

“While screaming to the world how much he wants Melania Trump to mediate saving 1,500 people in Oleshky, Putin continues to kill civilians 10 minutes away from my house, continues to bomb Kyiv and Zaporizhzhia,” he told the Daily Beast.

“Now Putin will be a ‘humanitarian’ for moving people from Oleshky to Russia," he said. "The Oleshky operation is truly the greatest victory of Russian propaganda.”

The first lady hosted an event at the White House on Thursday with delegations from both Russia and Ukraine in attendance, where both sides praised her efforts to achieve peace.

She said she had “acted immediately” to secure a ceasefire in Oleshky and described herself as the “exclusive intermediary” between the hostile nations. The event lasted about 15 minutes, and the first lady did not take questions from the press.

Nearly 800 people were evacuated from Oleshky, according to the first lady. The frontline Russian-occupied city in the Kherson region has been trapped in a horrific war zone since 2022, with residents facing months of severe food shortages.

Andrushchenko was even more blunt about the propaganda surrounding the operation.

“Using Donald Trump and Melania as their façade, Russian propaganda is building a campaign in order to blame Ukraine, put the ‘genocide,’ hunger in Oleshky on our shoulders,” he said.

“They are allowing American journalists in; they have brought a bunch of dubious reporters from Moscow. Not sure how Ukraine is supposed to react.”

President Volodymyr Zelensky has awarded the first lady the Order of Princess Olha, 1st Class, for her humanitarian work supporting Ukraine, including efforts to bring Ukrainian children home.

The Daily Beast reports that Ukrainians have mixed feelings about Melania’s involvement in the Oleshky evacuation. It helped people escape Oleshky while Russian strikes continued elsewhere, including Dnipro. It may have set a precedent for more truces on the frontline, but critics said it also handed Russia a propaganda coup. The report also raised concerns that moving Ukrainians out of occupied territory contributed to ethnic cleansing.

“Melania Trump brokered a ceasefire without a single independent monitor in the room, and Russia used that gap to stage exactly the picture it wanted the world to see,” Lyudmyla Yankina of the Ukrainian human rights group Civil Fortis told the Daily Beast.

Special envoy Steve Witkoff came under fire from U.S. lawmakers and Ukraine for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” following Russia’s release of U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard on October 21.

title: Arab bloc signals willingness to back coalition seeking to oust Netanyahu
content:
A veteran Arab lawmaker in Israel says his bloc is willing to break with decades of precedent and join forces with Jewish-led parties in a shared bid to end Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's long rule.

We want to do things that we did not do in the past in order to remove this criminal government, Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Arab Joint List, told The Associated Press.

But any such partnership could be politically fraught for both sides. For the Joint List, it would mean backing a government unlikely to end Israels wars or curb settlement expansion in the occupied West Bank. For Netanyahus opponents, it would mean aligning with parties that not only criticize Israel's policies, but reject its identity as a Jewish state.

RELATED STORY | Israel's elections are running to a new scramble to build coalition government

After historic voter turnout delivered Arab-led parties a record share in Israel's parliament, Tibi said the Joint List is willing to support an anti-Netanyahu government without joining it. That could reassure Jewish-led factions that view them with suspicion and satisfy their own constituents. It would still give the Joint List major influence.

Only one Arab party has ever served in an Israeli government, in 2021. But that party, Raam, is much more conciliatory than the Joint List and held fewer seats. Raam is willing to join another anti-Netanyahu government as a partner, but any such arrangement would still need the support of the Joint List.

If the Jewish-led parties reject such a partnership, then it would prove Israel is an ethnocracy, not an absolute democracy for all citizens, Tibi said.

The Joint List's positions put it at odds with most Israelis

Most of the Palestinian population in what is now Israel fled or was expelled during the 1948 war surrounding its creation. Those who remained were granted citizenship, including the right to vote, and today they and their descendants make up some 20% of the population.

Many Jewish Israelis have historically viewed Arab-led political parties with suspicion. That distrust has been reinforced by lawmakers who have defended or praised Israel's enemies.

The Joint List, a coalition of three left-wing and nationalist parties, rejects what it refers to as the racist Zionist consensus in Israel. It calls for partnering with Jewish Israelis who support a Palestinian state in the West Bank, Gaza and east Jerusalem, territories occupied in the 1967 Mideast war. It rejects Israels identity as a Jewish state, calling for equal rights for all its citizens.

Many Jewish Israelis see that as support for the countrys enemies at a time of war. Netanyahu has encouraged such sentiments, lodging unproven accusations of electoral fraud against the Arab-led parties and portraying them as a threat to national security.

A dilemma for Netanyahu's opponents

That creates a dilemma for Netanyahus main opponents, led by former general Gadi Eisenkot.

In the campaign, they portrayed Netanyahu as a corrupt leader who failed to prevent the Oct. 7, 2023, attack and then blocked a public inquiry into it. They cast the election in existential terms, saying Netanyahus far-right government threatened Israels democratic institutions.

They won 48 seats in the 120-member Knesset, compared to 53 for Netanyahus coalition. The Joint List won 11 seats and Raam won 8, making them crucial to forming an anti-Netanyahu majority.

The Joint List could help an anti-Netanyahu bloc take power by voting for it or by abstaining to lower the threshold needed for a majority. Either arrangement could allow opposition parties to form a government without requiring the Joint List to become part of their administration. Joining could put its lawmakers in the uncomfortable position of being part of a government waging wars in Gaza and Lebanon that they oppose.

Some of Eisenkots allies welcome Arab support while others are opposed, pointing to past statements by Joint List leaders they argue deny Israels legitimacy or support its enemies.

Tibi said he was under no illusions that a partnership with Netanyahus opponents would end the wars or bring about a Palestinian state. But he said a repair government would improve the lives of Palestinian citizens, by ending Netanyahus rule and also potentially addressing local issues like a wave of violent crime in Arab communities.

It's unclear what conditions would be required

Eisenkot has said Arab-led parties must meet certain conditions in any partnership, including calling Hamas a terrorist group that needs to be destroyed.

Tibi said the conditions do not apply to parties like the Joint List that want to provide outside support.

The Joint List and Raam have denounced the Hamas-led Oct. 7 attack and any violence against civilians. But they have refused to brand Hamas a terrorist group or call for its destruction, saying that doing so would justify Israels devastating military campaign in Gaza.

Tibi said both the Oct. 7 attack and Israels response to it were immoral.

RELATED STORY | Trump reverses course on Israel aid amid Tuesday's midterm election

The veteran lawmaker has long been a lightning rod for right-wing attacks on Arab parties. During Israels 2019 elections, Netanyahu, popularly known as Bibi, campaigned on the slogan Bibi or Tibi? to warn voters that opposing him meant relying on Arab-led parties to form a government.

Tibi said Tuesday that the election result had turned the slogan on its head.

When he said Bibi or Tibi, he incited against Arabs, he said. Now, its Tibi, because Arab voters went in a very massive way to take part in the elections. Its definitely our story this time.

title: Israel's elections are running to a new scramble to build coalition government
content:
Eyes worldwide are still on the electoral race in Israel, where Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu faces a new challenge in parliament.

President Isaac Herzog wrapped up consultations earlier Thursday on forming a new government. Neither Netanyahu nor challenger Gadi Eisenkot won a parliamentary majority in the elections, setting off a scramble for coalition partners.

So where do things stand now? And what does this mean moving forward?

Scripps News spoke with Ruth Eglash, the senior Israel correspondent for the Jewish Telegraph Agency.

"President Herzog has been meeting with the representatives of the 11 parties that passed the electoral threshold and that do have a place in Israel's parliament," Eglash said. "He's met with most of the parties. He still has to meet with the two main parties, which is Netanyahu's Likud party and, as you mentioned, his challenger Gadi Eisenkot's Yashar party."

RELATED STORY | Netanyahu bloc falls short of majority as Israel enters coalition talks

"It's looking pretty clear that the president will ask Gadi Eisenkot to begin the process of trying to put together a coalition. Neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot have a clear path to forming that coalition. Any coalition in Israel needs a minimum of 61 seats in order to have a majority in the Israeli parliament and there's no clear path for either party to reach that number."

Watch the full interview with Eglash in the video above.

title: Bomb threats hit more than a dozen European flights, forcing diversions and emergency landings
content:
A wave of bomb threats Thursday forced flight diversions and emergency landings across Europe after more than a dozen flights were targeted.

One plane headed from Dublin to Rome was diverted to a military base in France, with all 157 people on board safe. Authorities say security sweeps have so far found no explosives or suspicious materials.

The incident follows several similar hoax threats earlier this week. Airports in Madrid, Milan, Bucharest, Warsaw and London were among those targeted.

Some flights arrived at their destination safely but were ultimately searched by experts, while others had to be diverted. For example, four flights headed to Prague were threatened with some kind of explosive device being on board. But once they all arrived, they were searched and no explosive devices were found.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | US removes all Air Force bombers from UK base following new threat

UK Secretary of State for Transport Heidi Alexander has described the threats as a malicious hoax. Heathrow Airport has also dismissed that it was the subject of a bomb threat, saying it didn't believe it was a credible threat. As a result, no actions were taken to shut down airport operations in any way.

It remains unclear exactly who is behind these threats or how long they may continue. European Union transport chief Apostolos Tzitzikostas said it's also unclear whether all of the bomb threats this week are linked, or whether there is one group behind all of the same threats.

The UK Department of Transport has made it clear that London's Metropolitan Police Aviation Section is working with its international counterparts to try to figure out exactly what is happening and where these threats are emanating from.

There has been one claim made in Italy by a group which says it is an anti-feminist organization that wanted to make the skies turn red. However, that has not been verified as a credible claim, so it remains unclear whether these threats are coming from an individual, a group, a hostile state, or none of the above.

title: More than 600,000 rally across France to demand higher wages and school funding
content:
Frances Interior Ministry said more than 600,000 people rallied Thursday across France, including in Paris, to demand higher wages and support the student protest movement, piling fresh pressure on the beleaguered government.

After more than a month of large, recurring protests across France, major rallies took place again in Paris, Lyon, Marseille and elsewhere, most of which were peaceful. The Interior Ministry said the figures were still provisional.

RELATED STORY | French protesters defy heavy police presence in new demonstrations

The Paris march proceeded peacefully Thursday afternoon, drawing a massive crowd, including students carrying signs reading, Inequalities seriously jeopardize our future and We cant spend our whole lives just trying to make a living. Workers and retirees also joined, demanding higher wages and pensions.

About a third of Frances high schools were closed or unable to operate, some because of student blockades and others because teachers were on strike. Public transportation was disrupted in some areas. The Eiffel Tower was also closed.

Police are prepared but tensions flare again

Interior Minister Laurent Nuez said that 70,000 police officers were deployed, backed by armored vehicles, drones and helicopters. Police have been criticized for injuring protesters with heavy-handed tactics.

Many demonstrations in recent weeks have been marred by violence, which authorities blamed on masked far-left radicals seeking to incite insurrection and others intent on looting.

Authorities in the western region of Brittany said masked individuals tried to block roads in Rennes. They said young people, often accompanied by adults, committed serious acts of violence, including throwing steel balls at police.

Authorities also reported tensions, scuffles and other incidents in the cities of Lyon, Nantes, Pau, Orlans, Rennes and Toulouse.

Unions aim to send a warning

Frances main unions warned that the country is on the brink of recession and that layoff plans are multiplying. Fuel, food products, rent, gas, electricity everythings going up except wages and pensions, they said in a joint statement.

France is mired in debt and is one of the worst economic performers in Europe, along with Italy and Belgium.

We need to give every single children here in this country a proper future, said Garance Blaise, a 21-year-old university student taking part in the Paris march.

It's all about the way we dont know whether well get a job or not. And our parents, they know that and they agree with us and they also have things to ask for, she said. So I think the movement is already global, it is already all over Europe and its not just students, its the whole population.

Corinne Cucchini, from the Private Healthcare Federal Union, joined the Paris demonstration to denounce staff shortages and a lack of equipment at the private hospital in Paris where she works. Our demands focus on raising wages and the working conditions, she said.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | France wakes up to wreckage of a night of rioting after protests turned violent

Fabien Villedieu, national secretary of the SUD-Rail union, took aim at President Emmanuel Macron 's centrist government and the national rail company, SNCF.

When the government is not reasonable, when the head of the SNCF is not reasonable we simply do what weve always done in France, which is to go on strike, he said at the Gare de Lyon station in Paris.

Before the strike action, the government had been negotiating with unions a familiar scenario in French politics in hopes of limiting the protest movement, which has resulted in France's most violent civil unrest in years.

Protests are drawn into election campaigning

The movement began in September with a protest over staff shortages at a high school southeast of Paris and spread nationwide. It drew students demanding more education funding and then broadened to workers seeking better pensions and help with soaring fuel prices and other costs.

Thursday's demonstrations come as the campaign to succeed Macron as president next May heats up, with political leaders seeking to capitalize on the movement. Macron is constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term. Far-right contender Marine Le Pen is the favorite to win.

Some candidates participated in the Paris march, including veteran far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mlenchon, Green leader Marine Tondelier and Raphal Glucksmann, who represents the moderate left.

There is a sense of absolute frustration at the governments failure to operate, said Paul Smith, an associate professor of French history and politics at the University of Nottingham in England. Whoever wins the presidential election is going to have a stack of problems to cope with.

Its very difficult to see exactly where things go, he said.

title: GOP insiders say one official is about to quit and point the blame at Trump
content:
On Thursday, new bombshell reporting revealed that one of President Donald Trump's top Cabinet officials may be preparing to resign. According to GOP insiders who spoke with the Independent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio appears to be leaving the administration in order to protect himself from midterm blowback as he ramps up a 2028 presidential run.

As the Independent explains, "Even before the disastrous midterm results — when the Republicans lost both the House and the Senate — senior party sources in the US and senior figures in the UK government told the Independent that Mr Rubio could quit his senior role in President Donald Trump’s administration. The sources doubled down on the expectation after the midterms gave a damning indictment of the Trump presidency, with the Democrats seizing Republican strongholds such as Kansas and Texas. Mr Rubio is one of up to five members of Mr Trump’s current Cabinet who are thought to be preparing to 'run for the hills' in the aftermath of the midterms humiliation. One Washington insider told the Independent that Mr Rubio needs to 'distance himself from the Iran war and pin that one on Trump.'" Sources say that Trump may also lay the blame on Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth — whose impeachment is being called for even by members of his own party — with Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles also targeted as potential scapegoats.

As one insider, an ally of Rubio, elaborated, "It makes complete sense for him to step down and leave the administration. Rubio is the leading candidate at the moment to be the [Republican] nominee. He’s definitely ahead of [Vice President JD] Vance. But he cannot run while he is still secretary of state and being tied to the administration will only harm his prospects anyway.” Immediately after the GOP's midterm massacre, Vance was quick to blame the war in Iran in a clear effort to distance himself from it. “The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone … The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night," wrote Vance in his scathing remarks. "Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.” Meanwhile, many have noted that Rubio has played a "quieter" role in the war, with others helming negotiations despite the fact that his position makes him the country's top diplomat.

One senior UK government source told the Independent, “We are looking to see what he will do after the midterms. It seems unlikely that he will stick around. He would make a strong presidential candidate and we expect him to run.” Another Republican source asserted, “Rubio will be gone after the midterms. There will be about four or five them running for the hills." As this source noted, “The country has completely turned against Trump. People cannot even say where Iran is on a map and do not get this war. The cost of gas has really p—— people off.” They added: “Once the Democrats control the House and Senate we are just going to see attempts at impeachment and nobody wants to stick around for that.”

title: Nigeria Health Watch builds AI-readiness with an internal wiki
content:
About the organisation: Nigeria Health Watch is a communication and advocacy non-profit focused on improving health outcomes in Nigeria. Originally launched as a two-person blog in 2007, it has since expanded into a broader organisation that today is involved in solutions-driven journalism, community health monitoring, advocacy and research. Its team of permanent and freelance staff and volunteers comprises more than 60 people. 

Building the ‘brain of the organisation’

To some degree, every organisation struggles with institutional knowledge. As years go by and staff members come and go, it’s seemingly unavoidable that documents, multimedia files and other resources become scattered and effectively lost across online platforms, servers and local hard drives.

This was the problem that Nigeria Health Watch tackled during their participation in NextGen AI Leaders, a WAN-IFRA programme in partnership with the Google News Initiative. The programme is designed to help young media leaders reach the next stage in their careers through responsible AI deployment and strategic leadership.

During the programme, Chibuike Alagboso, Director of Media Programmes at Nigeria Health Watch, began the process of building an internal wiki, a “brain of the organisation,” in order to better preserve organisational memory.

According to Alagboso, there was a strong feeling within the organisation that access to important resources tends to disappear, especially after employees leave: “You might as well not have those materials, because they are scattered all over the place and you can’t access them. You might not even know they exist.”

Even when a specific file is needed for a project – a concept note, or a photograph – “we often find ourselves in situations where we have to spend a lot of time looking for it,” he said.

Start with a vibe-coded prototype

Today, Nigeria Health Watch is involved in a wide range of activities, but the organisation’s roots go back to a blog that was started by two friends interested in covering health care in the country. 

That foundation is still strong, Alagboso said: “We still write, we still produce content, we’re very active on social media.” The organisation’s regular output includes thought-leadership and opinion pieces, and it has a particular focus on solutions journalism.

Before joining the NextGen AI Leaders programme, Nigeria Health Watch had explored various types of AI use, from content generation and social media amplification to transcription, summarisation and analysis of large troves of documents.

As Alagboso began to develop an internal wiki to better capture organisational knowledge and resources – their most ambitious AI-driven initiative to date – his first step was to build a prototype that he could share with the IT team.

Having a vibe-coded prototype was tremendously helpful, Alagboso said: “It was easier for me to quickly translate my thinking into something visual, as opposed to trying to explain it, or draw it, for colleagues.” 

Screenshot: The vibe-coded prototype of the internal wiki that Alagboso passed on to the IT team.

The actual development of the tool was delayed because of the organisation’s annual conference and a website overhaul, but the IT team have now built the frontend interface, the backend for uploading resources, and the cloud infrastructure. 

The biggest step remaining is the collection and uploading of resources into the tool. The goal is to have a working version for team members to use by the end of the year.

‘The potential is huge’

Alagboso is optimistic that the internal wiki will make a significant impact, especially in terms of efficiency and saving time.

“It will have the context of everything we have done: projects, concept notes, stories, assets, all that. The potential is huge.” 

“It’s going to reduce the loss of institutional memory, because you can easily find things that happened even before you came into the organisation,” he said.

The clear upshot of having an easily searchable archive of past resources is that “it’s easier to create, it’s going to save time to build new things,” he said. “Rather than having to go back to a clean slate, there’s context to start from.”

Vivianne Ihekweazu, Managing Director of the organisation, commented on the internal wiki’s development: “Nigeria Health Watch creates an environment where our teams can express their creativity and explore new approaches to communications and advocacy. Our internal wiki reflects this commitment.” 

“Preserving knowledge takes foresight, but passing it on is even better. The wiki will preserve the knowledge and ideas generated through our work so they remain accessible when colleagues leave, giving future teams a foundation to build on. We hope to share what we learn with other organisations and help them build similar tools,” she said.

We spoke to Alagboso to learn more about how the NextGen AI Leaders programme helped shape his views on AI leadership. This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

‘Start with the problem’: Q&A with Chibuike Alagboso

WAN-IFRA: How did your perspective on AI leadership evolve during the programme?

Chibuike Alagboso: The main learning was about change management: you can’t just sit in your office and think, “This is what we need to do, this is how we build it, and now we have to get team members to buy into it.” You have to start by thinking about who the stakeholders are, who the blockers are. And from the beginning think about how to engage them.

Naturally, there might be some resistance in trying to push AI adoption and experimentation. How have you dealt with that?

It’s actually the reverse. Rather than resistance, our problem is more the overuse of AI, which we are now trying to cut down. We’re putting in some guardrails with the creation of an AI policy. It’s important to know where to draw the line: Where can we use AI? Where can we not use it?

I picked up an important leadership lesson during the programme: as leaders, it’s our responsibility to know when to ask others to slow down, even when we’re trying to drive innovation. Because AI use can get all over the place, it can be overwhelming. We have to know when to say “no.”

Was there a significant leadership challenge, and what did it teach you?

My main challenge concerned getting the tech team to take ownership and run with the wiki. The challenge was about managing time better, even though I do empathise, because I understand there are a lot of things on their plate. The biggest lesson there is to put scheduled check-ins in the calendar, so that even if you miss a goal, you have a check-in to know where you are and what the next steps are.

What milestone felt like a true breakthrough?

A big one was being able to visualise [the internal wiki] with a prototype rather than describing it. Another milestone was with the backend, the cloud infrastructure, that was set up. Also, we have a lot of resources and assets that we want to connect to the wiki, but we decided to prioritise multimedia assets, especially pictures, because we have pictures all over the place: in Google Drive, Microsoft SharePoint, hard drives… We made the important decision to make that the priority and start putting all that together. 

Has participating in the NextGen AI Leaders programme influenced your role or career path?

I believe it has put me on a certain pedestal, as far as AI leadership is concerned. If any conversation in the organisation is happening around AI, I usually get invited to be in the room. The programme has put me in a very strategic position, and if anything concerning AI innovation or business development comes up, I’ll definitely be involved.

If you could give one piece of advice to another media leader trying to implement AI right now, what would it be?

Start with the problem. That’s what I tell my team members. Don’t build something just because AI is the shiny new thing. You have to start with a clear problem. Once you have that figured out, you can see how AI can help you solve that problem. 

If you are clear on that, maybe you realise it’s a problem with a process and it’s something that you need to tweak. If you plug AI into a process that is not working, it will actually make it even worse. So start with the problem, understand the problem, then ask how AI can help address it.

title: With control of Congress, here’s how Democrats could stop Trump’s war in Iran
content:
The Democrats’ sweeping victory in the US midterm elections puts them in a stronger position to interfere with President Donald Trump’s agenda. This includes his deeply unpopular and costly war against Iran, which could be among their first priorities.

As president, Trump will be able to veto any legislation aimed at ending the war. But the Democrats still have another powerful card up their sleeves: cutting off funding for the war.

There are caveats, however. History suggests exercising this power could trigger a political confrontation that may backfire. And even if the Democrats succeed in ending the war, they may not be able to reverse the damage it has done to the US’ global standing.

The limits of legislation

Democrats will have three main options to try to force the war against Iran to a close. Two of these, however, face significant limitations.

The first – and perhaps most obvious – option is through legislation. There are a few different ways to do this.

One approach is to pass a resolution calling for an end to the war.

Congress already attempted this in June, passing a concurrent resolution (with the support of some Republicans) that directed the president to either withdraw US forces from hostilities against Iran or seek the approval of Congress before continuing. This was done under the War Powers Resolution of 1973.

These so-called concurrent resolutions are, however, widely seen as non-binding. Intended to express the opinion or will of Congress, they are generally used to deal with internal matters within Congress.

Trump ignored it. A similar resolution then failed in the Senate in September.

For such a resolution to be binding, it would need the force of a law passed by Congress, which the president would likely veto. To overcome that veto, the Democrats would need the support of a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate. This would require a significant number of Republicans to cross the aisle.

Exercising oversight

A second option for the Democrats is to launch a series of congressional investigations into the way the war has been conducted. This would likely include public hearings, subpoenas and demands for documents from the Trump administration.

The Democrats may also attempt to impeach senior officials in the Trump administration.

If Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat tipped to become the next speaker of the House, wants to appease some of the more progressive voices in his party – or the hardline voices on the Iran war or against Trump – Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth could be targeted for impeachment.

But the grounds for such proceedings are unclear at this stage, and even with the Democrats’ new Senate majority, he would be unlikely to be convicted unless a significant number of Republicans crossed the aisle.

More pertinently, congressional investigations are a protracted process, and unlikely to bring the war to a swift end.

The ‘power of the purse’

The more immediate power that Congress has to end the war swiftly is in Article I, Section 9 of the US Constitution, which states:

No Money shall be drawn from the Treasury, but in Consequence of Appropriations made by Law […]

This is known as the “power of the purse”.

Once the new Congress is sworn in in January, every new dollar that Trump’s Department of War wants to spend needs to be approved by the House and the Senate.

A Democrat-controlled Congress could put a clause into the defence budget, prohibiting funds from being used for hostilities against Iran. Trump could veto this, but this would mean blocking the paycheck for everyone in the military, as well.

The Democrats tried this very approach in 2007, attempting to force a timetable for a US withdrawal from Iraq. Then-President George W. Bush vetoed it, but it became a political football, with both sides accusing the other of leaving US troops unfunded.

The Democrats ultimately backed down due to the growing risk of backlash from voters.

Today, this approach would carry a similar risk. Are the Democrats willing to put their political credibility on the line if the president accuses them of letting American soldiers down? Who blinks first?

Republicans face a reckoning

As the dust settled on Wednesday, Trump himself acknowledged the Iran war had played a role in the Republican Party’s crushing defeat. But he doubled down on the decision, saying he would do it all over again if necessary to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon.

Vice President JD Vance was less defensive. In a detailed statement posted to X, Vance bluntly declared the war was the reason the Republicans lost. He added, “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there”.

Vance has long criticised US military involvement in overseas conflicts, but in his role as vice president has publicly backed Trump’s actions against Iran.

This week’s overwhelming Democratic victory has made it much easier for Vance – and other Republicans – to now break ranks with the president.

The balance of power has shifted

For Trump, bringing the war to an end now would mean humiliation. The US has so far poured almost US$50 billion into a military campaign with few tangible achievements.

On top of that, Iran has learned that the Strait of Hormuz is a chokepoint it can control. The same is true for the Bab al-Mandeb Strait off the coast of Yemen, where the Iran-aligned Houthis have attacked commercial ships.

These costs will outlast the Trump presidency. The war might definitively bring to an end the unipolar global order Washington built after the end of the Cold War. The biggest winner may not be Tehran, but Beijing.

Markus Wagner received funding from the Australian Department of Defence as principal investigator for the Weaponised Trade project.

title: Whose fault is the GOP’s cataclysmic defeat? 3 theories are gaining steam on the right.
content:
Republicans began picking through their party’s post-midterms wreckage Wednesday to ask about — and argue over — how things went so, so wrong in President Donald Trump’s second term.

Tuesday’s blue tsunami not only washed out Republicans’ House and Senate majorities, it carried Democrats into office even in deep red strongholds like South Carolina, Kansas, and possibly Mississippi. It seemed to be a decisive thumbs down from the electorate on the second Trump administration.

These results also mark the effective start of the battle to determine what the Republican Party will become after Trump — both who the 2028 GOP presidential nominee will be, and what the party will stand for overall.

Within hours of the results, a sort of narrative warfare began to unfold, as different politicians, advocates, and factions tried to advance their preferred accounts of what exactly went wrong, who should get the blame, and what the party should change for the future. Here are three theories of what went wrong that are already starting arguments between big names on the right.

Was the war by far the most important thing – or just one problem among many?

The conversation about what went wrong is especially important for Vice President JD Vance, who remains the frontrunner for the GOP presidential nomination, but is inextricably tied to an administration that increasingly looks like a failure. So it was noteworthy that he offered his own account of what happened.

Vance’s post-mortem glancingly mentioned a few issues, such as “cost of living/inflation,” and floated that he’d be open to changing immigration “enforcement” (though he reiterated he’d never support “amnesty”). He also cited voters’ belief that the United States should “change our relationship to Israel,” perhaps helping explain why Trump announced on Election Day that he’d decided to end aid to Israel after this year.

Yet there was one factor Vance wanted to be sure got most of the blame: the Iran war.

“The reason we lost is the war,” Vance wrote. What’s more, he claimed that “everyone knows” that is the case, and that “any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

That position is no surprise coming from Vance, who has long been a critic of the hawkish GOP foreign policy establishment, and who had hoped to help steer Trump’s second term on a different course. 

Vance is associated with an “America First” faction that was deeply skeptical of US involvement in foreign conflicts, particularly in Ukraine and Iran.

But Trump ignored their advice, sided with the hawks, and launched his Iran war early this year. And though Vance stood by that decision publicly, he now wants it known that he was right all along. 

Curt Mills, executive director of the American Conservative magazine and a critic of the hawks, told me Wednesday that Vance had a tremendous opportunity to help negotiate an end to the conflict: “He’s in a pole position to get us out of this mistake, and I think if he does do that, he will be associated with ending the war, not starting the war.”

The right’s internal conflict between the hawks and the America Firsters, has long been bitter and personal, and goes beyond Vance. Aspects of it played out publicly among commentators Wednesday, with hawks like talk radio host Mark Levin deriding the idea that the war sank Trump. 

“The mid-terms were not lost over a single issue.  And anybody with a functioning brain knows that,” Levin posted on X. He added that, to the extent the war harmed Trump politically, it was the fault of the America Firsters’ campaign to “undermine” it.

But right-wing commentator Ryan James Girdusky argued to me that the war hurt Trump’s coalition beyond just driving up energy prices. “In 2024, TikTok was all, ‘Trump is great, Trump is the man,’” he said. “What’s the vibe on TikTok today? It’s, ‘You’re at war for Israel.’ That is a completely different narrative, and that’s a mainstream narrative on TikTok.”

Is this outcome a rejection of Trumpism – that necessitates something very different?

Another narrative some began advancing was that the midterm elections were a repudiation of Trumpism in general — and, particularly, all the ways Trump deviated from the GOP’s pre-Trump conservative principles. 

The exact specifics varied, but the conservative commentator Erick Erickson summed up the gist of it by writing:

It was gas prices. It was the war. It was also the corruption. The incompetence. The tariffs. The playing nice with Russia. The impression of cruelty. The overly aggressive deportations. The accidental arrests of American citizens who were Hispanic. The arrogance. The ballroom. The reflecting poll. The golf courses. The arch. The Qatari 747. The aggressive redistricting push. The threats against enemies.

There was also Sen. John Curtis (R-UT), who criticized “a hastily executed war, headline after headline of scandals, a ballooning $40 trillion debt, and unpredictable tariffs” while saying it was “time for Republicans to return to the principled conservative values that once defined us—and that we’ve steadily abandoned over the last decade.”

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, a past and perhaps future Republican presidential candidate, had some pointed criticisms for the Trump administration even before the results were in. This week, he said that in addition to failures on affordability and the Iran war being a “big, big drag,” the administration’s aggressive approach to immigration under former Homeland Secretary Kristi Noem had created “unnecessary” conflicts. 

But DeSantis also emphasized another issue: corruption.“This swamp here is the worst it’s ever been,” he said. “Look at the amount of money these people are making, who are in the administration,” he went on, specifically calling out Trump lawyer Alina Habba for reportedly getting a $10 million a year contract while advising the Justice Department.

Then on Wednesday, DeSantis gave a lengthy press conference in which he portrayed the results as “close to an extinction-level event for Republicans.” Again, he cited the cost of living and corruption, and said that he himself does not trade any stocks while he’s in elected office.

What can Republicans do about the economy?

There was widespread agreement on the right that Trump had failed to address voters’ concerns about affordability and high prices.

There was much less agreement on why, exactly, Trump had failed on the economy — and what Republicans should do instead.

To the GOP’s free market faction, Trump had blundered with his tariffs, which, in addition to being handled chaotically, helped drive prices up. Curtis, the senator from Utah, mentioned tariffs and a failure to address the debt as major errors from the administration.

Those sympathetic to the populist right were more reluctant to blame the tariffs per se. Gidurksy told me that “the tariffs didn’t do what the anti-tariff audience said they were going to do” — that they did not cause economic catastrophe or raise prices as much as economists had predicted. 

Indeed, beyond the tariffs, many on the populist right believe that the Trump administration’s true failure was not delivering on their economic populist rhetoric. For instance, Trump’s biggest legislative accomplishment — the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — was mostly orthodox conservative Republican policy, focused on cutting taxes (particularly for the wealthy) and paying for it by slashing Medicaid and SNAP benefits.

But outside a couple of working-class flourishes, like exempting tips from taxes, it did little to address the broader affordability problem. Gidursky told me that the administration’s most acute problem was that gas prices, interest rates, and health insurance premiums kept getting more expensive, and the administration simply didn’t manage to address that.

“Life is too expensive,” right-wing commentator Benny Johnson posted on X. “Especially for young people. This is a crisis. Communists will win on the ‘affordability’ question if we don’t end the war and fix prices.”

Still, coming up with an agenda that can actually address those voter concerns is more challenging, especially with the deficits and inflation concerns potentially constraining both parties from considering major new tax cuts and benefits. And making major long-term headway on spending cuts would likely require looking at programs like Medicare and Social Security that voters punished Republicans in the past for trying to remake, and that Trump moved the GOP away from considering touching. This tension between offering voters more direct help or retreating to austerity is likely to loom over the 2028 presidential campaign. But for now, Republicans are still struggling to figure out a clear agenda on the economy that resonates with voters. 

“Voters are signaling they are unhappy with the economy, the Iran War, and corruption,” the influential right-wing activist Christopher Rufo posted. “It’s about policy.”

title: At $835M, tonight’s Powerball is among the top 10 jackpots in the game’s history
content:
A lucky player could win an estimated $835 million in Wednesdays Powerball drawing and secure the games second largest prize of the year.

Wednesdays grand prize, which could also be paid in the United States as a one lump-sum payment of $357.9 million before taxes, trails the $1.04 billion prize won in Illinois in August, according to the Multi-State Lottery Association, which runs Powerball.

While Wednesdays potential winnings total less than a billion dollars, the jackpot would rank as the tenth largest in Powerball history if won.

The biggest Powerball jackpot of all time is $2.04 billion won in California in 2022.

The current jackpot is also the first one fully built by players on either side of the Atlantic.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | UK players joining Powerball could drive US jackpots even higher

Powerball sales expanded to the United Kingdom in July, but this is the first time British players have been able to buy tickets from the beginning of the multi-drawing stretch.

By expanding the player base internationally, Powerball jackpots are expected to grow faster, creating bigger prize opportunities for players without altering the games $2 ticket price or jackpot odds, Multi-State Lottery Association said in a July news release.

Should there be a winner in the UK, they will be paid over 30 years rather than a lump-sum cash option.

The drawing is set for Wednesday at 10:59 p.m. ET. The odds of winning Powerballs jackpot are 1 in 292.2 million.

title: Kyiv's power now travels 200 miles, and Russia knows the weak point
content:
Kyiv no longer produces its own power. It can't.

On Wednesday, Russian attacks cut power and water across the capital and the surrounding region for hours. Residents were told to fill up at public drinking fountains. Emergency centers opened in the hardest-hit neighborhoods, handing out hot tea and places to charge phones. Water and power came back after repairs.

Russian strikes have gutted Kyiv's power plants. The city's two biggest heat-and-power stations have been hit dozens of times this year.

RELATED STORY | Zelenskyy says Ukraine got no early warning from partners as Russia hits the power grid again

On Tuesday, three more heat-and-power plants in Ukraine went dark. Russia fired 289 attack drones, 17 ballistic missiles and 59 cruise missiles at nine regions, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. DTEK, Ukraine's biggest private power company, said all three of its plants stopped generating and called it one of the "most serious attacks ever." No one was hurt at the plants.

Overnight into Wednesday, Russia sent 310 more drones, 81 of them jet-powered. Ukraine's air force said it shot down or disabled 272.

So where does Kyiv's power come from now? Mostly nuclear: three plants, roughly 200 miles away. They are the Rivne, Khmelnytskyi and South Ukraine nuclear plants. A fourth, Zaporizhzhia, is occupied by Russia.

The weak point is everything in between: high-voltage lines and a handful of big substations. And Russia knows it.

Hit a reactor, and you risk a radiation disaster. Hit the wires, and Kyiv goes dark anyway.

But even that tactic poses risks. On Tuesday, three drones went after the substation Khmelnytskyi's reactors rely on. Ukraine's energy minister called it a threat to "the nuclear safety of all of Europe."

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Russian drone strikes crowded Ukraine train platform, killing at least 13

Zelenskyy said halting strikes on energy and critical infrastructure is among Ukraine's priorities for U.S.-brokered peace talks Nov. 10-11 in Abu Dhabi.

Meanwhile, Kyiv is relying on a workaround called "islands": strategically placed, gas-fired plants that keep hospitals and water pumps running.

It's a Band-Aid, covering a fraction of what a city of 3 million needs.

And here's the twist. Analysts say the islands break the grid into pieces, all of them vulnerable to Russian attacks that appear aimed at making Ukraine's capital uninhabitable.

title: WAN-IFRA condemns arrest of Japanese journalist
content:
WAN-IFRA, the World Association of News Publishers, condemns the criminalisation of journalism in Russia and has called on Russian authorities to immediately release Japanese journalist, Yuki Imai, detained on allegations of espionage.

Imai, an accredited Japanese correspondent for Hokkaido Shimbun, was arrested on 13 October on Sakhalin Island, in Russia’s Far East, just north of Japan as he was getting ready to leave the country. He was subsequently transferred to Moscow, accused of gathering defence related information for Japanese intelligence – a claim rejected by Japan.

Stig Ørskov, WAN-IFRA’s CEO said: “Gathering information in the public interest is a fundamental part of journalism. Security laws must not be used to punish legitimate reporting, intimidate journalists or turn journalists in to bargaining pawns in political disputes.”

Imai was working in Russia on a journalist visa, with Russian foreign ministry accreditation. Based in Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk, his work covered Russia’s Far East and regional relationships. His last report on 5 October, described the presence and everyday lives of North Korean workers on Sakhalin.

David Walmsley, President of WAN-IFRA’s World Editors Forum and editor-in-chief of The Globe and Mail said: “The gathering of  information by reporters is the entire purpose of responsible journalism and Imai is no different. It is to the dismay of his colleagues across the industry that his responsibility has been perversely turned into accusations of wrongdoing. Imai should be immediately released.”

WAN-IFRA urges its members, national media associations and the wider international media community to take every opportunity to protest Russia’s actions, and the intimidation and arrest of journalists.

title: Trump just said he was ending aid to Israel. He might actually mean it.
content:
President Donald Trump announced Tuesday that the US would soon cut off military aid to Israel.

During an Election Day interview with Fox & Friends, Trump said of Israel, “We were giving them $4 billion but it’s cut off at the end of the year.”

When asked to explain this position, Trump said that Israel was a “very successful country” that didn’t need Americans’ money — and that the aid had become an “easy target” for “lunatics like [Democratic Michigan Senate candidate Abdul] El-Sayed” in the midterm elections. Trump also suggested that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu agreed with this reasoning and supported a cessation of US aid to his country.

Of course, Trump says a lot of things. If all of his policy declarations could be taken at face value, then US soldiers would now be patrolling the streets of Gaza, while American hoteliers redeveloped its coastline.

Further, Trump’s remarks Tuesday morning seem to have been ad-libbed. The Israeli Treasury Department reportedly had no knowledge of a supposed joint agreement to end US aid. And existing US law provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual funding through 2028.

All this said, Trump didn’t pluck his Election Day rant out of thin air. Rather, his remarks actually reflect a prominent strain of thinking among Israeli leaders and security experts. In their view, America’s cash may no longer be worth the political blowback that it invites.

Given this Israeli sentiment — and the souring of American public opinion toward Israel — the United States might very well draw down aid in the near future (although, probably not as soon as “the end of the year”).

The Israeli case against US aid to Israel

During a May interview with 60 Minutes, Netanyahu said he would like to “draw down to zero the American financial support, the financial component of the military cooperation that we have.”

Amit Halevi, a lawmaker in Israel’s parliament and member of Netanyahu’s party, spelled out the logic of his position last year. In a pamphlet outlining his vision for the US-Israel relationship, Halevi said US military aid “creates a false narrative of dependency, weakens Israel’s global standing and subjects it to political pressure.” Halevi met with the leadership of the Heritage Foundation — arguably, the GOP’s most influential think tank — in 2025, shortly after Heritage had released its own controversial call for the (very gradual) phasing out of US aid to Israel.

Many on the Israeli right believe that such aid compromises Israeli sovereignty. As the retired Israel Defense Forces general Amir Avivi told Breitbart in 2024, aid “puts on Israel lots of restrictions,” which prevent it from pursuing its security interests with a free hand. Similar concerns have been voiced by former Israeli Prime Minster Naftali Bennet and ex-Israeli ambassador to Israel Michael Oren.

Their argument boils down to two observations:

  • There are many forms of US support that Israel would struggle to do without — but financial aid is not one of them.
  • Direct financial aid provokes political blowback in a way that other, more essential forms of US assistance do not.

There is evidence for both these points. In 2025, Israel spent about 7.9 percent of its GDP on the IDF. To sustain its 2025 level of military funding — without American cash — Israel would need to dedicate 8.5 percent of GDP to its military. This might irritate Israel’s taxpayers. But it would scarcely threaten Israel’s ability to pursue whatever foreign policy it sees fit.

By contrast, Israel does need access to American military hardware. It has the money to fund its own military. But to adequately provision it, Israel must be allowed to purchase American-made fighter jets, among myriad other forms of martial technology. And the Israelis would also have a tough time doing without its broad military, diplomatic, and intelligence alliance with the United States.

That alliance has attracted some criticism on the American left and right this year — particularly, after the US partnered with Israel to launch a war against Iran.

But Israel’s American critics seem to have found the aid issue uniquely politically potent. Which makes sense: A voter doesn’t need to have any strong opinion about the Israel-Palestine conflict to oppose sending billions of dollars to a wealthy foreign country. Unlike proposals for an arms embargo or sanctions, cutting off aid speaks directly to Americans’ material interests; that money could be going to US citizens but is flowing to the Israeli military instead.

In his Senate race, Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed has tried to tap into this isolationist sentiment, describing his plans for slashing aid to Israel — and increasing benefits for US citizens — as an “America First” agenda.

Meanwhile, in a controversial ad, an outside group supporting El-Sayed’s candidacy made this argument in blunter terms, portraying a couple forced to pare back their grocery list, in order to save enough money for “killing Palestinians.”

US aid to Israel is not actually responsible for Americans’ rising grocery bills (although, the war in Iran plausibly is). But the broader isolationist argument has wide resonance. In a recent survey from the Chicago Council on Global Affairs, a majority of Americans favored either reducing or ending aid to Israel. And whether or not Trump’s aid comments referred to a solid plan, his political aides swiftly used them to reclaim the “America First” banner from Democrats like El-Sayed.

Faced with these dynamics, it isn’t hard to see how an Israeli leader might think it best to beat a strategic retreat on financial aid. 

A phase-out of US aid may be coming, whether Israel likes it or not

To be clear, Israel’s leadership is by no means united in favor of Trump’s impromptu proposal. Indeed, even those who support winding down US aid have insisted that this withdrawal of financial backing must be gradual. And Gadi Eisenkot, the man most likely to become Israel’s next prime minister, is a staunch advocate for indefinite US aid. On Tuesday, Eisenkot assailed Netanyahu for his purported agreement with Trump about winding down such assistance. Both Israeli leaders are currently trying to cobble together a parliamentary majority through alliances with small political parties, after each failed to win such a majority outright in Israel’s recent elections.

Still, it is quite plausible that Netanyahu genuinely told Trump that he was open to phasing out US aid, given the Israeli prime minister’s public remarks on that subject.

In any case, authority over US spending ultimately lies with the American people’s elected representatives, not Israeli officials. On the US left, right, and center, political winds are blowing against aid to Israel. With some of that country’s own leaders and admirers bowing to such gusts, the draw down of American aid to Israel might now be a matter of when, not if.
