title: Israel’s Arab parties could end Netanyahu’s rule — if his opposition lets them
content:
The dust is beginning to settle a week after Israel’s first national election since Hamas’s attack on October 7, 2023, and the war Israel waged on Gaza in response. Neither Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu nor his opponents won the 61 parliamentary seats needed to govern.

Now the fate of the next government hinges on a less-discussed part of the Israeli electorate: Arab citizens, who voted in record numbers and whose parties have emerged with more leverage than ever before. They are not to be confused with the roughly 5.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza, who live under Israeli control but are not citizens and cannot vote in national elections.

Although Israel has become a fault line in both American parties, with Democrats split over arms sales and whether to call the war in Gaza a genocide, and Republicans over whether Israel pulled the United States into war with Iran, these were not the central issues in the recent election.

Voters and candidates alike treated the election as a referendum on Netanyahu himself, who has governed Israel for most of the past 17 years and is currently on trial for corruption. And Netanyahu did lose support in this election: His right-wing and religious coalition fell from 64 of the Knesset’s 120 seats in 2022 to 53, while 67 seats went to parties that ran against him. 

Nineteen of those 67 opposition seats were won by two Arab parties, Ra’am and the Joint List, on a historic surge in turnout among Arab citizens of Israel. Arab parties had held just 10 seats after the last election.

Key takeaways

  • Israel’s election ended in deadlock, and record Arab turnout nearly doubled Arab parties’ seats to 19, the most ever.
  • A crime wave in Arab towns while Netanyahu’s far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir ran the police drove Arab voters to the polls.
  • Depending on the details, a Jewish-Arab coalition could reshape Israeli politics, but it won’t end the occupation or reverse course in Gaza.

But most of Israel’s Jewish parties have long treated a governing coalition that depends on Arab votes as taboo. Netanyahu spent the campaign portraying Ra’am and Joint List politicians as supporters of terrorism, and several of his Jewish opponents promised to never govern with them. Whether the four Jewish-led opposition parties that call themselves the “change bloc” will break that promise is now the central political question hanging over Israel — with major implications for Arab and Jewish citizens alike, and for what kind of country they share.

“There’s been a fair amount of commentary from American Jewish groups that over a million Arab citizens can vote, and that’s true, but the big asterisk is it matters only if those votes are taken seriously and if Arabs are treated as potential partners in a coalition,” Ilan Goldenberg, the chief policy officer for J Street, a liberal pro-Israel group founded as a counterweight to AIPAC, told me. “Otherwise it’s a pretty empty symbol, and it says something else about Israeli society and Israeli politics.”

Polling suggests most change bloc voters would accept a government that relied on Ra’am, if not the Joint List, whether inside the coalition or backing it from outside in exchange for policy commitments. Their leaders have been more cautious, though, partly because most Jewish Israelis still oppose an Arab-Jewish coalition and the politicians worry about losing those voters in the next election. Critics see that caution as the problem: Rather than try to bring the Israeli public along, the Jewish opposition leaders campaigned on rejecting an alliance they might need to form any kind of government at all.

It’s a pivotal moment for supporters of a liberal, democratic Israel, for those pushing sanctions and boycotts — some of whom want an end to Israel as a Jewish state — and for the roughly 900,000 Arab citizens who turned out to vote for urgent improvements in their daily lives. The next few months will decide who governs the country, whether Arab voters get real influence over policy or become further marginalized, whether pressure on Israel from abroad grows or fades, and whether anything changes for the Palestinians it rules.

Why Arab voters showed up

For Arab voters, this election was different in two ways. The Arab parties were more united than ever on a single priority — getting rid of Netanyahu — even if it meant working with Zionist parties whose vision of a Jewish state they’ve long opposed. And calls to boycott the vote, which Islamist and Palestinian nationalist groups within Israel’s Arab community have pushed in past elections on the grounds that voting legitimizes the state, were far more muted this time around. 

The prime motivating factor for Arab voters was Netanyahu’s coalition itself, the most right-wing government in Israel’s history. Its national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who was once convicted of inciting racism after displaying a sign reading “Expel the Arab enemy,” has overseen the police while organized crime has killed record numbers of Arab citizens. Homicides in Arab communities more than doubled between 2022 and 2025, and police solved just 12 percent of them in the first half of this year. Netanyahu’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, who has said there is “no such thing as a Palestinian people,” also froze hundreds of millions of shekels promised to Arab towns, arguing the money would reach criminals. In 2025, Britain and four other countries sanctioned both men for inciting violence against Palestinians.

“The feeling is the state has completely failed to address criminal violence,” Yousef Munayyer, a Palestinian citizen of Israel and the head of the Palestine/Israel program at the Arab Center Washington DC, told me. “Brutal murders go uninvestigated and unsolved, and in many corners there’s a belief that the Israeli intelligence services are intentionally turning a blind eye.” 

Hassan Jabareen, the executive director of Adalah, a legal advocacy group for Palestinian citizens of Israel, told me the Arab parties have been deliberately keeping their demands to things an anti-Netanyahu government could practically deliver, like fighting crime, ending the demolition of Bedouin homes in southern Israel, and stopping settler violence in the West Bank. 

“We are not going to say to end the occupation, we are not going to ask for withdrawal from Syria,” Jabareen said. “Those issues, we know that they won’t agree with us, and the right-wing will use it against them, and they themselves won’t agree.”

Though Ra’am and the Joint List did not make Gaza central to their campaigns, Jabareen said the national election was a rare opportunity for Arab voters to express their anger at the war, something they’ve been heavily barred from protesting over the last three years. He added that Palestinians in Gaza and the West Bank have been “happy and proud” of the record turnout of Arab citizens.

The choice facing Gadi Eisenkot

The “change bloc” is an alliance of four Zionist parties with little in common beyond wanting Netanyahu gone. Its leader is Gadi Eisenkot, a former army chief who sat in Netanyahu’s war cabinet after October 7, lost a son in Gaza, and quit the government over its handling of the war. His new centrist party won the most seats of the four. The others are a party led by two former prime ministers, the settler-right hawk Naftali Bennett and the centrist Yair Lapid, and Yair Golan’s party, the last of Israel’s Zionist left. The fourth is Avigdor Lieberman’s, hawkish on security and built on secular Russian-speaking immigrants who want the ultra-Orthodox out of government.

The four were split on Arab parties during the campaign. Golan was the only leader explicitly open to governing with them. Eisenkot set four conditions for any coalition partner, including recognizing Israel as a Jewish and democratic state and Hamas as a terrorist group, and said in September that no Arab party met them. (Arab leaders and many critics saw these conditions as a way to shut Arabs out without saying so.) Bennett, who in 2021 led the first governing coalition ever to include an independent Arab party, said this time he wanted only Zionist parties in government, and Lieberman, who sat in that same 2021 coalition, also ruled out relying on Arab parties again.

Ori Kol, a progressive campaigner who worked for Golan’s left-wing party, told me most Jewish opposition voters “were shocked” on election night, expecting the change bloc to win more seats.

“What people really expected is that Netanyahu voters would not turn out as they did, because the logic was after three years of war, two failed wars against Iran, attacking Qatar, the sanctions, and the incredible physical, emotional and economic toll on the country every Israeli living here has experienced, that Netanyahu would pay some sort of cost,” he said. And while Netanyahu’s coalition did lose about a dozen seats compared to 2022, his party still did better than expected, beating the final polls from three major Israeli broadcasters.

So what is the resistance to forming a Jewish-Arab government? Part of it is plain prejudice, a refusal to accept Arab parties as legitimate partners in governing a Jewish state. Arab parties have supported or joined an Israeli government only twice, briefly, in the 1990s and in 2021, and both times the Jewish parties involved treated it as a one-off they’d rather not repeat. Both times, too, the Arab parties were just a handful of votes at the margin, while this time they would represent nearly a third of the coalition. 

A vocal liberal minority of Israelis say that’s exactly the change the country is overdue for. In the week since the election, thousands have rallied to demand their leaders form a Jewish-Arab government. Some activists organized a pressure campaign outside Eisenkot’s home, while others have signed petitions, including one led by writers and artists, and another by Israeli healthcare professionals.

The other main hurdle, which can be hard to disentangle from bigotry, is electoral fear. Jewish opposition leaders worry that a Jewish-Arab coalition would be fragile from the start, and that if it collapsed in the near future, they would pay the price in the next election. Israelis vote on security above all, and Netanyahu leverages those concerns shamelessly. Two days before this past election, for example, he posted on X an AI-generated image of a mushroom cloud over Tel Aviv, warning of a second Holocaust if he lost. On election night he warned that it was “forbidden” to form a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties. (This didn’t stop Netanyahu himself from negotiating with Ra’am in 2021, when he needed its votes.)

Ra’am, for its part, has spent the last few months trying to make itself an easier partner for Zionist parties to accept. In August its leader, Mansour Abbas, put a Jewish former deputy security minister in the No. 2 slot on the party’s electoral slate, and a few months earlier Ra’am cut its formal ties to the religious council that had guided its decisions, to show it answers to no one but its voters. Abbas has also repeatedly condemned the October 7 attack.

The Joint List is more nationalist, and one of its party leaders was forced out of the race in October over an article he published the day after October 7, calling the attack an “important historical event.” That leader has since said his language was badly worded and he did not mean support for it. The Joint List may not want to be formally in the coalition anyway. Its leaders have said they’d rather support an Eisenkot government from the outside, which would let them push for concessions on crime and budgets without having to share responsibility for the coalition’s decisions on Gaza and elsewhere.

For now, the Arab parties are signaling they don’t want to drive a hard bargain with Jewish leaders given the risk of Netanyahu staying in power. Over the weekend, one of the Joint List’s leaders said his party would back Eisenkot’s choice for Knesset speaker when the new parliament convenes on November 10. “We want to be part of the correction, part of the hope,” he said, adding that his party would “swallow frogs” to get things done. The Joint List’s chair also said the party was “truly ready” to help build a majority in the coming weeks. Opposition leaders have reportedly been in contact with both Joint List officials and Abbas. 

Eisenkot, for his part, posted a statement over the weekend that read as tailored to exactly that arrangement, Ra’am inside and the Joint List outside. He repeated the four conditions he set during the campaign and wrote that “the door to the government we establish will be open to any elected official who accepts these principles.” But he also described the state he wants as “Jewish, democratic, liberal and egalitarian,” a word choice seemingly aimed at Arab citizens. And he said partners could satisfy his national-service condition through “civilian service,” not just the army, a voluntary version of which most Arab citizens tell pollsters they’d support.

The sticking point is Eisenkot’s demand that all partners declare Hamas a terrorist organization, something Abbas has repeatedly said he considers a risk to his life and his family’s. Hamas has a record of killing Palestinians accused of collaborating with Israel, and Abbas has faced death threats before.

But over the weekend Abbas signaled, according to Channel 12, that Eisenkot’s conditions need not keep Ra’am out of a government, which suggests the two sides may be able to negotiate a compromise. 

What a Jewish-Arab coalition means for Israel’s friends and critics

For supporters of a liberal, democratic Israel, bringing Arab parties into government would signal that Arab citizens have a say in who governs the country, and undercut the claim that they are shut out of power. Whether that proves true depends on what those parties actually get, in cabinet posts and in policy commitments.

Still, Israel’s democracy stops at the Green Line, the boundary that separated Israel from the West Bank before the 1967 war. More than 3 million Palestinians on the other side of it live under Israeli control with no vote in the government that rules them, and the same is true of the 2 million in Gaza. No election inside Israel changes that.

After last Tuesday’s election, most major American Jewish organizations released statements praising Israel’s democracy, citing its high turnout as proof. For example, AIPAC, which did not return requests for comment, praised turnout as reflecting Israel’s “vibrant democracy and rich diversity.” The Jewish Federations of North America cheered Israel for its “deep commitment to democratic principles and civic participation.”

J Street and New Jewish Narrative were exceptions, with J Street’s statement calling on the Jewish opposition to form a government with the Arab parties. New Jewish Narrative said Arab citizens “must be allowed a full voice in what comes next.”

Munayyer, of the Arab Center Washington DC, has little patience for the democracy talk at this moment. “People who are using this opportunity to talk about Israeli democracy, they’re not serious people,” he told me. Palestinian citizens did win historic numbers, but if the millions who live under Israeli control could actually vote, “they’d probably have 60 seats, not 19.” That, he said, is what makes it apartheid, noting South Africa held regular elections, too.

J Street’s Goldenberg was clear that a coalition with Arab parties would not by itself be a reason to ease pressure on Israel. The United States, he said, should decide what’s in its own national interest and respond when an Israeli government acts against it, whether on settler violence or on Gaza. But he argued that most Democrats have not given up on Israel. “I think the overwhelming majority of Democrats are not in a position of viewing Israel as irredeemable,” he told me. “What they want is a change in behavior.” 

A government that depended on 19 Arab seats, he added, would be the clearest possible signal that there’s potential for change. “I can’t think of any single action the Israeli opposition could take that would buy Israel more goodwill,” Goldenberg said. “And I can’t think of anything that would further confirm for Democrats that this is not an Israel we can work with than a failure to try.”

Hadar Susskind, the president of New Jewish Narrative and a dual citizen who flew back to vote, doubted American Jews would have much influence over the forthcoming coalition talks. But if a new government forms, he told me, liberal Zionist groups like his see “a lot of positive opportunity” to work in both directions, pushing the new government to deliver real change and Congress to engage with it and hold it to account.

That possibility, a repaired relationship between Israel and the United States, is exactly what many of Israel’s staunchest critics are worried about. The Boycott, Divestment, and Sanctions (BDS) movement’s official statement on the election called Western attention to it a “desperate attempt” to rehabilitate Israel as a democracy and pin Gaza war crimes on Netanyahu alone. For BDS supporters and many other anti-Zionists, engaging with any Israeli government, however it’s composed, normalizes a state they deem illegitimate.

The journalist Mehdi Hasan, who runs the outlet Zeteo, made a narrower version of the same argument, saying his worry throughout the election has been that “political and media elites” will use it to push for a “reset” that could improve Israel’s standing in global public opinion. The push to condition military aid and sanction settlements gained ground around the world largely because of Netanyahu and his far-right ministers, and a new government could make those efforts harder to sustain even if Israel’s policies on the ground barely shift.

The paths from here

What would a Jewish-Arab government actually change? Natan Sachs, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute in Washington, flatly rejected the idea that an Eisenkot government would be no different from Netanyahu’s. It’s true that both want Hamas gone and Iran boxed in, and that neither is going to offer the Palestinians a state anytime soon. But Eisenkot, Sachs told me, would be slower to use force, would treat Arab citizens as part of the country rather than a threat, and would reverse the damage Netanyahu has done to the courts and the civil service. 

Palestinian citizens turned out in huge numbers to make a former IDF chief prime minister, he said, “because they see the difference, so I would defer to them.” A coalition with Arab parties wouldn’t end the occupation or freeze settlements, but it would take the West Bank away from Smotrich and Ben-Gvir, the two ministers who’ve pushed hardest for annexation.

Even a short-lived Jewish-Arab coalition would matter, Jabareen of Adalah told me. “Even if it’s just for one or one and a half years, they can do a lot of things,” he said, pointing to forming a state commission of inquiry into the security failures before October 7, repealing Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul, and appointing Supreme Court justices. Beyond that, Arab leaders want to be inside the government to make sure its budgets reach their communities, with more money to fight violence and invest in construction and jobs.

Even before a governing coalition forms, the Jewish opposition parties can work with Ra’am and the Joint List in parliament, which convenes on November 10. Together they hold 67 of 120 seats, enough to pass laws and make appointments even without controlling the government. The first test will be replacing Netanyahu’s handpicked speaker, who controls what comes to a vote, which everyone in the opposition wants.

Almost any governing coalition will require some of the Jewish opposition leaders to break a campaign promise or two. The experts I interviewed were divided on how much that practically matters at this stage, and several noted it would hardly be the first time an Israeli politician had reneged. Eisenkot could also turn to the ultra-Orthodox parties, though that would likely mean compromising on the military draft exemptions his whole alliance campaigned against. President Donald Trump and Israeli President Isaac Herzog may also push for a so-called unity government with Eisenkot and Netanyahu. Whatever Eisenkot chooses, there is enormous pressure to reach a deal rather than go back to the polls, because few expect Arab citizens or the Israelis who flew in from abroad to turn out the same way in a repeat election, and a lower turnout would likely favor Netanyahu.

Kol, the campaigner who worked for Golan’s party, said what the moment requires is courage. 

“Centrist leaders have shown an alarming amount of passivity,” he told me. “There’s been a lack of willingness to carry people and lead.”

title: Trump reverses course on Israel aid amid Tuesday's midterm election
content:
President Donald Trump said in an Election Day interview with Fox News that the United States will not provide $4 billion in aid to Israel, claiming the country no longer needs the assistance.

Trump said the United States will continue to sell weapons to Israel.

His comments marked an abrupt reversal from his previous position, including when he signed legislation in July funding aid to Israel.

However, Trump acknowledged Tuesday that the money could be better spent domestically, including on reducing the national debt.

You can consider it barter. You can consider military aid or cash, Trump said. Look, we give them $4 billion of things and money, and they dont need it. And I was approached by Bibi Netanyahu, and weve been talking about it for a couple of years because its a lot of money.

During the interview Tuesday, Trump said aid to Israel has become a talking point for progressive Democratic candidates in the midterm election. Funding for Israel has been a focal point in Michigans Senate race between Abdul El-Sayed and Mike Rogers. El-Sayed has expressed strong opposition to providing aid to Israel.

The best talking point that these lunatics have on the left, they are lunatics, have no idea how great our country has become, Trump said. We are a beacon. Our country is the greatest country anywhere in the world, and two years ago we were a laughing stock. The left using $4 billion payment, and everybody knows about it, no secret, as a signal of unfairness and we can't allow that to happen. I don't like that; it is too easy.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has not publicly responded to Trump's comments that Israel does not need the funds.

title: US has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, US official says
content:
The U.S. has conducted defensive strikes on some Iranian targets in the Strait of Hormuz, a U.S. official says.

Iranian state television reported that explosions were heard on Qeshm Island. The official, who wasnt authorized to comment publicly and spoke Monday on condition of anonymity, said Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets had been targeted.

The strikes, which appeared to be limited as opposed to a full return to hostilities, came on the eve of crucial American midterm elections. President Donald Trump has previously said the U.S. wouldnt launch strikes on Iran before the midterms.

The unpopular Iran war and the resulting impact on U.S. gasoline prices and other parts of the economy have been a vulnerability for Republicans as they try to keep control of Congress.

Vice President JD Vance told reporters earlier Monday that he just spoke to Trump about talks with Iran and said that the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement.

He offered measured optimism on Monday that a deal can still be struck to prevent President Donald Trump from following through on his threat to potentially order new strikes on Iran after the crucial midterm elections in the United States.

Vance sent a letter to Irans security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, last week, but the White House has offered scant details about the contents of that correspondence. Trump told reporters that letter was focused on assisting Iran with medical supplies and various things.

But Vance on Monday suggested there's reason to believe that the U.S. and Iran could still come to an agreement.

Vance's comments came as the region remains on edge about the prospects of the U.S. resuming full-scale operations against Iran. The backchannel efforts are playing out as Israel and some Middle East allies lobby Trump on the way ahead in the 8-month-old war that's rattled global markets and wreaked havoc on Iran.

RELATED STORY | Iran war's cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion

Netanyahu pushed Trump for strikes in a weekend call

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is pushing for another wave of strikes on Iran after Tuesday's elections in the United States, according to two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter.

A return to full-scale war with Iran could help Netanyahu to form an emergency government after he and his far-right allies lost their parliamentary majority in last week's elections. Trump has alternated between threatening major strikes and pushing for a deal with Iran.

The two officials said diplomatic efforts have made progress, with Qatari mediators holding two rounds of talks last week with Iranian officials. The two officials said the mediators are trying to advance a framework for Iran to cease its attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the U.S. lifting its blockade on Iran's ports.

They said more talks are planned for this week. The two officials spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing classified briefings they had received from American, and in one case Israeli, officials.

One official said Netanyahu was working with senior officials in the U.S. administration to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign and that the president does not appear to have made a decision.

Netanyahu pressed for strikes during a call over the weekend with Trump, who would not commit to taking military action, according to a person who was briefed on it.

Other U.S. allies in the Middle East are warning against more strikes, saying that would destabilize the region and could lead Iran-allied Houthi rebels in Yemen to step up their attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, a third regional official said. Iran-backed militias in Iraq could also get involved.

The Israeli government did not immediately comment. The White House did not directly respond to questions about Netanyahu and Trumps discussion of potential new strikes during the weekend call.

Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Salman said he spoke by phone on Monday with U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth about the latest regional and international developments" and the Houthis' continued attacks on Saudi Arabia.

RELATED STORY | Hegseth fires Pentagons chief planning officer as renewed action against Iran looms, source says

Trump downplays scale of Iran conflict on Election Day eve

Netanyahu had pushed for renewed strikes even before the Israeli election as he sought to highlight his security credentials to a public deeply scarred by Hamas' Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

But the war has also loomed large for American voters ahead of Tuesday's midterm elections.

Oil prices dropped sharply on Monday as renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war between the U.S. and Iran appeared to show signs of headway. Rising prices at the pump, a byproduct of the war, have been a weight on Trumps Republican Party as it tries to maintain control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump noted the drop in a speech in Washington on Monday, which was billed as his closing argument to Americans, and sought to minimize the scale of the conflict, which has cost U.S. taxpayers at least $47 billion.

I dont know if you even call it a war, because we havent been doing any fighting for months, Trump said.

Netanyahu has not commented on Iran since the Israeli election, and there was no word from his office on the latest call with Trump.

Iran says it is prepared for war while pursuing diplomacy

Iran wants guarantees that the U.S. will implement its side of any agreement. The U.S. and Israel have twice attacked Iran while it was engaged in negotiations over its disputed nuclear program.

Iranian officials say publicly they are prepared for war or diplomacy.

The new supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, met with Irans military chiefs and said the response to any kind and level of threat from the U.S. or Israel should be immediate and without geographic limits, and urged an expansion of the list of potential targets.

A recent analysis by The Associated Press found that Iranian strikes on more than two dozen U.S. bases since the start of the war have caused billions of dollars in equipment damage.

Khamenei has not been seen publicly since the opening strikes by Israel and the U.S. on Feb. 28, which killed his father, the previous supreme leader.

Irans security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, told state television that the tone has completely changed from the U.S. and called it a very good sign. He also gave no details about the letter he received from Vance, which Iran acknowledged last week, and said he had not responded.

Meanwhile, Vance told reporters on Monday that the Republican administration's foremost concern is Iran agreeing to take substantive action on its nuclear program.

We do think that there is a pathway there, but it really does require a firm commitment and a verifiable commitment that they dont rebuild that nuclear program, Vance added.

Cost of war with Iran now at $47.1 billion

Arab allies are caught in the middle

October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz since March, as Iran has tried to ramp up economic pressure on the U.S. to get it to lift its blockade.

The mood was grim at the Manama Dialogue, an annual security summit in Bahrain organized by the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

United Arab Emirates presidential adviser Anwar Gargash told attendees the U.S. and Iranian stances are far apart, and if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst.

Gulf nations have spent billions of dollars to boost their defense capabilities since the war began. Egypts Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty told the gathering in Bahrain that the next escalation will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere.

China will send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters Monday.

title: FBI blames North Korea for stolen billions from Binance in biggest hack in history
content:
The theft of billions of dollars from Binance within a matter of minutes, the biggest crypto heist in history, was orchestrated by North Korean hackers, the FBI said Saturday.

The bureau said in a statement that this week's attack was tied to malicious cyber activity by an entity known as TraderTraitor, the same actors behind a $1.5 billion Bybit hack last year.

The FBI asked crypto exchanges, blockchain analytics companies and others to block transactions linked to various addresses to make sure the money is not laundered to cover up its origins.

It also said its probe found that TraderTraitor was converting stolen assets primarily into a cryptocurrency called ethereum. The FBI expects that TraderTraitor will now attempt to convert the assets using DeFi and instant swap services.

RELATED STORY | Oct. 7 hostage families sue crypto firm Binance, saying it helped fund Hamas and other terror groups

Asked by reporters as he appeared on Saturday night during a Halloween party at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida, however, President Donald Trump suggested investigators weren't yet certain that North Korea was involved.

Im not concerned. Were learning about it," Trump said of the case. We dont know if its North Korea. Though he added that, it could yet be determined that it was.

Crypto expert Ari Redbord said he expects the hackers will break the stolen assets into pieces and try to launder them through smaller exchanges to evade detection, a process that could unfold over months.

Its bank robbery, in this case, at the speed of the Internet, said Redbord, chief policy officer at blockchain intelligence firm TRM Labs. However, we can also track and trace those funds in real time in order to build investigations, to disrupt and to seize back funds.

He added: Its just this cat and mouse game.

On Thursday, $6.3 billion in bitcoin and other digital currency was stolen from Binance, the world's largest crypto exchange, in what several crypto experts said bore the hallmarks of a North Korean hack.

The company said Saturday that it had enough set aside in the same digital currency that was stolen to cover 90% of the missing assets and promised that customers would be fully reimbursed.

title: Could Trump interfere in the US midterms – and what checks and balances could stop him?
content:
On Tuesday, voters across the United States will cast their votes in the 2026 midterm elections. All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the Senate are on the ballot.

Forecast models give Democrats about a 95% chance of winning a majority in the House. The Senate is a closer race, but Democrats go into Election Day with the edge.

But the vote itself may not be the end of the story. Earlier this year, more than a dozen election officials from both parties said they feared President Donald Trump was laying the groundwork to undermine the midterm results.

And according to a recent survey, seven in ten Americans doubt Trump will accept the results if his party loses.

So, what tools might Trump use to contest or disrupt the results? And are US institutions equipped to withstand interference from the president?

A watershed moment

While Trump himself is not on the ballot, the stakes of these elections are high. The president faces mounting pressure at home, particularly on rising inflation and a deeply unpopular war with Iran.

With Election Day fast approaching, Americans have already headed to the polls in droves. According to the University of Florida’s Election Lab, more than 54 million votes have been cast in early voting.

A Democrat-controlled House could open investigations, issue subpoenas and stall the president’s agenda for the rest of his term.

Republicans want to keep control of both chambers to keep pushing through Trump’s agenda, including the president’s top legislative priority, the SAVE America Act. This would require voters nationwide to show photo identification and proof of citizenship to cast a ballot.

What powers does Trump have?

On paper, there is very little a president can do to interfere in elections. The US Constitution lets states set the “times, place and manner” of congressional elections, and only Congress can change those rules. The president’s only role is signing or vetoing election laws.

What the president does control is the federal government, which includes the Department of Justice (DOJ), Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), Department of Homeland Security and the Postal Service. He can direct these agencies through executive orders, but an executive order cannot override state election law.

Courts agree. In June, a federal judge permanently blocked most of Trump’s first election-related executive order, which would have forced people to show documents proving citizenship when registering to vote.

Also in June, the Supreme Court ruled states can keep counting mail ballots posted by Election Day that arrive later.

But the agencies he does control still give him ways to apply pressure at three critical points: voting, counting and certification.

Three pressure points

The first pressure point is voting itself. In March, Trump ordered the Postal Service to refuse to deliver mail ballots to voters missing from a list states would have to submit. But a federal judge blocked this move, and the Supreme Court subsequently upheld this decision, so mail voting will go ahead unimpeded.

The DOJ has announced it will be sending about 1,000 election monitors to all 50 states, its largest effort ever. However, these monitors can only enter polling places with local officials’ permission.

A second pressure point is the count. The DOJ has demanded full voter rolls from 49 states and the District of Columbia. It planned to check them against a Homeland Security database to find non-citizens. It has sued 30 states, and no court has ruled in the DOJ’s favour. Last month, a judge struck down the policy nationwide.

The third pressure point is certification, which is the formal sign-off on election results by state and local officials.

Trump says he will accept the outcome “if they’re honest elections”. If Trump disputes the results, the pressure will fall on these officials to certify them, as it did in 2020 when he pushed Georgia’s top election official to “find” him votes.

More drastic measures

Some options for disrupting the outcome of this election are more extreme.

The last step in this process will come on January 3 2027, when the new House is sworn in. The Constitution makes each chamber the judge of its own members’ elections. Some fear that Republicans could refuse to seat Democratic winners.

The House last refused to seat a certified winner in 1985. However, House Speaker Mike Johnson – the top Republican in the House – has called the idea of going down this road “absurd”.

The most extreme option would be for Trump to declare a national emergency. A leaked draft executive order proposed declaring one over alleged foreign interference, then banning most mail ballots and forcing voters to re-register in person. It relies on unfounded claims about foreign interference and voting machines similar to those Trump made in July.

Trump said he had never heard of the draft, and legal experts say the laws it cites give no such power to the president.

What checks and balances are in place?

Each pressure point meets a check. The first is that there is no national election system for a president to take over. Thousands of officials from both parties run the vote, and many have spent months planning for possible federal interference.

The courts are the second check. They have already struck down Trump’s attempts to prevent the delivery of mail ballots and blocked the DOJ from obtaining full voter rolls.

The third check is Congress itself. Two lawmakers, Democrat Josh Gottheimer and Republican Don Bacon, are asking House members to pledge to seat every certified winner. They hope their pledge will make it harder to justify blocking the swearing-in of any winners come January 3.

What to watch for

The first signs of potential interference will come on election night. Some states count mail ballots last, so early leads can shift in the days after polls close. Claims of fraud or victory before the count is finished would be a warning sign.

In the days that follow, observers will also watch whether the DOJ presses its cases against California, Washington and Alaska over alleged non-citizen voting, and whether federal agents will try to seize ballots or records.

Then comes certification. Most states sign off on results by late November or early December. Counties certifying on time, without court orders, would show the system is working. The last marker is January 3, when every certified winner should be sworn in.

So, the clearest test will come in the weeks after Tuesday’s election: will the president prove his critics right, or will he accept the verdict of voters?

title: Germany blames infiltrators as Gen Z protests turn violent
content:
Cost-of-living protests in Germany turned violent on Saturday evening with police using water cannons to disperse crowds and masked rioters smashed shop windows, as officials warn the day of rallies organized by a youth-led movement was infiltrated by extremist factions.

Saturdays action across Germany, organized by the Gen Z has got this! movement, railed against the high cost of living, underfunding in education, environmental concerns and a potential reintroduction of mandatory military service. It follows a wave of similar protests which have swept Europe, including significant unrest in France, which saw a third straight weekend of rallies.

Despite organizers calling for the protests to remain peaceful, violence broke out in some German cities, most notably in Frankfurt and Cologne. Police used water cannons while masked protesters smashed shop windows.

Speaking to German tabloid Bild, Germanys interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt said that violent left-wing groups and troublemakers from migrant communities hijacked the peaceful protests, without elaborating further.

RELATED STORY | French protesters defy heavy police presence in new demonstrations

The interior minister for the state of Hesse, which includes Frankfurt, warned that around 100 clearly identified left-wing extremists infiltrated the citys protest as the evening descended into violence and looting.

It is shameful how this event here in Frankfurt has ended, Roman Poseck said.

Poseck said he was determined the violence that has rocked France would not be replicated in Germany.

We all have those images from France in our minds looting, burning houses, burning police vehicles, and attacks on police officers, he said, according to Reuters. France must not be held up as a model in this regard.

In Frankfurt, police said Molotov cocktails were thrown at emergency personnel and shop windows were smashed. Officers arrested a suspect and seized two weapons after windows were broken at a gun shop. According to German news magazine Der Spiegel, several people broke into shops in downtown Frankfurt and over 30 people had been temporarily detained in city by the late evening.

Police in Cologne said water cannons were used after some protesters set off fireworks during a march in the city center. Our measures are directed against troublemakers and violent individuals not against peaceful participants, the police said in a statement.

In Hamburg, riot police responded after barriers were set on fire and emergency service workers were attacked. There has been an increase in incidents of emergency personnel being pelted with pyrotechnics and construction (materials) our riot police are taking immediate action against this, the police said.

Berlin police wrote on X that 27 officers in the German capital had sustained minor injuries and just under 60 people had been detained for offenses including property damage, assault, and resistance against emergency forces.

The movements organizers have sought to distance themselves from the ensuing violence. We had no influence on what happened after the demonstrations ended, a spokesperson from their press team was quoted by Der Spiegel as saying.

Organizers of Gen Z has got this! planned the day of action to coincide with Halloween, to maximize turnout and visibility. According to the organization, 120,000 people attended the protests across Germany on Saturday.

We are young people who no longer want to watch decisions being made about our future without us, the movement states on its website.

Speaking for his reasons for joining the movement, an 18-year-old student protester in Munich told Reuters, The government has offered no response to our concerns other than to continue making cuts and piling further burdens upon us. In the eastern city of Dresden, demonstrators held placards reading, The rich want war, the youth want a future! and Youve screwed up Gen Z will sort it out.

Europe-wide protests

More nationwide protests from the Yellow Vests movement took place in France on Saturday, in what was billed as thethird act of demonstrations, following earlier protests on October 17 and 24.

This time, however, they were more scaled down than before. The French Interior Ministry said 320,000 people protested across the country on Saturday, with 70,000 turning up in Paris; a significantly smaller number than the 550,000 who demonstrated on October 17 and the 410,000 who showed up last week.

The French protests were mostly peaceful, except for a few incidents. The Interior Ministry said in a statement that radical elements at the tail end of the processions in several cities. including Bordeaux, Toulouse, Rennes, Lille, Nantes, Marseille, and Lyon, attempted to enter city centers with the intent to cause damage and engage in looting.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Curfews imposed as France confronts widespread violence and looting

Protests over soaring housing costs also swept Portugal and Italy on Saturday. In the Portuguese capital, Lisbon, thousands marched to demand Portugals center-right government withdraw a rental bill they say will worsen the countrys housing crisis.

In Italy, protests largely led by student groups and workers rallied against inflation, stagnant wages and unaffordable housing in cities including Turin, Bologna and Milan.

title: French protesters defy heavy police presence in new demonstrations
content:
Hundreds of thousands of mostly young protesters took to the streets across France on Saturday in a third consecutive weekend of demonstrations over living costs and education.

About 70,000 police and gendarmes were deployed across the country, and Paris marches were rerouted to the capitals edge. Youth-led demonstrations were also reported in Germany and Italy.

France's government estimated that 320,000 people protested nationwide Saturday, fewer than in previous protests but still a significant turnout. Mass protests on Oct. 17 that deteriorated into some of France's worst rioting in years drew more than 500,000 people around France, and demonstrations on Oct. 24 drew 410,000, according to government estimates. Organizers turnout estimates are much higher.

French Interior Minister Laurent Nuez warned of a very high risk of disorder, especially after dark on Halloween. Police had arrested thousands of people following riots and looting that marred the largely peaceful protest marches the previous two Saturdays.

At Porte de Bagnolet, on the eastern edge of Paris, thousands gathered behind a line of students who led the march hand in hand. Security agents from the CGT, one of Frances largest labor unions, were keeping watch at the front of the gathering, while police were massed on side streets.

The Interior Ministry told reporters that of the 320,000 protesting Saturday, 70,000 people are estimated to have turned out for the main protest in Paris, which police moved outside the city center to reduce the risk of unrest around government buildings and tourist sites after a last-minute court battle.

The marchers grievances are diverse.

RELATED STORY | Curfews imposed as France confronts widespread violence and looting

Each group carried its own banner: high school students, climate activists and people angry about the cost of living.

A few Halloween costumes stood out in the crowd, including a zombie Michael Jackson from Thriller, a pirate and someone dressed as Spider-Man. Protesters waited calmly, chanting and singing through megaphones.

Corentin Cabreux, a 21-year-old student, said that he lives in a state-run student residence where there are damp stains all along the bottom of my walls, whole sections peeling off, cockroaches everywhere, rats.

The crowd streamed along the Boulevards des Marchaux, the ring of avenues that skirts the edge of Paris, in a march that was joyful for hours. Techno music blasted from speakers, a painter at work along the route drew cheers from the crowd, and some marchers went trick-or-treating. A police helicopter hovered overhead as the sun set slowly over the city.

Later, clashes broke out near Porte de Charenton, where the march ended. Protesters hurled glass bottles and fireworks at police. Officers responded with volleys of stun grenades and tear gas. The blasts echoed through the streets, and smoke filled the air as dusk fell.

Many peaceful marchers turned back, coughing, their eyes streaming with tears, and left the march, some scattering into the nearby Bois de Vincennes, one of the largest parks in Paris.

Police impose curfew and other measures

The rallies started last month as a movement of high school students protesting neglected buildings, teacher shortages and a university admissions system seen as unfair to disadvantaged students. Labor unions and others angry at President Emmanuel Macron joined in with a variety of demands.

RELATED STORY | France grapples with worst rioting in years after cost-of-living protests turn deadly and violent

While the vast majority of protesters have been peaceful, groups of troublemakers routinely target police with fireworks and projectiles. Some protests have degenerated into rioting and looting including unrest on Oct. 17 that appeared to take the government by surprise. Police have responded with tear gas, dispersion grenades, water cannons and other tactics that have resulted in severe injuries.

Macron said that Saturday's marches would stay out of city centers to protect shops. Police also barred people from entering Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. to 6 a.m. Saturday and Sunday.

Unaccompanied minors face a separate 9 p.m. curfew around the Champs-Elysees. A Paris court on Wednesday suspended an earlier curfew on minors as a serious and illegal infringement of freedom of movement.

title: Will Melania Trump save Ukraine?
content:
In the last month or so, President Donald Trump’s on-again-off-again relationship with Ukraine — which has ranged from kicking Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy out of the White House in early 2025 to promising new air defense missiles this summer — has once again run cold. Trump has excoriated Zelenskyy for successful Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil and gas infrastructure, called for Zelenskyy’s ouster, and gifted Russia a sanctions reprieve.

Trump also hasn’t had much success brokering a ceasefire, much less an end to the war (an announced “energy ceasefire” fell apart-near instantly earlier in October). First Lady Melania Trump, however, has.

She reportedly played a (limited) role in arranging a partial ceasefire for the frontline Ukrainian city of Oleshky, which has been hit especially hard by the war and is currently occupied by Russia. 

The pause, which is scheduled to run through the weekend, allows food and aid to get in and for a civilian evacuation. While limited, it also shows that both Ukraine and Russia are potentially willing to come to the negotiating table. 

After the Trump-Vladimir Putin rapprochement, though, some critics worry that the US is more likely to take Russia’s side — or at least step away from Ukraine’s — both in the war and in any possible peace talks. 

To break down what the Trumps are up to, how serious the concerns of Trump abandoning Ukraine for Putin actually are, and what could come next, Today, Explained co-host Sean Rameswaram spoke with Alex Ward, a national security reporter for the Wall Street Journal.

Below is an excerpt of Sean’s conversation with Ward, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full podcast, so listen to Today, Explained wherever you get podcasts, including Apple Podcasts, Pandora, and Spotify.

Let’s start with the most unexpected news out of this war in recent days: that Melania Trump brokered a ceasefire.

It’s possible she had a role. I’m going to personally, without too much reporting, say that it was probably more Pope Leo.

Melania stole Pope Leo’s ceasefire?

I think a little bit. Look, this ceasefire is not a small thing. It is a humanitarian ceasefire in the southern Ukrainian city of Oleshky. It allows humanitarian aid to get in. The critics would say this allows the Russians to re-arm and regroup, and I guess at the same time also the Ukrainians. 

The question is, does it actually have that much influence over the war? No, it’s a very, very small targeted ceasefire. But it is a potential signal that deals can be made. 

The Russians are very much saying, look at Melania Trump, look at how important she was to all this. And if I’m the Russians, I would love to be saying things like that because then President Trump feels like the Russians are being very generous towards my wife and to my family, and therefore I side with them. 

It feels very convenient that the Russians are pumping that up and that even the White House is pumping up Melania Trump’s influence. I don’t want to discredit her. I’m sure she did work on this.

When did she become a negotiator in this war?

From the beginning, she has been trying to get children kidnapped by Russia back to Ukraine.  That has been a major focus of hers in this war. 

Is she the driving force behind this ceasefire? Is she the number one reason it happened? It’s totally possible. There’s just a lot of skepticism out there about whether Kyiv and Moscow were brought to the table and browbeaten by the First Lady. Again, very possible, but both sides, being Ukraine and Russia, have an incentive to play up her role.

The ceasefire is just relegated to one city. How come?

That’s all they could agree to. If we’re looking at this war at a bigger scale, there’s been a massive discussion about how to get an end to the Ukraine-Russia war. 

The US last week was able to broker a commitment to have trilateral talks between the Ukrainians, Russians, and the Americans with the goal toward ending the war. And you’ve heard President Zelenskyy of Ukraine say, “We can call it ceasefire. We can call stop the killings. We can call freeze the conflict.” 

Putin goes, ‘No, thank you. I would like basically a handover of the territory that I want, even though I’ve been unable to conquer it after nearly five years.’ It’s unclear if they’re even going to get into the room for those trilateral negotiations. Even if they do, it’ll probably be at a lower technical level. 

So are we ever going to get to the point that Putin and Zelenskyy and Trump get in a room, all hold hands and say ‘war over’? I highly doubt it, but that is the goal they’re after. You see the Trump administration, the Kremlin, and Kyiv all point to this Oleshky ceasefire as, like, ‘Hey, this could be a model for the much bigger deal.’

I want to be clear that this Oleshky thing is important. It really is aimed at a humanitarian ceasefire since there’s a lot of food that isn’t getting in, a lot of people are suffering and this potentially leads to some relief. But there are a lot of people around Ukraine and many bombed-out cities that are going, “Hey, what about us? We are hungry too. We don’t have certain services.” 

Winter is coming, and the Russians have bombed out a lot of Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, which is going to make this winter potentially very brutal, as a lot of folks will not have heating or the necessities they need to survive really cold temperatures.

Steve Witkoff called Vladimir Putin a humanitarian, which had a lot of people shook because, famously, Vladimir Putin also started this war.

Yeah, it’s like calling Freddy Krueger a nails enthusiast. It doesn’t make a lot of sense. 

Has Vladimir Putin released Americans that he took hostage? Yes. Has he returned some children that his government, his forces have taken? Yes. I don’t know if that makes a humanitarian. That’s kind of like praising the arsonist for throwing a bucket of water on the house fire.

It’s not just calling him a humanitarian; it’s getting rid of the Lindsey Graham sanctions on Russia, which is essentially like handing Russia billions of dollars, right?

There’s a lot of weirdness here. First of all, on the Graham bill, it’s a weird bill, and frankly it’s a pretty bad bill despite the fact that Democrats and Republicans love it. 

What it basically calls for is tariffs on countries that purchase Russian energy. The way that Trump explains it is he waived the economic punishments, because otherwise the Russians would not have returned Stephen Hubbard and there might not have been this Oleshky ceasefire and there might not have been a bunch of other benefits.

Another argument President Trump was making for removing these tariff sanctions on Russia was that it would lower diesel costs here in the United States. Has that actually happened?

The Russians agreed to a diesel deal where they would basically export diesel to the United States. And in President Trump’s mind, that will lower costs because President Trump and political allies of his like Elon Musk of SpaceX say that is the reason diesel prices have skyrocketed across the US. 

However, when you talk to analysts and look at the data, it is the Iran war that has had a greater effect on diesel prices. Not to say that the Russia-Ukraine war hasn’t had any, but it’s much less because there is just very little Russian diesel in the American market, but also in the global market. 

What the US is receiving from Russia is not nothing, but effectively nothing because it’s just not enough to alleviate the diesel concerns across the country and to lower prices to a meaningful amount. And we can see President Trump is effectively scrambling to make good on his promises of lowering prices as the midterms approach, to the point that he’s willing to make a deal with the invading country in the war he’s trying to end in order to lower gas prices at home.

A lot of people see these developments and think that the United States’ allegiances have shifted, that we’ve maybe abandoned Ukraine at the moment. Is that fair?

I don’t think we can say that with any sense of certainty. President Trump has actually been on Ukraine’s side in certain cases, even rhetorically during a UN meeting, I believe it was last year. President Trump was presented with intelligence about how the Russians have been struggling to invade Ukraine. And then he released a statement saying basically, ‘Go Ukraine, go. Russia, you’re kind of losing here.’ And that made people go, ‘Oh, he’s on Ukraine’s side.’ 

And of course, after that whole Oval Office blowup with Zelenskyy, that relationship improved. But everyone’s always been kind of like, ‘Well, we know where Trump’s feelings are here. He wants a big deal with Russia. He wants an economic deal with Russia. He wants to improve relations with Vladimir Putin, and so he always returns to the mean, even if he flirts with Ukraine.’ 

But below President Trump’s unique style of dealmaking, the US intelligence community is helping Ukraine to defend against Russia. The US is selling weapons to Europeans for the Europeans to deliver to Ukraine. It is nowhere near the level of weapons support during the Biden administration, but that intelligence support seems to be at a higher level than during the Biden years. 

And it’s not like President Trump has purposefully hampered Ukraine’s defenses a lot. There are some questions about sudden intelligence shutoffs and delays of important weapons. I am not saying President Trump has been a staunch defender and a staunch supporter of Ukraine here. But if you look at the grand totality, Ukraine is still being defended by the United States. 

It almost seems like President Trump has an inability to pick a side. He’s playing both. In his mind, he thinks that’s the best way to get them both to the table and get a deal. But this is also the man that said he could do it in 24 hours and we’re nearly two years into his presidency. And right now the best we can get is, ‘Hey, maybe we can get the Russians, Ukrainians, and Americans to meet in a room for technical talks.’ 

It’s not nothing. And also, hey, we got a ceasefire in a town in Ukraine. It’s not nothing, but it’s nowhere near the big, potentially Nobel Peace Prize-winning deal that he’s searching for.

title: Pope Leo XIV casts mail-in ballot, becoming first pope to vote in US election
content:
Pope Leo XIV has become the first pope to vote in a U.S. general election, casting a mail-in ballot in a contest that will decide America's future as the Trump era slowly comes to an end.

The Vatican confirmed Friday that the Chicago-born pontiff had submitted a mail-in ballot in Chicago ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, citing his long-standing belief in civic participation.

Leo, formerly Robert Prevost, "has exercised his right to vote as a United States citizen" and has done so "whenever he was eligible to do so," the Holy See press office said.

Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in effect after Melania Trump, Pope Leo appeal to Putin

The statement said he had also voted while living in Peru whenever he was eligible. Leo lived in Peru as a missionary priest and bishop for over 20 years.

"The Holy Father expresses his belief in the right and the duty of citizens to participate in democratic processes," it added.

Leo holds U.S. and Peruvian citizenship, and is also the head of state of a foreign country, the Holy See. The city state is an absolute monarchy with no political elections.

This election, Illinois voters are deciding whether to elect Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker to his third term, and they're also filling an open U.S. Senate seat after longtime Catholic Democrat Dick Durbin's retirement. President Donald Trump is not on the ballot but he has campaigned hard to try to preserve Republican control of the U.S. House and Senate for the final two years of his second term.

Leo's vote was first reported by the Chicago Sun-Times, which quoted the chief of staff at the Will County clerk's office as saying the pope, registered at a New Lenox address, requested a mail-in ballot on Oct. 3.

The request was made just 10 days before Leo underwent surgery to remove a cancerous tumor from his right lung. Leo has been slowly resuming his activities at the Vatican after being released from the hospital Oct. 17.

It is unclear how Leo returned the ballot. The pope's older brother, John Prevost, was in Rome this week accompanying parishioners from St. Jude's, an Augustinian-run parish in New Lenox, Illinois. The elder Prevost attends Mass there, and Leo gave a talk at the parish in 2024 while still a cardinal.

Pope Leo needs no further cancer treatment after lung surgery, his doctors say

Prevost's past votes have gone Democratic and Republican

Since 2000, Robert Prevost has voted in five primary elections, requesting Democratic ballots twice and Republican ballots three times, according to records held by the Illinois State Board of Elections.

The records do not show which candidates he supported. Illinois voters must declare a party preference to receive a primary ballot. No such declaration is required in general elections.

While registered in heavily Democratic Cook County, Prevost requested Democratic primary ballots in 2008 and 2010. After moving to the more conservative suburban Will County, he requested Republican primary ballots in 2012, 2014 and 2016.

The records also show that he submitted ballots in every general election since 2000 except those in 2020 and 2022.

Clashes with Trump

Since becoming pope, Leo has drawn criticism from President Donald Trump for repeatedly condemning the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran and calling for dignified treatment of immigrants.

Earlier this year, Trump called Leo "weak" and captive to the "radical left."

Responding to Trump's public rebuke, Leo told reporters en route to Algeria in April: "I'm not afraid of the Trump administration or of speaking out loudly about the message of the Gospel, which is what the church works for."

"I will continue to speak out strongly against war, seeking to promote peace, promoting dialogue and multilateralism among states to find solutions to problems," he said.

The public dispute has subsided in recent months.

RELATED STORY | Pope Leo XIV: Not in my interest to engage Trump over Iran war

A pope who follows U.S. politics closely

Leo has made clear on several occasions that he follows local and national U.S. politics closely, and is not afraid to intervene.

He has repeatedly called for reflection and humane treatment for immigrants in his native U.S. amid the Trump administration crackdown and mass deportation program.

Recently, Leo reiterated official church teaching declaring the death penalty "inadmissible." He made the pronouncement in a social media post on the World Day Against the Death Penalty, which came as the U.S. announced plans to livestream an execution by firing squad. The plans were later scrapped.

In 2025, Leo intervened in a debate over abortion, after Chicago Cardinal Blase Cupich announced plans to give a lifetime achievement award to Sen. Durbin. The plans drew objection from some conservative U.S. bishops given the powerful Democratic senator's support for abortion rights. Leo called for respect for both sides, but he also pointed out the contradiction between people who call themselves "pro-life" but also support the death penalty.

Also in 2025, Leo said he was "very disappointed" that his home state of Illinois approved a law allowing medically assisted dying, which is condemned by the Catholic Church.

title: Netanyahu bloc falls short of majority as Israel enters coalition talks
content:
Israel's final election results confirmed Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahus bloc lost its parliamentary majority and that weeks of difficult negotiations among very different parties, from ultra-Orthodox Jewish to secular to Arab-led, lie ahead.

The results released early Friday showed Netanyahus bloc won 53 seats in Tuesday's election. The main opposition bloc won 48. Arab-led parties secured the other 19, a historic showing. Now parties must meet, bargain and seek a way to team up for at least 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.

Netanyahu, Israels longest-serving prime minister, remains in charge.

Now comes the truly hard part, centrist politician Yair Lapid said on X, urging patience and adding: If you want to know if somethings happening behind the silence youre hearing now, the answer is yes.

RELATED STORY | Arab-led parties gain leverage as Netanyahu falls short of clear victory

The president will task someone with forming a government

Difficult decisions lie ahead. Will the main opposition parties that campaigned hard to unseat the divisive Netanyahu make the politically sensitive choice to partner with Arab-led ones? Or will they toss their vows aside to team up with Netanyahu in a potentially fractious unity government?

Friday is when much of Israel starts winding down for Shabbat, and it was not clear who might be meeting with whom. Israelis debated possible coalitions and challenges, as some expressed traditional wariness around Arab parties and others insisted it was time for Israel to take a deep breath and embrace them.

There are options for all of this, not like in the United States, where there are only two parties, said Beny Engalrd, a resident of Tel Aviv.

The election results still need to be certified and submitted to the president next Wednesday. Then President Isaac Herzog will task someone with forming the new government. That could be the leader of the party that received the most votes Netanyahu or whoever leaders of the various parties believe is best suited.

If multiple attempts to form a government fail, Israel faces a new election early next year. Herzog this week said he will do everything in his power to avoid that scenario.

Netanyahu and Likud target Arab parties without evidence

In the hours before final results were announced, Netanyahu and his Likud party amplified unsubstantiated allegations that Arab-led parties had stolen the election, potentially with foreign assistance.

The opposition quickly accused Netanyahu of demonizing the Arab population, which makes up 20% of the population and showed up at the polls like never before in outrage over Netanyahus far-right allies like National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. His party lost seats.

In Netanyahu's first public comment Friday, he posted on X asserting it is forbidden to form a coalition with Arab parties.

The head of Israels election committee, Supreme Court Justice Noam Sohlberg, had said serious suspicions of foreign interference had been brought before him. In a letter to the Shin Bet security agency, Sohlberg said he could not verify the claims but asked the agency to investigate.

Israeli media reported that members of Netanyahus party were accusing Qatar of involvement a country that many Israelis view as a patron of Hamas, the Gaza-based militant group. Qatar issued a denial, calling the allegations ridiculous and dangerous.

As it announced results, the election commission said the investigation was based on classified intelligence. Acting Director General Dean Livne did not elaborate but warned that reports about the investigation had been entirely unfounded.

It does not affect the final results that will be submitted to the president, nor does it concern any particular sector of the population, he said.

By casting doubt on the vote, Netanyahu appeared to be trying to block any potential alliance between his opponents and the Arab-led parties. Netanyahu has suggested that it would be treasonous for chief rival Gadi Eisenkot or others to join with them.

The Shin Bet, seeking to calm tensions, said its investigation was not meant to cast aspersions on an entire section of the population that exercised its right to vote in a democratic and lawful manner.

The elections committee also sounded a note of caution in a letter written to a concerned member of parliament, saying that allegations of systematic violations of electoral integrity are baseless.

The committee wants findings from the Shin Bet within a week.

Opposition could assert control in the upcoming Knesset

Even as coalition negotiations begin, the new Knesset is expected to be sworn in Nov. 10. Once it convenes, Eisenkots bloc could join forces with the Arab parties to elect a new Knesset speaker, giving them control over the parliamentary agenda and potentially allowing them to advance and pass legislation before a new government is formed.

RELATED STORY | Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection

Already, hundreds of Israelis have been holding rallies urging Eisenkot and others to join forces with the Arab-led parties, a step that has happened only once before, briefly, in 2021.

I believe we should join forces and cooperate with the Arab parties, a legitimate population in the state of Israel, said Miri Sklair, a resident of Jaffa.

If Netanyahu loses office, that would set off a cascade of events that critics say he has desperately sought to avoid. He would be taken to account over yearslong corruption allegations, and an inquiry almost certainly would begin into security failures before the devastating Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack.

title: Russian drone strikes crowded Ukraine train platform, killing at least 13
content:
It is the scenario Ukraines railway system has spent months trying to prevent.

A high-speed Russian jet-powered drone struck a crowded train platform in Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 13 people, according to President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who called the attack horrific in a post on X.

Train No. 866, bound for Zaporizhzhia about 40 miles to the south, was at the platform when the drone hit. Passengers were still boarding.

Ukraines state rail operator said air raid sirens warning of a heightened threat had sounded before the strike. The drone arrived so quickly that station officials could not act in time to clear the open platform.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Russia-Ukraine ceasefire in one city in effect after Melania Trump, Pope Leo appeal to Putin

Dnipro is a city of roughly a million people and the main rail hub for Ukraines southeast, a gateway for civilians, soldiers and aid moving toward the front. Trains have become one of the few lifelines Ukrainians trust, which makes them a target.

In his post, Zelenskyy also asked how many strikes Russia has carried out since sanctions were lifted on certain Russian oligarchs and on Russias energy sector.

A few months ago, a Scripps News crew traveled from Kyiv to the same Dnipro station. On the return trip, just outside the city, the train stopped and passengers were evacuated to a nearby shelter.

That now happens daily on Ukraines railways. On Thursday, the warning came, and there was no time to heed it.

title: Trump risks US-Canadian defense operation by 'playing footsie with Putin'
content:
President Donald Trump’s growing alignment with Russia is now raising serious concerns among Canadian security experts. They warn that even if Canada builds closer ties to Europe, it may still not fully protect Canada from an increasingly erratic United States.

According to CBC News from the neighbors to the north, Trump has made several recent moves in support of Moscow: Secretary of State Marco Rubio invited Vladimir Putin to December’s G20 summit at Trump's resort in Miami. Trump then decided to abandon sanctions against Russia to send it $4 billion for diesel fuel.

Meanwhile, restrictions on aid are popping up in Ukraine. Trump pal Elon Musk has recently become a close friend of Putin and has put his thumb on the scale, slowing down Starlink for Ukraine. The Pentagon's watchdog announced it won't investigate Musk. A new Congress, however, is expected to. It has also been difficult for Ukraine to get more Patriot missiles.

"This is not Trump playing footsie with Putin," said national security and intelligence adviser Vincent Rigby, former adviser to the prime minister until 2021. "This is something far, far more serious, and strategically, this can't help but be a concern."

McGill University Russia expert Maria Popova similarly said Trump’s approach appears to be shifting from neutrality toward an open alliance with Putin again.

"We have to start thinking about where this trajectory ends up eventually," she said. "And it ends in the U.S. directly helping Russia's war effort."

Rigby agreed, saying that Trump and Putin's restored relationship raises new fears about Arctic sovereignty. In fact, he cautioned that it "could be the end of NORAD in a worst-case scenario." NORAD is the joint U.S. and Canada partnership that surveils the airspace of both countries and helps protect referring to the joint Canada-U.S. partnership to protect sovereign airspace.

Now there's the additional concern about Putin and Trump meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November APEC summit.

Experts have cautioned against normalizing a world divided by three men; such discussions could normalize a world split into American, Russian and Chinese spheres of influence, leaving smaller countries vulnerable to decisions made without their participation.

Canada is responding by strengthening its international partnerships, increasing defense capabilities and trying to preserve functioning institutions with Washington, the report described. Experts are seeing the value in building closer European cooperation when it comes to things like defense manufacturing, technology, financial infrastructure and satellite systems. It would help Canada be less dependent on the U.S. for networks and communications systems, given Elon Musk is so closely aligned with Musk and Trump.

Trump's pro-Russia push may not last much longer, with a Democratic House expected. Trump also has only 26 months left.

However, Rigby told CBC that he expects those next 26 months to be tumultuous ones.

"You are potentially going to see a president after next week being even more reckless, less restrained and more aggressive," he said.

title: 'How did we get to that place?' Father of deceased hostage speaks out after Israel's elections
content:
Israel's election results are coming into focus, but the question of who will lead the country may be far from settled.

And one of the biggest remaining issues for families of those killed and taken hostage on October 7th is accountability. Many want to see an inquiry into internal security failures.

That advocacy led to some tense moments outside of a polling place this week for the late Itay Chens father, Ruby.

"While standing there outside, speaking about investigation committee, a citizen started calling me names, Specifically, calling me a traitor and my son," Ruby Chen said. "And you ask yourself, how did we get to that place that my son, that was protecting the border of Gaza on October 7, was taken, kidnapped, fell while protecting Jewish people, someone would say something like that?"

Chen is also advocating for the U.S. Congress to launch its own inquiry into October 7th failures. Nearly 50 Americans were killed that day alone, and a dozen were taken hostage.
