title: Iran war's cost to American taxpayers grows to an estimated $47.1 billion
content:
The cost of the Iran war to American taxpayers has grown to $47.1 billion, according to a new estimate the Pentagon has provided to Congress. The fallout from the conflict has become a key issue in the midterm elections and could increase as President Donald Trump leaves open the possibility of renewed hostilities.

The figure from U.S. Central Command, which oversees operations in the Middle East, is as of Oct. 16 and offers the most up-to-date cost for the conflict since it was launched in late February by the United States and Israel. The latest price tag, obtained by The Associated Press this week, shows a $3.5 billion bump in U.S. spending since early September, when that figure stood at about $43.6 billion.

The growing cost of the unpopular war and its economic ripple effects on energy prices could hurt Republicans in next week's midterm elections. Voters on Tuesday will decide which political party controls Congress during Trump's last two years in office.

Gas under Trump 2.0 is now more expensive than it was under Biden

The Republican president has said new strikes on Iran are an option after the midterms and is sending more military resources to the Middle East, despite initially promising Americans a military campaign that would last only a matter of weeks. As the war's costs in lives, tax dollars and economic impact grow, most voters say they want Congress to prioritize ending the conflict, according to a recent AP-NORC poll.

The expense of the conflict and military spending in general are already a contentious issue on Capitol Hill, where the Trump administration is pushing for the passage of a historic $1.5 trillion military budget proposal. The White House also is asking lawmakers to approve a $95 billion package that would help fund the Iran war and other priorities.

Wednesday marks eight months of the war, which Democrats have been trying to end through legislation that has failed to pass the Republican-controlled Congress.

"Trump and his ego led us into this war with no plan, no authority, and no exit strategy," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York said in a news release. "Senate Democrats will continue to do everything in our power to end this disaster of a war and stop the costs, chaos, and corruption seeping from the White House."

In the latest estimate, the bulk of the war's costs are for replacing munitions, at about $29 billion. The advanced weapons most in demand and whose stockpiles have been drawn down are defensive missile interceptors, such as those launched by the Army's Patriot and THAAD systems, with a single Patriot interceptor costing millions of dollars.

High inflation and the Iran war put pressure on Republicans ahead of midterms

The Pentagon says about $11.9 billion is related to costs of operations, while an additional $6 billion is tied to equipment losses. The Air Force's costs are now $7.6 billion, and the Army's are more than $2 billion. The Navy's costs were listed at $1.45 billion, which is a significant drop from the $2.2 billion listed in early September.

When asked why the Navy's cost estimates decreased over the roughly six-week period, both the Navy and U.S. Central Command referred the questions to the Pentagon, which did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment on the new cost estimates.

The latest estimate does not include damage to U.S. bases in the Middle East, which the Islamic Republic has attacked with ballistic missiles and drones. A report from the Pentagon inspector general released last month said Iranian strikes have damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and other structures at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

The Pentagon's official tally lists 21 service members killed and 865 wounded in the conflict. That count includes troops who died in medical events and other situations that do not have a direct connection to the conflict, with 18 service members having been killed from Iranian strikes, combat aircraft crashes or disposal of Iranian drones.

While Trump has mused repeatedly about whether to make a deal with Iran or "finish them off," a third aircraft carrier and thousands of additional troops are making their way to the region. The Trump administration also has reduced staffing at some U.S. Embassies after receiving intelligence that Iran has stepped up efforts to target American personnel.

title: US cruise ship suspends three-year world voyage over fuel costs, leaving passengers in Cambodia
content:
A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.

The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000.

For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.

Navigating Europe's low river levels: What river cruise travelers need to know

The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.

Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $1,800 have reached an estimated $6,000 to $8,000 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran. The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.

Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the war in Iran began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.

"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday. "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees" while it tries to restructure.

"The company is working with residents to coordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.

Those on the ship had hoped to sail for years to come

Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.

Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.

Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.

Trump plans to loosen restrictions on methane emissions from oil drilling

Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.

"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."

The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.

For some, the venture was a risk worth taking

Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of traveling the world and living at sea.

Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.

"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don't want it to end," Larson said.

Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn't need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live it's just sad that it's all over."

Larson bought her cabin for $120,000, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.

"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising," she said.

The cruise began in Northern Ireland in 2024

The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.

Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.

Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3 1/2 years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, Northern Ireland, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.

The Odyssey is not the first cruise ship Sihanoukville has hosted in crisis.

In February 2020, the MS Westerdam was allowed to dock in Cambodia after being turned away at five ports in other nations because of fears of COVID-19, which just a month earlier had started to spread from China. It carried 1,455 passengers, more than 600 of them American citizens.

After being stranded at sea for two weeks, Cambodia's then-Prime Minister Hun Sen allowed it to dock for what he said were humanitarian reasons. Cambodia won plaudits as passengers were welcomed ashore and arrangements were made for them to fly home.

title: King Charles acknowledges ‘injustices of the past’ as Caribbean tour gets underway
content:
Britains King Charles III began his nine-day tour of the Caribbean region Tuesday, arriving in the Bahamas where he acknowledged the great suffering and injustices of the past as pressure mounts on Britain to apologize and pay reparations for its role in the slave trade.

Charles visit to the region will also take in Guyana and Antigua and Barbuda, where he and Queen Camilla will attend the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM).

Speaking at a youth rally in Nassau, Bahamas, the 77-year-old monarch acknowledged the countrys painful history and confirmed the legacy of slavery will be discussed by Commonwealth leaders at the biennial summit of 56 nations next week.

Charless first visit to the Caribbean as monarch comes amid renewed calls for Britain to make reparations for its role in forcibly transporting an estimated three million people across the Atlantic and into servitude in the New World.

FROM THE ARCHIVES | U.K. Protesters Topple Slave Trader Statue, Throw It In Harbor

Commonwealth Secretary-General Shirley Botchwey said last week the time had come to discuss reparations. Asked by Sky News whether the King should apologize for Britains historic role in the slave trade, Botchwey said: It wouldnt hurt to have that.

Thats what the countries have asked for, Botchwey added. I dont believe we can run away from it. But it is important to determine the form that reparations should take, and that is something that will emerge eventually.

Meanwhile, the Caribbean Community, or Caricom, a group of 23 member and associate member states, said last month it would push for reparations to be on the agenda at CHOGM.

The Caribbean has consistently asserted that reparations is fundamentally about justice, Caricom Secretary-General Carla Barnett said in a speech. It is about recognition, accountability and transformation, and about building a just and equitable future for the descendants of those who, as the chattel of colonial owners, endured untold suffering, loss of life and freedom.

The King can only act on the advice of his ministers when he represents the country abroad, and despite the renewed calls, he has continued to follow the British government advice against issuing a formal apology for Britains role in the slave trade. UK Foreign Office sources have told CNN that there is no legal case for reparations because slavery was not illegal at the time it was active.

Buckingham Palace has said he will not apologize during the Caribbean tour as such questions were matters for governments to address, but that he will not shy away from the darkest days of our past.

At the last CHOGM, in 2024, Charles acknowledged that the most painful aspects of our past continue to resonate. However, he stopped short of an official apology and did not directly engage on the subject.

Jonathan Reynolds, the United Kingdoms business secretary, said Tuesday that reparations are not a reasonable request. Reynolds told Sky News that he was sensitive to British history and that we should be able to talk about it but that past events should not be attributed to current generations.

In recent years, the British monarchy has adopted a more conciliatory tone when addressing the horrors of slavery. During a visit to Kenya in 2023, his first trip to a Commonwealth nation as head of the body, Charles said the wrongdoings of the past are a cause of the greatest sorrow and the deepest regret.

At least 12.5 million Africans were abducted and sold into slavery by European merchants between the 15th and 19th centuries, and Britain is estimated to have had a role in transporting about 3.2 million people.

When slavery was abolished in Britain in 1834, the government compensated slave owners the equivalent of 17 billion ($22.5 billion), but slaves received nothing, according to research by University College London.

King Charles has a busy schedule on Wednesday when he will hold an audience with the Bahamas prime minister and governor general. He will also meet the families of four Royal Bahamas Defence Force (RBDF) Marines killed when Cuban MiG fighter aircraft sunk HMBS Flamingo in May 1980, after a dispute over illegal fishing. He will also have an environmental engagement and finish his day at a garden reception.

title: Arab-led parties gain leverage as Netanyahu falls short of clear victory
content:
Anxious Israelis watched election results near completion Wednesday after the highest voter turnout in over a quarter-century, as no clear winner emerged and weeks of negotiating could lie ahead for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and an array of opposition parties trying to unseat him.

Arab-led parties made a historic showing, but its not clear if other opponents of Netanyahu's far-right government would form a coalition with them for a majority of seats in parliament. Issues around the Palestinians and their descendants remain incredibly sensitive in Israel.

Netanyahu seeks to remain the country's longest-serving prime minister. In defiant comments after the vote which showed his Likud party losing ground since the 2022 election he dismissed as treasonous the idea of partnering with Arab parties.

RELATED STORY | No clear winner in Israeli election, exit polls suggest, with Netanyahus fate uncertain

On Wednesday, Netanyahu warned against a dangerous government that might include them. He wont work with the Arab-led parties, whose constituents make up 20% of Israel's population, and they have also ruled out any partnership with him.

His top challenger, centrist former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has left the door open to partnering with Arab parties under certain conditions, including their recognition of Israel as a Jewish state and of Hamas as an extremist group.

But it's not clear whether some of Eisenkot's likely partners who have ruled out such an alliance will change their minds to force Netanyahu from office.

Israeli voters choose parties, not individuals. With 85% of votes counted, Netanyahus Likud party has 20.8% and Eisenkot's Yashar party has 16.1%. The official count does not indicate how many seats each will have in parliament, the 120-seat Knesset.

Emerging results indicated that neither Netanyahu's nor Eisenkot's coalition blocs would reach the 61 seats needed for a majority; local media projected 53 seats for Likud and allied parties, 48 for Yashar and allied parties and 19 for Arab-led parties.

Netanyahu faces a setback but not outright defeat

Nearly 78% of eligible voters turned out, the highest since 1999. Final results are expected by the end of the week, and will capture about a half-million absentee ballots yet to be counted from military personnel and diplomats.

Voting reflected unease over Netanyahu's alliance with the far-right and anger in a war-weary nation over military draft exemptions for the significant ultra-Orthodox Jewish population; the Likud party's share of the vote declined from 23.4% in 2022. But results suggest opponents were unable to capitalize on the grief caused by the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack to decisively push him from office.

One far-right partner losing support was national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir. For many Israelis, he represented the worst strain of Netanyahus government, openly taunting Palestinian detainees and asserting that many in Gaza are not even people.

Vote-counting suggested Likud would remain the largest party and best placed to be tapped to form a government by Israels president, Isaac Herzog. The president, however, isn't required to task the leader of the party holding the most seats.

We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections, Herzog said Wednesday.

The most obvious path to a parliamentary majority could involve Eisenkot partnering with Arab-led parties which have 14.9% of the votes counted but that's politically challenging. In a speech early Wednesday that focused on national unity, Eisenkot pledged to form a government and promised a new era an era of hope."

RELATED STORY | 2 Israeli soldiers, 2 Palestinian gunmen killed in West Bank attack

If no one can put together a majority coalition, new elections could be held early next year. Israel held five elections between April 2019 and November 2022 because of a similar stalemate. It is unclear whether thousands of Israelis living abroad would again fly back home to vote, and whether Arab voters would again surge to the polls.

Minority governments also are possible, but they must rely on cooperation from parties outside the government to pass legislation.

Arab-led parties could hold the key

Confronted with Arab parties strong election showing, Israelis have renewed a debate about identity.

We have no future here if we do not stop being afraid," said Yair Golan, whose Democrats party supports bringing Arab-led parties into a coalition. "We must no longer accept Netanyahus racist division between Jewish votes and Arab votes.

Israels Arab citizens are descendants of Palestinians who remained in the state after its creation in 1948. They often face discrimination and are viewed with wariness because of their solidarity with the Palestinian cause. That suspicion intensified after Oct. 7, even though Arab citizens were also among those killed and abducted.

The mood was joyful overnight at the headquarters of the United Arab List, the lone Arab party to ever join a governing coalition, briefly, in 2021.

We are here, we are not on the sidelines, party leader Mansour Abbas declared.

RELATED STORY | Trump endorses embattled Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for reelection

Some Israelis found that an unusual, if not uncomfortable, prospect.

We are little by little coming to a situation where we have to face reality," said Hanna Doukhan, a voter in Tel Aviv. "I dont see a possibility to form a government without the Arabs.

Others were hopeful. This would open the door to repairing our society" while preserving Israel as the national home of the Jewish people, said Eti Wissotzky-Cohen in Tel Aviv.

And in Nazareth, one of Israels largest Arab cities, Awni Zoabi thanked God for a possible return to rationality in a country where extreme rhetoric has increased. The Arabic language has become as if it were a crime," Zoabi said.

Attitudes over Netanyahu will shape the days ahead

Netanyahu has had a nearly unbroken 17-year rule. Israelis were divided over him even before the deadliest attack in the countrys history. The resulting wars, along with settler violence in the occupied West Bank, have stoked worldwide outrage, straining ties with Israels closest allies and fueling a rise in antisemitism.

Netanyahus supporters believe he is protecting Israels security and Jewish identity in the face of international pressure and liberal elites at home.

I prefer that (Netanyahu) assembles the coalition, said Ran Cohen, a Jerusalem resident. Hes the only one who knows how to do the job properly, knows how to speak to the world.

Detractors say Netanyahu, facing an ongoing corruption trial, dragged out the war in Gaza and its hostage crisis for political reasons. They say he is undermining Israels independent judiciary. And they accuse his government of allowing ultra-Orthodox religious Jews to avoid military conscription.

Eisenkot is viewed by supporters as a capable leader with sterling security credentials. His son and two nephews were killed in Gaza, and his backers believe that he feels deeply the country's pain. Parties that likely would partner with him have vowed to improve Israels international standing and work to conscript ultra-Orthodox men while bolstering the independence of the judiciary.

title: Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and his family land in Miami
content:
Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flvio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami on Wednesday after fleeing Brazil.

The stunning move came after 48 hours in which Bolsonaro refused to concede to Brazilian President Luiz Incio Lula da Silva and then threatened to attempt to annul the election result.

Bolsonaro's father, Jair Bolsonaro, also fled to Florida after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula before returning to Brazil three months later. On Monday, the U.S. said that it would grant visas to Flvio Bolsonaro and his family. Bolsonaro, a Trump ally, visited the White House in May.

Bolsonaro first fled from Brazil to Argentina and then Ecuador alongside his wife and two daughters, Argentina's migration authority said Wednesday a day after the 45-year-old senator and his family were granted United States visas by the Trump administration.

Brazil's Flvio Bolsonaro will be granted US visa after he defied a travel ban

Bolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil's Supreme Court for alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion in two cases. The court had ordered Bolsonaro to hand over his regular and diplomatic passports by noon Tuesday two days after he lost the vote to Lula. It remained unclear whether he had complied, but allies said late Tuesday he also has an Italian passport.

Argentina's migration authority said Bolsonaro, his wife Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and his daughters Carolina Figueira Bolsonaro and Luiza Figueira Bolsonaro crossed into the country at 10:50 p.m. Tuesday. They entered via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a primary border checkpoint linking Brazil to Argentina's northeastern province of Misiones.

"Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country," the Argentine migration authority said on X.

The authority said that at 11:30 p.m. local time, shortly after clearing immigration control, the four boarded a private charter flight operated by aviation company Baires Fly S.A. According to the filed flight plan, the aircraft departed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.

The move is almost certain to cause a big diplomatic rift between Lula and Argentine President Javier Milei, a Trump ally who traveled to Brazil to take part in Bolsonaro's campaign.

Bolsonaro lands in Miami

Flight tracking website FlightRadar24 showed that a plane fitting the description of Bolsonaro's landed in Guayaquil at about 4 a.m. local time, before taking off minutes later for Miami-Opa locka Executive Airport. The plane carrying Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami at around 9:30 a.m. EST.

Lula, who turned 81 on Tuesday, told several dozen supporters outside the presidential residence in Brasilia before the plane landed that he didn't have precise information about Bolsonaro's whereabouts, but said he had left Brazil.

"I regret that he left Brazil, because he could have stayed here and proven that the accusations are not true," Lula said. "This act of leaving Brazil is shameful."

Paulo Figueiredo, a close Bolsonaro ally who lives in the U.S., said in a short statement that he can't confirm information from foreign authorities, but added "Flvio Bolsonaro is well, in security and resting with his family." Figueiredo also said there would be a press conference Thursday in Miami to discuss the case.

Representatives of Brazil's government didn't immediately respond to requests for comment from The Associated Press.

U.S. President Donald Trump said early Wednesday that he would approve of Bolsonaro coming to the U.S., calling him and his family "fine people."

"The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible," Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, after returning from campaigning in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate, but stressed that he didn't endorse the election results.

Leaders all over the world and the Organization of American States, or OAS, endorsed the result and congratulated Lula, who was reelected by a margin of about 4.4 million votes in the second and final round.

On Tuesday, Milei's administration spokesman Adrin Ravier said "there is no asylum request (from Bolsonaro) and there is nothing more to add."

Lula is declared winner of Brazil's election as Bolsonaro rejects results

Bolsonaro visited his father, who is under house arrest, before leaving Brazil

The defeated candidate was served with a Supreme Court order to surrender his Brazilian passports Monday. In a video, he said he received it outside the home where his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest for attempting a coup following his 2022 election loss to Lula.

After that defeat, Jair Bolsonaro fled Brazil for Florida. He returned three months later.

Flvio Bolsonaro said on Monday in a video that he was attempting to organize opposition among his congressional colleagues to the election results. His eight-year term as a senator expires Jan. 31, 2027, which will also cause him to lose special jurisdiction at the country's Supreme Court.

Brazil's Supreme Court is investigating Bolsonaro for allegedly using a sports betting company to launder fraudulent deductions from government pensions paid to senior citizens. In a separate case, he is accused of accepting millions of dollars from a disgraced banker.

title: At least 68 dead after high-speed train slams into another in Spain
content:
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 68 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.

The central governments office for Castilla La Mancha confirmed the death toll had risen.

The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano Garca-Page, had said at least 80 people were injured as rescue workers continue to search in the wreckage for survivors and bodies.

It was the second major train accident in Spain this year.

WATCH | Death toll surges in Spain train crash

Death toll surges in Spain train crash

Spains rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. The accident was between two high-speed trains carrying hundreds of passengers and heading in the same direction from the capital Madrid to Seville in southwestern Spain, according to Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region.

RELATED STORY | Interoceanic Train derails in southern Mexico, killing at least 13 and injuring dozens

One ran into the tail of the other that had stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track.

Padilla said that the cause of the crash was not known. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Everything went flying when the trains collided, a passenger said

The crash, which occurred in a flat stretch surrounded by olive fields in between the towns of Urda and Los Ybenes, left one car shredded into bits of metal and other material, scattering debris down a gravel slope.

Spanish Health Minister Mnica Garca said that emergency workers were focusing on rescuing survivors and bodies from the two most damaged train cars. She said that the injured are being sent to different hospitals in the area.

It was a high-speed impact, so we are expecting this to be a tragedy, Garca said.

The accident involved a train from Spains state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. It appeared the RENFE train rammed the IRYO train, Spanish media reported. Garca-Page said 24 died in the RENFE train, and six in the IRYO one.

Passenger Ignacio Relao was traveling on the RENFE train. He told state broadcaster TVE that the train had stopped momentarily on the line before it started again and then crashed into the IRYO.

We all felt the train abruptly slowing down and then the impact, he said. The car leaned to one side like it was about to tip over. I hit my nose, everything went flying, luggage, cell phones. Everything shook.

Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.

IRYO, an Italian-owned company, said in a statement that it has activated its security protocols and is closely working with authorities.

The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galn, said that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to injured passengers.

A military emergency brigade was deployed to help emergency services, firefighters and police. Ambulances and medical helicopters made trips to and from the site, while unscathed survivors were put on buses.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Snchez canceled his agenda to focus on the crash. He wrote on X that he was dismayed by the serious train accident in Toledo.

Emergency services are working on site to attend to the affected passengers, wrote Snchez, who faces a national election next month. All my thoughts are with the victims and their families.

Spains King Felipe VI and Queen Letizia said in a short statement on X that they were following news of the accident.

We are deeply saddened and concerned by the train accident in Urda (Toledo), the royal couple said. We share in the grief of the families and loved ones of those who lost their lives, and we send our heartfelt support to the injured and all those affected.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, My heart goes out to the victims families and loved ones. Today, Europe mourns with you.

Spain's soccer federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled on Wednesday.

title: The global war on citizenship
content:
What do a Bollywood actor, a member of Congress, and Israeli directors have in common? 

It sounds like the beginning of a bad joke. The punchline, though, is that governments of India, the United States, and Israel, respectively, think they should be stripped of their national status.

Bollywood star Imran Khan, nephew of Bollywood superstar Aamir Khan, was told he has until October 28 (and since extended to November 2) to leave India, where he resides on an Overseas Citizen of India (OCI) card. India doesn’t allow dual citizenship, but OCI status gives individuals of Indian descent and their family members the right to permanently live, work, and study in India; its revocation uproots its holders from their homes and their lives. Khan had protested in a demonstration demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, India’s chief election commission. He is challenging the order in court.

Earlier this month, US Rep. Ilhan Omar’s home was raided by federal authorities who are reportedly preparing a case to strip her of citizenship, alleging that her father said she was 17 when she was really 18 when he filed her naturalization paperwork. President Donald Trump subsequently said that, because a federal court filing allegedly referred to her as “Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, a/k/a Ilhan Abdullahi Omar,” she should have to resign from Congress.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has intimated that Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, directors of the film NAZA, in which Abraham interviews Israeli soldiers and intelligence officers on Tel Aviv rooftops about how they assessed and decided to kill civilians in Gaza, could be stripped of their Israeli citizenship, saying he would pursue legislation to go after critics of the military who crossed a line. “We will revoke citizenship for anyone who defames IDF soldiers around the world — he will be deeply hurt in his pocket,” said Netanyahu, who cited the filmmakers as a potential example and called their work “intolerable.”

The move to strip citizens of their passports and their rights is not a new one, nor is it limited to these three countries. Perhaps most famously, Jews were stripped of citizenship by the Nazis in Germany and elsewhere in Europe in the 1930s and ’40s. To take a more recent example, over the summer, Russia passed legislation that effectively strips Russians abroad facing domestic prosecution on political grounds of their citizenship (the law takes away their property, freezes their bank accounts, and refuses them consular services).

Still, that three high-profile cases are coming from three countries that claim to be democracies raises the question: Why do reactionary leaders in democracies reach for denaturalization (or quasi-denaturalization, in the case of loss of OCI) as a weapon against political and cultural elites? What do they hope to gain? And, relatedly: What might they lose instead?

It’s not just about the high-profile targets

Reactionary leaders do not typically threaten to make an example of high-profile political opponents or cultural elites as a first step. In each of these cases, there are demographic groups — whole swathes of the population — whose governments have been trying to disenfranchise, denaturalize, or deport them (or some combination of the three) long before the recent spate of high-profile headlines. 

In India, there’s currently a politicized election integrity push that experts warn could illegitimately prevent tens of millions of voters from marginalized groups, especially Muslims, from participating in elections. What should have been a routine clean up of voter rolls ended up with 130 million — nearly 10 percent of the population — struck off the lists. The sweeping approach has raised widespread concern from critics that many voters will be incorrectly removed — and deep suspicions that this disenfranchisement is targeted and intentional.  

Mukulika Banerjee, a professor of anthropology at the London School of Economics, noted this happened after the position of chief election commissioner was made partisan and given immunity for life. And while normally in India (unlike in the United States) the onus is on the state, not individuals, to register voters, in this case, the state said that if people were to be put back on the voter rolls, they “had to produce a whole bunch of documents…which by implication affected the socially disadvantaged,” per Banerjee. 

That meant women, people from lower castes, rural voters — and, since “the Muslim population amongst the most seriously socially disadvantaged, the likelihood of Muslims falling in this category is very high,” Banerjee, author of Cultivating Democracy: Politics and Citizenship in Agrarian India, said. In places like West Bengal, where Muslims make up nearly 30 percent of the population, there were some assembly constituencies where, in elections earlier this year, the number of names deleted from the rolls was greater than the margin of victory, and while anti-incumbent sentiment was high and the BJP may well have won anyway, some, per Banerjee, are asking, “was this an attempt to choose the electorate, so to speak.”

In the United States, the Trump administration has made denaturalization a priority, hoping to find people they can make an example of as part of their broader immigration crackdown. They have already filed to strip dozens of Americans of their citizenship by claiming they lied on their naturalization paperwork (“Justice Department Moves to Strip Citizenship from 40 Criminals in Largest Single-Period Filing Under the Trump Administration,” a press release from earlier this month crowed). The White House also tried, unsuccessfully, to revoke America’s constitutional right to birthright citizenship, which could have left future generations far more vulnerable to removal or persecution.

And in Israel, Palestinians have long been made to feel the weight of citizenship — and the heft of its absence. This is not only true in, say, the West Bank, where Jews live as citizens but Palestinians live under occupation and military law, but in East Jerusalem, where most Palestinians are permanent residents, not citizens, meaning they cannot vote in general elections for the Israeli legislature.

“That is a tool that Israel has used in a different way that could easily be transplanted to citizens,” said Mairav Zonszein, senior analyst on Israel at Crisis Group. And if you can strip residency from Palestinians in Jerusalem, maybe you can strip citizenship, too. “If this government is reelected, I could see that becoming a less and less crazy idea” as what was once unthinkable becomes “normalized.” Palestinian citizens in Israel have expressed the same concern.

The chilling effect of deportation threats 

How — and why — does an aspiring authoritarian move from threatening the rights and status of demographic groups to going after elites?

Sometimes, the elites are — in addition to being outspoken and high profile — from the demographic group under threat.

Several years before Khan’s OCI status came under threat, the Modi government took journalist Aatish Taseer’s OCI card from him. This happened in 2019 — months after Taseer authored a Time story with “India’s Divider in Chief” plastered across the cover, after which the prime minister himself said, “Time Magazine is foreign. The writer has also said he comes from a Pakistani political family. That is enough for his credibility.” Taseer’s father was indeed a Pakistani political figure, but this was hardly some secret of which Taseer had made offhand mention; Taseer had written about his father and the role his absence and rediscovery in his life, including in his first book, Stranger to History: A Son’s Journey Through Islamic Lands.

And so with Imran Khan, Taseer said in a phone interview, there is an element of, “Just get the Muslim out” (Khan’s mother is Muslim). In Taseer’s own case, he said, he became “the Paki.”

The same is true at least in one high-profile case in the United States: Omar is Muslim and from Somalia, two groups that frequently attract the ire of the Trump administration. Recently, Trump urged Minnesotans to “fight back” against Somali immigrants before the state is “taken over.” Omar is also a prominent and progressive member of Congress. 

“It’s got these two levels,” Taseer said. “One is an ethnonationalist agenda. The other is a blunt instrument of coercion.” If you speak out too freely, Taseer added, “you won’t be able to return home.”

The blunt instrument, though, is more narrowly applied than, say, stripping people from voter rolls en masse. It is designed to cause fear among elites: journalists and actors and academics.

And it is meant, Banerjee said, to raise the price of protest.

The government’s first instinct, she said, is to call protesters terrorists and anti-nationals, rather than citizens exercising their rights: “They don’t seem to understand that to peacefully protest is there in…the constitution.”

And by taking a Bollywood star’s OCI status, the government can “make an example and say, look, we can take the biggest and the richest and the most prominent.” It is a message to the rich and the famous and the powerful: Do not think you are bigger than government coercion. You are not.

Whether it works is almost beside the point. Trump is facing an uphill legal battle in proving that an error committed by Omar’s father, if indeed any error exists, means she should lose her citizenship. Omar has said she sees the administration’s goal as exhausting and intimidating her to the point she leaves politics — something she says will not happen. 

And, it’s unlikely, Zonszein said, that Abraham and Szor will actually be stripped of citizenship given Israel’s own judicial protections. But, “It’s an empty threat, but one that works, because it chills dissent, it stifles it, it makes people scared.”

It also suggests that, regardless of whether you’re a member of the targeted group, or have some special status that could set you apart, power can come for you, too. That can scare people out of speaking out for the marginalized. It can also alert them into the need for doing so.

“When it happens in a democracy, one has to always keep one’s radar attuned to who is suddenly becoming prey, whether it’s LGBT in Russia or now in Turkey or in this case in India, Muslims, Taseer said. ”It’s sort of — what they’re going to those people, they’re going to eventually do to the population at large. It’s not one of those things where they’re like, ah, let us do this little thing, and then you guys can all live happily ever after. It’s generally always accompanied by a deeper authoritarian turn.”

For example, in addition to threatening Abraham and Szor, Israel has revoked the entry permits of American Jews who volunteered to work with and protect Palestinian farmers during harvests and froze aliyah — the name for the process by which Jews abroad immigrate — of two Jews over their pro-Palestinian West Bank activism, which, as Israeli outlet Haaretz reported, could be a violation of Israeli law guaranteeing the right of all Jews around the world the right to move to Israel and become citizens. 

“I mean, anybody with their head on straight would say, if you treat one person this way, it’s not that hard to treat another person this way,” Zonszein said. “That’s pretty basic, obvious stuff.”

title: US to issue Flávio Bolsonaro and family visas after he defied a travel ban and left Brazil
content:
The United States will issue visas to the defeated Brazilian presidential candidate, Flvio Bolsonaro, and his family, allowing them entry into the United States, a State Department official told CNN.

Two sources earlier confirmed to CNN that Bolsonaro had left Brazil and headed to the US after losing Sundays presidential election. A US official initially told CNN that Bolsonaro was headed to Florida, but later said his exact destination in the US was unclear.

A Brazilian source close to Bolsonaro said that the politician had feared arrest in Brazil. He is currently under investigation by the countrys highest court for alleged acts of corruption, money laundering and currency evasion.

RELATED STORY | Lula is declared winner of Brazil's election as Bolsonaro rejects results

Brazils Federal Police canceled Bolsonaros passports after he failed to surrender them, affiliate CNN Brasil reported.

Speculation about his movements mounted after Argentine news outlet Infobae reported that Bolsonaro had left Brazil via Argentina after losing Sundays runoff presidential election against leftist President Luiz Incio Lula da Silva. The Argentine government said in a statement that it has no record of Flvio Bolsonaro entering the country.

Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro to turn in his passports within 24 hours on Monday. CNN has reached out to Bolsonaro, his political party and the Brazilian Federal Police for comment on the senators whereabouts.

Bolsonaro said Brazilian police had informed him of the order in person and told him he was banned from leaving Brazil. In a video posted to Instagram, the senator denied that he intended to flee.

One of the allegations against Bolsonaro is connected to potential illegal online betting platforms, and another to the production of a biopic about his father, Dark Horse, which federal police believe involved funds from Banco Master, a now-collapsed bank at the heart of a $7 billion Ponzi-like scheme in 2025. Bolsonaro denies all wrongdoing.

At the time of his departure from Brazil, there were no warrants for his arrest, but according to legal analysts, the act of defying the courts orders to surrender his passports could be enough reason for a warrant to be issued.

Right-wingers in exile

In leaving Brazil for the US, Bolsonaro joins a large community of Brazilian conservatives in exile including his own brother Eduardo, former Brazilian intelligence chief Alexandre Ramagem and podcaster Paulo Figueiredo.

Eduardo suggested shortly before the runoff election that Flvio ought to leave Brazil if his bid for the presidency failed. On Tuesday, Eduardo called rumors that his brother had fled a lie.

Flvios journey mirrors his fathers actions after losing the 2022 presidential election. Shortly after his loss, Jair Bolsonaro decamped for Orlando, Florida, where he remained for three months. During that time, hundreds of his supporters stormed the seats of power in the capital Braslia, vandalizing the supreme court, congress and the presidential palace in an attack reminiscent of the insurrection on the US Capitol in 2021.

IN CASE YOU MISSED IT | Trump administration revokes visa of Brazils ambassador to US, escalating diplomatic spat

Bolsonaro and his allies efforts to overturn the 2022 election results led to the former president being sentenced to 27 years in prison. US President Donald Trump, a prominent supporter of the Bolsonaro family, briefly imposed tariffs on Brazil in response to the criminal case against Jair. Trump claimed without evidence earlier this week that Lulas victory was rigged.

Bolsonaros leaving Brazil comes directly after his surprise loss to Lula over the weekend. The conservative politician was a strong favorite to win, but Lula managed to outmaneuver Bolsonaro Sunday, earning 4.4 million more votes in the second round. Bolsonaro initially refused to concede to Lula, saying his team would ask for the results to be annulled.

Bolsonaros Liberal Party reversed course days later. We recognize the presidential election results, party head Valdemar Costa Neto said, according to CNN Brasil. But we believe the issues raised need to be properly clarified.

title: Benjamin Netanyahu’s day of reckoning is here
content:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.

Another day, another hugely consequential foreign election. (If you’re wondering why all the world seems to be voting now, there’s no conspiracy — it’s largely coincidence!) 

Today we’re jetting off to Israel, where voters turned out in record numbers for what some analysts have called the most important legislative election in the country’s history. It’s an election that will determine whether Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stays in power — and could shape the future of Israeli democracy.

These are, after all, the first national elections since the October 7, 2023, attacks, and they’re a referendum on everything that’s happened since: the devastating war in Gaza, the widening conflict across the Middle East, and Netanyahu’s attacks on independent watchdogs, foreign media, and his political opposition.

Both Netanyahu and the opposition have depicted the election in existential terms. Quite literally, in some cases. Campaign banners for Netanyahu’s Likud party warned Israelis that they could cast a vote for a right-wing party…or for Palestine. Opposition leaders, meanwhile, are framing the election as a fight to preserve Israeli democracy.

Go a little deeper

Some of you, I realize, may question whether Israel qualifies as a democracy at all, given its treatment of Palestinians. Listen: I appreciate the complexity here! That complexity is central to the stakes of this election. 

Israeli democracy — whatever its asterisks — faces both an immediate threat and a more foundational problem. The immediate threat is, of course, Netanyahu and his more authoritarian impulses. A record seventh term would give him more time to weaken checks on his power.

The foundational problem, meanwhile, concerns who gets a say in how Israel is governed. The state rules over Palestinians who cannot vote in its national elections, while its own Arab citizens — who make up one-fifth of the population — face well-documented discrimination in areas including housing, land use, and family reunification. That marginalization also shows up in politics. Both Netanyahu and several opposition leaders have vowed not to work with Israel’s Arab parties to form a governing coalition. 

But that’s where this election could get interesting. Under Israel’s parliamentary system, Israelis essentially vote for a party, and parliamentary seats are allocated proportionally. Aligned parties then band together to try to form a coalition that can command the majority of parliamentary seats. 

A Netanyahu coalition would likely include, for instance, a number of right-wing, nationalist and ultra-Orthodox parties, while an opposition coalition would likely include Jewish parties from the left, center, and center-right. 

Either bloc could win enough seats today to govern without additional partners. (Polls closed at 4 pm ET, and we’ll have a fuller picture as the evening goes on.) But if the opposition falls short, it might need support from one or more of the Arab parties that some of its leading figures have lately sworn off. 

Should no one form a governing coalition, Israelis may have to vote again. But more importantly, for our purposes, the debate over partnering with Arab parties goes back to that “deeper foundational problem in Israeli democracy,” as Vox’s Zack Beauchamp once put it. 

As Zack argues, most Israeli Jews want to live in a democracy — but paradoxically, they want to live in a democracy that privileges some citizens over others. Netanyahu has tried to resolve that paradox by weakening Israel’s democratic institutions. 

Today’s election and its aftermath could show whether there’s appetite in Israel for a very different, pro-democratic approach. Democracy is 2-0 this week! We’ll soon see if it puts a third win on the board.

Sharing specific financial information with a chatbot raises privacy concerns, and chatbots are not licensed or regulated the way human advisors or accountants are. Think of them as financially savvy friends: helpful…but fallible!

title: Trump’s Canada squeeze backfires as US 'desperately' needs crucial import
content:
President Trump's effort to squeeze Canada is coming back to bite American businesses as a new report reveals just how hard it is for the US to find an alternative to something it has long purchased from its northern neighbor.

"This country desperately needs aluminum," Trump admitted during an August telephone rally for Oklahoma Republican gubernatorial candidate Mike Mazzei. He later added: "We don't have it. We get it all from Canada, for the most part, and we need it badly."

That admission now looks very odd as Trump has imposed a 50 percent tariff on Canadian aluminum imports, yet American companies still need the metal to make cars, build houses, manufacture aircraft, construct data centers and all sorts of other things.

The Wall Street Journal reported Tuesday that the tariffs have driven the premium paid for aluminum in the US to record levels, adding costs for businesses that have very few real alternatives.

Higher material costs could eventually make their way to car buyers and families trying to build homes.

The issue is decades old, as there were 24 operating aluminum smelters in America 26 years ago. Today, there are just four, with Canada providing about 70 percent of US aluminum imports.

It's not simply that Canadian companies can produce the metal cheaper. Aluminum production requires enormous amounts of electricity, so the advantage of having access to cheap power is crucial. Quebec's huge hydropower resources give its smelters an advantage that their American counterparts simply can't match.

There's an irony in the very fact that America helped Canada build its aluminum factories. During World War II, the US helped turn the remote Saguenay region of Quebec into an aluminum powerhouse to supply aircraft and munitions. Thousands of Canadians built smelters and a hydropower plant in freezing conditions in just 18 months, and the region has supplied American manufacturers ever since.

Rio Tinto is investing $1.5 billion in modernizing its operations in the region, while a proposed $4 billion smelter in Oklahoma is meeting resistance over pollution, foreign ownership, and the public money required to get it built.

That leaves US manufacturers paying more today, while Trump's domestic replacement remains very much in doubt.

Canada, in the meantime, has found other partners, with its aluminum shipments to Europe up 77 percent year on year through August, according to the Journal, indicating that producers are finding other markets as Washington makes their principal market increasingly difficult to access.

For American businesses, that creates another problem. Even if Trump eventually wants more Canadian aluminum, suppliers may have other places to sell it.

title: Trump’s rally words obliterates his own case for Iran escalation
content:
President Donald Trump has spent the past week campaigning across the U.S., delivering remarks that a poke holes in his case for war against Iran.

The Bulwark's Will Saletan cited 13 rallies or press gaggles in which Trump detailed his expectations for the war and reasons for it. Saletan noted the president's claims just don't add up.

Saletan's video is aimed directly at Trump voters, and he's using the president's own words against him.

At a Trump rally in South Carolina on Oct. 21, Trump claimed, "Half of the things I am telling you I did I never discussed in the campaign ... I never said we're gonna take over Venezuela beautifully. I never said we're gonna stop Iran from having a nuclear weapon. You know, we have to do it."

Saletan noted that the president is spot on he not only never told Americans he'd end up in a war with Iran, he told voter the opposite. Trump told voters he believed in "America First," and that meant "no new endless wars."

Another point came from Trump's claim that "we obliterated Iran's nuclear program" after the 2025 bombing. But in February 2026, he had to do it again.

He made the point with an NBC Montana reporter on Oct. 14 while visiting the state. Trump said, "And they will never have a nuclear weapon. It was all about the nuclear weapon and we've already done that with our B2 bombers. They will never have a nuclear weapon."

Despite his claim that the U.S. took out all of Iran's nuclear weapons a second time in February 2026, eight months later the U.S. remains.

Then, on Oct. 23, Trump told his audience in Florida, "We obliterated Iran's nuclear enrichment capacity with Operation Midnight Hammer. You remember that? Late at night, 1 in the morning."

Trump also said he knew then it would drive up gas prices, telling his Arizona rally on Oct. 14 that he expected the numbers to be much higher.

"This is a very small price, people," Trump told the audience. "But we have to meet tomorrow because the Islamic Republic of Iran is two weeks away from having a nuclear weapon."

Saletan questioned why Iran was two weeks away when Trump said he "obliterated" the nuclear program the previous year.

"So he decided to start a war at your expense to stop a nuclear program that he had already destroyed," Saletan said.

During an Oct. 2 rally in Alabama, Trump told the audience he promised the war would be over in a few weeks. At a rally in Oklahoma the day before, he similarly recalled promising that the war would be over in four to six weeks.

"And I said it numerous times that it would take four to six weeks to get rid of the Iran nuclear threat, and I did it in one night. That was when the B-2 bombers went in there," said Trump.

Saletan said that he appeared confused as the B-2 bombers went out last June, not in February.

So, why are we still there, asked Saletan. Trump told an audience in Kansas on Oct. 19 that the U.S. could leave at any time because he'd already achieved the objective.

"By the way, somebody said you could leave right now. It's true. We could leave right now. They're not going to have a nuclear weapon. Those B-2 bombers," said Trump

He repeated the same claim at the Alabama rally, noting, "It would take them years to rebuild."

So he believes that the U.S. defeated Iran's nuclear program and he believes that they're not interested in starting it again.

"It raises the question," said Saletan, "why don't we leave? And the answer from Trump is that he won't leave until Iran signs a permanent agreement."

Speaking to Newsmax on Oct. 15, Trump made it clear that the U.S. could pull out, but they may be back in a year. Trump said he's worried that he "may not be here" in a year. He didn't elaborate. Instead, Trump doubled down a few days later to reporters, saying he wanted a written guarantee from Iran. Former President Barack Obama secured a 25-year pause of the nuclear program in Iran, but Trump ripped that up.

title: The far-right just lost. Twice.
content:
This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day. Subscribe here.

Vox isn’t typically in the business of covering elections in far-flung locales like the central Balkans. (No offense whatsoever to anyone from the central Balkans!) But on Sunday, an insurgent student-backed movement in Serbia successfully toppled the country’s ruling right-wing political machine, creating an unexpected opening for democratic reform. 

Then, in another upset halfway around the globe, Brazilian voters reelected incumbent President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva over his far-right challenger, Flávio Bolsonaro. “Democracy always, dictatorship never again,” Lula said in his victory speech.

That’s two big repudiations of the nationalist right in 24 hours. Not quite enough to declare a trend, maybe, but sufficient to remind us that there’s still hope for the world’s embattled democratic institutions. 

More than that, these results offer evidence of something that sounds naive and Pollyannish in our current moment, but can (apparently!) still prove true: Organizing can be a powerful force for electoral change — both abroad and maybe here at home.

Go a little deeper

View Link

To be fair, the two elections differed considerably, and I don’t want to suggest it’s all sunshine and democratic renewal ahead for Brazil and Serbia. Bolsonaro is refusing to concede, for instance. And in Serbia, the victorious Student List still has to stand up a government, a prime minister, and a full policy platform — something the nascent movement has never done before. 

But academics and elections-watchers in both countries have credited the results in large part to mass protests and grassroots organizing that helped mobilize unexpected numbers of voters.

Serbian students began their movement in 2024, following the partial collapse of a railway station that killed 16 people. The government’s failure to fully explain the cause of the collapse — or hold anyone responsible — fueled months of marches, protest bike rides, and other demonstrations. That movement eventually grew into the Student List: an opposition electoral slate that fielded 250 candidates in Sunday’s parliamentary elections. 

The story in Brazil is quite different. Lula, the country’s leftist president, was actually poised to lose. Brazil uses a two-round popular vote to elect its president, and if no candidate secures more than half the vote in the first round, then the top two candidates proceed to a runoff election. Lula placed second in that first vote, after Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro and the heir to his father’s far-right political movement. 

To many Brazilians, that second-place finish served as a kind of wake-up call. “No runoff campaign in Brazil has ever brought so many people to the streets and onto social media,” Guilherme Casarões, an associate professor of Brazilian studies at Florida International University, wrote in an analysis of the surprise results. One WhatsApp channel dedicated to turning voters out for Lula grew to nearly 11 million followers, up from just 50,000 after his first-round loss. 

Looking at these projects abroad, I’m struck that American pro-democracy movements like No Kings haven’t achieved that kind of influence. Arguably, that’s in part a consequence of their failure to turn protest energy into actual political organizing — things like registering voters, knocking on doors, and fielding candidates. 

But there are some signs that may be shifting. No Kings has lately pivoted its focus, for instance, from mostly organizing protests to urging Americans — of both parties — to vote in the midterms. And Indivisible, one of the groups behind the movement, claims that early voting surged during the latest protests in the zip codes where they occurred.

It’s not exactly a central Balkan moment, but maybe it’s a hint of things to come. Elections can surprise you, after all. Just ask a Serb or a Brazilian. 

One link for later

➨ Leave your big life decisions to chance. (Sort of.) A team of researchers invited people to make a big life decision by flipping a coin and then tracked their happiness with the outcome. They found that, of the people who obeyed the results of the toss, the ones who changed something big were overwhelmingly happier. That doesn’t literally mean we should all resort to coin tosses, but it should tell us something important: We often tend to be too cautious about making major changes. 

Before you go…

  • Did you know…that in the 1870s and ’80s, spectators flocked to Madison Square Garden for long-distance walking competitions? Athletes walked up to 600 miles in six days, just going round and round the stadium. 
  • Today’s trivia: Which New Jersey city was the first predominantly white community in the US to vote in favor of school integration? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword. Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.)
  • Yesterday’s trivia: Last week we asked you for the radioactive noble gas with the chemical symbol Rn. That would be radon, once a trendy (deadly) ingredient in quack medicines.

title: 'Clunkers': Kushner’s dad flagged among 'flagrantly unqualified' Trump picks
content:
A new profile in The New Yorker examines the role of Charles Kushner, father of President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner, who's served as U.S. ambassador to France since 2025.

Discussing Trump's ambassador appointees, Eric Rubin, a former U.S. Ambassador to Bulgaria, told The New Yorker's Lauren Collins, “Every Administration has what we call ‘clunkers,’ but we’ve never had quite this number of flagrantly unqualified people.”

From the beginning, it was clear —even by Kushner’s own admission — that he didn’t have the experience required for the coveted role. But being the father of President Trump’s son-in-law seemingly trumped all prerequisites. Kushner has no previous diplomatic experience. The New Jersey real-estate developer never served as a diplomat or lived abroad before taking office in 2025. Because he does not speak the native language, there is a communication barrier that could hinder his ability to engage with his host country. Kushner said publicly that he knew “a limited amount about France” when he arrived in the country.

Since taking on the role, Kushner has not been received well by French government officials, primarily because he is viewed as disrespectful to French protocols, which has caused friction. In one example, author Lauren Collins notes that Kushner failed to meet with French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot when serious issues arose between the two countries. Kushner’s disregard for the meetings further complicated diplomatic relations rather than assisting in managing tensions between the United States and France. Kushner, instead, saw the meeting request as a form of reprimand rather than a chance to create reconciliation and understanding between the two. Explaining why he ignored the first summons, Kushner said, “I'm seventy-two years old. I'm not getting called to the principal at this stage in my life.”

Kushner has been publicly critical of France’s domestic policies, intervening when many believe he should not have. The author gives the example of Kushner visiting former President Nicolas Sarkozy in prison before criticizing Sarkozy's imprisonment, saying it was a “terrible slap in the face to France,” despite Sarkozy's conviction. Kushner himself has also been asked to answer questions about a controversial past, which includes tax fraud and intimidation schemes.

Kushner hasn’t seemed interested in the relationship-building crucial for his role, nor does he seem to have a presence at important events, such as official receptions and ribbon-cutting ceremonies. Instead, he prefers events that are deemed more entertaining to him, such as his efforts to bring an NFL regular-season game to Paris.

Kushner’s behavior has made many in the general public and internationally question whether he is an effective representative of the United States. Furthermore, it calls into question the long-term effects and how U.S. politics are viewed globally.

title: Trump fumes at Don Jr. behind closed doors over Russian wedding gift
content:
President Donald Trump isn't happy with his son, and reports say they've been battling over several issues in recent weeks.

The Wall Street Journal reported Friday night that corruption allegations are growing and are now on Trump's radar.

"The president has also privately complained to aides that his son Donald Trump Jr. exhibited bad judgment for allowing Russian businessman Umar Kremlev to pay for his post-wedding party in the Bahamas," the report said.

Trump Jr. recently married Bettina Anderson on a private island where friends and family were treated to lush food, beautiful weather and even a fireworks show. The island rental and events cost hundreds of thousands of dollars and the fact that it came from a Russian oligarch was yet another connection between the Trump and Russian nationals.

It makes it difficult for the president to claim that the probe into his campaign's ties to Russia was illegitimate when Russian oligarchs are handing out money and jobs to those who work with him.

Trump has said his son paid back Kremlev, though there's no indication of when or how.

The reporting came after it was revealed that Trump and Don. Jr. are also fighting over the Iran war.

“Remember when they said Trump would get us into a full-blown war with Iran?” Don Jr. wrote on X in April 2024, as Iran sent missiles and drones toward Israel. “Times like these should make us all realize how lucky we were to have Trump, his strength and his resolve.”

Behind closed doors, Don Jr. is ranting and raving about his father's war, The Atlantic reported earlier this week.

“Don has kept his views on the subject private, as he would never publicly break with his dad on an issue like this, but I can’t imagine anyone who knows Don would be surprised by his personal views on the subject,” said a person close to the president’s son. Trump Jr. wouldn't comment.

The White House, meanwhile, said in an official statement, “Iran has been decimated, and one way or the other, the conflict in Iran will be over very soon.”

Trump has said the same thing since April.

Meanwhile, the week wasn't a good one for Trump Jr., who has taken public blow after blow.

One example is his ex, Kimberly Guilfoyle, who was ousted last week after she allegedly shook down a GOP donor for cash to pay her American Express bill. Guilfoyle is now threatening a tell-all book about the Trumps from her close six-year relationship with Don Jr.

On Friday, Don Jr. was linked to a recent revelation that Russian energy giant Novatek was pulling the strings behind the curtain for a project, known as Polar Train, which would help with Alaska's infrastructure problem on the North Slope.

The Financial Times on October 24 that the venture was initially associated with Gentry Beach, a longtime friend of Donald Trump Jr. who also served as a finance vice chairman for President Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration.

"The venture was initially associated with Gentry Beach, a longtime friend of Donald Trump Jr. who also served as a finance vice chairman for President Donald Trump’s 2017 inauguration," said a report.

The Russian funds were going through the UAE-based company Tech Wave.

It's just another connection between Russia, the president and his family.

title: Fox News veteran demolishes Trump envoy’s 'absurd' Putin praise
content:
Fox News chief political analyst Brit Hume put President Donald Trump's special envoy Steve Witkoff on blast after he praised Russian President Vladimir Putin as a "humanitarian" during peace talks in St. Petersburg.

When asked about how he felt about the interaction, Hume did not hold back, calling Witkoff’s comment extravagant before adding: "The guy's a war criminal, for God's sake, and he's rained down bombs on civilians without regard to human life."

Hume, speaking with host John Roberts on Wednesday's edition of America Reports, called the Putin praise "absurd," pointing to Russia's war with Ukraine and the high civilian casualty count, with millions more displaced.

Witkoff gave the compliment after Putin announced the release of Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old American who had spent more than four years in Russian custody.

"You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that, I commend you, and I thank you again," Witkoff told Putin during their meeting.

Hubbard, a retired teacher from Michigan, was detained by Russian forces in Ukraine in 2022. Russian authorities accused the then-70-year-old of being a mercenary for Ukraine. He denied the allegations, and the United States determined that he was illegally detained.

Roberts excused Witkoff’s comments as diplomatic flattery, and Hume acknowledged that possibility, while seemingly taking a dig at Trump’s diesel deal with Russia

Hume then discussed Donald Trump’s reason for putting a pause on the Russia sanctions in Sen. Lindsey Graham’s bill.

The Fox News star said the president told reporters on the South Lawn that you don’t punish people you’re trying to strike a deal with.

“When you’re trying to get a guy out of what has been locked up for four years illegally, you don’t insult the guy,” Hume said. “Maybe you flatter him.”

North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis called the praise "embarrassing and outrageous," mentioning how the comment is insulting to the families of Ukrainian children killed or made homeless by the war.

Texas Sen. John Cornyn offered a rebuke, calling Putin a "stone-cold killer."

The criticism comes as Trump faces criticism for what many believe is capitulating to Putin’s demands and turning his back on Ukraine.

During the Fox News discussion, Hume also addressed Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky's willingness to freeze current battle lines as a potential starting point for peace talks.

Hume said the proposal now requires a response from Putin, who has rejected previous proposals to put the brakes on the fighting. He also noted that it challenges Trump, who has repeatedly blamed Zelensky for the lack of progress toward ending the war that Russia started.

title: Insiders reveal the singular theory guiding Trump’s historic world blunder
content:
Three sources close to President Donald Trump said that he has convinced himself that there is an evil actor meddling in the 2026 election to ensure Republicans lose.

The Atlantic's Jonathan Lemire and Simon Shuster reported late Tuesday that the president is operating under his own delusion that Ukraine is responsible for the effort to overthrow the midterms.

Ukraine understands that there are three major world events that could determine its future. One is the U.S. election. Another is the upcoming mid-November meeting in southern China, "where Russian President Vladimir Putin wants to meet with Trump and Chinese President Xi," the report said.

Finally, the G20 summit at Trump's country club in Miami, Florida is scheduled for mid-December. The authors noted that Trump had been dreaming about a peace agreement between Ukraine's president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Russia's Vladimir Putin, advisors told them. It isn't likely to happen.

The report cited one Ukrainian official, who said, “It looks like this is all happening without us."

While talks are ongoing, Trump's recent decision to announce a ceasefire without it being approved by either Russia and Ukraine prompted anger from the latter as they paused and Russia continued to bomb the country's civilians. At that point, Zelenskyy said, "We're done," according to NBC News. The report implied that Ukraine has been holding back on bombing Russia's oil infrastructure. Trump has desperately hoped to protect the refineries in Russia to keep the costs of fuel low ahead of the 2026 elections. It appears Ukraine believes continuing is in its own best military interest.

"Some in Trump’s orbit have suggested that the United States go further and stop sharing intelligence with Ukraine" the report said. "Trump’s deference to Putin has been a theme for a decade, yet this new round of kowtowing has handed Republicans another obstacle ahead of the elections."

The reference is to Trump's decision to deliver $4 billion to Russia for a small sliver of diesel in what is expected to be a failed effort to reduce fuel costs in the U.S. The price of oil is determined on a global scale. The main issue is supply disruptions from the Iran war and the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

Trump "blames those strikes for the rise in energy prices while ignoring the real culprit, Iran’s ability to defy the United States and close the Strait of Hormuz. He’s convinced himself, three people close to him have told us, that Ukraine’s attacks on the refineries are, in part, meant to undermine Republicans’ chances next month — and, by extension, Trump," the report said.

Trump hasn't responded to the attacks on Ukraine's civilian population and their electrical grid. In fact, Trump commented that Russia hasn't "been doing much." Zelenskyy responded with photos of dead children in a park.

The Atlantic reporters recalled the 2024 campaign when Trump promised he could end the war within his first 24 hours in office. He later added that he could probably solve it before he was sworn in.

Putin appears to have convinced Trump to hold a private meeting with Xi on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation meeting in China to discuss, among other things, Ukraine. Trump told reporters on Monday that he was open to it.

"It is no surprise that Trump is drawn to the idea," the report said. "His deference toward Putin is rivaled only by his regard for Xi, whom he hosted in lavish fashion at the White House last month. He has previously been intrigued by the idea of the three powers — China, Russia, the United States — dividing the globe into spheres of influence, although Moscow these days hardly wields the international clout of Washington or Beijing."

In the background, activists have been sharing memes claiming that after Russian data centers were bombed, pro-conservative, pro-Republican and far-right promotion significantly dropped. They've noted that since then, Republicans allege that Ukraine is meddling in the election, which activists think is an admission that they knew Russia was helping them.
