title: WSJ warns of Trump threat to 'blow up US global credibility'
content:
The Wall Street Journal Editorial Board panned President Donald Trump’s emerging alliances with hostile nations China and Russia against U.S. allies.

“It’s hard to know what President Trump is up to at any one moment because he operates so much on tactical impulse. But he has long coveted grand bargains with Russia and China, and that may be his motivation now as he hardens his hostility to Ukraine and Europe and courts a Yalta 2 summit with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping,” the board opined.

The WSJ was quick to point out that the Yalta analogy doesn’t even apply because the original team of the first Yalta summit, Stalin and Churchill were U.S. allies in 1945. But the trio do resemble Trump’s plan in the way they seek to “carve up the globe,” according to the WSJ, and that is “the danger with what Mr. Trump says he’s open to now.”

“As we wrote before the 2024 election, this was one of our main fears for his second term,” said the board, pointing out that Putin has floated a meeting with China and Trump to divvy up Ukraine — which would pose a clear threat to U.N. allies.

“A new triumvirate that divided the world into spheres of influence would blow up America’s global credibility as a reliable ally. U.S. allies may be punching bags these days, but the U.S. network from NATO to Japan, South Korea and Australia allows America to deter aggression and maintain peace before threats are dire,” said the board.

And all that damage is pointless, said the board, because Trump can’t “force Ukraine into capitulation.” Plus, Trump “would own the ugly scenes of carnage that followed if he pulled intelligence and targeting help.”

“Curb your enthusiasm about a China alliance as well,” warned the board. “Mr. Trump might want China’s promise not to help Iran, but … Mr. Xi wants Taiwan in his strategic soul, and he aspires to subdue the island without having to take the risk of a blockade or military assault.”

Xi, predicts the WSJ, will no doubt exploit any opening Trump provides to push the U.S. out of the Pacific, even if that means abandoning 23 million free people “across the Taiwan Strait.”

“Trump’s advisers may tell him that voters don’t care about the post-1945 ‘global order.’ But the public understands that China and Russia aren’t American friends, and they know looming trouble abroad when they see it,” said the board. “GOP lawmakers are already unhappy with the President’s appeasement of Mr. Putin, especially given that Mr. Trump has so far failed to rebuild the U.S. military.”

Handing over Europe to Russia, and the Pacific to China, would open a “major party division” at a time when Trump is rapidly cascading into his “lame duck” period.

“It’s true that Congress and the courts can’t stop a determined President on foreign policy, but they can make him pay a political price,” said the WSJ. “A second Yalta is arguably the worst idea of the second Trump term, and the President would be betting far more than his own legacy.”

title: Trump’s Greenland threats spark arctic power grab as Russia looms
content:
The European Union announced plans to strengthen its presence in the Arctic as rising temperatures, geopolitical tensions and competition for energy resources and critical minerals reshape the region, the LA Times reports. The move comes amid President Donald Trump’s threats to take control of Greenland, a self-governing territory of Denmark, and growing unease in Iceland after Trump posted a map depicting both islands in the colors of the American flag.

As the Arctic warms much faster than the rest of the planet, new challenges are emerging, including the opening of new shipping routes, increased Chinese trade through the region, and a Russian military buildup that is heightening security concerns. “When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned stability in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.

As a result, the EU wants to help set up a cable center which would assist in undersea communication efforts in the North Atlantic and Arctic. Russian submarines are suspected of preparing to sabotage critical underwater infrastructure in the region. The EU plans to use the funding to deploy cameras, sensors, and satellites to monitor the region and detect potential threats.

At the same time, the European Commission plans to support the development of a “sovereign, secure and resilient submarine cable” that would directly connect Greenland to the EU, per a new strategy document. The cable monitoring system would be part of a larger security hub.

In September, the United States and Denmark reached a security agreement concerning Greenland in an effort to ease tensions sparked by President Donald Trump’s threats to seize the territory. Trump announced the agreement on Truth Social, claiming Denmark would grant the U.S. “permanent control over security, and all other needs” in Greenland, including the establishment of a “large military presence” on the Arctic island.

Danish and Greenlandic leaders also voiced support for strengthening security in the region, while emphasizing the importance of respecting Denmark’s sovereignty and territorial integrity, as well as the Greenlandic people’s right to self-determination. The agreement was formalized by U.S. President Donald Trump, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen, and Greenlandic Prime Minister Jens-Frederik Nielsen, which some believe is a pivotal moment in negotiations over Arctic security and Greenland’s strategic future.

Trump has repeatedly dismissed the science behind global warming, despite the Arctic’s rapidly changing temperatures. He has called climate change “the greatest con job ever perpetrated on the world,” arguing that predictions by the United Nations and other organizations have been inaccurate. He has also criticized climate initiatives as a “green scam,” warning that countries embracing them risk economic failure, PBS reports.

title: Ex-Canadian leader maps out the historic trap Trump’s sleepwalking into
content:
Former Canadian Deputy Prime Minister Chrystia Freeland has a warning for Americans: Trump’s attempts to push Canada around are hurting the United States, and driving a longtime ally to look elsewhere.

Speaking with The New York Times’ Ezra Klein in a podcast published Tuesday, Freeland described a relationship transformed by tariffs and threats to Canadian sovereignty. A country Canadians once regarded as a trusted ally is increasingly seen as a threat.

Trump wanted Canada to become the 51st state. Instead, his pressure campaign is encouraging Canadians to strengthen ties with Europe and China and reduce their dependence on the United States.

Drawing on her experience negotiating with Trump during his first term, Freeland offered a straightforward rule for dealing with him: “We do not escalate, and we do not back down.”

What doesn’t work, she argued, is excessive flattery from leaders who believe they can manipulate Trump by appealing to his ego.

“Well, I’ll just sort of butter him up. I will outrageously flatter him, and maybe I’ll agree to some things he wants, but it will just be on paper. It won’t be real, and it will all be fine,” she said, describing the thinking behind an approach she rejects.

Freeland favors something less theatrical: stay calm, refuse to be intimidated and make clear that threats will not produce submission.

“I’m not going to suck up to you, I’m not going to be bullied by you, but also I’m not going to raise the emotional register with you,” she explained.

That matters because Canadians see the confrontation as more than a dispute over trade. Trump’s threats have made it a question of national independence — and Freeland said Canadians understand that defending it could come at a steep economic cost.

“This is an asymmetric confrontation. And it means it will be more painful for Canada. Canadians recognize that,” she said. But she remains confident they will “hold the line.”

Trump’s tariffs, meanwhile, are also hurting the Americans he claims to be protecting.

Canada supplies U.S. companies with materials they need to make other products: aluminum for manufacturing, lumber for construction and potash for fertilizer. Taxing those imports increases costs for American businesses, which can pass those costs along to consumers.

“So tariffs on Canadian goods make stuff in the United States more expensive, and then Canada’s retaliation actually has an impact,” Freeland said.paste.txt

She called the idea that America benefits from tariffs on Canadian aluminum “perverse.” Her argument is simple: making essential materials more expensive undermines the American companies that rely on them.

Freeland recalled that Canada responded to Trump’s first-term tariffs by targeting politically sensitive American products while trying to limit the damage to its own economy.

“The last time the United States imposed tariffs on Canada, we retaliated dollar for dollar. I was the minister responsible for that, and, ultimately, America dropped its tariffs,” she said.

The goal was to create pressure inside the United States. When American businesses and workers felt the consequences, they would have a reason to demand that Washington change course.

Freeland wants more of that pressure now: international allies coordinating their responses, businesses speaking out and Republican lawmakers challenging policies that hurt their constituents.

She also suggested the midterms could change the calculations of business leaders who have accommodated Trump. If Democrats take back the House and Senate in November, for example, it's possible they could try to change course with Canada and return to the way things were by reasserting their authority.

“If they see that President Trump and MAGA no longer deliver at the ballot box, you may start seeing some very different behavior,” she said.

Her larger warning is that America’s strength depends partly on other countries wanting to work with it. Treating allies as adversaries gives them a reason to find other partners — and, she argued, China is benefiting.

“The part about all of this that I find not just depressing but horrifying is that the biggest winner is China," she said.

title: Trump has 'nothing left to lose' — and Putin has everything to win: Krugman
content:
Nobel Prize-winning economist Paul Krugman argued on Tuesday that Donald Trump’s increasingly open support for Russian President Vladimir Putin is really more about refusing to hide his longstanding support for the foreign leader.

In the column, Krugman warned that Trump’s weakening political position is making him more willing to indulge his authoritarian instincts, like Putin.

David Sanger's recent reporting for the New York Times walked through the president's efforts to rehabilitate Russia after years of war against Ukraine.

“Russia, frankly, has been fine on Ukraine,” Trump claimed while speaking to reporters before leaving for a campaign rally.

“We’ve given a lot to Ukraine. They’ve given nothing to us. Remember that," Trump complained.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky replied to Trump's comment with a photo of a baby girl who was dead in a stroller after another Russian bombing of civilians in a park near a cafe.

Krugman agreed with Sanger's assessment that Trump's support for a dictator like Putin is unusual from an American president.

"What makes Trump’s support for Putin even more remarkable is that Russia has, by many accounts, been actively aiding Iran against America in the war Trump started. Who says so? Well, among others, Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. And the aid goes beyond intelligence sharing that has helped Iran target U.S. forces. Russia has also reportedly been sending Iran explosives and weapons components," said Krugman.

He wondered what Republicans would be saying if a Democratic president made the same move: "Even as that dictator was helping another nation kill American troops? They would be crying 'treason.' But this is all apparently 'fine' with Trump."

The reality is that Trump hasn't made a "pivot," the way the right appears to be claiming, said Krugman. When Trump claims "we" gave Ukraine "a lot," Krugman wondered what he means by "we," since Trump "cut off all economic and military aid to Ukraine as soon as he took office."

Krugman described it as a kind of "political bankruptcy" and the freedom to be the worst version of himself, which supports "corrupt, murderous dictators."

He also thinks that Trump resents Zelensky’s demonstrated courage.

The economist predicts much more is coming, largely because Trump has nothing left to lose if he flops in the midterms. Electoral pressures will no longer restrain the president and what he wants to get out of Putin.

"Trump can’t and won’t make America great again. But he can betray everything America stands for, and he’s doing it as we speak," Krugman closed.

title: Trump faces investigation threat in stunning GOP revolt over huge betrayal
content:
Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, U.S. Representative for Pennsylvania’s 1st congressional district, gave a fierce warning on Monday, October 19, when speaking of the recent alleged U.S. betrayal of Ukraine. He says he intends to hold any U.S. officials “fully accountable” if discovered that they were involved in limiting Starshield in Ukraine during a Russian missile attack last week. Fitzpatrick shared his lengthy response on X.

“I will be speaking with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and his team this week to discuss Starshield, sanctions, and other matters pertaining to the defense of our strong ally, Ukraine,” he wrote in part. He added: “I will be assuring President Zelenskyy that anyone who attempts to limit the use of Starshield for Ukraine will be fully investigated and will be held fully accountable, to include public congressional oversight hearings, and immediate harsh and punitive budget cuts to any responsible agency or agency head.”

His statement continued, adding, “Congress will unequivocally reaffirm that Ukraine is an indispensable ally to the United States, that Russia is a self-declared enemy of the United States, and that the United States will 100 percent support and defend the people of Ukraine in their fight for their own freedom against this brutal, illegal, and unprovoked Russian invasion.”

He says the country has a duty. “The United States must provide any and all defensive equipment that Ukraine needs to defend itself. The United States must not import a single drop of Russian oil,” he wrote, adding in part. “Sanctions against the Russian regime must be harsher and stronger than they’ve ever been before. Each and every one of these items will be brought to the House Floor—and each and every one of these items will pass on the House Floor by an overwhelming margin.” He also referenced former President Ronald Reagan, saying it’s the way Reagan would handle things, and that the U.S. should follow suit.

Zelenskyy has accused Trump of betrayal over the ordeal, saying he was blindsided by it. "It's a pity that we are losing, we are losing a strong partner," Zelenskyy said, as reported by Yahoo.

Starlink is a satellite internet network operated by Elon Musk’s SpaceX that provides internet access across the United States and other countries. Ukraine has relied on the network to support its defense against Russia throughout nearly five years of escalating war.

Because of the limitations last week, Zelenskyy said things were made difficult on their end. Trump has denied any involvement in interfering with Starshield. "I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon. And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been," he said on October 16 while speaking with the media.

title: 'Fair to say' Kushner-Ivanka Trump resort in Albania is 'dead': reporter
content:
Extremism reporter Will Sommer of The Bulwark believes Ivanka Trump and Jared Kushner's efforts to build a luxury resort in Albania are likely dead.

Albanians haven't stopped protesting the plan since the announcement, and over the weekend protesters burned their Supreme Court building to the ground. Meanwhile, the parliament and the education department have been vandalized, and the prime minister is in hiding.

The plan was for Trump and Kushner to spend $1.4 billion to $4 billion to build a luxury resort on Sazan Island and parts of the nearby Zvërnec peninsula along Albania's southern coast. The problem is that citizens don't want to lose access to their beaches, which are part of a protected ecosystem.

Allegations suggest the president and other government officials are being influenced by investors. Meanwhile, there are residents on the Zvërnec peninsula who claim that their homes and land were sold out from under them to Kushner and Trump. The dispute centers on government actions, not on Kushner directly stealing the land.

At the same time, the environmentally protected land is a habitat for flamingos. As Sommer explained, the community's love for the birds and other wildlife on one of the islands has prompted the activists to name their uprising the Flamingo Revolution.

A New York Times exposé revealed that the project has already cleared large amounts of land and built roads and bridges. This happened even while the government claimed that everything was on pause for an environmental assessment.

While it began as an issue over the resort project and ties to the Trump family, it has become part of a larger issue of fighting corruption.

"I don't understand why this land project is not just dead," said The Bulwark's Sam Stein. "Clearly, no one wants it."

"I think it's fair to say it's pretty dead," Sommer explained. "I mean, you know, some of the payments have been frozen because of various corruption questions. Now they're calling for the president to resign. And, so, I think at that point maybe he can hang on to his job. If he does that, I don't think he's going to say, 'Now back to building the resort.'"

Stein thinks that the resort was cursed from the start.

They went on to mock Ivanka Trump for her comments about the "beautiful hectares of land" after she mispronounced "hectares." The pronunciation and seriousness of Trump prompted the men to burst into hysterics.

"And she just walked on it. It was pristine," said Stein with a laugh.

"It was like a Cold War submarine base," Sommer said.

"With a bunch of flamingos that had ended up there," Stein continued. "We had to have it. It's going to be this big eco-friendly resort. And now we have a Supreme Court building burning down because of this dumb, dumb idea. Let it rest. They should come out and say 'We're not doing this. Don't burn anymore buildings.' It's one of those situations where they started the fire. They should put it out."

title: What Australia could learn from its Southeast Asian neighbours about power and the changing global order
content:
Successive Australian governments have reacted with alarm at China’s influence-building activities in Southeast Asia and the Pacific. They have passed foreign interference laws, tightened foreign investment regulations, and regulated university collaborations with institutions overseas.

They have executed a Pacific Step-Up and a plan for greater trade and investment with Southeast Asia.

And they have tightened security partnerships with the United States, aligning closely with the US strategy of balancing, deterring and containing China. Australia’s two major foreign policy initiatives of the past decade – AUKUS and the Quad – are intended to implement these strategies.

But as I noted in my Quarterly Essay earlier this year, there’s a paradox bedevilling Australian foreign policy. Our closest neighbours in Southeast Asia have reacted to China’s growing power and influence in very different ways to how Australia expects they should react.

While polling data and research shows many people in Southeast Asia worry about China’s growing influence and distrust its intentions, their governments have shown no interest in joining a coalition against China.

This represents a profound challenge to the way Australian policymakers understand the world.

A hedging strategy

In the realist school of foreign policy, a collection of small, relatively weak states facing a rising and threatening great power would be expected to react decisively.

This means Southeast Asian nations should be responding to the rise of China in one of two ways. The first is aligning with Beijing in the expectation that benefits will flow to China’s allies. The alternative is looking to “balance” China’s power by joining a countervailing coalition of nations.

However, Southeast Asian countries have done neither. Instead, they have elected to hedge. They are engaging China while simultaneously building closer links with a range of other powers, namely the US, Japan, India and Russia.

This has resulted in the most significant strategic divergence between Australia and its closest neighbours in how to deal with China’s rise – the most profound challenge to regional order since the second world war.

Understanding the roots of this divergence, and its implications, will be one of Australia’s more urgent priorities in the near future.

How Australia sees the world

As a mid-sized, free-trading, developed democracy, Australia is a strong supporter and beneficiary of the post-second world war international order. This order is based on:

  • the sovereign equality of states
  • healthy and authoritative multilateral institutions
  • open and rules-based trade and investment
  • universal and binding international law.

Australia has traditionally seen this order as part of the evolution away from the power- and conflict-driven decades of the early 20th century.

Australians have also viewed international power through a moral lens. When the most powerful country in the world shares and upholds the values Australia believes in – as has been the case since the arrival of the First Fleet in 1788 – power is an inherently moral force.

When this power is wielded by states that do not share, or actively oppose the values Australia believes in, it is seen as inherently dangerous and immoral.

As a result, Australia’s strategic policy is animated by a consistent urge to help uphold moral power against the challenges of immoral power.

The key dilemma for Australian policymakers is when this moral power acts against the international rules and order.

The consistent choices they have made in these situations tell us much about Australia’s “strategic imaginary”. This is the set of implicit understandings about how the world works and where a country fits into that world.

In supporting NATO’s bombing of Serbia in the late 1990s, the US-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, the NATO-led military intervention in Libya in 2011, and the recent US balancing against China, Australia’s leaders are making a clear judgement: the long-term preservation of America’s inherently moral strategic primacy is more important than the short-term morality of its actions.

Australia’s strategic imaginary mandates that it must – by its words and actions – ensure the US prevails, even if it can see the immediate damage the US is doing to the international order it supports.

How it differs from Southeast Asia

This all shapes which countries Australia looks to for guidance and solidarity as it navigates global affairs.

Australian diplomats and policymakers constantly refer to “like-minded” nations that share similar strategic imaginaries and support for the post-second world war order. These include the United Kingdom, western European states, New Zealand, Canada and Japan.

The strategic imaginaries of Southeast Asian countries, however, are very different.

Of course, this region is made up of countries of varying size, composition, wealth and type of government. Despite these differences, however, I would argue these states have relatively aligned strategic imaginaries arising from their common location, colonial and post-colonial histories, and record of regional solidarity.

In their journeys toward nation-building and development, these nations have had to be entrepreneurial and pragmatic. They’ve had to adopt political and economic strategies that work, rather than prioritise universal philosophical principles.

Southeast Asian nations also have a more ambivalent attitude to the post-second world war international order. It was created by countries that colonised them; they had no role in its development. Despite this, all will admit that, by and large, it has been conducive to their nation-building objectives.

What these countries object to is the US or other Western nations trying to impose their human rights and neoliberal economic principles on them.

Southeast Asian states do not see power through the lens of morality. To them, power simply exists in the world and must be dealt with.

In their view, the greatest threat to the region is the instability brought about by great power competition.

There is a shared belief that smaller, developing states are more genuinely committed to global stability and a just international order. This explains why Southeast Asian countries have reacted negatively to US actions that contravene international rules, particularly when carried out against weaker, developing countries. It’s seen as hypocritical. The US claims to uphold the rules-based order, but brushes it aside when it suits its interests.

This is why there’s been astonishing reluctance among Southeast Asian states to condemn Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

It’s also why there’s been a rise in solidarity between Southeast Asian nations and the rest of the Global South. Many believe there is an opportunity for the Global South to work together now to construct an alternative global order.

And it helps explain why Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto has become close with Russian President Vladimir Putin. At an economic forum in Vladivostok in September, in fact, he described his country as Russia’s “gateway” to Southeast Asia.

As a result of these differences, Australia’s anxieties about the erosion of the post-second world war order are not as intensely shared by Southeast Asian states.

Their pragmatic view of the world means they will adopt low-key, solidarity-driven actions to preserve the elements of the order that matter to them. But they’ll remain silent on Western concerns about the rupturing of the entire system itself.

Will Australia’s view of the world change?

For Southeast Asian countries, the country that wields power is less important than the way power is wielded. And at the moment, US President Donald Trump’s use of power is seen as being just as dangerous to international stability – if not more so – than Chinese leader Xi Jinping’s.

It is time for Australia to start understanding its northern neighbours in much greater depth. And it may be time for Australia to learn from its neighbours’ more pragmatic view of power as the world becomes more multipolar than it’s ever been.

Underpinning all of this is the question of whether Australia’s strategic imaginary will compel it to continue defending the old international order, rather than a pragmatic adaptation to a new one.

Can strategic imaginaries change? This is perhaps the most crucial question Australia faces today.

This is an edited version of the 2026 Menzies Lecture delivered at Kings College London earlier this year.

title: George Conway delivers brutal Trump swipe after he loses Nobel Peace Prize
content:
President Donald Trump did not win the Nobel Peace Prize again this year, and ex-Republican George Conway is laughing about it.

The award is given annually to those whose work was essential in making the world more peaceful and just the previous year.

Conway mocked the latest loss and teased a different kind of peace the president with bring about in the "not-too-distant-future."

"With deep sorrow and regret I must report that President Donald J. Trump did not win this year’s Nobel Peace Prize. I know how devastated all of you must be. But inevitably someday in the not-too-distant-future he will give the world something much greater to celebrate," he wrote on X on Friday.

Those in the replies couldn't help but note that having a woman of color win the prize instead made it much better.

"A woman of color, on the International Court of Justice for her work vs genocide, war crimes etc. That was a direct shot from the committee at Trump, Bibi [and] Putin. So Trump is gonna be p——," biomedical engineering student Ben Johnson replied.

South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay was named on Friday as the award winner “for her efforts to promote peace and international law," ABC News reports.

In 1967, Pillay became the first woman to open a law practice in South Africa’s Natal province, defending anti-apartheid activists. She became the first Black woman appointed to South Africa’s High Court in 1995, the details on the Nobel website said.

She also served as a United Nations high commissioner for human rights, so the committee highlighted her decades of legal experience in pursuing justice and accountability on the international stage.

The committee’s choice of Pillay focused on her lifetime of defending human rights and strengthening international justice.

Previous U.S. winners include former President Jimmy Carter, Vice President Al Gore and former President Barack Obama.

Trump has lobbied for the award but has never secured it.

Norwegian politicians fear that Trump could retaliate against their country if he doesn't win the prize, the Washington Post reported Thursday.

As the Post noted, vice rector for research at Oslo New University College Kjetil Tronvoll argued the committee should "suspend the prize for three years until he steps down, in order for him not to be unnecessarily provoked by it."

“Peace-promoting activities are more needed than any time before,” Tronvoll said. “But the prize committee has earlier shown very much a lack of contextual, deeper global knowledge to understand how sensitive this prize is, and they don’t do enough due diligence and risk-awareness analysis.”

title: Yemen is spiralling into another civil war that could swiftly engulf in the entire region
content:
The Middle East has seen many explosions of violence in recent years. But while the US-Iran war has grabbed the headlines this year, the rapidly escalating conflict between the Houthis and Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia risks becoming just as consequential for the region.

The complexity of Yemen’s internal conflict cannot be underestimated. The violence is linked to two major regional powers – Iran and Saudi Arabia – as well as the ongoing US-Israel confrontation with Iran over the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran backs the Houthis (also known as Ansar Allah or Partisans of God), while Saudi Arabia supports the Yemeni government (known as the Presidential Leadership Council or PLC). The United States is also standing beside its de facto ally, the Saudis, while Russia and China are aligned with Iran.

And Riyadh’s other regional allies, Turkey and Pakistan, have just agreed to activate their newly signed mutual defence pact and deploy troops to help defend Saudi Arabia if it’s attacked again.

Given how many actors are involved, the conflict could quickly spiral out of control and engulf the entire region, further destabilising global fuel supplies.

Houthis gaining ground

The US-Iran war has reached a stalemate in recent months. Tehran remains adamant that it controls the Strait of Hormuz, a conduit for 20% of the world’s daily supply of oil and liquefied natural gas before the war. And US President Donald Trump has been running hot and cold about how to end the conflict. Neither America’s military might, nor its maximum economic pressure, has worked so far.

Tehran’s Houthi allies, who control one-third of Yemen (including the capital Sanaa), entered the fray to support Iran earlier this year. They have tightened their control of the vital Bab al-Mandab Strait that connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean.

And they have made territorial gains in Yemen since July, with the aim of taking over the whole country, while also attacking Saudi oil facilities, tankers and its main airport in Riyadh. An attack in recent days again halted the pumping of oil through the East-West Pipeline, which Riyadh has been using to export oil via Bab al Mandab since the closure of the Strait of Hormuz.

Yemeni and Saudi forces have launched a counteroffensive in recent days in an attempt to retake all the territory held by the Houthis, raising the spectre of a return to a major civil war and a potentially dire humanitarian crisis for Yemenis.

Riyadh has asked Washington to carry out airstrikes on the Houthis, but Trump has declined the request to get actively involved, instead offering support from US intelligence and military analysts in the country.

Trump has been disinclined to expand the US-Iran war and get the US embroiled in another conflict while the potential for a restart of the war with Iran remains very real.

In addition, despite his denials that he is concerned, Trump will no doubt be aware of the impact of the Iran war on American consumers, with higher petroleum prices and cost of living pressures. His Republican Party is urgently trying to shore up its voter base with the midterm elections now just a month away.

Without direct US involvement, Riyadh has looked for support from its new security partners, Pakistan and Turkey. Before committing to deploy military forces to Saudi Arabia this week, the two had appeared cautious about getting involved – caught between the need to support Saudi Arabia and not to offend Iran and its strategic partners, Russia and China.

The renewed conflict has already taken a very heavy toll on the Yemeni people, with more than 800 killed, 3,000 injured and 158,000 displaced. This comes on the top of the hundreds of thousands of people who have died since the civil war and Saudi-led intervention began in 2014–15. These deaths were due to fighting, as well as indirect impacts such as hunger, disease, and lack of health services and infrastructure.

Where is this going?

The worse the fighting becomes in Yemen, the greater the impact on the world economy.

While the Strait of Hormuz remains partially inoperable due to the fear of ships being attacked, some tankers have managed to sail through after making deals with Iran’s new Persian Gulf Strait Authority, or with US escort protection.

The US energy secretary, Chris Wright, recently claimed 13 million barrels of crude oil were getting through the strait daily. This has been disputed by Iran.

On October 4, Iran’s parliamentary speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, said the strait will not reopen fully until the US meets Iranian demands. These include a ceasefire on all fronts, the lifting of the US blockade of Iranian ports and the unfreezing of Iran’s assets.

And after the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi ports and started attacking Saudi-linked ships in the Red Sea in July, disruptions in the global oil supply are expected to worsen.

At the root of this expanding and multi-dimensional crisis is the US war of choice against Iran. If Trump does escalate that conflict with more lethal force, Tehran is prepared to retaliate. It has warned the US’ Arab allies in the Gulf they could be targeted more severely than before.

The overall situation remains very explosive, unless Washington and Tehran pull back from the brink and opt for a negotiated deal. This seems like a distant goal, but it is still possible.

Amin Saikal does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.

title: Three years after October 7, global attention on Gaza has receded. The real test will come after Israel’s election
content:
This week marks three years since Hamas’ massacre of October 7 2023, in which some 1,200 people, most of them Israeli civilians, were killed and 251 taken hostage.

What followed were two years of devastating war waged by the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) in Gaza, which a UN commission of inquiry, leading genocide scholars and major human rights organisations have concluded amounted to genocide. Much of the strip lies in ruins and more than 74,000 Palestinians are dead, with thousands more believed to remain buried under the rubble.

A year ago this week, a US-imposed ceasefire was finally forced on both sides – though mainly on paper. While major IDF assaults have ceased, Israeli attacks in Gaza have continued, in addition to unbridled Jewish settler violence in the West Bank.

Despite this, global attention on Gaza has waned. As the US–Israeli war with Iran began dominating the headlines, earlier pledges by many states to help drive the peace process forward have proved once again wanting, even hollow.

Now, Israel is preparing for a highly polarised parliamentary election on October 27, which could be consequential for the entire region. If a less extreme government takes office, will the world’s attention to Gaza and the West Bank – and the pressure it has generated – hold?

What the peace plan delivered, and what it didn’t

The first phase of US President Donald Trump’s 20-point plan in Gaza largely succeeded. The remaining living Israeli hostages came home in exchange for close to 2,000 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, and the remains of deceased hostages were returned over the following months. Hundreds of thousands of displaced Gazans moved back to the north. Israeli forces pulled back to a “yellow line”, and the UN Security Council endorsed the plan and a US-chaired “Board of Peace”.

However, the world’s expectations for “all guns to fall silent” were soon dashed. A year after the ceasefire was signed on October 9 2025, the Gaza Health Ministry, whose figures the UN uses, reports close to 1,400 Gazans have been killed.

Aid remains restricted, meaningful reconstruction has yet to begin, and another winter is approaching for families living in tents and damaged buildings.

Without sustained international engagement, the second phase of the Trump plan has largely stalled. Hamas has not disarmed. An International Stabilisation Force intended to bring security to Gaza has yet to deploy, despite a US commander being appointed in January. And the technocratic Palestinian committee meant to run Gaza has not taken control on the ground.

Only last week did the Board of Peace unveil a six-month, US$2.45 billion plan to begin rebuilding, but this is a fraction of the US$71.4 billion it estimates recovery will require over a decade.

And all of this depends on Hamas surrendering its weapons. Israel will not allow reconstruction before full disarmament, and Hamas will not disarm on the plan’s terms. Reform of the domestically unpopular Palestinian Authority has been slow, and Israel’s right-wing government has been in campaign mode for months, with strong incentives to spoil the progress.

Recognition of Palestine by more than 150 states has not changed the reality on the ground. The international pressure that helped bring about the ceasefire has proved much harder to sustain since the worst of the violence ended.

Attention faded, but did not disappear

Media and public attention to distant atrocities is notoriously short-lived. It peaks with the most extreme violence and quickly subsides once violence becomes chronic, or once another crisis begins to dominate the news.

Gaza has followed part of this script. As mass casualty bombardments gave way to near-daily “lower-intensity” attacks, headlines receded. The US–Israeli war with Iran, which began in late February, absorbed much of the world’s limited attention span. Ukraine and, in short bursts, Lebanon, competed for what remained.

Most people rank foreign crises far below domestic concerns – health care, jobs and the cost of living – and the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has reached directly into people’s pockets through the price of petrol. Gaza, for most, never did.

A year ago, I warned that once the mass violence in Gaza ended, international attention would wane, making it easier for either side to derail the peace process. That is largely what happened, but not entirely.

What stands out about the past year is less the weakening of attention to Gaza than the extent to which some of it remained. While mass opinion largely moved on, elite opinion (some legislators, officials, commentators) and the smaller but highly committed body of concerned global citizens did not.

The latter drew on a Palestinian solidarity movement built over decades, turning outrage into a sustained global campaign – though some of their rhetoric and tactics also deepened polarisation, at home and in Israel.

Sudan, meanwhile, which the UN has described as the world’s largest humanitarian crisis, shows the flip side. With no equivalent global campaign behind it, it has struggled to hold the world’s gaze.

The invisibility of one crisis and the hyper-visibility of another are two faces of the same problem: which atrocities galvanise public opinion depends less on their severity than on who is organised enough to make us pay attention.

A deepening crisis in the West Bank

The sustained, if narrower, global pressure campaign on Gaza soon had a new source of outrage: settler violence in the West Bank.

The United Nations had recorded an average of six settler attacks on Palestinians a day by June of this year, a pace higher than any year on record. By July, killings linked to settler attacks had exceeded the total for all of 2025. Thousands of Palestinians have also been displaced as settlement expansion has accelerated.

Some European governments had already banned trade with the settlements; others, such as the United Kingdom, more recently found they could no longer afford to ignore the crisis. In September, London announced its ban, with Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband accusing “settler terrorists” of ethnic cleansing.

Although the European Union is Israel’s largest trading partner and the UK another important one, the economic impact of these measures will be modest since settlements export relatively little. The significance is mainly political.

Moreover, if the European pressure is meant in part to sway Israeli voters before the election, it’s unclear how effective it will be. Outside pressure before an election tends to rally a leader’s loyal base, and the global outrage over Gaza has already reinforced a siege mentality among many Israeli Jews.

The real external pressure, however, will need to come after the election.

The decisive stick for moving the peace process forward lies in Washington, given how much any Israeli government depends on US support. The main carrot for Israel would be normalisation of relations with Saudi Arabia – and with it much of the Arab and Muslim world. But this is a reward Riyadh has tied to a credible path to Palestinian statehood.

Another factor will weigh even more, and it is often underestimated: the Israeli public’s profound need for a sense of security.

Shattered on October 7, this need helps explain how the war in Gaza was fought, though it cannot excuse it – just as no grievance, whatever its roots, could justify Hamas’ massacre of civilians.

It will now shape how Israelis vote – and what any new government believes it can risk – far more than sticks or carrots from abroad.

Read more: Could a former IDF chief break Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power in Israel?

The harder test: shades of grey

Last year, I argued that meaningful progress in Gaza and the West Bank would require an Israeli government willing to make hard choices.

The October 27 election will be a test of whether one emerges. Polls suggest Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar could become the largest party in the Knesset (Israel’s parliament), but it may struggle to form a governing coalition without the support of Arab-Israeli parties, a prospect Eisenkot has refused to embrace.

A change of government would matter. It could bring a real effort to rein in settler violence, a more cooperative approach to the Board of Peace’s efforts in Gaza, and a state inquiry into the October 7 attacks.

However, it is less likely to bring a fundamental change in policy on Israel’s illegal occupation of the Palestinian territories. Eisenkot has ruled out a Palestinian state for the foreseeable future, and any coalition he leads would probably include right-wing partners.

Herein lies a paradox. Global action is most easily mobilised against clearly villainous actions and actors. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s current coalition, including far-right ministers such as Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich, has made the case for international pressure easy.

A more moderate-sounding, centre-right government would make it much harder to sustain. Governments that could not ignore Israel’s conduct under Netanyahu may ease off their pressure. Some media may treat an Eisenkot-led victory as a path towards resolution, and concerned citizens may struggle to keep people’s attention focused on an occupation that grinds on more quietly.

If sustained attention depends on extreme cases, then the quieter periods in between are where policies stall and abuses continue. The past year suggests that outrage alone cannot carry meaningful pressure through those periods.

Three years after October 7, the guns in Gaza are quieter, but far from silent. The question for the year ahead is whether the world keeps listening.

Eyal Mayroz served as a counterterrorism specialist with the Israeli Defense Forces in the 1980s.

title: Could a former IDF chief break Benjamin Netanyahu’s grip on power in Israel?
content:
Israel is heading to the polls on October 27 and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is facing perhaps the toughest political battle of his career.

He’s facing fresh allegations that he was warned of a major Hamas plot ahead of the October 7 attacks.

Professor of Israel Studies Dov Waxman tells The Conversation Weekly although Netanyahu denies it, many hold him personally responsible for the attacks because he didn’t take those warnings seriously.

Netanyahu has consistently deflected any kind of blame and has basically pointed the finger at the Israeli army, at the Israeli military. This is something that I think many Israelis are really appalled by: his refusal to take any sort of personal responsibility.

He’s also facing a new challenger: former chief of the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) and leader of the newly formed Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot.

Waxman says part of Eisenkot’s appeal is his authenticity. Eisenkot’s own son and two of his nephews died during the war in Gaza.

Clearly his own personal loss is part of the narrative he’s presented to the Israeli public about why there needs to be a change of government in Israel.

So who is Gadi Eisenkot, the career military man who could unseat Israel’s long-time leader?

Waxman says Eisenkot is considered to be on the centre right politically, but isn’t considered an ideologue.

[Eisenkot has] pledged that a government that he would lead would not establish or recognise the Palestinian state. When it comes to Israeli settlements in the West Bank, he is supportive of Israel’s settlement. At the same time, he has condemned settler violence in describing it as terrorism.

So he doesn’t share the same views as Netanyahu, but he’s certainly hawkish and on the right.

Regardless of whoever leads Israel over the next four years, Waxman says we shouldn’t expect a radical change in policy or its relationship with neighbouring states.

I don’t think this election is likely to result in any sort of really dramatic changes in Israel’s policies on the most important questions facing the country — namely the Palestinian question.

If Israel remains on its present course, that I think points to a direction of even greater international isolation and further kinds of extreme policies.

It’s not so much that things would change dramatically for the better if the opposition comes to power [but] things could get even worse if the current government remains.

Disclosure statement & credits

Dov Waxman is currently the scholar in residence at the Nexus Project, a non-profit organisation focused on combating antisemitism.

Newsclips in this episode from AP, BBC News, ABC News, CBS News and 9News.

title: Flydubai attack feeds into Netanyahu’s ‘protector’ narrative with crucial elections approaching
content:
The apparent attempted hijacking of a Flydubai flight carrying 170 mostly Israeli passengers was another reminder to Israelis of the constant threat of terror and war. Only the bravery of the chief pilot and passengers prevented a major disaster.

A few hours earlier, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu released a video warning of attempts to harm Israelis in the lead-up to the country’s general election on October 27. Initially, his opponents criticised this as a stunt to divert public discourse towards security concerns, and away from his part in the devastating failures that enabled the October 7 Hamas attacks.

But after the suspected terror incident on the Flydubai plane, Netanyahu can claim he was right. With the elections approaching, the longest-serving prime minister in Israel’s history is hoping he can still restore his image as “the protector of Israel”.

Netanyahu was quick to incorporate the plane attack into his campaign by posting on his social media accounts a video and images of him embracing and praising one of the passengers (a Netanyahu supporter) who stormed the cockpit, his shirt still stained with blood.

Growing criticism over October 7 failures

Despite public outcry, Netanyahu refuses to accept blame for the October 7 attack. He has blocked the creation of a judicial commission of inquiry to investigate what led to the attack, while failing in his attempts to set up a different investigative committee more favourable to him.

Netanyahu has repeatedly argued that security officials failed to warn him of the impending assault, saying “if they had woken him up” earlier on October 7, “things would have been very different”.

Recent reports, however, paint a different picture. Numerous media outlets have reported that Israel’s security agencies, as well as Netanyahu himself, received explicit warnings days before the 2023 attack. These came from high-ranking Arab officials (Egypt’s intelligence minister) and leaders (the United Arab Emirates’ Mohammad bin Zaid). A new book also claims Netanyahu received a direct warning from Hamas’ leader, Yahya Sinwar, the mastermind of the attack.

The prime minister and his top security officials, however, understood these warnings of an “earthquake” (to use Sinwar’s own term) erupting in Gaza as a demand for economic concessions for Palestinians.

Israeli decision-makers were captive to what is called a conceptzia in Israel – a detailed and entrenched set of assumptions about the enemy’s capabilities and intentions. (The term was coined to describe Israel’s intelligence failures before the 1973 Arab-Israeli war.)

In 2023, Netanyahu’s conceptzia, supported by many security officials who misread or were fooled by Sinwar, was that Qatari money going to Hamas would “buy quiet”, in the words of his critics.

Netanyahu approved the transfer of millions of dollars from Qatar to Gaza from 2018 onward. Yet, instead of assisting needy Gazans, Israeli intelligence believe much of these funds ended up feeding the growth of Hamas’ military abilities and underground terror infrastructure.

Can the opposition capitalise?

In the election, Netanyahu is facing strong opposition from the “ABBA” (Anyone But Bibi Again, in reference to Netanyahu’s nickname) bloc. His main rival is the Yashar! Party (which translates as “direct” or “straightforward”), headed by a former head of the Israel Defense Forces, Gadi Eisenkot, whose son was killed in the Gaza war.

Polls consistently suggest Yashar! will be the biggest party after the elections. Yet, forming a coalition may prove difficult because Eisenkot’s bloc is made up of a mishmash of right, left and centre-aligned parties, with little common ground except their goal of ousting Netanyahu. A similar coalition, under Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid, fell apart quickly in 2022.

Furthermore, many Zionist parties demand the next government be “Zionist-only”, refusing to participate in a coalition that includes the Arab Islamic party Ra’am.

Ra’am was the missing piece that enabled the creation of the Bennett-Lapid government after four consecutive elections ended in 2022 without anyone having a path to a governing majority. Without Ra’am, the ABBA bloc may not be able to form a coalition.

The fate of a few small parties that must pass the vote threshold to sit in the Knesset is a wild card that is almost impossible to predict. If votes from the pro- or anti-Bibi blocs are wasted on small parties that fail to meet the threshold, this could dramatically affect the result.

Until recently, the polls were consistently pointing to a change of government being likely. But in recent weeks, the polls have tightened between the pro- and anti-Netanyahu blocs because they do not count the Arab parties and centre-right Hendel/Zelekha party. (It remains to be seen if this party will even pass the threshold.)

October 7 looms large over the vote

A few days before the election, Israelis will sombrely commemorate the third anniversary of the October 7 terror attack. Almost 1,200 Israelis of all ages were massacred on that Black Saturday, with some 250 people kidnapped, countless women raped and whole neighbourhoods pillaged and destroyed.

In the war in Gaza that followed, more than 70,000 Palestinians have been killed, with vast stretches of the enclave left in ruins and 1.2 million people left without homes.

October 7 is everywhere in the heated election campaign. Many candidates are family members of victims or soldiers injured in the war. A poll of the unprecedented large number of young, first-time voters revealed that October 7 has dramatically shifted their views to the right.

What will worry many Israelis most is the election will again end with a deadlock. The Jewish state urgently needs a leader that can safely steer it in the face of increasing criticism over the Gaza war, a wave of ugly antisemitism globally and now incidents like the attempted Flydubai hijacking.

Netanyahu will certainly be seeking to project himself as the person who can meet these challenges – but so, too, will his opponents.

Ran Porat is a research associate at The Australia/Israel & Jewish Affairs Council (AIJAC) and Research Fellow at the International Institute for Counter-Terrorism, Reichman University, Herzliya, Israel. He is also a former IDF military intelligence officer.

title: Rubio hired tech firm after Kremlin-link warnings surfaced: report
content:
The State Department Secretary Marco Rubio awarded a $50,000 contract to Oxygen Forensics months after allegations about the firm’s Russian ownership and links to Kremlin agencies circulated within the federal government, according to a report.

PunchUp reported that the State Department granted the contract on August 28 via the U.S. Embassy in Zagreb, Croatia. The records indicate that the purchase order amounting to $49,999.76 was for "ICITAP - OXYGEN SOFTWARE", which is supporting a Justice Department initiative that collaborates with foreign law enforcement agencies. The award has a possible end date of September 1, 2027.

The contract was reached several months after Max Weissberg, a former employee of Oxygen, made a public claim that the Virginia-based company had been secretly controlled by Russian interests and that its software had been developed in Russia. According to PunchUp, Oxygen admitted in a lawsuit filed in August that government customers had asked the company about Weissberg's allegations as early as February 23 and that a document relating to the claims had been circulated among the Department of Homeland Security and other federal agencies.

Oxygen brought its lawsuit against Weissberg on August 28, the same day the contract with the State Department was awarded. The company rejected his claims, charged him with defamation and demanded damages in excess of $1.85 million.

On September 23, the Justice Department announced that Lee Reiber, the CEO of Oxygen, and the Russian national Oleg Sergeyevich Davydov had been arrested and accused of conspiring to commit wire fraud. The prosecutors claim that Reiber had hidden from American agencies the fact that Oxygen had been owned and controlled by five Russian nationals via a holding company based in Cyprus and that the company's software had been developed in Russia.

Federal prosecutors state that those same five Russians were also the owners of a Russian company which supplied versions of the software to customers allegedly comprising the Federal Security Service, the Investigative Committee of Russia, and the Ministry of Internal Affairs. It is alleged that the Russian owners of Oxygen kept on making major decisions of the company after their names had been taken off the public corporate records as a result of the broadened U.S. sanctions against Russia in 2022.

The Justice Department stated that its complaint does not claim that Oxygen's software included malicious code or had been used to gain unauthorized access to customers' systems or data; Reiber and Davydov are considered innocent until they have been proven guilty.

PunchUp also stated that in May 2025 the State Department gave Oxygen a contract which could be worth about $180,664.

When asked if the officials had known about the ownership allegations at the time the August agreement was approved, the State Department told PunchUp that it was “aware” of the claims and said it “takes seriously the security of its systems and the integrity of its procurement processes.”

title: Trump opens door to Russia deal that could enrage even his own GOP allies
content:
President Donald Trump has supported a plan that involves giving Russia some sanctions relief in return for the release of political prisoners, a move that could cause his administration to be at odds with Ukraine, the European governments and certain Republicans in Congress.

According to a report by The Atlantic, the initiative was put forward by John Coale, Trump's envoy to Eastern Europe, and it’s still in its early phases. Coale said to the magazine that he mentioned the idea to Trump following their talks about the release of prisoners, including Russian journalist and Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov, and that the president had then agreed for him to go ahead with it.

According to the proposal, Moscow would set free dissidents, journalists and other prisoners, while Washington could reply by relaxing a number of its economic restrictions. In Belarus, Coale has previously employed a similar strategy, whereby U.S. negotiations led to the release of hundreds of prisoners as Washington waived some of its sanctions and looked into trade agreements.

As Coale told The Atlantic, “All this stuff works toward the possibility of peace. The more interaction, the more trade-offs — either economic, prisoners, or whatever — leads step by step toward, hopefully, peace.”

The proposal follows by only a few weeks on the back of Trump signing legislation that authorizes tougher sanctions against Russia and countries that are carrying on major economic transactions with Moscow. According to Reuters, the law permits tariffs of up to 100 per cent to be applied to imports from countries that maintain significant trade with Russia or Iran.

Some lawmakers have urged Trump to impose greater costs on Moscow over the war in Ukraine, and therefore a shift towards sanctions relief could lead to tension within Trump's own party, especially if Russia has not agreed to a cease-fire.

Republicans, such as Sen. Mitch McConnell, have argued for tougher actions against Russia, while all but seven House GOP members backed the sanctions Trump signed last month.

Volodymyr Zelensky, Ukraine's president, has also stated that sanctions should not be relaxed before the fighting is over. Speaking to The Atlantic, he said that he would attempt to “block” such a decision and cautioned the United Nations that greater trade with Russia could provide Moscow with more resources to keep the war going.

“When someone gives Russia more money through trade, they give this war more time,” Zelensky said.

The White House stated that Trump was still focused on arriving at a settlement. According to an official speaking to The Atlantic, the President and his team are firmly committed to carrying on a constructive role in bringing about an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine.

Coale's suggestion could also open the way for renewed business relations between the United States and Russia in the areas of energy, minerals and other commodities. The basis of his approach is the belief that economic engagement can reduce tensions and provide incentives for peace.

Ukraine, together with a number of European officials, has adopted the contrary view, stating that the sanctions should stay in place as long as Russia carries on its military campaign.

title: New White House claim exposes Trump’s 'incoherence and incompetence'
content:
New claims out of the White House are "mind-boggling," according to a new analysis from MS NOW, and further expose President Donald Trump's "remarkable combination of incoherence and incompetence."

Trump recently hosted a controversial state visit from Chinese President Xi Jinping last week, after which David Perdue, the U.S. ambassador to China, made the "mind-boggling" claim that the president had asked his counterpart if he wanted to purchase American military hardware. Trump himself later denied hearing about such an offer, but also added, "they’d probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that, so maybe it’s a good idea."

Perdue's explanation came as he broke down Trump's conversation with Xi about U.S. arms sales to Taiwan, a longstanding point of contention with China. Trump supposedly tried to downplay the relationship, as Perdue explained it, arguing, 'Hey, we sell arms to other people around the world,' before he then “actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some at one point?' Official statements from the White House and State Department did not dispute that Trump brought up the idea to Xi, but stressed that no official offer is in place.

"This scenario, if true, is mind-boggling," MS NOW reporter Zeeshan Aleem wrote. "And if Perdue’s claims are not true and he was saying something false, that’s a significant and confounding problem, too, because it would not just be a major lie, but a foolish one... China is the only country in the world that threatens the U.S.’ status as the world’s preeminent military power, and the U.S. takes great pains to guard its technological edge against its rivals... Selling highly coveted U.S. arms to China would undermine the U.S.’ military advantage. It is common sense to not empower a country that lands on the opposite side of a lot of global geopolitical jockeying. Given that, for example, Trump asked Xi to curb assistance to Iran, it would not make sense to boost Beijing’s arsenal."

He added further: "If Trump made the offer, it would demonstrate total incoherence on China policy in the administration. Under the One China policy that has governed U.S. policy since 1979, the U.S. officially acknowledges China’s position on Taiwan but maintains informal diplomatic ties with the island nation, and crucially, routinely supplies it with billions of dollars worth of defensive arms... If the U.S. were to sell arms to China, it would undermine that entire calculation and would be akin to scoring an own goal."

Aleem also noted that, despite the alarming nature of the alleged offer, it was on some level "not surprising at all" coming from Trump, given that "he lacks even a rudimentary knowledge of how things like trade and diplomacy work, and has an even poorer grasp of — or commitment to — U.S. traditions in those spheres." It would have also fit with his well-established tendency to flout long-standing ties with democratic allies in order to better align himself with authoritarian states, whose leaders he openly admires.

"The capitals of the world are always watching Washington closely," Aleem concluded. "This episode shows a president who seems to have fewer and fewer wits about him — and a staff that lacks the competence or willpower to make up for it."

title: Privatised aid failed the people of Gaza. The world should learn not to repeat it
content:
For six months in 2025, the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation operated a radically different model for delivering food to Palestinians in Gaza.

The foundation didn’t disclose its donors, but received at least US$30 million from the US government. Many established aid organisations refused to cooperate, citing concerns about transparency and independent oversight.

Instead of distributing aid through hundreds of established humanitarian sites, the foundation concentrated distribution at just four heavily secured sites. Three were in a military zone in southern Gaza and one was in central Gaza City. Armed private security contractors helped operate the system.

The foundation says it distributed 187 million meals and demonstrated there was a better way to deliver aid to Gaza, which is reported to be adopted in US President Donald Trump’s Peace plan.

My new research shows this privatised, militarised model should stand as a warning against the risks of transforming humanitarian relief in occupied territories from an instrument of protection to one of control.

Protecting civilians

Humanitarian assistance in occupied territories must comply with international humanitarian law and human rights obligations. These are designed not merely to put food in civilian hands, but to protect the people receiving it.

Under these laws, the occupying power bears extensive obligations towards the civilian population.

These include ensuring access to essentials such as food and medical supplies, and facilitating humanitarian relief where the population is inadequately supplied.

An occupying power can regulate humanitarian operations for legitimate security reasons. It can inspect consignments, verify their humanitarian character and take measures to prevent aid being diverted for military purposes.

But those powers have limits.

Humanitarian relief must remain impartial and needs-based. Civilians must be treated humanely and without discrimination. Relief operations must also be sufficiently independent of political and military objectives to retain their humanitarian character.

This is where the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation model becomes legally problematic.

From hundreds of aid sites to four

Before the foundation began operating, humanitarian assistance had been distributed through more than 400 UN-coordinated sites across Gaza.

The foundation replaced this network with four large distribution sites. Their location was crucial.

Civilians south of Wadi Gaza could reach them only using routes that took them through heavily armed Israeli military units and bases.

People in northern Gaza faced long journeys. Access was particularly difficult for vulnerable people, including women, children, older people and people with disabilities.

Distribution was also unpredictable. At times, civilians received only minutes’ notice that a site was opening. Sometimes those sites would remain open only for very short periods.

This transformed receiving food into a potentially dangerous journey.

International humanitarian law requires aid to be distributed according to humanitarian need. A system that makes access particularly difficult for some of the most vulnerable civilians raises serious questions about whether it satisfies that requirement.

Privatising human need

The Gaza Humanitarian Foundation model also relied heavily on private security contractors.

Safe Reach Solutions provided security logistics, while UG Solutions secured distribution sites and interacted directly with Palestinians.

Some contractors reportedly had little or no humanitarian experience. Contractors were armed, and draft rules of engagement were reportedly provided only after distribution operations had already begun.

Private security companies are not automatically incompatible with humanitarian operations. They can, for example, protect civilians, escort aid convoys and secure humanitarian facilities.

But the distinction between protecting humanitarian operations and performing military or governmental security functions is important.

My research argues activities such as coercive crowd control, intelligence gathering, security screening and the use of force in civilian settings risk crossing that line.

Reports that contractors monitored people considered “suspicious”, shared information with the Israeli military and operated alongside facial-recognition surveillance, further blurred the distinction between humanitarian assistance and security operations.

Civilians paid the price

The consequences were serious.

Aid distribution points became sites of crowding, stampedes and shootings.

Thousands of Palestinians were reported killed or injured around distribution sites and aid routes.

Israel disputed casualty figures and maintained live fire near humanitarian centres was prohibited, except in response to an immediate threat to life.

Whatever disputes remain about individual incidents, the broader legal question cannot be avoided.

A humanitarian system should reduce civilian vulnerability. It should not require hungry civilians to expose themselves repeatedly to foreseeable danger to obtain food.

Outsourcing responsibility

There is another important lesson from the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation experiment.

Governments increasingly rely on private companies to perform functions once carried out by states or established humanitarian organisations.

But outsourcing a function does not necessarily outsource legal responsibility.

Under the Fourth Geneva Convention, an occupying power remains responsible for the treatment of protected civilians by those acting under its authority or control.

This means replacing an established humanitarian network with a privately administered system does not remove the occupying power’s underlying obligations to keep civilians safe.

Beyond Gaza

The Gaza Humanitarian Foundation operated for only six months, but its significance may extend much further.

The danger is that highly militarised private aid systems become a model for humanitarian assistance in future conflicts and occupations.

Humanitarian relief cannot be judged simply by how much food is delivered and distributed. It must also be judged by who can reach that food, what risks they must take to obtain it, whether assistance is distributed according to need, and whether the system protects human dignity and civilian life.

When access to food becomes connected to surveillance, forced movement, confinement or exposure to violence, the boundary between humanitarian assistance and military control begins to disappear.

This can be incompatible with international humanitarian law, but also with the central reason for relief operations to exist in the first place: to get essential goods to innocent civilians in war zones.

Shannon Bosch does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organisation that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
