title: Florida 'paying big price' for Trump’s Canadian trade war
content:
The U.S. has such a toxic brand that, despite the huge World Cup events, folks don't want to come to the U.S. on vacation and spend hefty tourism dollars.

Axios reported the new numbers this week, and a CNN report noted Monday the U.S. suffered a 20 percent drop in tourism in 2026 from 2025.

The U.S. Travel Association president Geoff Freeman explained that it isn't something happening around the world. This significant drop is coming from tourism only to the United States.

"Travel around the world is growing at a 5 to 10 percent clip, and it's dropping to the U.S. in the same numbers," he said.

CNN co-host Boris Sanchez asked how it would have been different if there hadn't been a huge World Cup event, and Freeman agreed it would have been far worse.

"This is a trend," he explained. "We welcomed nearly 80 million visitors in 2019. We haven't gotten back to that number any year since. While the rest of the world continues to grow, we obviously need to revisit our strategy to figure out what we're going to do to turn the tide."

There were already huge drops in tourism amid the COVID-19 pandemic. Now those numbers are falling even more.

It prompted the CNN hosts to ask what could possibly be causing this anti-American sentiment.

Freeman explained that it's more than just one specific thing.

"There's a variety of reasons they're not coming," he said. "Cost matters. It's because of the war in Ukraine. You can't fly over Russian airspace for Asian travelers. Certainly there are some for whom politics matters, and they're swearing off the United States. I think what's happening more often than not, though, is travelers are reading the foreign press. They're seeing these horror stories. They're worried that if I come here, I'm going to get detained. My device is going to be searched. They're fearful."

One story reported by The Guardian revealed 65-year-old British tourist Karen Newton was detained for six weeks after her tourist visa to the U.S. expired.

Becky Burke, a 28-year-old Welsh backpacker, was held for 19 days and led away in chains. The U.S. claimed she had to be detained "related to the violation of the terms and conditions of her admission." Burke's mother said she thinks the authorities misunderstood. She said that her daughter was trading work around the house for stays at various accommodations, the BBC reported. Burke's mother thinks that they considered this "employment" in the U.S. when she wasn't approved for that.

Still, Freeman said that stories like those are "a misperception of what happens."

He claimed that the World Cup helped dispel a lot of those stories, but it didn't help reset beliefs around the world about the U.S.

Given most tourism is to states like California, Florida, New York and Texas, Freeman said that those states are experiencing huge increases in cost.

"Florida is paying a big price for the drop in Canadian visitation," said Freeman. Canadians began boycotting the U.S. amid President Donald Trump's trade war.

Freeman explained that it isn't merely tourism; Canadian business travel has also fallen.

"People who would come to buy a Caterpillar tractor, they would come to go look at another American good. They're deciding to go to another country right now," said Freeman. "That's the loss we're feeling. Not to mention the fact that these people that come here, we know when they're here, they enjoy their time. They go home and tell their friends and family about the experience they had. When they don't come, it doesn't just cost us now. It costs us down the road because we continue to drive these travelers into the arms of other countries."

title: Trump may have blown the cover on a terror investigation tied to key US base
content:
Five men were released on bail after being arrested on suspicion of a terrorist attack in the U.K. on a base that has been helping the U.S. launch bombs into Iran.

Reporter and author James Ball wrote for The iPaper that there are still few facts available, but that a tip from a "concerned passerby" may have been what alerted authorities to a possible attack on RAF Fairford base in Gloucestershire.

It was "significant" enough that new Prime Minister Andy Burnham skipped a political football match at a Labor Party conference, said Bell.

RAF Fairford is the United States’ principal European forward operating site for long-range heavy bombers. So, if there were a successful terrorist attack, it could be a serious disruption to President Donald Trump's ongoing war with Iran. It would also make for a serious security crisis for both countries. The base is visibly associated with the U.S., though it remains on U.K. soil. So, even if an attack were limited, it would be seen as an escalation in the war with Iran.

Since it's a place with a lot of munitions, homes nearby could also be affected by such an attack. It means a high number of U.K. civilians would likely be harmed.

Bell explained that under normal circumstances, "the U.S. and U.K. governments would carefully coordinate to make sure their messaging was entirely in line in such situations."

But then there's Trump, who Bell characterized as not having the time to "bother with such details."

Popping off to reporters, Trump implied that the U.S. was somehow involved with the operation and then leaked details about the specifics publicly.

“We had them under investigation,” Trump said. “They were looking to do big ⁠damage to our fort and working with the British worked out great … we had them under view for a long time.”

He called them “fantastic” arrests and praised the “amazing job” the police had done. The problem, Bell explained, is that the U.K. never disclosed anything about the suspects, the duration of an operation or whether RAF Fairford was a possible terrorist target.

"It is hardly out of character for Trump to run roughshod over such national security concerns, though: over his two terms, he has built up a consistent pattern of being utterly unable to keep his mouth shut when a chance to show off – or to make a threat – presents itself," wrote Bell for iPaper.

Trump disclosing classified information isn't anything new. In one recorded conversation with reporters, Trump had an aide bring a classified military operation map he'd taken from the White House and showed it to the group. In another incident, Trump showed foreign leaders where the U.S. had stashed its nuclear submarines. He even told former dictator Rodrigo Duterte that he had two nuclear subs near North Korea.

Trump even leaked police investigation information from the 2017 bombing of the Manchester Arena.

He has also tweeted sensitive satellite intelligence images of a failed satellite launch in Iran that Israel's government shared with him.

Bell noted that last year, the Dutch decided that they'd begin restricting what intelligence they shared with the U.S. out of fears that there could be a “politicization of our intelligence and the violation of human rights."

Trump will be gone on Jan. 20, 2029, the report noted. Until then, Bell said most are "keeping their heads down" and keeping up whatever business they can.

National security is something different, however. "When the U.K. is trying to deal with what could be complex national security problems, not being able to rely on the discretion of the U.S. president is a major headache."

Bell closed by saying, "Trump’s indiscretion on this occasion will almost certainly prove to be harmless. Next time, we might not be so lucky."

title: GOP revolt grows as Trump gives 'stature and legitimacy' to Putin
content:
On December 14–15, 2026, the Group of 20 Leaders’ Summit (G-20) will be held at U.S. President Donald Trump's resort in Doral, Florida near Miami. Trump invited Russian President Vladmir Putin to attend, but on Friday, September 25, a group of seven Republican senators joined Democrats in urging Trump to "reconsider" the invitation.

In a bipartisan letter to Trump, the seven Republican senators — Texas' John Cornyn, Mississippi's Roger Wicker, Kansas Jerry Moran, North Carolina's Thom Tillis, Utah's John Curtis, Oklahoma's Alan Armstrong and former Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Kentucky) — wrote, "Given President Putin's continued actions against the Ukrainian people and U.S. national security interests, we urge you to reconsider granting President Putin the stature and legitimacy to appear in the United States as a world leader at the G20 Leaders' Summit."

The Democratic senators who signed the letter included Rhode Island's Sheldon Whitehouse, Colorado's Michael Bennet, Virginia's Tim Kaine, Connecticut's Richard Blumenthal, Delaware's Chris Coons and Arizona's Ruben Gallego.

The senators also told Trump, "It is troubling that, despite being sanctioned, these individuals have been given access to participate in G20 forums hosted in the United States. The G20 is intended to foster international cooperation on critical issues including finance, trade and global economic stability. As Russia continues its war against Ukraine and refuses to agree to a just and lasting peace agreement, its government should not be afforded a business-as-usual treatment alongside other nations at G20 events."

The Hill's Helen Huiskes notes that the Republican senators who signed the letter to Trump "went beyond the usual Trump critics in the GOP."

"Their support on the letter, which urged Trump to rescind any such invitation to Putin and any other sanctioned Russian officials, demonstrates how Senate Republicans generally still support Ukraine in its war with Russia, and some have become more willing to push back on Trump amid his low approval rating," Huiskes reports. "The letter also cited the recently passed Russia-Iran sanctions bill, named for former Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who was one of the staunchest defenders of Ukraine in the Senate before his death in July. That bill increased sanctions on Russia, hoping to squeeze it economically as its aggression in Ukraine continues four years after invading that country."

title: Hacked FBI files exposed medical info like blood tests and spouse details
content:
The FBI's hacked personal data didn't merely reveal contact information for 60,000-plus agents and officials; it also contained private details about blood and urine tests, the BBC reported on Friday.

The black-hat hacker group ShinyHunters stole the "fitness-for-work" medical examinations, including the files of an agent, a potential agent and even senior officials or deputy directors. That information includes doctors' notes and even medical conditions like a "shellfish and banana allergy" or even "high cholesterol." There is also information about an agent's spouse. The group has shared some of the samples of data they obtained with the extortion demands.

It could mean that agents remain vulnerable to scams, blackmail and targeted attacks, the report claimed. It could also mean that law enforcement officers could be more easily impersonated.

"The list maps thousands of agents against their medical and fitness records," Etay Maor, VP of threat intelligence at Cato Networks, told the BBC.

"Passwords can be reset if stolen, but medical records cannot, so once this data is out, it stays compromised for good. That permanence, applied across an entire workforce, is what makes this leak so serious," he said.

"Such data could be used for highly convincing phishing, impersonation, identity fraud, blackmail or even operations targeting law-enforcement personnel, making the potential implications particularly serious," said CyberSmart co-founder Jamie Akhtar.

The FBI has acknowledged only the breach so far. They haven't detailed how it happened yet, but they're "aggressively investigating it."

The BBC noted, "Unusually, the hackers are not demanding money. Instead, they are seeking a retraction of an FBI advisory published in May, which they claim 'offended' them."

Reuters reported that some of the hacked data included information on agents involved in investigations around Russia, China and drug cartels.

404 Media reported that the data may also have revealed a little-known FBI hacking unit with a secretive team.

The hackers told reporters they would publish the information in five days if their demands weren't met.

The records appear to relate to thousands of agents, including senior officials such as deputy directors.

Professor Ciaran Martin, the former head of the UK's National Cyber Security Centre, has described the hack — if confirmed — "as serious as it gets when it comes to data breaches."

According to the hackers, they found a vulnerability in an Oracle PeopleSoft cloud storage system being used by the FBI. Oracle is the company co-founded and currently led by top supporter of President Donald Trump, Larry Ellison.

They were able to gain access to multiple platforms, including FBIJobs, FBI BEAST, which handles background checks on employees and applicants, FBI MedLink, which stores medical records, and FBI BICS, which contains investigative information," the BBC said.

title: 'Bad foreign policy': Ex-ambassador rips Trump’s 'embarrassing weakness'
content:
Chinese President Xi Jinping is visiting Washington, DC for his meeting with U.S. President Donald Trump. The leaders, according to CNN, are "expected to discuss key issues" that include "trade, Taiwan and the war in Iran." Michael McFaul, who served as U.S. ambassador to Russia under former President Barack Obama, discussed the meeting during a Friday morning appearance on MS NOW — and was vehemently critical of Trump's handling of U.S./China policy as well as his ban of three major media outlets (CNN, MS NOW and Politico) from the White House press pool.

During the panel, MS NOW host Peter Alexander, McFaul and former CIA Director John O. Brennan argued that the timing — a press ban during a U.S. visit from the Chinese president — was terrible. Alexander pointed out that members of state-operated Chinese meeting were allowed in the White House while reporters from top U.S. media outlets were shut out.

McFaul told Alexander and Brennan, "This is embarrassing for the United States of America. We used to be the leader of the free world. Countries used to look up to us because of our freedoms of press … This makes us look weak. I don't understand why President Trump doesn't understand how to connect these dots when we are now talking about this, not talking about national interests that he might be pursuing with Xi Jinping today. That is a sign of weakness — not a sign of strength. So, it may be legal, but it's also really bad foreign policy."

The Trump/Jinping meeting comes at a time of escalating fears that the People's Republic of China, under Jinping, will invade Taiwan — an important ally of the United States.

Brennan was highly critical of Trump as well, telling McFaul and Alexander, "I think (Jinping is) able to see through Donald Trump's rhetoric."

The former CIA director made a comparison between Trump's meeting with Jinping and Obama's meeting with former Chinese President Hu Jintao in 2011. Brennan argued that while Obama made a point of highlighting the United States' press freedoms during the Jintao meeting, Trump was doubling down on a White House press ban during Jinping's visit.

Brennan told McFaul and Alexander, "That's because President Obama believes strongly in a free press, believes strongly in a rule of law … It underscores how much Donald Trump is abusing the rule of law, doesn't respect it … I think Michael would agree with me: Donald Trump's weakness right now (is) that he's afraid of the free press. He's afraid of being exposed. Even the red-carpet treatment of President Xi Jinping, which is, you know, going overboard — it sends a signal that Donald Trump needs Xi Jinping more than Xi Jinping needs Donald Trump. And the fact that he is engaged in these fights with the courts, with the Constitution — again, it just shows the world, and it shows, you know, hopefully all American citizens, just how afraid he is of being exposed."

title: NYT issues warning as Trump 'sycophants' prop up 'flailing presidency'
content:
The New York Times editorial board issued a stark warning that President Donald Trump's "flailing presidency is leaving Americans with the thinnest of hopes" for negotiations with China. The Times editors hope he makes it through the summit without making anything worse.

In a column Thursday, the board explained that for more than 100 years the United States has taken a "leading role in the world." But that could be coming to an end, along with losing "expanded prosperity, security and democracy."

"Mr. Trump shows little care for these benefits," the board said. "He uses international relations to seek personal enrichment, praise from sycophants and equal standing with authoritarians. His flailing presidency leaves Americans with the thinnest of hopes for this week’s summit: that he does not further damage the national interest."

Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in Washington, D.C. on Tuesday, where he was greeted with a red carpet, military flyover and, on Wednesday, will have a state dinner.

Still, the Times said that the "low expectations for the visit" underscore "the damage that Mr. Trump is doing to American influence and global well-being. He is an undisciplined politician who puts his personal interests above the nation’s, running an administration that has no coherent strategy for solving major problems. He is instead often exacerbating the world’s biggest problems."

There are three leading crises facing the world, and no single nation can fix them alone, the board said. But, there is a low bar, the Times confessed. They hope that the world won't let Trump get away with "the benefit of low expectations." Then the board confessed it's low expectations.

Currently, the world faces potentially catastrophic risks from artificial intelligence, the escalating effects of climate change, and the economic damage from disrupted shipping through the Middle East. The board wants to see cooperation between the U.S. and China over the issues, but Trump doesn't believe in climate change, doesn't intend to regulate AI and he's the one who destabilized the Middle East with the Iran war.

The column laments an unfortunate reality of the two leaders. They explain that Trump’s erratic, self-interested approach to foreign policy has weakened U.S. influence and made serious diplomacy harder. Meanwhile, Xi has been a difficult negotiating partner for Trump, with authoritarian tendencies.

The board hopes that China will still cooperate with the U.S. While Trump said that Xi supports an unregulated AI world, they, too, have fears about AI run amok; they, too, need a stable oil supply, and they've made great strides in clean energy.

The column concludes that Trump’s focus on personal enrichment, flattery,and status leaves the United States unable to lead on global threats. So, the board said, the best hope for the summit is simply that Trump does not cause further damage.

title: There are 'tapes of Donald Trump': Russia expert unloads explosive claim
content:
President Donald Trump's close relationship with Russia has long troubled observers. Now an author and Russia expert who recently wrote a book on Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin offered a theory as to why.

"President Donald Trump excessively appeases Putin out of fear because he knows the Russian dictator likely has serious dirt on him, the author Luke Harding has alleged," reported The Daily Beast's Vic Verbalaitis on Wednesday. "Appearing on The Daily Beast Podcast, Harding told host Joanna Coles that Trump, 80, is 'afraid' of the Russian president, 73, because of the Kremlin’s sweeping surveillance operations."

Verbalaitis added, "'The Betrayal: Trump, Putin and The New Age of Conquest' author said that while working as a correspondent in Moscow in 2007, he experienced firsthand the frightening extent to which the Russian government monitored him and his family. Harding described how the country’s Federal Security Service (FSB) broke into his family’s apartment and planted bugs, which they used to keep eyes on them even during their most intimate moments."

The Daily Beast journalist continued, "U.S. intelligence officials have already said Russia meddled in the 2020 election to benefit Trump." He wrote that "they made it clear that they were watching us because on one occasion, we came back from a family holiday in Berlin and they’d left a sex manual in Russian by the side of the marital bed, and I had to say to my wife, you know, ‘Darling, this really isn’t mine. The KGB have introduced this.’'"

After describing how he believes he was surveilled by Russian intelligence, Harding speculated that Trump is similarly alarmed.

“The reason I tell you this is that the... FSB, KGB, are adept at surveillance,” Harding told The Daily Beast. “They break in and watch everybody. And of course, that means there’ll be... tapes of Donald Trump.”

Writing earlier on Wednesday, another foreign policy expert broke down how Trump's handling of foreign policy has empowered both Russia and another rival superpower to the United States, China.

"In his first book, 'A World Restored,' Henry Kissinger argued that a stable and legitimate order rests on a limited consensus: an understanding among the major powers about what he called the permissible aims and methods of foreign policy," Brookings Institute senior fellow and former foreign policy adviser to President Joe Biden, Thomas Wright, wrote for The Atlantic. "Governments can compete intensely and violate rules without seeking to overturn the system itself. The danger arises when a major power becomes so dissatisfied with the limits imposed upon it that it adopts a revolutionary foreign policy."

In February Joseph Bosco, who served as China country director under Secretary of Defense Donald Rumsfeld from 2005 to 2006, argued in The Hill that Trump's foreign policies have sacrificed America's greatness.

“History will brand the U.S. failure to ensure Ukraine’s victory and prevent Taiwan’s fall as the time when America fell from greatness and her ‘cunning’ but miscalculating enemies plunged the world into a new global conflict,” Bosco explained.

title: Trump roasted for flinching during military flyover while Xi remains stoic
content:
President Donald Trump visibly flinched during a military jet flyover while he met with Chinese President Xi Jinping for a summit on Wednesday. The media noticed — and decided to mock him for his seeming frailty.

"What happens to Trump here?" liberal commentator Ed Krassenstein wrote on X. "Did he just have a mini stroke?"

The Daily Beast observed that "the 80-year-old president recoiled at a flyover, ducking and baring his teeth, while Xi Jinping stood stoically beside him."

New York Times bestselling author Don Winslow "now you see why Trump got 5 deferments from Vietnam. Even just the SOUND of a plane flyover is too much for the fat baby in makeup and a diaper. Look at the President of China. No reaction."

Liberal commentator Keith Olbermann posted that "Trump shoulda just let that White House pool boycott alone. Look what he bought himself."

Meanwhile the popular account Republicans against Trump simply wrote "Holy s——."

Liberal commentator Jim Stewartson broke down the footage by saying, "Watch Xi in comparison. It’s not that loud, but Trump’s brain does not filter input correctly anymore due to his worsening frontotemporal dementia. The sound made his nervous system go into full overload — which registers as pain. Note the glove. It is not cold. Sad."

Meanwhile pro-Trump pundit Nick Sortor, who often contributes to Newsmax, wrote "LMAO! A surprise SUPERSONIC BOMBER flyover at President Trump's welcome ceremony for Xi Jinping just caught EVERYONE off guard It was a B-1 Lancer with FULL afterburner, RIPPING through during the Star Spangled Banner Freaking legendary."

Experts have observed other signs of Trump's apparent decline. Speaking to AlterNet earlier in September, psychiatrist Dr. David M. Reiss — who co-authored the book “The Dangerous Case of Donald Trump: 27 Psychiatrists and Mental Health Experts Assess a President" — warned AlterNet that the mainstream media is not adequately covering the president's mental health issues.

"The press is treating it as if this is just him," Reiss told AlterNet. "No, this is a very disturbed — in a vernacular, deranged — person. He says things that don't make sense, goes on for two hours. This is not normal behavior, not productive behavior, and obviously a lot of it is lies. So the diagnosis really isn't relevant. What's relevant is: if this was a friend, if this was a relative, would you say this person needs help if they're not getting it — and if they are getting it, they should see a different doctor because it's not being treated effectively."

He added, "That's not what the press is saying. The press is acting like this is just his style, or making bizarre excuses, or ignoring it."

title: Trump baffles allies by literally rolling out the red carpet for China
content:
China's President Xi Jinping is headed to Washington D.C. on Wednesday, and President Donald Trump reportedly intends to actually roll out a red carpet to celebrate the leader and his allies don't understand why.

Politico's "Playbook" said Wednesday morning that, despite the AI arms race, expectations are low that any meaningful agreement between the U.S. and China will happen.

"The summit is shaping up to be heavy on pomp and light on major breakthroughs," said Politico.

“Apart from the notification mechanism, there's almost zero chance that there will be some kind of meaningful U.S.-China AI safety dialogue, where the governments agree to anything real,” said Liza Tobin when speaking to "Playbook." She was the former director for China at the National Security Council during Trump’s first term.

Another administration official was just as dire: “There isn’t a deal to be had on AI. There’s not. This is not realistic, and I don’t know that there ever will be.”

The White House simply intends to pretend that there was some kind of deal so Trump can have his "win."

When asked what must happen for the White House to call the meeting a success, "Playbook" was told by a senior White House official: “We’re going to say that regardless."

A former Trump official said that the U.S. doesn't have any cards to play, the report said.

"There’s 'no pressure point' right now that would force China to the table," the report said, citing the ex-official. Indeed, the U.S. has cut so much of what it's getting from China that there is little incentive.

Steve Bannon likes it that way. He told Playbook that there should be “no chips, no distillation — America must quarantine the CCP from any access to compute power or intellectual property that allows them to compete in AI."

Meanwhile, Republicans aren't happy about Trump's ceremonial flattery. Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), who chairs the Senate Armed Services Committee, complained from the floor on Tuesday.

"Mr. President, every minute of dialogue, our commander-in-chief should keep in mind that his guest is a brutal, unelected and oppressive dictator who seeks to dominate his neighbors and whose massive military arsenal is aimed directly at the United States," Wicker said.

CNN reporter David Sanger said that most people don't recall what happened the last time a president went to greet a foreign leader at Andrews Air Force Base, much less hold flyovers and other performances.

"And in fact, that's more of a greeting than he got when [Trump] arrived in Beijing. And the trip in May, I remember, I was on that trip. He got a big welcome," said Sanger. "And, you know, the Chinese military was out in Tienanmen Square ... But we didn't have the kind of flyovers. And what you're going to see."

The second main point, he said, is that Xi fully recognizes that Trump is in a moment of weakness.

Xi "knows about the coming elections," Sanger said. "He's looking at the kind of poll numbers that you were you were discussing yesterday morning, particularly the approval ratings on foreign affairs. He understands the president is stuck in Iran with no easy way out, and that he has done nothing to make that any easier. In fact, we believe that the Chinese have been providing the Iranians with at least some basic technology and intelligence that probably has helped them target those bases in the Middle East."

title: Conservative National Review tears up Trump for tanking US 'reputation'
content:
President Donald Trump got a major pushback from the United States' North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) allies when he threatened Greenland with annexation. In a biting editorial, the conservative National Review argues that Trump's Greenland push was a "diplomatic" debacle — from hurting the United States' "reputation" to undermining key U.S. alliances.

The Review, in its editorial, emphasizes that while Greenland is important to the U.S., Trump handled things badly at a considerable "cost."

"To be clear," the conservative Review says, "Trump was right about one big thing: that Greenland merited much more attention than it had been getting. The Arctic may not have warmed up by as much and as quickly as Al Gore and others claimed it would, but it has done so by enough to render it much more accessible than before. As a result, it is becoming a zone of geopolitical competition for its resources and, more simply, because of location, location, location. For obvious geographical reasons, that increases the already-considerable importance of Greenland to this country."

The Review editorial continues, "The island is a potential back door through U.S. defenses and a key North Atlantic vantage point. Moreover, in an era of supply-chain anxiety, it has potentially valuable mineral resources, including rare earths."

But Trump, the Review laments, made things "painful" in ways they didn't have to be.

"Asking politely to upgrade the existing agreement might well have delivered just that — and done so without creating all the geopolitical self-harm," the Review explains. "Unfortunately, Trump went about defending the U.S. strategic interest in a different way, and that was the wrong way. The core of the problem has been that, despite his own nationalist instincts, the president is oblivious when it comes to the national sensitivities of others. Originally, he had imagined that Greenland could simply be bought: essentially, it would be 'a large real estate deal.' This was not, unsurprisingly, how the Danes and Greenlanders saw it. The president's adding the threat of stick (tariffs and hints of worse) to the promise of carrot caused a major rift within NATO and did damage to our reputation as a reliable ally."

According to the Review, "stressing the fact that Danish and Greenlandic sovereignty will be left intact" is in the United States' best interests.

"If and when an agreement is concluded," the Review writers argue, "the best way to maximize its benefits to the U.S. will be to repair the diplomatic damage that this episode has caused by rebuilding a deeper relationship with Denmark and Greenland."

title: Russia’s parliamentary elections will not be a referendum on the Ukraine war – or anything, really
content:
Russia is not a democracy. However, Russia does have elections – many of them, in fact.

From September 18-20, Russian voters will elect their national parliamentary representatives (to the Russian State Duma), as well as 11 governors, deputies to 39 regional assemblies, and deputies to other lower-level representative bodies.

The elections will be the first parliamentary elections since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, this will not be a barometer of public opinion about the war, the state of the Russian economy, or, well, anything.

Russians have many reasons to be disenchanted with President Vladimir Putin’s regime. The war is now in its fifth year, with an estimated 1.4 million battlefield casualties (including 450,000 deaths). Some 30,000 Russian soldiers are either being killed or injured a month. Ukraine is also increasingly bringing the war home to Russians with frequent drone attacks.

Yet, these elections will be carefully stage-managed to guarantee a favourable result – and a continued strong mandate – for Putin’s party.

Elections under dictatorship

Most modern dictatorships are not run by decree; they hold nominally multiparty elections in an effort to legitimise their systems as democratic and consensual. This is called “electoral authoritarianism”. Today, it is the most common form of authoritarian government in the world.

These elections perform a variety of functions for authoritarian regimes. In Russia, they help the Putin regime gauge the mood of the electorate, gather information about Russia’s voter base, and mobilise its key supporters.

Putin still holds all of the power in Russia, and traditionally and constitutionally, the president stands above the other branches of government.

Yet, parliament still exists – nominally. It has been controlled by the United Russia party since 2003.

Although the party is a strong vehicle of support and mobilisation for Putin, he is not a party member. This reflects the historical role of the president being “above the fray” of Russian party politics, which former President Boris Yeltsin started.

However, for these elections, Putin has positioned himself closer to United Russia by appearing several times at its party congress. He’s likely done this to boost the party’s sagging popularity and demonstrate he strongly endorses the party of power.

Russia has a select number of approved parties that are allowed to take part in elections because they are ultimately loyal to the Kremlin. These include ostensible opposition parties, such as the Communist Party and the nominally liberal New People party. They offer the veneer of a diverse electoral packaging, even if the product is the same.

But more democrats sat in the last Soviet parliament from 1989–91 than have have been in the Duma over the last two decades. Indeed, there have not been any bone fide democratic deputies in the Duma since 2007. This was when new election laws were ushered in following terrorist attacks in the North Caucasus, which skewed the playing field against democrats to the benefit of pro-Kremlin parties.

While Russia’s political parties have been offered surprising independence at times in the past, this has declined markedly since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Today, nearly all parties are united in support of the war.

The only party that has been opposed to the war is the pro-Western Yabloko party. It has existed since 1993 and been allowed to run in previous elections. This is because its platform of pro-Western liberalism has fairly limited electoral appeal and Putin’s regime has been able to keep it in check through repressive actions.

This year, however, Yabloko’s parliamentary candidates were blocked from taking part in elections for the first time. Both of the party’s deputy leaders, Lev Shlosberg and Maksim Kruglov, also received long prison sentences for “discrediting” the Russian military and “spreading false information about the war”.

Another anti-war candidate planning to run for parliament, Boris Nadezhdin, was also convicted on spurious charges that will keep him out of the elections.

Voting in Russia: carrots and sticks

Electoral authoritarian regimes generally try to avoid overt election fraud to maintain a democratic facade. However, they constantly look for ways to interfere with them.

For example, remote electronic voting will be used in many regions this year. Critics say this provides the state with an easy and largely untraceable way of manipulating the vote, if it so chooses.

Ensuring these elections function smoothly and appear legitimate will also mean maximising turnout. One problem is that elections with pre-determined outcomes struggle to attract the attention of voters.

The Putin regime therefore offers material incentives to vote. This includes creating a carnival-like atmosphere at polling centres with raffles, vouchers and even cars on offer as prizes for voting. It has also used more coercive measures, such as putting pressure on biudzhetniki, employees of state institutions, to vote for the ruling party.

In the occupied regions of Ukraine, voting is likely to be particularly coercive. It may literally be carried out at the barrel of a gun.

However, even in electoral authoritarian systems, governments have to permit some uncertainty of the outcome to legitimise the process, and surprises can occur.

In 2018 and 2019, for instance, the nationalist-oriented Liberal-Democratic Party of Russia won majorities in the municipal and regional Dumas of Khabarovsk in Siberia, and its candidate won the governorship.

The tight grip the regime keeps on its elections and the barring of troublesome opposition candidates is not a sign of regime strength. Rather, it reveals a substantial degree of anxiety on the part of the regime.

In reality, these elections demonstrate that the Putin regime is struggling to contain opposition to its rule amid the ongoing social and economic strain posed by its floundering war in Ukraine.

title: Five years into AUKUS, what do we have to show for it? We’ve measured progress on three key metrics
content:
This week marks five years since US President Joe Biden, UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and Australian Prime Minister Scott Morrison announced AUKUS, a trilateral security partnership composed of two parts: Pillar I, the nuclear-powered submarine program, and Pillar II, a collaboration on advanced defence capabilities.

Since then, AUKUS has survived multiple leadership changes and national reviews or public inquiries in all three countries. At a time of heightened geopolitical risk, the case for acquiring the subs to help protect Australia’s access to sea-lanes and contribute to regional stability has endured.

But this milestone needs to be put in context.

For one, when AUKUS was announced on September 15-16 2021, we had very few details. The actual plans for the delivery of nuclear-powered submarines to Australia came much later, in March 2023.

And AUKUS still has a way to go. We’re barely a tenth of the way into the implementation of the 30-year “Optimal Pathway” for the program in its totality.

We’re at least six years away from receiving our first US-built Virginia-class submarine, and at least 15 years from receiving the first AUKUS-class submarine, to be co-developed and co-produced here and in the United Kingdom.

Still, five years after the initial announcement, it’s worth gauging what Australia has to show for a program the government has said is “too big to fail” and is without a “Plan B”.

We’ve tried to bring clarity to this question by focusing on three indicators of progress:

  • how much money Australia has invested so far

  • the development of Submarine Rotational Force-West (SRF-W) in Perth

  • the state of US submarine production and fleet size.

Though by no means exhaustive, these three metrics offer a snapshot of where the program stands at the moment, and the challenges that must still be overcome.

Read more: In view of Trump’s review of AUKUS, should Australia cancel the subs deal? We asked 5 experts

1. What Australia has spent so far

Australians are justified in wanting to know how much money their government has invested in AUKUS, and where it has gone.

When the Optimal Pathway was announced in 2023, the Albanese government costed it at 0.15% of GDP annually over the life of the program. This would amount to roughly A$268 billion to A$368 billion over three decades.

Since then, the A$368 billion figure has been widely cited by the media as the ultimate price tag.

Crucially, at the time, a third of this total – around A$122.9 billion – was set aside as contingency funding to absorb the delays and cost pressures that come with a 30-year program. In other words, it may not actually be spent.

Accurately tracking Australia’s overall spending to date is difficult. Since 2023, there has been a flurry of government statements announcing or promising funding to support various aspects of AUKUS over different time frames. These figures are scattered across portfolios, and are sometimes announced and then folded into the forward estimates of the federal budget. Some are projections, rather than down payments.

Both the Liberals and Greens have pressed the government to share updated costings for AUKUS. Budget papers do not offer an itemised account nor a consolidated overall figure for the program so far.

With no central database for AUKUS spending, we set out to build one.

We went through public announcements, portfolio budget statements, annual reports and strategy documents, and attempted to trace everything that’s been spent, announced, promised or projected.

What we’ve come up with hardly qualifies as a ledger. Still, it reveals three important things.

First, the bulk of the funding announced in Australia has gone to infrastructure, across three main sites:

  • A$12 billion on the Henderson Defence Precinct, a shipbuilding and submarine maintenance hub on the west coast

  • A$8 billion to expand HMAS Stirling so it can host US and UK submarines under SRF-West from 2027, and Australia’s own fleet of submarines from the early 2030s

  • A$8.5 billion to the Osborne Nuclear-Powered Submarine Construction Yard, where Australia’s nuclear submarines will be built.

Second, Canberra is investing in the UK and US submarine industrial bases to support the delivery of the Virginia-class and future AUKUS-class submarines to Australia. This reflects the additional demand Australia’s submarines will put on production and maintenance capacity in both countries.

This has included US$2 billion (about A$2.8 billion) to the US in three instalments, with a further US$1 billion (A$1.4 billion) in instalments pledged over the next decade.

Canberra has also paid A$310 million to the UK for components needed to build nuclear submarines and has committed an additional £2.4 billion (about A$4.6 billion) over a decade to expand the UK’s submarine production capacity.

Third, AUKUS will consume a growing share of the Australian defence budget, even if the government follows through on its commitment to increase spending to 3% of GDP by 2033.

In 2023, the Parliamentary Budget Office projected annual AUKUS spending to be roughly A$2.2 billion per year over the program’s first four years, rising to more than A$8 billion annually for the next three decades. This means most of the spending is still to come.

There’s a long list of various capabilities required to meet Australia’s future defence requirements. If the Defence budget does not grow sufficiently and AUKUS eats into those programs, the overall investment in these capabilities could become lopsided.

2. A new submarine base in WA

Until the Virginia-class submarines arrive, we still need to make sure our near-term defence needs are being met. We also need to be ready for when our subs show up.

This is where Submarine Rotational Force-West comes in.

The first phase of the AUKUS program involves frequent visits by US and UK submarines to HMAS Stirling in Perth from next year. These subs won’t be formally based in Australia; they will rotate in and out.

But these aren’t mere pitstops. Australians are being trained in how to maintain the ships and handle their weapons. Some US submarines already have Australians serving onboard. These initiatives are helping to prepare Australia to maintain our own nuclear-powered submarines when they come online.

The US is also setting up local operations to provide services, logistics and operational support to these rotating submarines and their crews. This will be the only location outside US and UK territories in the Indo-Pacific where these subs can receive sophisticated maintenance support.

Crucially, these facilities will be beyond the range of most (though not all) of China’s growing missile capabilities.

Successive National Defence Strategies have emphasised that an enduring US military presence in the region is fundamental to Australia’s security and contributes to regional deterrence. This is also the view of Australia’s closest partners in the region, such as Japan.

This is why leading Australian experts have argued SRF-W is perhaps “the most significant aspect” of AUKUS for Australia’s immediate security interests.

So, even if Australia won’t have its own AUKUS submarines for years, it will become increasingly capable of operating them, while simultaneously embedding a more resilient US naval presence in our region.

As far as near-term payoffs go, this shouldn’t be understated.

3. US submarine availability

Sceptics in both the US and Australia have expressed doubt about Washington’s willingness to sell at least three submarines to Australia beginning in the 2030s, given how much it relies on them and how long it takes to build them.

Indeed, the speed of US submarine production has been under particular scrutiny. The conventional wisdom is production needs to hit around 2.33 boats per year to meet both US and Australian requirements.

There are no consistent public records for the actual production rate, but the estimates are sobering.

New builds have averaged 1.1–1.3 submarines per year since the COVID pandemic, down from a high of 1.9 per year from 2016–19. US Navy leaders anticipate reaching two subs per year by 2032 – still short of the 2.33 goal.

Yet, production rates only tell part of the story. If Australia is supposed to receive in-service submarines from the US, understanding the state and size of the existing fleet is just as important.

In 2016, the US Navy declared it needed a force of 66 submarines to counter growing Chinese and Russian threats – up from a previous requirement of 48.

But since then, the US’ submarine fleet size has gradually declined, with older submarines retiring at a marginally higher rate than their modern replacements (the Virginia-class subs) have been introduced.

This reflects the difficulties Washington has had speeding up production, even with US$15 billion (about A$21 billion) in navy investments since 2018, contributions from the Australian government, and a growing number of Australian companies supporting US shipbuilding.

What’s more, since 2016, between 25–33% of the US submarine fleet has been undergoing maintenance, at significant financial and operational cost. For Australia, addressing that backlog will be as important as boosting US production rates.

Australia is already helping to ease these challenges with investments at Submarine Rotational Force-West and its own shipyards. If the AUKUS partners take full advantage of these developments, this could increase the number of boats available to the US Navy – and, by extension, to Australia.

So, while the US has a mountain to climb to boost sub production, that won’t be the only factor that determines the timeline for Australia’s AUKUS fleet.

Where does this leave Australia?

Of course, these three metrics tell only part of the AUKUS story so far.

Ultimately, however, delivering submarines to Australia is the point of the Optimal Pathway. Our analysis points to both successes and challenges, but at three years into a complex 30-year project, an incomplete picture is probably what we should expect.

Though reliably measuring progress is difficult, it would be disingenuous to say Australia has nothing to show for its investments to date. Important gains have been made in strengthening deterrence and building the workforce and industrial capacity for Australia to maintain and operate a fleet of the most advanced naval systems in the world.

title: Ratko Mladić: the war criminal who became a martyr for Bosnian Serbs
content:
To most of the world, he was the “Butcher of Bosnia”. A brutal murderer who wanted to eradicate Bosnian Muslims and Bosnian Croats in pursuit of an ethnically pure “Greater Serbia”.

Ratko Mladić was the commander of the Bosnian Serb military during the Bosnian War of the 1990s. He orchestrated the 1995 Srebrenica massacre, which resulted in the deaths of more than 8,000 Bosniak men and boys by Bosnian Serb forces.

Mladić died in The Hague in late August while serving a life sentence for war crimes and crimes against humanity. He was laid to rest this week in Serbia with full military honours, drawing thousands of mourners. The scenes angered the families of the victims of his crimes, and the European Union.

Olivera Simic was 19 years old when the war broke out and she was forced to flee the country.

Now an international law professor at Griffith University in Australia, she told The Conversation Weekly podcast that she’s found it difficult to see the public mourning over the death of a convicted war criminal.

I think I spent all my life trying to understand what really happened back then. People often think if you survive war, you know everything about war and you must know why it happened and what happened. But that’s not necessarily true for most of us.

Simic said that for many Serbs and Bosnian Serbs, Mladić is still seen as a martyr who defended the Serbian people during the war.

What concerns me the most is the normalisation of these images [for] young people who were born after the war.

This is what they are exposed to […] not the evidence [that was] presented at his trial, but rather through this pop culture of Mladić as a war hero.

More than three decades after the conflict, Simic said Mladić’s death is reopening old wounds in Bosnia and Herzegovina and showing how divided it remains.

Everyone talks about their own […] victimhood. But there is little reckoning and dealing with the past when it comes to owning your own responsibility and accountability for some things that happened in the 1990s.

That also needs to happen if we are going to move on.

title: The rebuilding in Nepal needs to start now. This is what worked after an earthquake a decade ago – and what to avoid
content:
In the aftermath of the devastating flash floods in Nepal on August 26, the immediate priority was to save lives and meet the urgent needs of victims. But the relief efforts must also begin laying the foundations for the future.

This requires a delicate balancing act. The early days after a disaster are crucial for ensuring a long-term recovery sets off in the right direction.

This means addressing challenging questions about how and where to rebuild homes, even while rescue efforts are ongoing and debris is being cleared. It also means ensuring aid agencies and policymakers are investing humanitarian funding in the right way and listening to communities.

After a 7.8-magnitude earthquake struck Nepal in 2015, killing nearly 9,000 people, I led a review of the recovery efforts of 15 of the largest international NGOs and their partners, which had received around US$100 million of funding from the United Kingdom’s Disasters Emergency Committee (DEC) and the Canadian Humanitarian Coalition.

While that earthquake was very different to the recent flood catastrophe in terms of scale, spread and severity, there are still many lessons about what to do after a disaster – and what not to do.

Cash is important

Communities need cash after a disaster. Where markets are working, this money gives people greater control over what they need most. While this is derided by some as potentially wasteful (“What if they spend it on the wrong thing?”), the overwhelming evidence shows that it works.

In my review after the 2015 quake, I found the immediate transfers of cash to survivors by NGOs working with local banks was highly effective. These survivors were able to prioritise what to spend it on, such as medicine, food or rent.

Direct cash transfers was also at the top of the United Nations’ appeal to donors after the floods last month “to give families the dignity to buy essential goods while stimulating local economies”.

But one of the most important findings from our review is that all this money can’t just be allocated for short-term relief.

Several months after the 2015 earthquake, far too many NGO staff told me they were still operating in response mode, providing the basic necessities to victims. As one field worker said, “it is only about relief, there is nothing on development”, while a senior NGO manager said, “we’re still in delivery mode, the conversations [about the future] aren’t happening”.

Thinking about the future means supporting farmers to re-establish their livelihoods, for instance, or repairing water systems to ensure access to safe drinking water.

Big decisions on housing

Short-term temporary housing for victims can also be problematic, if not handled the right way. Shelter usually takes up much of the money spent in post-disaster recovery efforts. In 2015, this accounted for 55% of the funds provided by the DEC.

In my view, funds shouldn’t be spent on elaborate temporary shelters, which has unfortunately been a focus of too many misguided international design saviours following disasters. These types of projects should never be taken up by serious aid agencies or responsible governments.

If temporary shelters are needed, local materials and local skills work best. Permanent rebuilding as quickly as possible is the goal, especially for Nepalis now, given winter is arriving soon.

Our 2015 review found a mixed bag of housing responses. The best efforts involved training up local carpenters and masons to a proficient standard to build quality shelters quickly. In other cases, aid providers with little or no technical skills oversaw complex housing projects, with worse outcomes.

Where to rebuild is also important. Unlike the situation after the 2015 earthquake, where rebuilding tended to take place in the same location, riverside communities devastated by the floods in Nepal today may need to be rebuilt elsewhere, given further deluges from melting glaciers are a real possibility.

This will be a hard decision to make, given the strong connections many communities have to their villages and land. But these decisions need to be made very quickly, as temporary housing has a habit of becoming permanent.

Rebuilding also requires materials. After the 2015 earthquake, bureaucratic red tape and corruption hindered the recovery by delaying the arrival of much-needed supplies from overseas, such as corrugated iron sheets. Bribes were demanded at border crossings, for example, which slowed progress.

International NGOs and donors are well attuned to the risks of corruption following disasters and must resist the paying of bribes in Nepal today.

And when aid money is funnelled through government agencies, there is always misappropriation, even when auditing takes place.

This will undoubtedly be a concern during the flood recovery, given Nepal ranks 109 out of 181 countries in Transparency International’s annual perception of public sector corruption index.

Listening to communities

Finally, aid agencies need to listen to the people they seek to serve.

Affected communities need to be seen as agents of their own recovery – not the “helpless victims” that some newspaper headlines would have you believe.

In 2015, there were too many instances in which community engagement was limited due to speed or sacrificed because of needless donor contracting requirements.

One independent survey undertaken at the time asked residents if their particular problems were being addressed by aid agencies. A resounding three-quarters said “very little” or “not at all”.

Women, in particular, felt their specific needs weren’t being addressed – adequate shelter, financial support, health care, and clean water and sanitation.

The aid agencies on the ground in Nepal now will hopefully be undertaking needs assessments to tailor their support in the most effective manner. This must be a continuous process to make sure communities are heard.

title: Even if it doesn’t form government, the far-right AfD has shaken Germany’s political establishment to the core
content:
The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party has sent shock waves across Germany – and the world – by trouncing the opposition in a state election over the weekend. But will the party actually be able to govern?

In an election that saw record-high levels of voter turnout, the AfD captured more than 44% of the vote in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt. This is more than double the party’s result in the 2021 state election.

As is normal in German politics, however, the AfD has fallen short of an absolute majority and would need to go into coalition with another party to govern – if only just.

Traditionally, Germany’s major political parties on both the left and right have committed to maintaining a “firewall” between the AfD and government. This means none of them would go into coalition with the far-right party.

The result has nonetheless threatened to upend German politics, which has successfully prevented a far-right party from returning to power since the second world war.

The AfD has garnered more votes than any party in Saxony-Anhalt in more than ten years. This is the same branch that the government body charged with protecting German democracy has formally described as an extremist right-wing party because of its “numerous anti-Muslim, racist and antisemitic statements”.

The concern now is what this state election presages about far-right successes to come.

Why did the AfD do so well?

Political analysts have long tried to paint the AfD as an East German phenomenon – and continue to do so. But this is only part of the story.

In the most recent federal election in 2025, the AfD was the second-most popular party in many German electorates. And in almost all national polls this year, the AfD comes out on top as the country’s most popular party.

Even a coalition of Germany’s historically strongest parties – the Christian Democratic Union (CDU), the Social Democratic Party (SPD) and the Greens – would, on current polling, struggle to form a federal government today.

Tellingly, this lurch to the far right in Saxony-Anhalt came at the expense of the CDU, which leads Germany’s current federal government under Chancellor Friedrich Merz. As an exit poll after the election made clear, 88% of voters in the state believed that if Merz’s government had implemented better policies, the AfD would not be as strong in the state.

For his part, Merz has made the mistake of trying to push what was a popular centre-right party under Angela Merkel much further to the right in an attempt to win over disgruntled voters. Instead of mollifying disillusioned AfD voters, though, Merz has simply pushed far-right talking points into the mainstream, prompting some conservative voters to support the extremist AfD.

Despite the AfD’s clear anti-migrant stance, this election was not merely a referendum on immigration, as some would like to paint it.

In fact, only 16% of voters in exit polls said immigration was their primary concern. The economy and education ranked higher as concerns, with immigration closely followed by the lack of basic infrastructure and services and employment opportunities.

Voters in the state felt their quality of life was slipping away and blamed not only migrants, but also mainstream politicians and those they collectively dismiss as die Bonzen – the “fat cat bosses” who have enriched themselves during a cost-of-living crisis.

Is a coalition possible?

The only party that could join the AfD in coalition would be the minor BSW party (Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht). The BSW is a splinter party founded by a once-prominent member of the Left party, an ostensibly democratic socialist party.

Since leaving the Left Party, however, BSW has almost entirely flipped from its earlier democratic socialist beliefs to become increasingly nationalistic.

Indeed, it has moved so far to the right that after the Saxony-Anhalt election, it immediately held out the possibility of coalition with the AfD, emphasising their “overlap”.

For its part, the AfD is currently maintaining its refusal to accept any coalition government. Instead it is threatening to send the state of Saxony-Anhalt back to elections in an attempt to gain an outright majority.

This is not entirely unrealistic. Now that the party is in striking distance, it would only take a minor party like BSW to slip under the 5% vote threshold needed to earn a seat in state parliament for the AfD to secure an outright majority.

A uniquely German result?

While the dark shadows of Germany’s Nazi past continue to shape outside understandings of voter behaviour in Germany, its move to the right is not happening in a vacuum. Disillusionment with liberal democracy is growing elsewhere in Europe and beyond.

In Italy, the already right-wing prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, is currently under pressure from even more extreme parties. The anti-migrant Reform party is still riding high in the polls in the United Kingdom. And France’s perennial threat to liberal democracy, Marine Le Pen, is the frontrunner for next year’s presidential election.

The conditions that have allowed the AfD to rise in Germany are thus hardly unique. There is a more fundamental erosion of democratic norms happening globally that is allowing the furthest extremes of far-right nationalism to become electable.

What this could mean for globally significant issues such as the unity of the European Union, the war in Ukraine and the future of NATO in Europe remains to be seen.

Matt Fitzpatrick receives funding from the Australian Research Council.

title: 9/11 anniversary: democracy was not doomed to fail in Afghanistan – the US did not live up to its promises
content:
After the signing of the Munich agreement in 1938 that allowed Nazi Germany to annex part of Czechoslovakia, Winston Churchill spoke of the fate of that country in a powerful speech in the House of Commons:

Silent, mournful, abandoned, broken, Czechoslovakia recedes into the darkness.

The same could now be said of Afghanistan, 25 years after the September 11 attacks and subsequent US invasion that forever changed the country.

Sadly, there is now little inclination in Western policy circles to reflect deeply on Afghanistan’s experiences since then.

All too often, one instead encounters orientalist stereotypes that imply the post-2001 experiment with democracy was always doomed to fail, depicting the Taliban as somehow the true embodiment of “Afghan culture”.

This is despite the fact the Asia Foundation, in its highly regarded Survey of the Afghan People, reported that 88% of respondents in 2021 had “no sympathy at all” for the Taliban.

Afghanistan’s experience after 2001 deserves more careful study than this, if only because it offers useful lessons for the future.

What went right – and wrong

In all the postmortems on the US-led mission to oust the Taliban from power and bring democracy to Afghanistan, it is easy to lose sight of what was achieved during the two decades of the Afghan Republic.

As I recount in my book, coauthored with Afghan researcher and lawyer Ahmad Shuja Jamal, much went wrong, but a great deal also went right.

A generation of young Afghans was raised in an era of globalisation. By 2021, nearly 70% of the population used television to get news and information. Average per capita incomes increased and a vibrant civil society developed, fostered by the freest media in the region. Health outcomes improved across a range of indicators and access to education for girls also expanded (spectacularly in urban areas).

These achievements were sometimes exaggerated by Western donors, but they were real nonetheless, and not trivial.

However, much went wrong. The process of institutional design from 2001, heavily influenced by the United States, led to an overcentralised and complex state. Too much power was given to the president, resulting in a “neopatrimonial” system in which formal institutions became entwined with patronage networks.

The combination of bureaucratic complexity and a flood of aid money fuelled corruption. And from 2009, some elections were marred by fraud, which senior Western officials culpably failed to confront.

Even more seriously, the new Afghan National Army (ANA) was designed to be interoperable with its US counterpart. This made it heavily dependent on US civilian contractors to maintain the sophisticated equipment it was given, and acutely vulnerable if and when such services dried up.

International developments also had a dire effect on Afghanistan. The US invasion of Iraq in March 2003 sucked a great deal of oxygen out of US operations in Afghanistan at a critical time for the country’s democratic transition.

This “greenlighted” a resumption of malign meddling by Pakistan, which had been the Taliban’s original patron from 1994 and was desperate to block the consolidation of a pro-Indian government in Kabul. This was a problem far beyond the capacity of the Afghan Republic to handle.

Successive US presidents failed to bring effective diplomatic pressure to bear on Islamabad to cease its meddling, seemingly hoping it would simply go away. In 2021, the chairman of the US Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Mark A. Milley, testified that never “effectively dealing with Pakistan” was a critical error on the part of the US.

This was compounded by a grave misreading of the Taliban movement by Washington, legitimising the terrorist group as a partner in an ill-conceived negotiating process that purported to offer “peace” for the Afghan people.

Year after year, the Taliban – not the Afghan government or its Western backers – had been responsible for a clear majority of civilian casualties in Afghanistan. Nonetheless, under President Donald Trump, the US in 2018 commenced “peace” negotiations with the Taliban, excluding the Afghan government.

This itself sent a dangerous signal. But worse was to come on February 29 2020 in Doha, Qatar, when a US envoy, Zalmay Khalilzad, signed an exit deal with the Taliban.

Thomas Hobbes’ warning that “reputation of power is power” was seemingly lost on the US.

The tragedy of Afghanistan today

The irony was that most foreign forces had left Afghanistan at the end of 2014. The Taliban’s aim in negotiating with the US was instead aimed at detaching the Afghan Army from the civilian contractors vital to its survival. And the US negotiating team walked straight into the trap.

With then-president Joe Biden recklessly following the path laid out by his predecessor, the scene was set for the tragic sequence of events in August 2021: the chaotic withdrawal of the remaining US troops, the collapse of the Afghan republic and the return of the Taliban.

Biden’s approval ratings plummeted and were never able to recover. It was his Bay of Pigs moment.

For a US audience, the Taliban sought to project themselves as reformed and “inclusive”, and some US policy experts who supported the abandonment of Afghanistan continue to whitewash the group to this day. One historian has even argued “the Taliban have not ruthlessly oppressed the Afghan people”. Nothing could be further from the truth.

Afghans are enduring unprecedented misery today. The Taliban regime has no constitution, and it openly rejects democratic choice. It functions as a totalitarian tyranny, with the Taliban leader, Hibatullah Akhundzada, producing ever-more repressive decrees on the basis of a kind of Führerprinzip (Adolf Hitler’s “Leader Principle”).

There is no rule of law, and ordinary Afghans are entirely vulnerable to the arbitrary exercise of power. Most notoriously, the Taliban’s practice of gender apartheid has led to its international isolation once again, with only Russia willing to grant it formal recognition.

With no institutionalised basis of legitimacy, the regime depends on coercive control to survive. And while brutal, it is also brittle, not least because of the recent breakdown of its relationship with Pakistan.

The botched US exit from Afghanistan cast a long shadow. The Russians smirked, and invaded Ukraine six months later. Hamas celebrated, too.

A further lesson may be that US promises are of little value in the long run. Afghanistan’s status as a “major non-NATO ally” of the US proved meaningless. Presidential term limits function as “promise limits” too.

And there’s a final warning for the future. The first Taliban regime was overthrown in 2001 because it had hosted Osama Bin Laden’s al-Qaeda terror group. Afghanistan remains an operating base for terrorist groups today, as a recent expert report to the UN Security Council makes clear.

But the greater danger comes from the Taliban’s establishment of ever-widening networks of madrasas (religious schools). A new study by the Hamrah Network, an expert Afghan organisation operating in exile, paints an alarming picture of these schools.

With more than 3.65 million students enrolled, the danger that radicalised students could pose in the region and beyond should not be underestimated. These madrasas are a veritable time bomb.

title: Why Israel and Turkey are trading insults and jockeying for power in neighbouring Syria
content:
When Israeli jets struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria on August 18, Israel said the attack was meant to stop Turkish forces from deploying there to help rebuild Syria’s army.

US intelligence found no evidence to support the claim, and Turkey and Syria denied any such plan.

In the weeks since, Israel and Turkey – the two countries with the most powerful militaries in the region – have traded their harshest words in years.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office has branded Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan an “antisemitic tyrant”, while Erdoğan has accused Israel of being a “terror state”.

Israeli media also reported this week that Turkish warships have approached Israeli vessels in the Mediterranean Sea and forced them to change course.

Both governments say they do not want war. So, why are two close US allies – one a NATO member, the other a nuclear power – suddenly circling each other over Syria?

The tensions are tied to Syria’s collapse in late 2024 when a rebel army led by now-President Ahmed al-Sharaa overthrew dictator Bashar al-Assad’s regime.

Syria’s two powerful neighbours have since exploited this moment very differently: Turkey has acted at the invitation of the Syrian authorities, while Israel has not. It therefore has no legal basis to police Syria’s territory or determine its security and political future.

Rushing to fill a power vacuum

When al-Sharaa came into power as Syria’s new leader, Turkey became the main backer and military partner of his new government.

Turkey undoubtedly wants a strong, unified state anchored to Ankara and has agreed to train and equip Syria’s army. Ankara has also stationed about 20,000 troops inside Syria, ostensibly to help maintain Syria’s territorial integrity and prevent attacks from Kurdish separatists over the border.

However, some believe its real intentions are to expand its presence to central Syria as a bulwark against Israel.

Turkish tensions with Israel did not begin over Syria. The countries’ relations began hardening in 2023 over Israel’s war in Gaza. Erdoğan called Israel’s campaign a genocide and joined South Africa’s case against Israel at the International Court of Justice. Turkey also suspended trade with Israel over the war.

Israel, meanwhile, wants a Syria too weak and fragmented to threaten its northern frontier.

In the hours after al-Assad fell, Israeli aircraft destroyed much of what remained of Syria’s military. Israel has since pushed past the Syrian border to Mount Hermon, declaring southern Syria off-limits to the country’s armed forces.

Its deeper worry is that a larger Turkish presence would limit its own freedom to operate in Syrian skies.

While both countries have stationed their forces inside Syria, there’s a crucial distinction: Turkey is there at Damascus’ invitation; Israel is there against its wishes. Legally, that distinction matters.

Clear law, selective enforcement

Article 2 of the UN Charter prohibits the use of force against the territorial integrity of any state. Israel’s pledge to keep its troops in a “security zone” in southern Syria has been rightly called a violation of this law.

Israel has made similar moves in the past. In 1967, it captured Golan Heights in the Six-Day War against Egypt, Syria and Jordan and officially annexed it in 1981. The UN Security Council declared this annexation “null and void”.

Last week, Syria’s UN ambassador, Ibrahim Olabi, told the UN Security Council that Israel’s continued occupation of Mount Hermon was “a blatant defiance of international legitimacy and the resolutions of this council”.

Syria also has the right under international law to raise an army and choose its own partners. Syria insists it alone will decide its alliances.

However, the bodies that enforce these rules – in particular, the UN Security Council – act only when the major powers allow. And because the United States has veto power on the council, it provides diplomatic cover for Israel.

This is one reason Syria is looking to strengthen ties with regional partners such as Turkey, as a way of pressuring Israel without resorting to conflict.

Turkey may be doing the same thing, signing a mutual-defence pact with Saudi Arabia and Pakistan that gives it other friends outside its US and NATO alliances.

What happens next

Open war remains unlikely for now. The Trump administration is the key to ensuring this as a close ally to both countries.

Tom Barrack, the US ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria, has been trying to keep the peace through back-channel talks. He has not been afraid to criticise Israel’s behaviour, though, calling its strike on the Syrian airbase last month an “unnecessary escalation”.

The situation remains volatile. Because Israel claims the right to strike whatever it dislikes in Syria and Turkey has deployed troops in the country, this raises the risk miscalculation could result in open conflict.

The deeper question is what is being obscured – that only the people of Syria have the right to decide Syria’s future.

Self-determination belongs to people, not just governments. Yet, for Syrians, there is no settled path for them to exercise this.
